title.rendered: India grew through a year of shocks. Who paid the bill?

content.rendered:
Review period: 14 November 2025 to 13 November 2026, India Standard Time. Published retrospectively on 14 November 2026. Earlier tariff and tax decisions appear where they establish the baseline. This is not a chronology pretending that later evidence was available at the time of the original decision. Each statistic below retains its observation period and release vintage.

India’s economy did not experience a single, neatly identifiable shock over the past twelve months. It absorbed overlapping changes to American tariffs, oil supply, domestic tax rules, inflation measurement, labour protections and borrowing costs. The economy kept expanding. Yet an economy can grow rapidly while households experience higher food bills, workers move into lower-quality jobs, governments spend less than budgeted, and exporters encounter a different commercial reality at the border. That is why the useful question is not merely whether India grew. It is who carried the risks, who received the benefits, and what the evidence can actually establish.

Five outcomes run through this investigation: household purchasing power; access to decent work; productive private investment; fiscal capacity and public project execution; and India’s ability to finance its external obligations. These are not interchangeable. They come from different official series and time periods. Treating one headline number as the score for all five would conceal more than it reveals.

The annual economic ledger: five numbers, five different questions

The figures above are sourced respectively to the 12 November CPI release, 10 November PLFS quarterly bulletin, 31 August national accounts release, 1 June provisional fiscal accounts, and the 13 November Reserve Bank of India balance-of-payments release. The interactive evidence scorecard explains the comparators, uncertainties and follow-up tests for each series.

1. The external shocks changed the cost of doing business

The trade story began before this review window. The United States announced its reciprocal tariff programme in April 2025 and later imposed additional measures affecting Indian goods. The economic incidence of a tariff cannot be understood from a country-wide rate alone. At the firm level, the outcome depends on tariff classification, exclusions, rival suppliers, contracts, exchange rates, and how much of the added cost an American buyer or Indian exporter can absorb. The August 2025 Russian-oil-related surcharge was a prior-stage shock. It should be linked to the later measures, not collapsed into one permanent rate.

On 7 February 2026, the United States and India described a framework for a prospective interim trade agreement. A framework is a negotiating or political milestone; it is not automatically a line-by-line tariff concession an exporter can claim. Later litigation and administrative actions introduced further legal distinctions. Then, on 23 July, the U.S. Trade Representative announced its final forced-labour Section 301 measures, putting India in the 10% tier for covered goods, subject to exemptions and the precise operative notice. India’s relative position could improve against a supplier paying more even while its own absolute tariff burden remained substantial.

That difference matters to a textile exporter. Imagine an Indian manufacturer and a rival offering identical pre-tariff prices. If the rival faces a higher applicable duty, the Indian firm may regain price competitiveness. But that cannot be converted into a forecast for textile employment without matching actual customs lines, buyer substitution, supplier capacity and utilisation of any rival-country quotas. The same logic applies to chemicals, engineering goods and other covered products. The first question is the legal rate for the shipment; the second is whether orders moved.

Trade agreements supplied a very different kind of change. The India–UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement entered into force on 15 July 2026. By contrast, India–EU negotiations concluded on 27 January 2026, while the India–New Zealand agreement signed on 27 April still required ratification according to the government’s subsequent trade-agreement status register. A negotiated deal, a signed treaty and a preference legally usable at customs are three distinct economic stages.

The practical consequence is that export opportunity must be measured through product eligibility, rules of origin, certification costs, shipping and actual preferential trade. A small exporter may find a nominal tariff advantage too expensive to claim. A larger firm may use the preference but still lack buyers or production capacity. The tariff timeline, trade-deal timeline and landed-cost model preserve those stages separately.

2. Oil was a supply problem, an exchange-rate problem and a fiscal problem

Oil prices and the exchange rate exert different pressures on the same importer. A more expensive dollar price increases the global cost of an equivalent barrel. A weaker rupee raises its domestic-currency value even when the dollar benchmark is stable. Multiply the two to get a simple benchmark for exposure, then remember that the price of an actual cargo also reflects grade, freight, insurance, contract timing and hedges. The two market prices can reinforce each other or partly cancel out.

The energy shock also reached people who were not directly buying crude. A commercial LPG restriction can alter the number of meals a restaurant can prepare even if its listed price is unchanged. Higher petroleum costs can affect trucks through cash flow and later through delivery charges. Fertiliser support can protect administered bag prices while supplies at the village level remain uneven. A fuel-tax cut may limit the immediate retail increase but reduce a government revenue stream. These effects fall on different balance sheets, and they should not be added up as one aggregate cost without matching units and periods.

During the March supply disruption, the government reported commercial LPG allocation at 70% of the pre-crisis allocation. An allocation below baseline is evidence of a restriction in an important channel. It is not by itself the share of actual cylinders delivered to each restaurant. The distinction becomes particularly consequential when one firm has a storage buffer while another must purchase daily. India also announced fuel-excise relief on 27 March. That could cushion household and business prices while changing the fiscal allocation of the shock.

In October, the RBI’s dollar facility for three public-sector oil marketing companies changed the mechanism through which they could meet immediate foreign-currency demand. It did not eliminate the fundamental oil bill. Liquidity support changes the point of purchase and the strain on a market; sustained import expenditure still depends on volumes and prices. The 52-week oil, rupee and trade archive records the recurring benchmark exposure with original EIA and Federal Reserve data. It is a historical research reconstruction prepared in November 2026, not a set of articles actually published week by week during the preceding year.

3. Inflation returned to the centre of household economics

India changed its measurement instruments during the year. A new CPI series with a 2024 base was introduced in February 2026, while national accounts also moved to a revised 2022–23 base. Better statistical methods or revised baskets can make the measurement more relevant, but changes to a published series are not the same as a sudden improvement in households’ material conditions. Old and new data should be compared only with appropriate bridging and source vintages.

The October 2026 CPI release reported headline inflation of 6.09% year on year, compared with 5.54% in September. Food inflation was 8.94%, compared with 7.74% in September. Rural and urban headline rates were 6.63% and 5.41%. These are inflation rates relative to a year earlier, not the month-to-month increase in the index. Indeed, the combined CPI index moved from 109.49 in September to 110.05 in October, a smaller month-on-month move than the annual rates might suggest.

Households do not experience an identical weighted basket. A family devoting a large share of its expenditure to staple foods faces a different price exposure than one spending more on services or housing. But it is not enough to invent two household weights, multiply them by published food inflation and call the difference a measured welfare gap. We need actual observed expenditure profiles and earnings trajectories before estimating who became poorer in real terms.

The previous September 2025 GST Council decisions lowered statutory rates on many goods. Whether consumers retained those benefits depends on the retail price at the point of sale, promotional cycles, inventory, firms’ pricing and input costs. Neither an announced cut nor a later change in headline CPI is alone proof of pass-through. The correct empirical test compares matched products whose tax rates changed with similar products whose rates did not, while controlling for timing and cost shocks. Our GST calculator labels itself as a statutory incidence scenario, not a retail-price estimate.

4. Stronger employment did not settle the question of better work

The July–September 2026 Periodic Labour Force Survey provides real positive evidence: for people aged 15 or older, the unemployment rate under the survey’s current-weekly-status measure eased from 5.4% in April–June to 5.1%. The worker-population ratio rose from 51.7% to 52.7%, and the labour-force participation rate rose to 55.5%. Thus the falling unemployment rate was not simply a statistical consequence of fewer people seeking work.

The composition, however, complicates a simple victory narrative. Rural self-employment accounted for 62.7% of rural employed workers, up from 61.4% in the previous quarter, and the rural share working in agriculture rose to 56.7% from 52.9%. The urban regular wage or salaried share edged up to 49.6%, while urban unemployment remained around 6.8%. A seasonal expansion of rural farm work can raise participation and employment without establishing an equivalent increase in predictable wages, annual hours or social insurance.

The labour codes that commenced in November 2025 and the final Central Industrial Relations Rules notified in May 2026 make another distinction unavoidable: a statutory entitlement is not the same as an accessible remedy. The labour-rules investigation tracks grievance committees, retrenchment procedures, the reskilling fund and the gap between central and state coverage. To evaluate the reform, we need worker receipts, complaint resolution times, processing delays and changes in durable formal employment, not merely the count of government notifications.

Similarly, a rural jobs statute that changes guaranteed days, administrative rules or financing arrangements should be evaluated by requests for work met, time to payment and actual person-days delivered. The best test for households is the predictable income and protection they can secure, especially between agricultural seasons. The unemployment rate is one important outcome; it is not the entire labour market.

5. Investment was stronger on paper, but “private capex revival” needs proof

The national accounts for April–June 2026, the first quarter of FY2026–27, reported real GDP growth of 7.8% year on year and real gross fixed capital formation growth of 11.9%. Using the expenditure-side constant-price levels in the source release, private consumption and fixed investment each added approximately 3.95 percentage points to the change in GDP, before accounting for other components and the statistical discrepancy. These are expenditure contributions, not identified causal drivers.

Investment can rise because government agencies are laying roads and power lines, listed corporations are expanding capacity, households are building homes, or enterprises are replacing machinery. All enter the broader national accounts in different ways. It would be wrong to present the full 11.9% increase in GFCF as a private corporate investment boom. An investment boom that broadens productive opportunities should eventually be visible in new projects actually commissioned, independent company investment, machinery use, freight costs, energy reliability and employment.

The Controller General of Accounts’ provisional FY2025–26 outturn also clarifies the government’s own capital-spending story. Direct Union capex was budgeted at ₹11,21,090 crore, subsequently revised to ₹10,95,755 crore and recorded provisionally at ₹10,69,119 crore. The shortfall against the original Budget Estimate was ₹51,971 crore, or about 4.64%. That is an execution gap in the fiscal ledger. It is not evidence that every unspent rupee represents a failed project, nor proof that every spent rupee created a productive asset.

The Economic Survey’s case for public infrastructure was economically plausible: reliable transport, power and logistics can make private production profitable. Yet a promise to crowd in private investment remains a hypothesis until linked to concrete output and investment behaviour. For a new highway or freight corridor, that means measured travel time, cargo volumes, demand for industrial land, later factory entry and a comparison that accounts for why the route was chosen. The capital expenditure audit distinguishes the budget, cash spent, asset commissioned and asset utilised.

6. Monetary policy travelled through loans with a lag

The RBI reduced the repo rate to 5.25% in December 2025 and later raised it in October 2026 as inflation risks evolved. The direction of the policy rate does not tell us the timing of the average borrower’s EMI. Floating-rate loan benchmarks reset at different dates; new lending and existing loan portfolios are repriced differently; banks can alter spreads, fees and loan composition; and deposit rates create a separate transmission channel.

The empirical test is a matched time series for the policy rate, weighted average rates on new and outstanding rupee loans, and term deposit rates, with clear source release months. A downward movement in the average fresh-loan rate can reflect a shift to less risky borrowers rather than identical clients receiving cheaper credit. Conversely, aggregate outstanding rates may barely move while newer loans are already repricing. That is why the RBI transmission notebook records the appropriate definitions and releases rather than promising that all borrowers automatically receive a repo-rate change.

Higher rates can temper demand and inflation persistence, but the trade-off is not symmetric across households and firms. A salaried household with a floating-rate mortgage, a capital-constrained small business and a cash-rich depositor have different balance sheets. An interest-rate change that helps depositors can hurt leveraged borrowers. Understanding that distribution is more useful than assigning a single label of “good” or “bad” to tightening.

7. India financed its goods deficit, but the quality of finance matters

India’s latest available balance-of-payments release, dated 13 November 2026, gives a clean accounting decomposition for April–September 2026. The goods balance was negative US$176.1 billion. Net services brought in US$105.0 billion; current transfers added US$77.7 billion; net primary income was negative US$32.4 billion. Together these components produced a current-account deficit of US$25.8 billion. This compares with a partially revised US$18.0 billion deficit in the corresponding half of 2025.

The arithmetic can be checked directly: −176.1 + 105.0 + 77.7 − 32.4 = −25.8 (all US$ billions). A merchandise trade headline reports just one component. It does not indicate what India ultimately owes the world on the full current account. Services earnings and personal transfers cushion a goods gap, while investment income paid to foreign claimants can widen it again.

The financing side is especially important this year. The RBI’s table reports a net capital-account aggregate, under its own published classification, of positive US$92.6 billion in April–September 2026, compared with US$11.6 billion in the corresponding prior period. Within banking capital, net NRI deposits were unusually large at US$125.6 billion, against US$6.1 billion a year earlier. The reported overall balance was positive US$66.8 billion. These figures show that financial inflows can coexist with a current-account deficit. They do not make the goods deficit disappear.

There is a second distinction. A bank’s foreign-currency deposit liability may supply dollars today, yet its maturity, cost and eventual repayment still matter. Reserve transaction flows and the valuation of the outstanding reserve stock are different measures. A positive overall balance is not proof of permanent external safety. Foreign capital can be borrowed, temporary or reversible. Any judgement about resilience should assess the maturity structure, currency composition and what happens when an exceptional financing window ends.

The Dollar Cushion workbench lets a reader change separate goods, services, transfers, income and financial-flow assumptions for a named period. It preserves the RBI’s reserve-flow sign convention and explicitly does not forecast an exchange rate. The larger analytical question is how far recurring service exports and remittances can finance an energy and investment bill without excessive dependence on short-duration external funding.

8. Industrial and social policy will be judged by delivery, not approval

A new semiconductor programme, storage incentives, mineral processing support and infrastructure commitments can all address important strategic vulnerabilities. But a cabinet approval is an input, an investment award is a different input, and an operating factory is an output. A subsidised plant that is not commissioned or cannot obtain materials is not equivalent to productive capacity. Comparing schemes by total announced rupees also ignores risk, scale and time to deployment.

The same standard should apply to social programmes. More nominal coverage under provident-fund rules does not necessarily mean more take-home pay today, since deductions and employer costs may change. A rural road programme that counts sanctioned kilometres without measuring all-weather travel can overstate economic access. A childcare scheme can increase female employment only if services are reliably available during working and commuting hours. The real outcome may be waiting times, delivered services or better access to jobs.

States matter because they implement major parts of the economy. Their own revenues, tax devolution, interest commitments and pension bills shape the funds available for new investment and welfare delivery. A Union cash transfer is not necessarily the same as spending at the state level in the same month. An informative federal comparison has to consolidate appropriately and separate grants from loans, expenditure from releases, and financial approvals from usable capacity.

What changed, what remains uncertain, and the editorial verdict

This was a year of real measured growth and a changing economic risk allocation. The GDP and labour data are not fictional. The domestic economy demonstrated resilience in output and participation. The official inflation and external-account figures are equally real. They show that a robust headline does not spare households from food-price pressure or remove the need to finance a substantial import bill. And the financial and capital-expenditure data warn against confusing an announced policy, a recorded transaction and a durable outcome.

The evidence gives us at least four tensions to follow. First, growth versus real incomes: are workers receiving earnings increases that compensate for different household price baskets? Second, public versus private investment: where have public assets created independently observable new production? Third, formal protection versus access: do workers actually receive entitlements within useful time limits? Fourth, external financing versus underlying resilience: how much of the current-account gap can be sustained through recurring export and transfer receipts, and how much depends on temporary liabilities?

A responsible ranking of the shocks would require common exposure denominators, credible counterfactuals and evidence of distribution. We do not yet have all of them. It would be false precision to declare that tariffs, inflation, oil or the Budget “caused” a particular fraction of the year’s growth on the strength of simultaneous changes. Our judgment is therefore narrower and stronger: India kept producing and investing through the shocks, while the durability and distribution of the gains remain open empirical questions.

This investigation is part of What Shaped India’s Economy, the eight-series research archive. Readers can examine the 48 dated milestones, the five-outcome scorecard, the original research commissioning register and the Research Library. Each future follow-up will be linked to the evidence that changed, and later revisions will be dated rather than silently rewritten into the historical record.

Primary documentary record

  • MoSPI: October 2026 consumer price index and food inflation (12 November 2026)
  • MoSPI: PLFS July–September 2026 quarterly bulletin (10 November 2026)
  • MoSPI: April–June 2026 GDP and expenditure estimates (31 August 2026)
  • Controller General of Accounts: FY2025–26 provisional unaudited accounts (1 June 2026)
  • RBI: September and April–September 2026 balance of payments (13 November 2026)
  • USTR: Section 301 forced-labour measures (23 July 2026)
  • India: UK CETA entered into force (15 July 2026)
  • Indian government: status of trade agreements (2026)
  • RBI: October 2026 rate decision
  • Ministry of Labour: Industrial Relations (Central) Rules, May 2026

excerpt.rendered: India grew through tariffs, an oil shock, inflation and new policy frameworks. A source-linked review of what happened to households, work, investment, government spending and external resilience, without confusing growth with prosperity.

title.rendered: The Survey promised investment. The accounts reveal what was actually spent.

content.rendered:
Historical baseline: Economic Survey 2025–26, tabled 29 January 2026. Accounts checked through the provisional FY2025–26 release of 1 June 2026. Retrospective publication: 14 November 2026. India’s investment narrative is often told with a budget allocation. But a Budget Estimate is a plan to spend, not proof that money reached a construction site or that an asset is being used. The Economic Survey’s case for sustained public capital expenditure was plausible. It can now be tested against the Controller General of Accounts’ later, unaudited figures.

The number in the Survey and the number in the accounts

Chapter 9 of the Economic Survey 2025–26 recorded a FY2025–26 central capital expenditure allocation of about ₹11.21 lakh crore. It described this as part of a sustained build-out of infrastructure, with a rise from ₹5.92 lakh crore in FY2021–22. The original Budget at a Glance provides the exact FY26 Budget Estimate: ₹11,21,090 crore. It also separately reported ₹15,48,282 crore in effective capital expenditure, which incorporates grants for the creation of capital assets. These are not two alternative measures of the same cash payment.

The CGA’s provisional accounts put FY2025–26 direct Union capital expenditure at ₹10,69,119 crore. The revised estimate was ₹10,95,755 crore. Relative to the original Budget Estimate, provisional spending was lower by ₹51,971 crore, or about 4.64%. Relative to the revised estimate, the shortfall was ₹26,636 crore, or about 2.43%. These are arithmetic differences between published figures for the same fiscal year, not project-level evidence of cancellation or delay.

The budget-to-provisional difference matters, but its sign does not by itself tell us whether the investment programme failed. Capital expenditure can undershoot because a tender attracted fewer bids, because a project faced land or procurement issues, because projected prices fell, because loans were released later than anticipated, or because the government revised priorities. Some of those explanations point to poor execution; others could reflect efficiency or a change in demand. The accounts alone do not distinguish them.

The fiscal bridge, in original rupee units

One rupee out of the capital budget is not necessarily one rupee of direct physical works by a Union ministry. The CGA records ₹1,99,691 crore of loans disbursed within FY26 capital expenditure, or roughly 18.7% of the aggregate. Loans can support investment by states, agencies or other recipients, but the lender’s cash disbursement is not the same as asphalt laid, megawatts commissioned, passengers carried or a project’s financial return. A responsible investment dashboard has to track both the financial transaction and the physical result.

The Survey’s higher ‘effective capital expenditure’ measure included grants-in-aid to create capital assets. Grants may finance state and local projects, and are recorded differently from the Centre’s own capital spending. Adding the entire effective-capex figure to direct capital expenditure would double count components. Comparing the FY26 Budget Estimate for effective capex directly with the CGA’s ₹10.69 lakh crore provisional direct capex would also be invalid: the definitions differ.

Spending did not disappear into a fiscal vacuum

The same provisional CGA accounts show total Union expenditure of ₹49,05,151 crore, compared with revised estimates of ₹49,64,842 crore. Revenue expenditure was ₹38,36,032 crore. Interest payments were ₹12,42,575 crore, while major subsidies amounted to ₹4,53,854 crore. Net tax revenue to the Centre was ₹26,23,264 crore, and total non-debt receipts were ₹33,85,982 crore. The reported fiscal deficit was ₹15,19,169 crore. These are distinct accounting categories, not a bill of how much each individual household paid.

Why do these surrounding numbers matter? Public capital expenditure competes for fiscal space with existing commitments, transfers and debt-service requirements. A rising interest bill can make it harder to sustain a high capex-to-GDP share without tax increases, cuts elsewhere or more borrowing. But a budget is not a household envelope: the timing of revenues and expenditure, the economy’s nominal size and the terms of debt all matter. The capital spending programme needs to be judged in the context of both asset quality and fiscal sustainability.

The multiplier is a research hypothesis, not a receipt

The Survey cited studies suggesting that infrastructure spending can have a medium-term output multiplier on the order of 2.5 to 3.5 under the modelling assumptions used in those studies. It would be incorrect to multiply the provisional ₹10.69 lakh crore outturn mechanically by 3.5 and call the product the realised gain in GDP. The cited multiplier is not a cash-return statement, nor is it necessarily applicable unchanged to every project, year, state and macroeconomic environment.

The real effect of public infrastructure depends on whether an asset removes an actual constraint. A road can reduce time and wastage if firms and workers use it. A port improvement may add little productive value when access roads are still congested. A power line can create valuable capacity but remain underused because the last-mile connection or tariff agreement is missing. A perfectly completed project and an economically productive project are related but not identical concepts.

Consider an illustrative ₹1,000 crore public investment in freight infrastructure. If it lowers logistics costs by ₹80 crore annually for many years, the economic evaluation would weigh those savings, maintenance, environmental effects, crowding-in and the opportunity cost of public funds. The ₹80 crore figure is assumed. It is not an estimate for any real railway, port or highway. An appraisal that counts only construction spending mistakes the input for the outcome.

Does public capex crowd in private investment?

A stronger public logistics network can make privately financed warehouses, factories and export contracts profitable. In that case public investment crowds in private investment. But government borrowing may also compete for savings or raise financing costs under some conditions, and private firms may delay spending if demand is uncertain. One cannot conclude that crowding-in occurred because the national accounts report an increase in gross fixed capital formation. That includes public, private and household investment, and the classification varies by release and data source.

Evidence of crowding-in should link a specific improvement in public infrastructure to private decisions that would otherwise not have happened. Follow industrial land purchases, project awards, construction, installed machinery, plant utilisation, freight-time reductions and firm entry. Ideally compare places that acquired a new capacity connection with appropriately matched places that did not, recognising that routes are not selected at random. The same caution applies to claims that public capex necessarily crowds private investment out.

Private corporate investment statistics are narrower than aggregate GFCF. Company capex reported in financial statements, project-completion records and surveys of capacity utilisation provide independent cross-checks, though they are disproportionately weighted toward visible or listed firms. Micro and small enterprises may respond with a delay and are underrepresented in many financial datasets. A proper test of a ‘broad private investment revival’ needs the whole distribution, not the largest announcement.

The state-government problem

States can receive interest-free or concessional central loans and grants to finance investment. The FY26 budget included sizeable capital support to states, including a ₹1.50 lakh crore outlay for long-term interest-free loans, according to the original fiscal statement. But the same transaction can appear as a Union loan disbursement and later as state project expenditure. Adding both without consolidating public-sector accounts exaggerates the aggregate investment effort.

A useful state comparison should show approvals, cash received, cash spent, contractor payments, projects commissioned and service outcomes on a common timeline. States with similar announced allocations may have different land-acquisition processes, procurement capacity, supplier markets and own-revenue positions. A higher-capex share is not always more productive if the capital is spent on assets with weak demand or high maintenance burdens. Fiscal room also varies after salaries, pensions, interest and legally committed schemes.

What the June provisional accounts can and cannot settle

The provisional data allow a defensible statement: the Centre spent about 95.4% of its original FY26 capital-expenditure Budget Estimate and 97.6% of its Revised Estimate. They do not by themselves tell us which projects missed milestones, whether the quality of new roads improved, or how many private firms invested because of public spending. Nor do they independently verify the Survey’s general claims about logistics efficiency, integrated planning or productive spillovers.

The comparison must preserve the observation and release dates. The Survey was tabled in January 2026 and used a forward-looking FY26 allocation. The June CGA release incorporated the completed financial year and was explicitly provisional and unaudited. Later final accounts may differ. The correct historical reconstruction keeps both figures rather than overwriting the January baseline with a June revision and presenting it as what the Survey knew.

An investment scorecard that can actually be maintained

The next annual research series should have five stages for each major programme: Budgeted → Released → Spent → Commissioned → Utilised. Budgeted is an intention, released is a transfer, spent is the government account, commissioned is the physical asset and utilised is the benefit being delivered. These should be separate fields with sources and dates. Do not score a scheme as successfully implemented merely because a ministry booked the money or awarded a contract.

For a road project, utilisation might include sustained freight volumes, travel times, safety outcomes and maintenance condition. For a transmission line, it might include dependable transfer capacity, congestion and served energy, not just rated megawatts. For irrigation, it can be dependable water at the farm and crop outcomes rather than just canal length. The harder work of economic journalism is collecting these denominators and keeping them consistent when project boundaries change.

The strongest conclusion today is neither that India’s public investment strategy automatically worked nor that missing 4.6% of budgeted capital spending disproves the Survey. It is that the fiscal accounts provide a credible first audit and a sharper question. Did the ₹10.69 lakh crore recorded as capital spending generate usable public assets, and where did those assets induce new production, private investment and work? That is where the Survey’s promise must be tested.

The state fiscal-room comparison, the Union Budget dashboard and the dated economic chronology provide additional context. A dedicated Budget-to-Outturn research table will preserve the three fiscal vintages and their original source records.

Primary sources

  • Economic Survey 2025–26, Chapter 9, investment and infrastructure
  • Union Budget 2025–26, Budget at a Glance, original Budget Estimates
  • Controller General of Accounts: FY2025–26 provisional accounts
  • Ministry of Finance: 1 June 2026 provisional accounts announcement
  • RBI Bulletin: FY2025–26 provisional fiscal comparison

excerpt.rendered: India budgeted ₹11.21 lakh crore in FY26 Union capital expenditure. Provisional accounts report ₹10.69 lakh crore. The gap is measurable, while the productivity of the resulting assets needs a different test.

title.rendered: India’s labour-code rules changed the procedure. Enforcement is the harder test.

content.rendered:
Historical record: the Industrial Relations Code framework commenced on 21 November 2025; draft Central Rules were published on 30 December 2025; final Industrial Relations (Central) Rules were notified on 8 May 2026. Retrospective published: 14 November 2026. A change in labour law is often described as a change in the cost of hiring and firing. The more precise question is who can invoke the procedure, how quickly it operates, which government is responsible, and whether the worker receives what the law promises.

Three dates, three legal events

India’s Industrial Relations Code framework replaced the earlier legislative arrangements for industrial disputes, trade unions and standing orders. The draft Central Rules circulated as G.S.R. 930(E) on 30 December 2025 for public objections and suggestions. Those were proposed procedures, not an already-final set of central rules. On 8 May 2026, the Ministry of Labour and Employment issued the final G.S.R. 342(E), stating that it would take effect on its publication in the Gazette. The official notice records that submissions on the draft were considered.

The Code and the subordinate Rules do different jobs. The Code creates rights, obligations, categories and decision powers. Rules tell institutions which forms to accept, which committee to constitute, what notice to give and how to process disputes. A worker’s practical protection often depends on the latter. An entitlement to a hearing means less if employees cannot learn the procedure, obtain representation or track a case to resolution. Equally, an employer’s ability to plan a restructuring depends on clear procedures and predictable decision times, not only the nominal statutory threshold.

Who is actually covered by the Central Rules?

The word Central matters. These 2026 Rules apply where the Union is the appropriate government under the Industrial Relations Code, including specified central undertakings and industries such as railways, banks and mines. The state government is the appropriate authority for many other establishments. An employer in a privately owned manufacturing plant cannot assume the central notification automatically supplies every locally operative procedure. State-level rules, court decisions and transitional arrangements need their own review.

This division creates a research challenge for comparisons across states. Counting central notifications may overstate progress where state implementation differs. Conversely, finding a delay in one state’s rulemaking does not prove that every worker in that state lacks all protections. A transparent implementation tracker needs the date, issuing authority, provision, coverage, procedural form and whether cases are actually being filed under it.

Works committees and individual grievances

Under the Code, establishments with 100 or more workers may be subject to a works-committee requirement under the relevant government direction. The Central Rules describe committees of up to 20 members with employer and worker representation, prescribed office-bearers and meetings at least once in three months. These institutions are intended to address common issues before they become industrial disputes. Their success is not measured by the number of committees entered into a register. It should be measured by representation, frequency of meetings, issues raised and resolutions implemented.

Grievance Redressal Committees are another mechanism, generally covering qualifying establishments with 20 or more workers. The final Central Rules recognise representatives selected through negotiating unions or councils, and contemplate worker-selected representatives where no such body exists. PRS Legislative Research notes an implementation weakness: the detailed manner for choosing worker representatives where no recognised union or council exists is not fully prescribed. That is an institutional gap with economic consequences. A formal committee offers weak protection if employees cannot select a trusted representative without retaliation or procedural uncertainty.

The value of these mechanisms is conditional. If a complaint can be resolved at low cost before a prolonged dispute, the worker may regain unpaid wages or correct an unsafe practice faster, and the firm may avoid disruption and litigation. But if meetings are perfunctory or the committee cannot secure compliance, the process may delay access to more effective remedies. A useful evaluation compares grievance resolution times, repeat complaints and whether workers can appeal, not just the stock of committees.

Retrenchment, closure and the 300-worker threshold

For specified establishments such as factories, mines and plantations with 300 or more workers, the Code establishes a prior-permission framework for layoff, retrenchment and closure. The Central Rules detail applications and notice periods: at least 15 days before the proposed layoff, 60 before retrenchment and 90 before closure, subject to the particular legal provisions. Different transactions, exceptions and establishments can have different requirements. This is not a claim that a firm with 299 workers can freely disregard every other obligation under labour law.

Threshold-based rules affect incentives. In principle, compliance costs that change discontinuously with headcount can influence how firms define establishments, outsource work or schedule expansion. But observing that firms cluster below 300 workers is not proof the legal threshold caused it. Technology, industry, market size, reporting gaps, and access to capital can create similar patterns. A convincing study would compare otherwise similar firms around the threshold, before and after legal implementation, while accounting for measurement and strategic employment reporting.

An employer facing an unpredictable approval decision may delay restructuring even when preserving an unviable position is costly. Workers, meanwhile, need time to organise, contest and search for alternative income. Lawmakers therefore confront a genuine trade-off between the ability to adjust a business and the social cost of sudden employment loss. The operative question is whether safeguards are accessible and predictable enough to protect workers without converting a statutory hearing into arbitrary delay.

The reskilling fund gives us a measurable promise

One especially testable provision is the Worker Re-skilling Fund. The final Central Rules describe an employer contribution equivalent to fifteen days of the retrenched worker’s last drawn wages, to be deposited within ten days, with payment into the worker’s account on the prescribed timeline. PRS summarises a forty-five-day transfer requirement. That creates three distinct records: the retrenchment event, the employer’s transfer to the fund and the worker’s receipt. An ’employer deposited’ statistic is not the same as a ‘worker received money’ statistic.

For illustration, suppose a retrenched worker’s daily wage is ₹900. Fifteen days’ wages equal ₹13,500. If the employer makes the required payment but the worker receives it months late, its protective value is lower than a timely ₹13,500 payment because the worker may have immediate rent, food and job-search expenses. This is a numerical illustration, not a claim about actual wages or compliance. It captures the relevant outcome: not merely whether the contribution was booked, but whether a household had access to liquidity during unemployment.

Even timely support cannot be equated with reskilling. The contribution may ease the worker’s search constraint, yet its usefulness for training depends on course quality, recognition, employer demand, travel costs and the worker’s time. If the fund simply pays a lump sum, measuring enrolment or placements after retrenchment is necessary before attributing skill gains to the scheme. A credible evaluation would also distinguish workers who would have found a new job without the fund.

Where the rules remain incomplete

The PRS analysis finds that several matters delegated under the Code are not fully specified in the final Central Rules, particularly aspects of trade-union procedures and grievance representation. The 2026 rules also do not straightforwardly repeal every earlier trade-union regulation. The legal transition can therefore leave questions about which forms or procedures remain operative. This is why it is risky to tell employers or workers that one Gazette has resolved every issue in the industrial-relations framework.

The strongest argument for the 2026 notification is that specifying applications, notices, conciliation, settlements and worker payments makes the statutory framework more usable. The strongest counterargument is that procedural detail alone may not create bargaining power, effective enforcement or swift adjudication. Firms can comply on paper while employees do not obtain remedies; conversely, overly uncertain enforcement can deter legitimate investment and formal jobs. Both outcomes require evidence rather than a predetermined ideological answer.

How we should measure the reform

An evidence register should follow each central and state rule from draft publication to notification to operating forms and case outcomes. For works and grievance committees: record affected establishments, membership, meeting frequency, resolved complaints and average duration. For restructuring: track applications, approvals or denials, processing times, appeals and observed layoffs across firm sizes. For the reskilling fund: count eligible workers, employer contributions, actual worker receipts and elapsed days. Publish state and sector denominators so the evidence is not reduced to raw totals.

It should also separate descriptive associations from causal policy estimates. For example, if formal manufacturing employment rises after May 2026, that alone cannot establish that the Industrial Relations Rules created jobs. Firms were simultaneously facing exchange-rate changes, tariffs, investment incentives, credit conditions and changes in demand. A study needs a credible comparison group, attention to contemporaneous shocks, and administrative data that capture the firms and workers intended to be treated.

The December draft and May final text are therefore a meaningful historical sequence, but their significance will be determined by the lives of workers and employers under the rules. The next follow-up should be a side-by-side, clause-numbered draft-to-final comparison, and then an implementation scorecard with actual cases. The Kakistocrat economic chronology records the key dates; the underlying labour-code coverage offers the earlier context. Where a link to an earlier report proves unavailable, the underlying Gazette remains the canonical source.

Primary documents and independent legislative analysis

  • Draft Central Rules, G.S.R. 930(E), 30 December 2025
  • Final Industrial Relations (Central) Rules, G.S.R. 342(E), 8 May 2026
  • PRS Legislative Research: Central Rules, scope and unresolved procedures
  • The Industrial Relations Code (Amendment) Act, 2026

excerpt.rendered: India’s December 2025 draft labour rules became final Central Rules in May 2026. Procedures for worker complaints, retrenchment, representation and reskilling matter only if they are implemented and measured.

title.rendered: India moved its GDP deadline because the evidence arrived late

content.rendered:
An extra week changed the information available

Historical decisions and releases: 12 May and 5 June 2026. Retrospective published: 14 November 2026. India’s annual GDP number is often treated as a single verdict on the financial year. It is better understood as a sequence of estimates. In May 2026, the National Statistics Office changed its provisional annual and fourth-quarter GDP release calendar, moving publication from the last working day of May to 7 June, or the preceding working day when that date fell on a holiday. The estimate for FY2025–26 was consequently published on 5 June. The statistical reason reveals why a few days can change what the country is able to measure.

In the 12 May announcement, the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation explained that listed companies had up to 60 days after the financial year ended to file their Q4 and annual audited financial results. Many submitted near the 31 May deadline. The corresponding March Union government accounts also arrived with a lag of around two months. Publishing the year’s provisional GDP on the last working day of May meant the statistical office was often racing the very evidence it needed.

This is not a trivial calendar matter. The economy does not produce a real-time full census of every factory, professional firm, retailer and government department on 31 March. GDP is a constructed measure that combines direct surveys, company filings, administrative records, prices, indicators and assumptions. A release made too early relies more heavily on partial observations and extrapolation. A release made later can incorporate more actual returns, although even a later provisional estimate remains subject to revisions.

The June number, with its precise vintage

The 5 June MoSPI provisional release put FY2025–26 real GDP at ₹323.12 lakh crore, up from a first revised ₹299.89 lakh crore for FY2024–25, implying growth of 7.7%. It reported nominal GDP of ₹346.36 lakh crore versus ₹318.07 lakh crore, or 8.9% growth. The fourth quarter’s real output was estimated at ₹87.77 lakh crore, compared with ₹81.40 lakh crore a year earlier, giving 7.8% year-on-year growth.

These numbers were the June 2026 vintage, not permanent constants. MoSPI had introduced a GDP series with a 2022–23 base in February, replacing the 2011–12 base. The February second advance estimate incorporated information through the third quarter. The June provisional estimate added Q4 evidence and updated indicators. A researcher who places the February second advance estimate and June provisional estimate in the same chart without identifying their information sets risks implying that the economy itself changed between the two releases. The underlying period, FY2025–26, was already over.

A later National Accounts Statistics revision notice explained that updated producer prices, the revised industrial production series and administrative data were incorporated into earlier annual and quarterly estimates. This is why the June figures should remain labelled as June figures even after newer numbers appear. Replacing the older value everywhere with the latest one may be useful for a current level, but it erases the historical evidence available to a forecaster or policymaker when the original decision was made.

What drove the measured annual increase?

The expenditure identity is GDP = household and government final consumption + investment + exports − imports + the remaining accounting components, including inventories, valuables and the statistical discrepancy. The June constant-price release allows a transparent accounting decomposition using the same base and same published vintage.

Private final consumption rose from ₹166.99851 lakh crore to ₹179.93871 lakh crore, a change of about ₹12.94 lakh crore. Dividing that increase by the prior-year real GDP of ₹299.88619 lakh crore gives approximately 4.32 percentage points of the year’s 7.7% real GDP growth. Gross fixed capital formation rose from ₹96.47792 lakh crore to ₹104.34799 lakh crore, a change of about ₹7.87 lakh crore, contributing approximately 2.62 percentage points. These are accounting contributions, not independent econometric estimates of what fiscal or monetary policies caused.

Government final consumption added about 0.56 percentage points. Exports added roughly 1.42 points while higher real imports subtracted about 1.35 points. Stocks, valuables and the discrepancy together account for the rest. Adding rounded terms can differ slightly from the official growth rate. The exercise shows why saying simply that ‘investment drove growth’ is too imprecise: households made a larger absolute contribution to the measured annual increase, while the fixed-investment component grew faster in percentage terms than consumption.

The most important limitation is that the national-accounts fixed-investment total includes investment by government, public corporations, private firms and households. It cannot by itself demonstrate a broad-based private corporate capital-expenditure boom. Nor does a stronger consumption component establish equal purchasing-power gains across income groups. Both claims need other evidence, from budget accounts, balance sheets, labour surveys, retail prices and income distribution.

Why Q4 financial statements matter

For incorporated firms, the measured value added may draw on accounts of revenue, intermediate costs, inventories and operating activity. A financial statement arriving near 31 May can replace a projection with a more detailed account of what the firm actually earned and spent in January–March. That matters especially in industries where selling prices and input prices diverge. A producer can report higher nominal sales because it charged more, because it sold more units or because it changed its product mix; those explanations imply different real growth.

Suppose a factory’s nominal output rises from ₹100 to ₹115 while its intermediate purchases rise from ₹70 to ₹85. Nominal value added rises from ₹30 to ₹30, a zero change, even though output sales increase 15%. If the output and input prices changed by different amounts, the constant-price result could differ again. The example is illustrative; it is not a figure for any Indian firm. It demonstrates the need for detailed industry data and suitable price indices rather than treating sales growth as real value-added growth.

Updated company results also matter for the composition of the economy. Large listed manufacturers and small unincorporated firms may experience different demand and input-cost shocks. A dataset biased toward early-filing large companies can paint an incomplete picture if the rest of the economy is struggling. The 2022–23 GDP series introduced methodological improvements that use additional surveys and administrative sources, but those source improvements cannot remove all reporting lags, measurement error or the problem of estimating activity in firms that report infrequently.

The fiscal accounts need their own clock

Government spending contributes to measured demand, but the Union’s monthly public accounts are neither identical to the national-accounts government-consumption concept nor sufficient to determine general government expenditure. Capital outlay, subsidies, tax receipts, interest payments and loans affect different parts of the accounts. State expenditure and public enterprises matter too. If March cash accounts arrive only after a two-month lag, rushing the GDP release can increase reliance on estimates or incomplete classifications.

The May scheduling note explicitly cited the fiscal-data lag. That fact matters when analysts claim a quarterly GDP outcome reflects either a late surge of government spending or an abrupt fiscal slowdown. Before drawing that conclusion, one must verify whether the indicator came from final cash accounts, budget estimates, provisional ministry records or a statistical extrapolation. A budget allocation is not expenditure, and a recorded cash payment can finance goods delivered at another point in time.

The policy danger of mixing series and vintages

The new base year is another source of possible confusion. The 2011–12 and 2022–23 series employ different data inputs and methods. An old-series nominal GDP level cannot be compared mechanically with a new-series quarterly level to manufacture growth or decline. The statistical office has subsequently explained cases where estimates of the same period changed because the base, producer-price inputs, industrial-production indicators and other records were updated.

The same problem affects fiscal ratios. If the denominator for debt-to-GDP is updated while the stock of debt remains measured in rupees, the ratio can change without new borrowing. If an investment share or tax-to-GDP ratio is quoted with one vintage and compared with a previous estimate under another, the apparent trend can be partly methodological. The correct response is to preserve vintages in a research database and recompute ratios using consistent denominators, not to declare the old or new number politically convenient.

A reproducible research workbook should therefore hold at least six columns for each GDP observation: economic period, release date, base year, price basis, estimate stage and value. The estimate stage may be an advance estimate, second advance estimate, provisional estimate or later revision. A second table should record the actual source and revision reason. That would let readers ask both ‘What do we know now?’ and ‘What did policymakers know when they acted?’.

What did extra time buy, and what did it not buy?

Delaying the publication by days offers a plausible improvement in information completeness and may reduce later revision volatility. But it is not proof that the June provisional estimate was more accurate than every earlier estimate. More recent company filings can themselves be corrected, administrative coverage may change, and unorganised-sector information still lags. The relevant evaluation would compare the size and bias of revisions before and after the new schedule across several years, controlling for changes in methodology and the unusual scale of the 2026 base revision.

There is also a real cost to waiting. Fiscal and monetary policymakers, researchers, investors and citizens need timely GDP information. A later release can arrive after a decision that would have benefited from current data. Statistical agencies therefore face a classic trade-off between timeliness and completeness. Shifting a date by a week is justified if it substantially improves source coverage without making the release too late to inform useful decisions. MoSPI’s explanation gives a testable reason; evaluating its success will require observing future vintages.

What would change the conclusion?

The strongest case for the calendar change is that waiting until after the bulk of listed-company results and March fiscal data are available produces a more representative provisional estimate. Evidence that would strengthen it is a documented decline in the size of subsequent revisions for Q4 and annual GDP relative to comparable past years. Evidence that would weaken it is that the extra time makes little difference to input coverage or that large revisions continue for other reasons and the change only delays information.

The June 2026 release should therefore be read as an advance in the information set, not the final word on FY2025–26. It reported solid annual real growth and an important rise in household consumption and investment, but neither total contains enough information to declare a lasting private-investment revival or shared growth in living standards. The analytical gain is to ask what evidence each estimate includes and why it changes.

For readers, the story continues through Measuring the Indian Economy, the growth-divergence dashboard, and The Kakistocrat’s February base-year analysis and August investment analysis. The three investigations answer different questions: how the series is constructed, how the evidence arrived and what the spending components imply for private investment.

Original sources

  • MoSPI: 12 May 2026 change in GDP provisional-release date
  • MoSPI: 5 June 2026 provisional annual and Q4 GDP estimates, including full tables
  • MoSPI subsequent National Accounts Statistics revisions
