title.rendered: The forced-labour tariff changed India’s trade position before it changed the factory

content.rendered:
The proposal and the final order were different economic events

Historical milestones: 2 June and 23–24 July 2026. Retrospective publication: 14 November 2026. In June, the United States proposed additional tariffs linked to whether trading partners prohibited imports made with forced labour. In July it adopted a final scheme, including a 10% additional duty for covered Indian-origin imports. Treating those two announcements as a single tariff event obscures how the cost changed, how India responded and what exporters actually had to pay at the border.

The original 2 June USTR finding covered 60 economies and proposed different additional-duty rates of 10% and 12.5%, with product exemptions and a contemplated textiles mechanism. The 23 July final action placed India in the 10% group. The 28 July Federal Register notice made the legal distinctions, product exemptions and shipping dates explicit. This article examines the economic transmission, not merely the diplomatic headline.

What the United States was investigating

The Section 301 inquiry was framed around a trading partner’s failure to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on importing goods produced wholly or partly with forced labour. It is not the same question as whether a particular Indian factory used forced labour. The US allegation concerned the importing country’s legal and enforcement regime, and the resulting possibility that goods made with coercive labour could circulate through international supply chains and compete with compliant producers. A country-wide duty is a blunt response to that institutional problem.

USTR initiated the investigations in March 2026, examined submissions and consultations, and made its actionability determination in June. Following comments and public hearings, the final notice invoked the policy discretion of Section 301 to impose additional charges subject to exemptions. The stated objective was to encourage foreign governments to enact and enforce import prohibitions, while protecting competition in the US market. That creates an immediate economic tension: a duty can raise the price of goods regardless of whether the particular shipment has documented clean sourcing. The policy’s incentive therefore acts at the country-policy level, while its bill is presented on a specific customs entry.

How India entered the 10% group

The June proposal contemplated a higher tier for economies that lacked qualifying prohibitions or commitments. India’s Ministry of Commerce statement of 25 July described the final 10% rate as a reduction from the originally proposed 12.5% for India. The US Federal Register notice states that India adopted a forced-labour import prohibition after publication of the June proposal, and cites this among the considerations for India’s final tariff treatment.

India’s Directorate General of Foreign Trade issued Notification No. 23/2026–27 on 13 July, inserting forced-labour provisions into the Foreign Trade Policy 2023. The provision concerns goods produced wholly or in part using forced labour and is accompanied by procedures for examination and action. The exact operative date must be read from the official Gazette wording and any subsequent notification, rather than inferred solely from a headline or a US announcement. The policy response may have affected India’s classification in the US trade action, but that does not establish that labour-rights violations were immediately detected or eliminated by the new import framework.

India’s position in the lower tier is therefore best understood as a relative tariff result, not an exemption from the new policy. An additional duty of 10% still creates a cost wedge. Nor did India gain a unique 10% rate: Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and the United Kingdom were among the other economies placed in the 10% group. For a buyer deciding between India and Bangladesh on a product subject to identical tariff treatment, the new Section 301 measure alone does not change their relative prices.

Why the tariff has to be calculated product by product

India was placed in an additional 10% Section 301 category for non-exempt covered goods. The extra duty is generally applied in addition to ordinary customs duties, rather than replacing the product’s most-favoured-nation rate. For certain other economies, including some goods of the European Union, Taiwan, Japan, Korea and Switzerland, the final scheme included a net of MFN mechanism. These are not equivalent tariff structures. A comparison that assumes every exporting economy simply adds the headline percentage to its ordinary tariff will misstate the competitive position.

Consider an illustrative Indian shipment with a customs value of $100,000, an ordinary 5% US duty and no exemption or other applicable special measure. The ordinary duty is $5,000; the additional 10% Section 301 duty is $10,000; total duty on this simplified basis is $15,000. If the June proposal had resulted in a 12.5% additional rate instead, the additional duty would have been $12,500, a $2,500 difference for this consignment. These assumptions are illustrative. They are not a verified landed bill for an actual Indian HS code.

The actual bill can depend on the Harmonized Tariff Schedule classification, origin, entry date, specific exemptions, other lawful tariff measures, trade remedies, valuation rules and administrative guidance. A product listed in an exemption annex cannot be assessed as though the blanket country headline applies. The Kakistocrat landed-cost calculator can be used to explore two assumed suppliers, but it does not replace the applicable US tariff schedule, customs ruling or professional classification decision.

The customs clock mattered

The final US notice applied additional rates to qualifying goods entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption, on or after 12:01 AM US eastern time on 24 July 2026. It contained a narrow in-transit exception for merchandise loaded before the cutoff and entered before 12:01 AM eastern time on 28 July. The relevant legal trigger was customs entry under the notice’s definitions, not the date on which an Indian exporter had signed a purchase order.

That small window can shift the costs of a shipment substantially. A vessel’s departure, arrival, entry for consumption, warehouse withdrawal and cargo release are not necessarily the same event. A firm that priced a sale in early June could face a different duty at arrival if its contract did not allocate the tariff risk. An importer might renegotiate, seek a concession, delay future orders, change shipment timing where lawful or absorb part of the cost. The largest immediate effect can be on cash flow and contract margins, before any factory changes its output.

Who pays the additional tax?

The US customs authority collects the duty from the importer of record. That tells us who has the legal obligation, not who bears the final economic cost. The importer may reduce the price offered to its Indian supplier, pass some cost into the US retail price, accept a smaller margin or reduce orders. Where alternative suppliers can rapidly replace the Indian product, the Indian exporter may face stronger pressure to cut its dollar price. If the imported input is highly specialised or competitors face similar duties, more of the cost may remain with US buyers.

An illustrative $100,000 shipment facing $10,000 extra duty might be renegotiated so the exporter concedes $4,000 and the importer absorbs $6,000. That split is simply an example, not a measured incidence rate. The actual split depends on demand elasticity, supply alternatives, inventory, contracts and the firms’ relative bargaining power. Any serious claim about the policy’s impact on Indian exports needs matched product-level quantities, unit values and counterpart prices, not a single country-wide export growth rate.

For labour-intensive manufacturers, tariff uncertainty can be as important as the duty itself. A buyer may withhold orders until a supplier can prove origin and document inputs; a smaller exporter may struggle to finance the working capital needed for longer customs clearance. Even a supplier whose inputs satisfy relevant requirements can lose competitiveness if the buyer faces a higher country-specific duty. For US buyers, the same risk may encourage diversification across origin countries, but a diversified supplier list is no defence if common inputs trace back to the same opaque source.

The textile mechanism was not a universal India exemption

The final notice directed USTR to establish tariff-rate quotas when feasible for specified textiles and apparel from Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia and Malaysia, tied to those economies’ purchases of US cotton or textile inputs. India was not named among those four TRQ beneficiaries. This matters because a quota allowing some shipments at a reduced additional rate could alter competition for a particular garment order even when India and Bangladesh both appear in the general 10% tariff group.

Crucially, the notice described the TRQ mechanism as something to establish when feasible. It did not make an automatic quota entitlement available to every listed exporter on 24 July. The final economic effect must be tested against later implementing notices: exact covered tariff lines, quota size, use of US inputs, proof requirements, allocation and the dates when quota entries actually became available. A forecast of future competitiveness should not be presented as a customs rate already in operation.

Does an import ban eliminate forced labour?

Prohibiting forced-labour goods from entering a market can give purchasers an incentive to verify their supply chains and shift away from abusive production. It can also encourage governments to improve domestic enforcement, since the absence of credible import controls can create trade costs for otherwise compliant exporters. The objective of preventing coerced work is distinct from the fiscal impact of collecting duties, and success cannot be inferred from how much tariff revenue is raised.

The policy’s weakness is the imperfect link between country-level sanctions and the conditions in a given factory. A country can enact a prohibition without building the investigative capacity needed to find concealed abuses. Buyers can move assembly to another location while continuing to source inputs from an upstream supplier with poor labour practices. A successful regime needs credible evidence, targeted investigations, traceable supply chains, proportionate enforcement and a process for firms to contest an adverse finding. Its effectiveness should be measured in improved detection and labour conditions rather than legal text alone.

India’s July policy change is therefore a beginning, not the endpoint. The next Indian evidence should include implementation procedures, investigations launched, findings, customs seizures or exclusions, judicial review where relevant and measurable changes in supply-chain due diligence. Likewise, an evaluation of the US tariff should look for genuine compliance improvements rather than merely a rise in landed prices. A lower tariff group can be an incentive to reform; it is not proof that reform was fully enforced.

What would establish the economic effect on India?

A careful product-level study would first identify the Indian HS lines affected after exemptions. It would then compare shipment volumes and prices with similar goods from countries facing different treatment, separating exporters that compete in the same US product markets. The legal implementation date and the shipment date should both be recorded. Monthly trade data require attention to front-loading, timing delays and contracts signed before the new duty. The analysis also needs to account for other US tariffs or trade measures operating at the same time, otherwise a Section 301 estimate may absorb unrelated changes.

The strongest apparent benefit of India’s move from the proposed 12.5% tier to the final 10% tier is lower duty relative to that counterfactual for covered non-exempt goods. It is not the same as a 2.5% improvement over the duties exporters actually paid before the final action. The June figure was a proposal, not a tax then being collected. One cannot record avoidance of a hypothetical tariff as an increase in observed export revenue.

The strongest reason to think the final order mattered is that relative border prices influence procurement decisions and contract bargaining. The strongest counterargument is that products exempt from the action, competing countries facing similar rates, or firms with highly specialised orders may see little incremental competitive effect. We should also ask whether more effective forced-labour enforcement improves worker welfare and sourcing credibility, even where the tariff itself reduces commerce.

How the story continues

The chain of events is now clear: a March investigation, a June proposed duty and request for comment, an Indian policy response in July, a 23 July final decision and 24 July applicability subject to the notice’s entry and exemption provisions. The next stage is to measure actual shipments, tariff utilization and enforcement. A reader interested in the larger sequence can follow America’s Tariff Reset timeline and the earlier analysis of exporters’ bargaining position. The economic question is how a legal intervention changes orders, profit margins and supply-chain practices, not whether a tariff headline sounds favourable.

Original documents

  • USTR determination and proposed action, 2 June 2026
  • USTR final determination, 23 July 2026
  • Federal Register final notice, 28 July 2026
  • US Presidential memorandum, 23 July 2026
  • India Commerce Ministry, 25 July 2026
  • USTR investigation document register

excerpt.rendered: June’s forced-labour tariff proposal and July’s final US order had different implications for Indian exporters. The difference turns on the legal tariff, exceptions, customs date, incidence and textile quotas.

title.rendered: The RBI held its rate in February. Borrowers kept repricing.

content.rendered:
Why a rate hold can still change a borrower’s bill

Historical decision: 6 February 2026. Retrospective published: 14 November 2026. When the Reserve Bank of India left its policy repo rate at 5.25% in February, it did not announce that the cost of credit would stop changing. The rate on a new bank loan and the rate paid by a borrower with an older floating-rate loan are different prices. They reprice on different contractual schedules and respond to funding costs, risk, competition and earlier policy decisions with different delays. The February hold is an unusually useful point from which to observe those differences.

The Monetary Policy Committee’s 6 February resolution records a unanimous decision to leave the repo rate at 5.25%, the standing deposit facility at 5.00% and the marginal standing facility and Bank Rate at 5.50%, while maintaining a neutral stance. The decision followed a cumulative 125-basis-point easing since February 2025. A central bank can keep the next overnight-policy price fixed while earlier changes travel gradually into loan contracts and deposit pricing.

What the data said when the MPC met

The RBI’s 30 January release provided weighted average lending-rate data through December 2025. The average rate on fresh rupee loans had moved from 8.71% in November to 8.28% in December, a 43-basis-point decline in that particular comparison. The weighted average rate on outstanding rupee loans fell from 9.21% to 9.06%, only 15 basis points. These are samples of loans issued or held during different periods, not a panel that tracks the same households at both dates.

A borrower taking a fresh loan in December could therefore face a substantially different market from a household still servicing an older loan. It would be a mistake to say the typical existing borrower immediately received the whole 43-basis-point fresh-loan decline. It would also be a mistake to use the smaller 15-basis-point movement in the outstanding aggregate to conclude that new lending prices barely responded. The two statistics answer different questions.

The February Governor’s statement summarised cumulative transmission during February–December 2025 as 105 basis points on fresh loans against the 125-basis-point repo reduction, while distinguishing the rate effect from changes in the mix of loans. The same statement reported a 95-basis-point decline in fresh deposit rates and a 41-basis-point softening in outstanding deposit rates. These are different aggregate price indices, and their changes should not be mechanically attributed entirely to the repo path.

The loan mix can move the average even when a bank changes no rate

Imagine Bank A issues ₹100 crore of home loans at 8% and ₹100 crore of unsecured loans at 14%. The simple weighted average rate is 11%. Next month, suppose it issues ₹150 crore of home loans and ₹50 crore of unsecured loans at exactly the same product rates. The weighted average on fresh lending falls to 9.5%, even though the quoted price of neither product changes. This example is illustrative. It shows why fresh-loan averages reflect both pricing within loan categories and the distribution of lending across categories.

The problem becomes harder across the entire banking sector. Changes in which banks supply credit, which borrowers qualify, the amount and tenor of each loan, collateral quality and the share of floating-rate contracts can all move the published average. A year of monetary easing might encourage high-quality borrowers to refinance and lower the average new-loan rate even if borrowers facing greater credit risk see much smaller concessions. Looking only at the aggregate would miss who obtained cheaper credit.

This is also a reason not to take a movement in aggregate rates as a causal estimate of pass-through. A clean interest-rate effect would compare like with like, holding the lending mix reasonably constant. RBI researchers have subsequently examined decomposition methods that separate rate and weight effects. The underlying issue is exactly what households and firms need to understand: an aggregate average can change without any one contract repricing by the headline amount.

The February observation and what came afterwards

The RBI’s 27 February release, containing January observations, showed the fresh-loan average rising relative to December, while the outstanding-loan average edged down to 9.04%. One month’s increase in the fresh-lending average after an easing cycle is not proof that banks collectively reversed their posted rates. It could reflect changes in credit mix, firm risk, product composition or the pricing of funding. Subsequent RBI releases may also revise the comparison month.

The 30 March release placed the February fresh-loan rate at 8.44% against a revised January comparison of 8.49%, while outstanding rupee loans declined to 9.00% in February from 9.04% in January. Reading the two releases together shows why a data notebook must preserve vintages: the first published January figure and the later comparison are not identical. A chart that silently splices them may manufacture an extra movement that is part of data revision, not a change in borrowing conditions.

By September 2026 the outstanding-loan rate was reported at 8.96%, unchanged from August, and the fresh-loan average had fallen from 8.61% in August to 8.51% in September, according to the 30 October release. Policy itself had changed direction in October, when the MPC increased its repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50% and adopted calibrated tightening. The February hold should therefore be understood as one chapter in a continuing credit cycle, not an indication of where borrowing costs would stand forever.

Existing floating loans, new loans and deposits transmit policy differently

External-benchmark-linked loans may reset in line with their contractual benchmark and reset frequency, but a customer’s total rate also includes an agreed spread and any applicable contractual changes. A margin linked to credit risk or a change in loan product can make two borrowers with the same benchmark face different rates. MCLR-linked loans are based on the bank’s marginal funding cost and reset according to the loan contract. Fixed-rate loans are even more insulated from immediate movements in the repo rate. Loan-rate transmission is therefore a sequence of contractual events rather than a simultaneous repricing of the country’s outstanding debt.

Deposits can be slower or faster, depending on whether the money is being placed in a new term deposit or remains locked into an older rate. A bank may have to compete for new funding even while the RBI is easing. The January release showed the weighted average fresh term-deposit rate rising from 5.59% in November to 5.67% in December, while the outstanding term-deposit average eased from 6.73% to 6.68%. Funding competition and maturity structure can counter the mechanical impulse of a lower repo rate. Bank lending prices need to cover operating costs, expected credit losses, capital costs and a margin as well as the cost of funding.

Who benefits first, and who waits?

A large company with an existing relationship, strong financial statements and access to bond markets may be able to bargain for competitive borrowing terms. A smaller manufacturer dependent on working-capital credit can be more exposed to the bank’s own funding costs, collateral rules and risk premium. A housing borrower with an external benchmark may receive a contractual reset before a borrower on an older MCLR contract. Savers with maturing deposits can encounter a different renewal rate even when the interest received on their previous deposit has not changed. None of these outcomes can be quantified from the single national average alone.

Consider an illustrative ₹40 lakh, 20-year housing loan with a fixed remaining tenure. At an interest rate of 9.0% the equated monthly instalment is approximately ₹35,989. A 25-basis-point reduction to 8.75%, if fully applied with tenure unchanged and standard monthly compounding, brings the instalment to roughly ₹35,349, a difference of about ₹640 a month. Actual lenders may hold the instalment fixed and shorten the tenure instead. Prepayments, reset dates, fees, principal outstanding and contractual terms affect the realised saving. A claim that every borrower saves this amount would be incorrect.

Why the MPC could wait while banks were still adjusting

A rate hold gives policymakers time to see how earlier easing changes financial conditions and demand. Another cut before the existing reductions are transmitted could add stimulus while observed lending prices still contain an incomplete response to earlier policy. But a hold is not necessarily restrictive: if inflation declines, the inflation-adjusted policy rate rises even with a fixed nominal repo; if inflation accelerates, the opposite may occur. The right monetary stance depends on expected inflation, the growth outlook, credit conditions and the distribution of the policy’s effects.

The February resolution described a neutral stance, not a commitment never to cut or raise rates again. The choice was to preserve flexibility as the global trade environment and domestic indicators evolved. Policymakers also face an attribution problem: a fall in loan rates after a repo cut is consistent with transmission, but the same period may see changes in risk appetite, credit demand, government borrowing, bank capital and global interest rates. A credible assessment should follow these variables rather than isolate one central-bank decision and assume it explains every market movement.

What an economist can reproduce

The simplest useful comparison puts the repo rate, the rate on new rupee loans, the rate on outstanding rupee loans, new and outstanding term-deposit rates, and the one-year median MCLR on the same timeline. The observation month must be distinguished from the RBI’s publication date. Missing months should remain missing instead of being interpolated as if the interpolation were an observation. Any change in the RBI’s published comparison series should be recorded as a revised vintage.

The Kakistocrat’s RBI transmission research notebook provides source-linked observations, a calculation method, downloadable CSV and Python reproduction code. The earlier December 2025 rate-cut analysis asked who obtained cheaper credit, while the later September transmission report examines the eventual responses. The February hold belongs between them.

The question the February decision leaves us with

The record supports a careful conclusion: the MPC held the policy rate steady, and the cost of bank credit continued to adjust. What it does not support is a single ‘percentage of the repo cut passed on’ that applies equally to new home loans, old floating business credit and deposit accounts. Those markets have different contract structures and compositions. The strongest argument for watching the aggregate is that it captures the price of actual lending in the economy. The strongest argument for caution is that it cannot hold the types of loans constant.

The next decisive evidence would show matched loan products across banks and borrower groups, with known reset dates, consistent contract terms, and clear separation between rates and loan mix. Until then, the appropriate policy question is not simply whether a repo reduction reached ‘the average borrower’. It is which borrower got what rate, on what date, under what contract, and whether cheaper credit financed additional productive activity rather than only replacing more expensive debt.

Original source documents

  • RBI MPC February 2026 resolution
  • RBI Governor’s February 2026 statement
  • RBI January 2026 lending and deposit rates release
  • RBI February 2026 lending and deposit rates release
  • RBI March 2026 lending and deposit rates release
  • RBI October 2026 lending and deposit rates release

excerpt.rendered: The MPC held at 5.25% in February 2026, but fresh and outstanding bank lending rates kept adjusting. The sequence shows why a policy-rate hold is not a credit-price freeze.

title.rendered: GST 2.0 cut tax rates. Which consumer prices actually fell?

content.rendered:
The tax announcement and the price question

Historical event: 3 September 2025; principal implementation: 22 September 2025. Retrospective reviewed: 14 November 2026. The GST Council’s 56th meeting reshaped India’s indirect-tax schedule. The central promise was that lower tax rates on many everyday goods and services would improve household purchasing power. One year later, the fair question is narrower and harder than whether the reform looked generous on paper: which consumers actually paid lower retail prices, and how much of the initial tax reduction was absorbed before it reached the till?

The Council moved toward two principal tax rates, 5% and 18%, alongside a special 40% rate for selected supplies. Its original 3 September recommendations and accompanying official FAQs specified a generally applicable 22 September commencement, with specified tobacco products subject to separate treatment. A recommendation, the legally operative notification and the shelf price are three distinct objects. The date of a government announcement is not necessarily the date on which a wholesaler’s stock or a retailer’s price tag changes.

The reform should be judged in three ledgers, not one: the statutory GST rate; prices paid by buyers of eligible products; and revenue received by the Centre and states. Each is affected by a different set of decisions. A lower tax rate can coincide with a higher retail price if production or distribution costs increase at the same time. Total GST receipts can grow despite lower rates if taxable sales, imports or compliance expand. Neither result settles whether the policy delivered the intended relief.

The arithmetic of a tax cut is not the same as the arithmetic of relief

Take a product whose pre-tax price is ₹100 and whose tax falls from 18% to 5%, assuming an unchanged taxable base and no other tax complications. Its old customer price is ₹118. Full pass-through produces a new price of ₹105, a saving of ₹13, or about 11.0% of the original sticker price. The tax rate fell by 13 percentage points, but the consumer price did not fall by 13%. That difference matters in judging media claims about the size of a discount.

If the seller passes on only half of the ₹13 statutory saving, the new price would be ₹111.50, a fall of 5.5% from ₹118. The remainder is retained somewhere in the supply chain or offsets other costs. This is a transparent illustration, not an observed rate of pass-through for Indian businesses. Conversely, stronger competition or lower wholesale costs could make the final price fall by more than the immediate tax arithmetic implies.

The apparent simplicity also hides input-tax credits. A firm’s effective burden depends on whether it can claim credits on inputs, what exemptions apply, and whether its suppliers change their prices. A zero rate or exemption cannot always be modelled as a straightforward subtraction from the sale price when earlier input tax becomes non-creditable. The relevant comparison is therefore a matched item of the same specification, tax treatment and seller, not a national average for an entire industry.

What the price evidence says

A subsequent study from the National Institute of Public Finance and Policy provides a useful early check. In working paper 444, GST 2.0: Do Lower Tax Rates Translate into Lower Consumer Prices?, Sacchidananda Mukherjee and Shivani Badola compared average CPI movements for selected commodities over four months before the restructuring and four months after it. They report uneven adjustments: prices for many food, household and personal-care items continued rising, while several higher-value durables, including motor vehicles, bicycles, tyres, air conditioners and some appliances, showed declines in the CPI measure.

That finding weakens the assumption that a statutory cut automatically creates a uniform fall in recorded retail prices. It does not establish that retailers retained a particular share of the tax reduction. The pre-and-post comparison covers months with other moving costs, discounts, seasonal demand, inventories and changes in product mix. A household food item becoming dearer after the cut could still be cheaper than it would have been without the cut. The missing counterfactual is the core identification problem.

The more defensible reading is that price transmission differed by product. A durable with relatively transparent list prices and concentrated national distribution may adjust differently from goods sold through many layers of wholesalers and retailers. Perishable food prices move with harvest conditions and transport costs. Personal-care items can have branded retail prices but changing pack sizes, promotional offers or discounts. Those possibilities are hypotheses to test against matched prices and supply-chain evidence, not explanations to assert merely because the series moved differently.

The revenue ledger is a different story

The official October 2025 collection release recorded gross GST receipts of ₹1,95,936 crore, up 4.6% from ₹1,87,346 crore a year earlier. Gross domestic receipts rose only 2.0%, from ₹1,42,251 crore to ₹1,45,052 crore, while the import component rose more strongly. This is exactly why the aggregate growth rate cannot be treated as the effect of the rate restructuring on domestic transactions. Import composition and other differences matter.

For November 2025, a subsequent parliamentary reply reported ₹1,70,276 crore of gross receipts, versus ₹1,69,016 crore in November 2024, an increase of about 0.7%. The October and November growth rates were lower than a simple story of rising nominal consumption might suggest. But the receipts are neither a clean estimate of forgone tax revenue nor an estimate of the household benefit from the reform.

Cash collection is not the same thing as tax accruing on transactions in the same calendar month. Filing and payment schedules, imports, refunds and adjustments can alter the relationship between the date of a sale and the reported collection. Gross versus net receipts also matter. The Kakistocrat’s earlier analysis of the November figures examined the divergence between imports and domestic receipts. The price question adds a separate incidence test to that fiscal account.

Who would be expected to receive the benefit?

A cut in consumption tax starts as a reduction in the tax wedge between the seller’s net price and the buyer’s gross price. How the benefit is split depends on demand, supply and market structure. If consumers have good substitutes and retailers compete strongly, sellers have a greater incentive to lower sticker prices. If local supply is constrained, demand is relatively insensitive to price or the sale involves a product that is difficult to compare, more of the statutory relief may be retained upstream. Neither side’s share can be inferred from the legal incidence of GST alone.

For policymakers, distribution also matters. A given reduction in the price of a regularly purchased necessity may free more cash in a low-income household’s monthly budget than an equally large percentage reduction in a rarely purchased durable. But a product-specific rate cut benefits only buyers of that product, and some of its benefit can accrue to higher-income consumers who buy more of it. One cannot calculate the distributional payoff from a list of headline tax rates without household expenditure weights, actual pass-through and a baseline price path.

For businesses, the reform could lower working-capital costs and ease inverted-duty problems in addition to any final retail-price effect. The GST Council also recommended measures affecting refunds and procedures; those have to be assessed by effective notifications and processing times, not by assuming the whole change happened on 22 September. In October 2026, the 57th GST Council meeting focused substantially on registration, returns, refunds, adjudication and other process changes. The reform story therefore extends beyond the initial change in rates.

What a credible estimate of pass-through would require

An appropriate study should start from a published list of product-level tax changes, not broad industry labels. It should match products by size, grade and seller wherever possible; track shelf prices before announcement, during stock transition and after implementation; and distinguish posted prices from promotions and actual transaction prices. Tax-invoice data, scanner data and carefully sampled consumer prices would help. The comparison needs products whose GST rate did not change, alongside controls for broader inflation, promotions and seasonality.

A useful event-study specification would compare log prices of treated and otherwise comparable untreated products around the effective date, including product, outlet and calendar effects where the data permit. The coefficient on treatment after the rate change is an estimate of relative price movement, not automatically a causal tax-incidence parameter. Its credibility depends on parallel pre-trends, no simultaneous product-specific policy shocks and the quality of the comparison group. Check pack sizes and quality changes so that ‘cheaper’ does not mean less product for the same price.

A second exercise should measure the government’s side with a comparable domestic tax base. Published gross GST can be decomposed into domestic, import and cess components, then adjusted conceptually for refunds, taxpayer coverage and changes in the taxable base. One must avoid applying the average statutory rate to aggregate collections: goods and services carry different effective rates, exemptions and input credits, so the collection-to-consumption ratio is not the enacted tax rate.

The judgement, and what would change it

The September 2025 reset offered a plausible channel for real household relief, but the early evidence supports a heterogeneous rather than universal price effect. The NIPFP comparison gives good reason to be cautious about promises of automatic relief on essentials. It gives less reason to dismiss the reform altogether: some durable-goods prices fell, and an observed increase in another product’s price is not the same as an estimate of what would have happened absent the cut. The tax measure and the subsequent macroeconomic environment need to be separated.

The strongest counterargument is that even incomplete measured price reductions can coexist with meaningful avoided increases, lower compliance costs or faster working-capital recovery. That is possible. The evidence that would strengthen this interpretation is product-level matched-price analysis with a convincing comparison group, combined with firm-level information on net prices and input credits. The evidence that would weaken it is persistent, widespread retention of the statutory saving after adjusting for input costs and seasonality.

The next chapter should test a limited basket of clearly identified products with reliable data, rather than claim a national pass-through percentage that no such dataset yet supports. The reader can follow the evolving fiscal side through the Policy Ledger and the broader Politics of Public Money timeline. A parallel interactive calculation can show the exact implied price saving under different pass-through assumptions. That is what the statutory arithmetic can prove. Real-world incidence requires observation.

Primary sources and research

  • 56th GST Council decision, 3 September 2025
  • Official implementation FAQs, 3 September 2025
  • NIPFP Working Paper 444: price comparison, 2026
  • Ministry of Finance: October 2025 collections
  • Parliamentary reply: November 2025 GST receipts
  • 57th GST Council meeting, 8 October 2026

Try the calculation: The companion GST pass-through calculator lets readers change the original sticker price, statutory tax rates, purchase quantity and assumed consumer share of the saving. Its results are illustrative, not an empirical estimate of realised price transmission.

excerpt.rendered: The September 2025 GST reset lowered statutory rates. Evidence a year later shows uneven consumer-price adjustments, while domestic GST receipts tell a separate story. An incidence test.

title.rendered: India’s October goods deficit widened from September and narrowed from a year ago

content.rendered:
India’s goods trade deficit rose to $39.88 billion in October from $30.21 billion in September, according to Commerce Ministry figures released on 13 November and reported by Reuters. Compared with October 2025, when the gap was $42.58 billion, it narrowed by $2.70 billion. The monthly increase matters for near-term demand for dollars. The year-on-year comparison gives more weight to export growth. The policy question is how much of the import surge will persist and how much of the export gain reflects more goods shipped. Reuters on the 13 November release · Year-on-year figures · Official September baseline.

Imports rose almost three times as much as exports

Goods exports rose $5.07 billion from September while imports rose $14.74 billion. The difference, $9.67 billion, is the widening in the goods deficit. Gold imports increased by $3.71 billion, about 38% of that widening. Holding everything else at October levels and gold at September’s level would still leave the gap nearly $6 billion wider than in September. That remainder includes every other change in the goods account. Assigning it all to oil would obscure changes elsewhere. Reuters on exports, imports and gold · Commerce Ministry’s September release.

Festive demand offers a reason for part of the gold increase to unwind. A jeweller can import inventory ahead of a holiday and sell it over several weeks. That concentrates the demand for dollars around the shipment, even if the eventual sales are spread out. The import value can also rise because the dollar price is higher or because the mix of shipments changes. To distinguish those explanations, compare physical quantities and implied unit values across the months around the festival, allowing for the calendar to shift from year to year. A subsequent fall in gold imports would narrow the goods gap if the rest of the account held steady. Reuters on gold buying ahead of Diwali.

Services offset about half the goods gap

The ministry estimated October services exports at $40.51 billion and imports at $20.72 billion. The implied $19.79 billion services surplus offsets just under half the $39.88 billion goods deficit, leaving an estimated combined trade gap of $20.09 billion. The RBI’s latest monthly services observation is for September and is provisional. It recorded $39.305 billion in receipts and $20.097 billion in payments, a $19.208 billion surplus. Comparing that with October combines a provisional observation and an estimate. A modest revision could change the apparent month-to-month movement in the surplus. October services estimates reported by Reuters · RBI’s provisional September services data.

The quarterly current account also includes investment income and transfers such as remittances, with goods and services reported on a balance-of-payments basis. The financial account captures flows such as foreign investment. A services firm collecting dollars from overseas customers provides a source of foreign exchange even when merchandise importers need more of it. Portfolio flows can move in either direction at the same time. The timing of settlement and hedging further limits what the monthly goods release alone can explain about the rupee’s movement. Our analysis of the RBI’s quarterly external accounts.

What would make the export improvement durable?

The strongest case for a more positive reading is the year-on-year goods comparison. October exports rose from $34.11 billion to $49.47 billion, a gain of $15.36 billion. The narrower October-to-October deficit gives that gain more substance than the monthly deficit headline suggests. If shipment volumes keep rising across several products and markets, producers may be winning repeat orders. Employment would benefit most where those orders raise domestic activity and require additional workers. Gross export values leave the size of that effect uncertain, especially when production uses substantial imported inputs. October merchandise figures and year-ago comparison · Trade data by product and destination.

The year-on-year arithmetic also shows why the improvement should be described precisely. October goods imports were about $12.66 billion higher than the year before, based on the published deficits and export totals. Exports increased $15.36 billion, so they covered the entire increase in imports and another $2.70 billion. That is a useful measure of the change in the dollar value of goods traded. It leaves open whether exporters shipped more units, sold higher-value products or received better prices for similar shipments. October comparison reported by Moneycontrol.

For import-dependent businesses, the distinction between an inventory build and a sustained rise in costs matters for financing. A firm buying ahead can place a smaller order next month. A firm paying more dollars per tonne for fuel or components may have to absorb the cost, renegotiate prices or reduce production. Smaller firms with limited access to working capital have less room to carry costly inventory. Exporters earning dollars can receive more rupees per dollar of revenue when the currency weakens, while firms that use imported components face higher local-currency costs. The balance depends on input shares, contracts and payment dates.

For policymakers, the evidence supports watching the next few shipments before drawing a conclusion about underlying import demand. If expensive inputs are doing most of the work, measures that reduce delays or help viable small firms finance inventories would address a different problem from weak export competitiveness. If volumes rise across a broad range of inputs, the relevant question becomes whether those purchases are feeding domestic sales, capital investment or later exports. Import and export values can rise together in an economy whose firms buy intermediate goods abroad. Their growth tells us little about the domestic value added until we know what those firms are buying and selling.

The next data should answer three questions. Do gold quantities and values return towards their pre-festive levels? Do imports excluding petroleum and gold keep rising across several months, and do quantities move with values? Does the RBI’s eventual October services release confirm the estimated surplus? For exports, compare the same product and destination across several periods, then check whether values are rising because shipments are larger or unit prices are higher. A narrower gap after gold demand normalises, alongside stronger export volumes, would support the view that the monthly widening was temporary. Continued increases outside gold, particularly if services receipts disappoint, would make the financing question more pressing.

excerpt.rendered: India’s goods deficit reached $39.88 billion in October. Gold accounted for about 38% of the widening from September, while the estimated services surplus offset nearly half the goods gap.

title.rendered: India’s bank lending to services is surging. Who is borrowing?

content.rendered:
India’s banks expanded their outstanding credit to services by 28.3% in the year to September 2026, up from 9.9% a year earlier. The RBI’s separate release on non-banking financial companies, or NBFCs, puts their services credit growth at 17.3%, down from 23.0%. The bank figures were released on 30 October and the non-bank figures on 6 November. Read together, they show why a fast-growing bank credit category can tell us as much about who funds a loan as about who ultimately uses the money. In this case, some of what banks call services credit goes to financial intermediaries that can lend to households and businesses in other sectors. RBI bank credit release · RBI non-bank credit release.

The two books are growing in different places

Bank services credit growth accelerated by 18.4 percentage points, while NBFC services credit growth slowed by 5.7 points. Outstanding non-bank services credit still grew. At the same time, growth in the NBFC retail book accelerated by 5.1 points, with housing, loans against gold jewellery and vehicle loans among the categories the RBI identifies. Non-bank industry credit growth slowed by 2.8 points, and the RBI described infrastructure credit in that book as subdued. These are growth rates in nominal outstanding balances. They combine new borrowing, repayments and other changes to the stock. A borrower who takes a new loan to repay an old one can generate a new disbursement while leaving the amount outstanding broadly unchanged. RBI’s September NBFC breakdown.

The bank report identifies NBFCs alongside trade, commercial real estate, transport operators and professional services as contributors to services growth. The RBI’s October Monetary Policy Report separately identifies NBFCs as the largest recipient of bank credit within services in the first half of the financial year. This makes the intermediary channel material. Direct lending to businesses in trade or transport can also be expanding quickly. The size of each channel has to be measured from the underlying balances. Comparing headline growth rates alone gives no weight to the different starting sizes of the sectors. RBI’s bank breakdown · RBI Monetary Policy Report, Chapter II.

Follow the borrower through both balance sheets

Suppose a bank lends ₹100 crore to a non-bank lender, which uses the entire sum to make new vehicle loans. At the first step the bank has a ₹100 crore claim on the lender. At the second step the lender has ₹100 crore in claims on the vehicle buyers. Adding the two balances gives ₹200 crore in gross claims at the two links, while final vehicle borrowers owe ₹100 crore. The gross number can be useful for mapping exposure between financial firms. A measure of final borrowing would consolidate the two steps. The example illustrates the accounting. Published sector totals do not trace each borrowed rupee to a particular end use.

Banks can fund a specialist lender with a dealer network or local staff better placed to assess a small borrower’s cash flow. That arrangement can expand access in markets where a bank would find it expensive to originate and service small loans directly. It can also allow a lender to refinance older debt, replace bond funding or hold a larger liquidity buffer. Each would generate a different effect on new credit for households and firms. Better access is most convincing when borrower counts, loan terms and volumes move together. A larger funding line alone gives little information about interest rates, fees or which applicants now qualify.

The indirect channel can matter when funding tightens. A non-bank lender that needs to refinance before its customers repay may face higher funding costs even if its existing loans are performing. It can pass those costs on when it originates new loans, reduce loan sizes or pull back from borrowers who cost more to serve. Small transport operators and households with few alternative lenders would feel that adjustment sooner than a large company able to issue debt. For banks, monitoring the concentration of their exposure to intermediaries serves a different purpose from monitoring how much direct credit reaches manufacturers or service businesses.

What would show that the expansion is broad-based?

The strongest case for reading the bank figures as a sign of wider demand is that several operating sectors are expanding alongside intermediaries. Trade and transport finance can rise as firms carry more inventory and move more goods. Stronger direct lending in those sectors would support that interpretation, especially if it coincides with higher real activity and wider participation among smaller borrowers. Some of the same increase could come from the cost of carrying the same stock at higher nominal prices. A persuasive demand story would show both stronger volumes and a larger pool of borrowers, with repayment performance holding up across successive loan cohorts. RBI’s sector commentary.

The reporting dates matter. The bank release uses 30 September 2026 for the current comparison and 3 October 2025 for the earlier reference. The RBI moved the last reporting fortnight to month-end from December 2025. The sector breakdown covers 41 selected banks, while the headline non-food growth rate uses the all-bank return. The non-bank sample covers major NBFCs and housing finance companies, with September 2026 figures provisional. Use each series on its own terms, then compare the direction and composition of growth. Adding the published percentages or treating the two samples as a consolidated national balance sheet would misstate the result. Bank release methodology · NBFC sample and provisional status.

A reproducible test for the next release

How much of the increase in bank services credit disappears when loans to NBFCs are removed? Take the services and NBFC outstanding balances in RBI Statement I at both reference dates. Subtract the NBFC balance from services at each date, then calculate the annual change in that residual. Divide the annual rupee increase in bank credit to NBFCs by the rupee increase in total bank services credit to estimate their contribution, where the denominator is positive. Repeat for August and the next release, recording the reporting dates. Compare that contribution with changes in the separate non-bank retail, services and industry balances. A large, persistent contribution from NBFC funding would support the intermediary explanation. Rapid growth in the residual across multiple sectors would strengthen the case for broad direct borrowing. This exercise can test composition, while identifying ultimate borrowers requires more granular data. RBI bank workbook · RBI non-bank workbook · Economy dashboard.

The next labour bulletin and quarterly GDP release provide independent checks on the real economy. The official calendar lists the October labour bulletin for 15 November, with holiday releases moving to the next working day, and quarterly GDP for 30 November. Hours, employment and output can help distinguish wider demand from a rise in financing needs among existing borrowers. The September releases already establish a shift in the composition of credit growth. Evidence that direct borrowing and activity are rising together would justify a stronger reading. MoSPI advance release calendar.

excerpt.rendered: Bank services credit grew 28.3% in September as non-bank services lending slowed. The RBI’s two releases show how funding for lenders can lift the headline while credit to final borrowers takes a different path.

title.rendered: India’s inflation crossed 6% as monthly price increases slowed

content.rendered:
India’s retail inflation rose to 6.09% in October from 5.54% in September, according to the National Statistics Office’s 12 November release. The provisional reading is above the Reserve Bank of India’s 6% upper tolerance level. The same release shows the national price index rising 0.51% from September, down from a 0.69% monthly rise the month before. The annual rate and the monthly movement answer different questions. October strengthens the case for another rate increase if price pressure keeps spreading, while the monthly figures give the RBI a reason to examine where it is spreading before committing to a sequence of hikes. MoSPI’s October CPI release · Inflation-target notification.

How the annual rate rose as monthly price gains slowed

The headline index went from 109.49 in September to 110.05 in October, an increase of 0.56 index points. A year earlier the published index was 103.74 in both months to two decimal places. With that comparison base essentially flat, the annual inflation rate would rise by roughly 0.54 percentage points from the latest monthly price gain alone. The published increase was 0.55 points, consistent with the calculation once rounding is allowed for. The threshold crossing therefore reflects a real increase in the price level against a flat comparison base. The slower monthly rise is a separate observation. Both monthly figures are unadjusted and a single comparison cannot separate seasonal patterns from changes in underlying momentum. MoSPI, national indices and Annexure IV.

Food explains about two-thirds of the monthly increase

The Consumer Food Price Index rose 8.94% from a year earlier, compared with 7.74% in September. Its monthly increase eased to about 0.94% from 1.30%. To estimate how much of October’s overall monthly increase came from food and beverages, use the broader division in the main CPI. Its index rose 1.01 points, from 111.77 to 112.78. Multiplying by its 36.75% basket weight gives about 0.37 of the headline index’s 0.56-point increase, or roughly two-thirds. That is a contribution to the month’s index movement, using rounded published figures. The food-only index used in the 8.94% headline excludes some categories included in the broader division. September CPI, Annexure I · October CPI, Annexures I and II.

Even within food, the price changes differed sharply. Onions were 116.22% dearer than a year earlier, while potatoes were 14.24% cheaper. Rural headline inflation reached 6.63%, against 5.41% in urban India. A household spending a large share of its income on food has less room to absorb these increases without cutting other purchases. A farmer’s exposure depends on which crops they sell, whether they have a marketable surplus and what they buy. Consumer price data show what buyers pay at retail. They cannot establish how much of the increase reaches producers or intermediaries. MoSPI, rural and urban rates and selected items.

The case for tightening rests on what happens beyond food

The strongest case for a December increase is that the upward pressure is already showing up across more categories. Reuters counted 19 of 43 subgroups at or above 4% annual inflation, up from 14 in September. That is an unweighted count. The RBI’s October resolution also discusses breadth, using the share of the basket by expenditure weight. Those measures can move differently if the categories crossing the threshold are mostly small. MoSPI’s division figures show annual transport inflation rising from 5.01% to 5.84% and restaurants and accommodation rising from 9.36% to 10.06%. Actual rent inflation was almost unchanged, at 2.36% in October against 2.37% in the September release. Reuters on subgroup breadth · September annexures · October annexures · October MPC resolution.

A restaurant can raise prices to recover food, electricity or delivery costs. The same price increase can also reflect firm customer demand that lets the business widen its margin. The two explanations have different implications for a rate decision. Tighter credit can curb discretionary spending and restrain follow-on price increases. It raises debt-service costs for borrowers whose rates reset and makes working-capital finance more expensive for some businesses. It has little direct effect on how quickly food stocks reach markets. The case for tightening is strongest when demand, expectations and business pricing suggest that an initial cost shock will persist after input costs ease. RBI discussion of demand and second-round effects · Our analysis of the October rate increase.

What the RBI can verify before December

The 7 October increase took the repo rate to 5.50%. The RBI projected 6.0% inflation on average for October to December. One monthly reading of 6.09% is close to that quarterly baseline and leaves two months to determine the average. The statutory failure test also uses quarterly averages. For an overshoot, it requires inflation above the upper tolerance level for three consecutive quarters. The December meeting is scheduled for 2 to 4 December, and MoSPI’s release says the November national CPI is due on 14 December. The committee will have to judge persistence from other incoming evidence before the next official CPI report. RBI resolution and meeting dates · RBI’s inflation-target framework · MoSPI, release schedule on page 4.

The evidence that would strengthen the case for another hike is a sustained rise in the weighted share of faster-inflating items, firmer inflation expectations and repeated price increases in services with limited exposure to food or fuel. Wholesale vegetable prices and arrivals can help show whether the food shock is easing, while credit growth and lending rates can show how the October move is reaching borrowers. If food prices cool and broader measures level off, a pause would give the previous hike more time to work. If pricing pressure keeps broadening after food and energy costs stabilise, a further increase becomes easier to justify. October raises the stakes for that assessment and gives the committee a clear reason to test the breadth of the shock.

Follow the observed India CPI series and read the 12 November morning edition for the labour data and the Cabinet’s farm-input and credit decisions.

excerpt.rendered: October CPI rose 6.09% from a year earlier. Monthly price gains slowed, and food and beverages accounted for about two-thirds of the latest rise. The RBI’s December decision turns on whether price pressures keep spreading.

title.rendered: The Kakistocrat Daily Desk, 12 November 2026

content.rendered:
Morning cutoff: 8:30 a.m. IST, 12 November 2026. The 11 November Cabinet package extended two credit guarantees and approved new spending on fertiliser support and metro infrastructure. The latest labour survey shows where employment increased and where it barely moved.

Lead judgement

The Cabinet’s ₹62,370 crore rabi fertiliser package is defensible as short-run insurance against a global input shock. The policy should still be judged against a harder counterfactual. Did it preserve balanced nutrient use and timely availability, or did it simply defend the price of selected bags while leaving the urea distortion intact? Read the fertiliser analysis.

The July to September labour survey provides qualified good news. Participation and employment increased together, so the lower unemployment rate is not an artefact of people leaving the labour force. The rise in agriculture and rural self-employment, alongside almost unchanged urban employment, means job quality and persistence are the next tests. Read the labour analysis.

India policy radar

  • Credit guarantees for micro enterprises. The Cabinet extended the Credit Guarantee Fund for Micro Units to 31 March 2031 with a ₹5,000 crore corpus. The government says the facility can support ₹12.6 lakh crore of PM Mudra lending over five years and reduced the annual guarantee fee from 1% to 0.75%. The analytical question is additionality. A guarantee is useful when it expands sound lending to borrowers constrained by collateral, not when it merely shifts expected losses from lenders to the public balance sheet. Track first-time borrowers, interest rates, repeat borrowing, delinquency by vintage and lender recovery effort. Cabinet release.
  • Stand-Up India. The scheme was extended for five years to 31 March 2031 with a ₹4,111 crore guarantee corpus and a target of at least 2.5 lakh additional women, SC and ST entrepreneurs. Loans range from above ₹10 lakh to ₹1 crore with guarantee coverage of 85% and a 0.5% fee. The target should be evaluated on enterprise survival, employment, revenue and repeat access to unguaranteed credit, not sanctions alone. Cabinet release.
  • Noida Metro extension. The Cabinet approved 8.449 km and five elevated stations from Noida Sector 51 to Greater Noida Sector 04. The scheme briefing values the project at roughly ₹2,390 crore. That is about ₹283 crore per route-kilometre before considering financing and operating support. The proper appraisal needs expected peak and off-peak ridership, interchange penalties, bus integration, land-value capture and operating subsidy. Connectivity claims should be converted into measurable travel-time savings. Cabinet release.
  • RBI liquidity. The Reserve Bank’s 11 November money-market release reported ₹7,331 crore of marginal standing facility borrowing for 10 November at 5.75%. One day does not establish systemic stress. The signal becomes meaningful if high-cost borrowing persists across institutions while overnight rates, collateral conditions and variable-rate operations confirm tightness. RBI money-market operations.
  • Inflation release due today. MoSPI’s advance calendar schedules the October all-India CPI for 12 November. No claim about the number is included before the official release. The afternoon policy watch should separate food momentum, core inflation, base effects and month-on-month seasonally adjusted movement. MoSPI advance release calendar.

Sources

MoSPI PLFS release · Rabi fertiliser decision · CGFMU extension · Stand-Up India extension · Noida Metro extension

title.rendered: A fixed DAP price and late subsidy rates are steering farmers towards India’s scarcest fertiliser

content.rendered:
India’s rabi fertiliser subsidy is large enough to shield farmers from this year’s global price shock. Its design is the problem. On 11 November the Cabinet approved nutrient-based subsidy rates for phosphatic and potassic fertilisers covering 1 October 2026 to 31 March 2027, at an estimated cost of ₹62,370 crore, about ₹24,418 crore more than last rabi. The rates apply to a season that began six weeks earlier. At the same briefing, Information and Broadcasting Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said a 50 kg bag of diammonium phosphate, or DAP, would still sell for ₹1,350. Fixing the price of one product while its substitutes float, and setting the rates after the buying season has begun, pushes demand towards DAP, the fertiliser India finds hardest to source. Cabinet release on rabi 2026–27 NBS rates · PTI report of the Cabinet briefing

The scheme was built to let prices move

The Nutrient Based Subsidy scheme, in force since April 2010, pays manufacturers and importers a fixed amount for each kilogram of nitrogen (N), phosphate (P), potash (K) and sulphur (S) contained in 28 grades of fertiliser. Companies then set the retail price. The logic is that a farmer choosing between two products sees prices that reflect what each contains and what it costs to supply. Urea works the other way: its retail price is fixed and the government absorbs whatever the gap turns out to be. Cabinet release on rabi 2026–27 NBS rates

The new per-kilogram rates are steep. Nitrogen rises to ₹94.21 from ₹43.02 a year ago, an increase of about 119 per cent. Phosphate rises to ₹66.11 from ₹47.96, about 38 per cent. Sulphur rises to ₹10.42 from ₹2.87, and potash stays at ₹2.38. Business Standard reports that the package also includes special assistance for sulphur and extends the “special provisions” that apply to DAP to imported and domestic triple superphosphate and imported monoammonium phosphate. Business Standard on the rabi rates and special packages · BW Businessworld on the nutrient rates

What the rates imply for a tonne of DAP

DAP contains 18 per cent nitrogen and 46 per cent phosphate. A tonne therefore carries 180 kg of N and 460 kg of P, and the nutrient rates translate directly into a subsidy per tonne. The same calculation reproduces the ₹29,805 a tonne the government published for rabi 2025–26, which is a useful check on the method. PIB note on rabi 2025–26 NBS rates · PTI on kharif 2026 rates

Add the farmer’s ₹1,350 a bag, or ₹27,000 a tonne, and a tonne of DAP sold at the fixed price brings its supplier about ₹74,370 from NBS and the farmer combined. Compare that with what DAP costs to land. Indian Potash Limited bought about 1.35 million tonnes in a May tender at $930–935 a tonne, cost and freight, and late-August assessments for India were $915–935. At an illustrative ₹94 to the dollar, $925 is about ₹86,950 a tonne before duty, port handling, bagging, inland freight and dealer margins. The gap of about ₹12,600 a tonne, roughly ₹630 a bag, before those domestic costs, has to come from the special DAP provisions, and the Cabinet release does not publish their rate. In practice the government has promised to cover whatever DAP costs. That makes DAP a price-controlled product inside a scheme designed for floating prices. Angel One on the May DAP tender · Fertilizer Daily on late-August DAP prices

These figures are illustrative. Actual landed costs depend on when cargoes were contracted, the exchange rate on payment and the costs of moving product inland. The direction of the result does not.

Complex fertilisers carried the risk instead

The NP and NPK “complex” grades received no such guarantee. S. Sankarasubramanian, chairman of the Fertiliser Association of India, told Business Standard that NBS rates are generally based on a six-month average of international prices and that the previous revision had not captured the sharp rise in input costs. Companies raised the prices of NP and NPK grades, which the paper reports rose by around 40–50 per cent, and cut production. Domestic output of complex fertilisers in September was 0.59 million tonnes against a target of 1.06 million tonnes, a shortfall of about 43 per cent. The FAI chairman also said the usual consumption split of roughly 60 per cent complex grades and 40 per cent DAP had tilted towards DAP over the last two seasons because of the heavy support for it. Business Standard on complex fertiliser prices and output

From a farmer’s side the choice is straightforward. Phosphate has to go in at sowing. A bag of DAP at a guaranteed ₹1,350 competes with complex bags that have become far dearer. Choosing DAP is sensible for each farmer. For the system, it concentrates demand on the product with the greatest import exposure: industry estimates put India’s import dependence for phosphoric acid and finished DAP at 80–90 per cent. When concentrated demand meets a constrained pipeline of cargoes and rail rakes, the adjustment shows up as queues rather than prices. Fertilizer Daily on DAP import dependence and the Haryana shortage

In mid-October Haryana’s agriculture department suspended Indian Potash Limited’s authorisation to sell non-subsidised fertilisers in the state, saying the company had placed DAP rakes in Jhajjar and Jind instead of prioritising Sirsa and Hisar as directed. Farmers in Sirsa and Fatehabad were queuing outside distribution centres from early morning. Queues have several causes, including rail allocation, cargo timing and dealer behaviour, so they do not prove that the price structure caused the shortage. They are what a price-capped product in excess demand looks like. The Tribune on the Sirsa shortage and IPL suspension

The tilt also works against agronomy. DAP supplies nitrogen and phosphate but no potash or sulphur. The Kakistocrat argued last month that soil testing matters only if it changes what farmers buy. A price structure that makes DAP the cheapest route to phosphate pulls the other way.

Late rates shift risk onto suppliers

The timing compounds the distortion. Rabi rates for 2025–26 were approved on 28 October 2025. Kharif 2026 rates came on 8 April for a season starting on 1 April. This year’s rabi rates arrived on 11 November for a season that began on 1 October. A company that bought cargoes in August and September for rabi sales did not know what subsidy those tonnes would earn. Selling a complex grade under that uncertainty means extending credit to the government at an unknown price. The rational response is to make and stock less of the grades whose support is uncertain and more of the grade whose price the government has promised to protect. September’s collapse in complex output is consistent with that. ANI on the 28 October 2025 rabi decision · PTI on the 8 April kharif decision

This year the weather has lent the government time. After a monsoon 13 per cent below normal, rabi sowing on 30 October covered 37.56 lakh hectares, 46 per cent less than a year earlier. Wheat covered 19,000 hectares against 3.34 lakh hectares. Delayed sowing pushes peak fertiliser demand into the weeks after the Cabinet decision. That is luck, not design. Business Today on rabi sowing to 30 October

The Budget pays, and so does the back of the queue

The fiscal cost is now clear. The kharif 2026 allocation of ₹41,533.81 crore and the rabi allocation of ₹62,370.02 crore together come to about ₹1.04 lakh crore for phosphatic and potassic fertilisers. The Budget estimate for the whole year was ₹54,000 crore, so the outlay is about 92 per cent higher. Business Standard reports industry and expert estimates that total fertiliser subsidy, including urea, could exceed ₹3 lakh crore against a Budget estimate of ₹1.71 lakh crore. That is the same shock moving onto the Budget that this site traced through fuel taxes in April. Business Standard on the FY27 subsidy bill · Crisil on the Budget split between urea and complex fertilisers

The other payers are less visible. A price cap delivers its benefit to whoever gets the bag. A farmer who cannot find DAP at ₹1,350 pays through a delayed sowing, a premium from a private dealer or a substitute product that may suit the soil less well. The subsidy per bag is identical. Access to it is not.

The case for holding the price

The strongest argument for the government’s approach is that this is a bad year to let prices move. Moisture is short, sowing is late and many farmers must buy inputs before they have any income from the crop. A visible, stable price for the most widely used phosphatic fertiliser limits panic buying and protects working capital. Switching mid-season to a different instrument, such as a per-hectare cash transfer, would need land records and payment systems that cannot be rebuilt in a few weeks. Letting DAP move towards import parity, which on the illustrative figures above would be well over ₹4,000 a bag before inland costs, could cut application exactly where it matters most for yields.

The new rates also raise support for complex grades sharply. For a common grade such as NPK 10-26-26, the implied subsidy rises from about ₹19,070 a tonne in kharif to about ₹27,230, an increase of roughly 43 per cent. The FAI expects this to bring complex prices down and rebalance demand. If that happens quickly, the distortion narrows on its own.

That is a fair case for generous support during a shock. It is a weaker case for delivering that support through an open-ended guarantee on one product and late, backward-looking rates on the rest.

Support that does not choose the product

Three changes would keep the protection while removing the steer. First, set the season’s rates before it starts, using a published formula linked to import prices with scheduled adjustments within the season, so companies know what a tonne will earn when they contract cargoes. Second, publish the DAP special package per tonne, so the true support per kilogram of phosphate can be compared across products. Third, aim for equal effective support per kilogram of each nutrient, whichever bag it arrives in. A farmer’s cheapest route to phosphate should depend on chemistry and logistics, not on which product carries a political price.

What would change the judgement

The test comes in the next two months of production and sales data. If complex fertiliser output and sales recover towards target and DAP’s share of phosphate sales falls back, the problem was mainly the late timing, and the new rates have fixed it. If DAP’s share keeps rising while complex output lags, the fixed price is doing the steering, and the next kharif decision should address the guarantee rather than only the rates.

Part of a series

Testing India’s subsidies

Semiconductors, AI compute, minerals, green hydrogen, small hydro and factory power: what each subsidy should be made to deliver.
