title.rendered: India has borrowed Indonesia’s export ban for a market that works nothing like nickel

content.rendered:
India’s new ban on exporting lithium-ion battery black mass borrows the legal form of the best-known resource policy of the past decade, Indonesia’s ban on exporting nickel ore. The economics underneath are different. Indonesia’s ban worked as industrial policy because it controlled an input the world needed in enormous volumes, so processors moved to the ore. India’s black mass market is small, has few buyers and depends on collectors who can stop collecting. The useful lesson from Indonesia is less about whether export bans work than about who gains bargaining power when the export option disappears, and what that does to the supply of the material itself.

What India has prohibited

On 10 November the Directorate General of Foreign Trade amended the export policy for ITC(HS) code 85491400, which the notification describes as lithium-ion battery black mass, from “free” to “prohibited”, with immediate effect and until further orders. Black mass is the powder left after end-of-life batteries and battery manufacturing scrap are shredded. It contains recoverable lithium, cobalt, nickel and manganese. The government says domestic recycling and refining capacity “is not being fully utilised due to inadequate feedstock availability”, that some recyclers have had to import material, and that the ban complements the ₹1,500 crore incentive scheme for critical mineral recycling approved in September 2025. Commerce ministry release on the black mass prohibition

The ban replaces a leaky permit system. Black mass was already classified as hazardous waste, so exports needed permission from the environment ministry and a DGFT licence. EVreporter reported a year ago that several shredding facilities were nonetheless exporting it as non-hazardous material under other codes. Prohibition is easier to enforce than a licence that customs officers must second-guess. EVreporter on black mass export curbs and industry views

The policy completes a pair. Six days earlier the Cabinet approved ₹2,814 crore of capital support for lithium and nickel processing plants, which The Kakistocrat argued should be judged by supply that works in a disruption. One measure builds refiners. The other guarantees them feedstock.

How Indonesia used its ban

Indonesia’s 2009 mining law required domestic processing. The government banned nickel ore exports in 2014, relaxed the ban in 2017 when smelting capacity was not ready to absorb domestic ore, and reimposed a comprehensive ban from 1 January 2020. Before the ban Indonesia mined about 71 million tonnes of ore a year and exported about 65 million tonnes of it raw, mostly to China. Chinese firms, led by Tsingshan, responded by building smelters in Indonesia. Nickel-related exports rose from about $6 billion in 2013 to nearly $30 billion in 2022. Mining.com on the 2014, 2017 and 2020 phases · ASPI Strategist on ore volumes and Chinese investment · East Asia Forum on export values

The ban was not costless. A WTO panel ruled in November 2022, on a complaint by the European Union, that the export ban and the domestic processing requirement were inconsistent with Article XI:1 of the GATT and were not justified as a temporary measure against a critical shortage or as necessary to enforce domestic law. Indonesia appealed in December 2022 to an Appellate Body that cannot hear cases, which leaves the ruling in limbo. WTO dispute DS592

The mechanism matters more than the headline export numbers. Hiau Looi Kee of the World Bank and Enze Xie of Zhejiang University model the ban as pushing the domestic nickel price below the world price, because a few midstream steel firms gain buying power once miners cannot sell abroad. In customs data, the domestic value added of iron- and steel-using exporters rose about 5.6 per cent by 2022 relative to other industries. Average firm size in those industries fell, which the authors read as lower productivity, and they attribute the problem to incumbents with monopsony and monopoly power. Even in the success story, the first effect of the ban was a transfer from ore sellers to domestic processors. Kee and Xie, “Nickel, Steel and Cars”, November 2025

Three differences that change the result

Scale. Indonesia withheld tens of millions of tonnes a year from a market that had no ready substitute. India’s black mass market is measured in thousands. In February 2024 the founder of Lohum, the largest Indian recycler, estimated national output at 400–500 tonnes a month and his company’s share at about 70 per cent, with three or four regular producers. Output has grown since, but a Korean or Chinese refiner will not build a plant in India to secure volumes of that size. The ban hands the material to buyers already here. Fastmarkets interview with Lohum’s founder

Buyer concentration. The domestic refining capacity cited in the debate sits with a few firms. Attero says it can refine 15,000 tonnes of black mass a year, Rubamin 10,000 tonnes and Exigo 7,600 tonnes. On the other side are shredding-only recyclers, which one industry executive told EVreporter make up more than 80 per cent of the country’s lithium-ion recycling industry and receive better payments from overseas refiners. The two sides dispute the size of that gap. Exigo’s business head cited claims that Indian refiners pay about 2 per cent less, while others say international refiners offer much higher recovery rates. EVreporter on capacity and payables

Supply that responds to price. Indonesian ore stays in the ground if its price falls; mining margins shrink, but the resource does not vanish. Black mass has to be gathered from used phones, laptops and vehicle packs, often by informal aggregators, then transported and shredded. A lower price for black mass lowers the price that shredders can pay for scrap batteries, which reduces collection or diverts batteries to informal dismantling. The resource itself is elastic. That is the decisive difference from nickel ore.

Why small changes in payables matter

Black mass is priced as a percentage, or “payable”, of the value of the metals it contains. In early 2024 Indian material was reported to fetch 70 per cent of contained value delivered to Korea for nickel-cobalt-manganese black mass and 62.5 per cent for cobalt-rich lithium cobalt oxide material, which still dominates Indian scrap because it comes from consumer electronics. Fastmarkets on Indian black mass payables

Take an illustrative tonne of cobalt-rich black mass whose contained metal is worth ₹10 lakh. At a 62.5 per cent export payable, minus an assumed 5 points for freight and handling, the shredder nets ₹5.75 lakh. Suppose collecting, transporting and shredding the scrap costs ₹5 lakh. The margin is ₹75,000. If a domestic buyer without foreign competition offers 55 per cent, the shredder receives ₹5.5 lakh and the margin falls to ₹50,000, a cut of a third from a 2.5-point change in the payable. At 52.5 per cent, the margin halves. These numbers are assumptions, not market data. They show why a small change in bargaining power can have a large effect on whether collectors keep buying scrap batteries.

Europe chose a narrower tool

The European Union faced the same worry about black mass leaving for Asian refiners and chose a different instrument. In March 2025 the European Commission classified black mass as hazardous waste. Under the Basel Convention and EU waste shipment rules, that bans exports to countries outside the OECD, including China, while shipments within the EU and to other OECD members continue under prior notification and consent. China moved the other way, allowing imports of black mass that meets set standards as a non-waste product from 1 August 2025. European Commission on the black mass classification · National Law Review on the diverging EU and Chinese rules

The case for a full ban

The strongest argument for the government is coordination. A refiner will not invest without dependable feedstock, and a shredder will not sell domestically without dependable buyers. A period of guaranteed domestic supply can break that deadlock, especially when domestic recovery has strategic value during import disruptions. A licensing regime had already failed to stop mislabelled exports. Overseas refiners with large scale can also outbid domestic plants for a while, which keeps India dependent on processing abroad.

Supply may also grow regardless of price. Lohum’s founder expects scrap from new Indian battery factories to reach as much as 20 GWh a year as about 200 GWh of manufacturing capacity is commissioned. Producers also carry extended producer responsibility obligations under the Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022, which give them a reason to deliver used batteries to registered recyclers whatever the black mass price. Fastmarkets on India’s expected scrap volumes

Those points justify keeping feedstock at home while domestic refining scales up. They do not justify ignoring the buying power the ban creates.

Tests that keep the ban honest

Four measures would show whether the prohibition is building an industry or redistributing margins. Publish a monthly benchmark of domestic payables against international reference prices less freight, by chemistry. Track formally collected battery tonnage and extended producer responsibility certificates against the years before the ban. Set a review date, after which the ban becomes a licence tied to the utilisation of domestic refining capacity, so exports resume if domestic buyers leave material unprocessed. Ask the Competition Commission to watch buyer concentration in a market where one firm reported a 70 per cent share.

The judgement would change with the data. If domestic payables stay within a few points of export netbacks and collected volumes rise, the ban is doing what Indonesia’s did at its best: solving a coordination problem. If shredders report stockpiles, collection falls or payables drift persistently below export parity, it is doing what the World Bank found in Indonesia’s midstream: moving rents to a few processors at the expense of the supply the policy needs.

Part of a series

The economics of strategic dependence

Where India depends on a single foreign supplier for something it cannot easily replace, and what it costs to build an alternative: critical minerals, battery materials and the inputs that sit behind them.

title.rendered: Three customs questions decide whether a trade deal’s tariff cut is real

content.rendered:
A trade agreement does not lower the duty on a shipment. It lowers the duty on a list of tariff lines for goods that meet its conditions. Whether a particular consignment pays the lower rate is decided later, at the border, by three questions: what customs says the good is, where it says the good was made and what it says the good is worth. Most disputes about whether a trade deal is “working” turn out to be about one of the three. The current argument over bulk Scotch whisky is a clear example, and it is a useful template for reading the news about every deal India has signed.

The case that shows the machinery

The India–UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement entered into force on 15 July 2026. India cut its duty on UK whisky from 150 per cent to 75 per cent, with a schedule that takes it to 40 per cent by the tenth year. In October, Reuters reported that India’s Directorate of Revenue Intelligence had visited premises linked to Pernod Ricard and Diageo’s Indian unit to examine whether some bulk Scotch imports had been wrongly classified for the lower duty. About four-fifths of Scotch imported from Scotland arrives in bulk, and much of it is blended in India with locally made spirit. Vinetur, citing Reuters, on the DRI inquiry · Vinetur, citing Reuters and The Financial Express, on the classification dispute

Nobody disputes that India granted the concession. The argument is about whether this product falls inside it. The Kakistocrat argued in July that the agreement’s real test was whether firms could use it. The Scotch case shows the mechanics of that test.

Question one: what is the good?

Every traded good is assigned a code in the Harmonized System, an international nomenclature that is common to six digits. India extends it to eight digits in its customs tariff. A trade agreement’s tariff schedule lists concessions line by line, so a preference exists only for goods classified under the lines it names.

The whisky concession sits under heading 2208, which covers spirits, and subheading 2208.30 for whisky. The schedule explicitly covers Scotch in containers larger than two litres, so bulk shipments were part of the bargain. Investigators are reported to be considering whether concentrated bulk Scotch that is later blended or diluted should instead fall under heading 2106, a residual category for food preparations not elsewhere specified. That heading carries no concession, so the duty would stay at 150 per cent. Importers argue that the product is whisky whatever happens to it after import, and that a specific description should take precedence over a residual one. That is a general principle of tariff classification, and it is likely to be central to the outcome. Vinetur on headings 2208.30 and 2106

The stakes are easy to calculate. On an illustrative consignment with a customs value of ₹10 lakh, a 75 per cent duty is ₹7.5 lakh and a 150 per cent duty is ₹15 lakh. Classification decides which of the two applies. Because bulk dominates volumes, it effectively decides how much of the whisky concession is real.

Firms can buy certainty before shipping. India’s Customs Authority for Advance Rulings, with benches in New Delhi and Mumbai, gives written rulings on classification, valuation and origin before goods are imported. A ruling binds customs and the applicant for that transaction for three years unless the facts change. A ruling helps only the firm that asked for it. When a classification question affects an entire industry, a public circular or instruction from the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs can settle it for every importer at once. TaxTMI on advance rulings under Chapter V-B of the Customs Act

Question two: where was it made?

A preference applies only to goods that “originate” in the partner country under the agreement’s rules of origin. Typical rules ask whether a good was wholly obtained there, whether processing changed its tariff classification, or whether a minimum share of its value was added locally. Scotch whisky is a simple case, because it must be made in Scotland. A laptop assembled in a partner country from imported parts is not, and origin is where many electronics and textile claims fail.

India has put the burden of proof on importers. Since 21 September 2020, the Customs (Administration of Rules of Origin under Trade Agreements) Rules, known as CAROTAR, require an importer claiming a preferential rate to hold information showing how the origin criteria are met, and they set out how customs can verify a claim with the exporting country. A certificate of origin is necessary, but it is no longer treated as sufficient on its own. PwC overview of CAROTAR 2020 · ELP on CAROTAR obligations

Origin rules also explain why Indian exporters often ignore the preferences they have. The Global Trade Research Initiative estimates that only 20–30 per cent of India’s eligible exports use FTA benefits, against 60–70 per cent of partner-country exports to India. Many partners already charge low most-favoured-nation tariffs, so the saving from proving origin is small. A worked comparison makes the point. On a $50,000 shipment facing a 4 per cent tariff, the preference saves $2,000. If documentation, certification and supplier records cost $1,500, the claim is barely worth making. Facing India’s higher tariffs, a foreign exporter shipping into a 12 per cent duty saves $6,000 on the same shipment, which easily covers the paperwork. The compliance costs in this example are assumptions. The asymmetry they illustrate is the one GTRI describes. Outlook Business on GTRI’s utilisation estimates

Question three: what is it worth?

Most Indian duties are ad valorem, levied as a percentage of the good’s assessable value. That value normally starts from the transaction price, but customs can reject a declared price, particularly between related companies, and assess duty on a comparison with similar imports. A lower tariff rate reduces the incentive to understate value. It does not remove it. At 75 per cent, every ₹100 knocked off the declared value still saves ₹75 of duty.

Valuation is the third live issue for Scotch. In a filing dated 24 January 2026, Indian authorities alleged that Pernod Ricard’s Indian unit had undervalued its bulk Scotch concentrate imports by 67.49 per cent and sought about $314 million in back taxes. Pernod India rejects any suggestion of wrongdoing and says officials selectively compared its prices with a rival’s while excluding importers that paid less. The case predates the agreement, but it will shape how customs treats bulk Scotch under the new rate. The Drinks Business, citing Reuters, on the valuation dispute

How the three questions combine

The value of a preference to a firm is roughly the tariff margin multiplied by the assessable value, discounted by the chance that customs rejects the claim and the cost of delay while it decides. Classification and origin determine whether the margin applies at all. Valuation determines what it is applied to. A concession can look generous in the treaty text and be worth much less if any of the three is uncertain. Detained cargo adds storage costs and ties up working capital even if the importer eventually wins.

This is also why the remedies differ. A classification dispute is usually settled by a circular, an advance ruling or a tribunal decision on the tariff heading. An origin dispute goes through verification with the partner country’s authorities. A valuation dispute runs through assessment, adjudication and appeal. Knowing which question is in play tells you how long a dispute is likely to last and who can resolve it.

A checklist for the next trade-deal headline

When an agreement is announced, ask which tariff lines it covers and how quickly the cuts are phased in. Some concessions take ten years to reach their headline rate, and some come with quotas, as the apple quota in the New Zealand deal showed.

Ask what the origin rule is for the products that matter, and whether exporters must obtain certificates or can certify origin themselves.

Ask whether customs has issued instructions or advance rulings on contested products, because those documents decide the border treatment that the treaty text leaves open.

Ask for utilisation data. A preference that few firms claim is a concession on paper.

The Scotch case will probably be settled by the first of those instruments. The Financial Express reported that the commerce secretary told industry on 2 November that the ambiguity would be resolved and India’s commitments honoured, with the commerce and finance ministries working on a solution within the existing legal framework. The document that emerges, most likely a classification instruction, will decide what the 75 per cent rate is worth. Vinetur, citing The Financial Express, on the 2 November meeting

Part of a series

India’s trade deals

India’s agreements with the UK, EU, New Zealand, the US and Russia, each judged by whether firms can actually use them.

  • 26 Dec 2025

    The apple quota is the real test of India’s New Zealand trade deal

  • 30 Jan 2026

    India’s EU trade deal will pay off if exporters can meet Europe’s rules

  • 27 Feb 2026

    The US tariff reset changes India’s bargaining position

  • 17 Jul 2026

    The UK–India trade deal’s real test is whether firms can use it

  • 11 Sep 2026

    India’s Russia trade target should be judged by repeat export orders

  • 11 Nov 2026

    Three customs questions decide whether a trade deal’s tariff cut is real

All series →

excerpt.rendered: A trade deal cuts duty on a list of tariff lines. Whether a shipment pays the lower rate depends on what customs says it is, where it was made and what it is worth. The Scotch whisky dispute shows all three tests at work.

title.rendered: India’s unemployment rate fell. The quality of work is the next test

content.rendered:
India’s quarterly Periodic Labour Force Survey for July to September 2026, released on 10 November, reports an unemployment rate of 5.1% for people aged 15 and above under Current Weekly Status. That is down from 5.4% in April to June. Labour-force participation rose from 54.6% to 55.5%, and the worker-population ratio rose from 51.7% to 52.7%. Because participation and employment increased together, the fall in unemployment is more encouraging than a decline caused by people leaving the labour force. It is still not evidence of a broad-based improvement in job quality. MoSPI release, 10 November 2026 · PLFS Quarterly Bulletin

The headline points to a genuine improvement in labour absorption, particularly in rural India and among women. The composition makes the result more cautious. Much of the rural movement coincided with a higher agricultural and self-employment share, while urban employment barely changed. Policy should treat the release as evidence of participation, not yet proof of more productive or secure work.

What the survey measures

Current Weekly Status classifies a person according to activity during the seven days before the survey. It is useful for detecting relatively recent labour-market conditions. It is not identical to the usual-status measure based on a longer reference period. Nor is the unemployment rate the share of the whole adult population without work. It is the share of the labour force that is available for or seeking work but unemployed under the survey definition.

The arithmetic matters. In a hypothetical group of 1,000 adults with the published rates, 555 would be in the labour force. An unemployment rate of 5.1% implies about 28 unemployed people and roughly 527 workers. That matches the published worker-population ratio of 52.7% after rounding. In the previous quarter, 546 people would have been in the labour force and about 517 employed. The comparison suggests roughly ten additional workers per 1,000 adults, alongside a larger labour force. It is a rate-based illustration, not an estimate of the number of jobs created nationally.

Agriculture accounted for a larger share of rural work

Rural unemployment fell from 4.8% to 4.3%, while rural labour-force participation rose from 56.9% to 58.1% and the rural worker-population ratio rose from 54.2% to 55.6%. Those movements are internally consistent. They also occurred in a quarter when the share of rural workers in agriculture rose from 52.9% to 56.7%. The rural self-employment share increased from 61.4% to 62.7%, while casual labour declined from 22.5% to 21.7%.

Agriculture can absorb labour quickly during a busy crop season. That is economically valuable when it raises production and household income. It does not necessarily represent a structural shift into higher-productivity work. Self-employment includes employers and successful own-account enterprises, but it can also include unpaid helpers and workers accepting low returns because better alternatives are scarce. Employment status is therefore not a quality ranking by itself.

The year-on-year baseline tempers the quarter-on-quarter excitement. Rural unemployment was 4.4% in July to September 2025, close to the new 4.3% reading. Rural participation rose from 57.2% to 58.1% over that year, which is more meaningful. The central question becomes whether the additional participation is accompanied by higher hours, earnings and productivity after the agricultural peak passes.

Urban India tells a different story

Urban unemployment was 6.8%, essentially unchanged from 6.7% in the previous quarter. Urban participation edged up from 50.2% to 50.4%, while the worker-population ratio moved from 46.8% to 46.9%. Urban regular wage or salaried employment increased slightly as a share of workers, from 49.3% to 49.6%. These are small movements. They do not support a claim of an urban hiring boom.

This split matters for macroeconomic policy. Urban formal and regular employment influences household credit, housing demand and durable-goods consumption. Rural employment often depends more directly on agriculture, public works and local demand. An aggregate unemployment rate can improve even when the part of the labour market most closely linked to sustained non-farm productivity changes little.

The female participation gain deserves two readings

Female labour-force participation rose from 33.2% to 34.7%, while the female worker-population ratio increased from 31.3% to 32.8%. This is one of the strongest signals in the release. More women were counted in the labour force and at work. The quarterly bulletin also shows a sharp rural-urban difference, with rural female participation at 39.2% and urban female participation at 25.5%.

One reading is optimistic. Improved access to jobs, transport, credit, childcare or flexible work can allow women who want paid work to enter. Another is more cautious. Household income stress can push additional family members into low-paid self-employment or unpaid work. The survey rates alone cannot distinguish an opportunity effect from a distress effect. Earnings, hours, employment status and reasons for not working are needed.

The distinction has policy consequences. If transport and safety are the constraint, urban mobility and workplace design matter. If unpaid care is the constraint, childcare and public services can change labour supply. If the increase is concentrated in low-productivity agricultural work, skills programmes without local labour demand will have limited effect. The next step is diagnosis, not celebration.

Unemployment is not enough

A low unemployment rate can coexist with underemployment. People who work a small number of hours, earn very little, or do work below their capacity are still classified as employed. India also has a large informal economy where job security, benefits and written contracts vary. A complete labour dashboard should therefore combine unemployment with earnings, hours, real wage growth, formal payrolls, enterprise surveys and transitions between employment states.

The survey’s expansion is useful here. Quarterly bulletins now cover rural as well as urban India and include estimates of broad employment status and industry. The next analytical gain would come from consistent public microdata and uncertainty measures that allow researchers to test whether changes are statistically meaningful and which groups drive them.

The strongest counterargument

The strongest case for taking the headline improvement at face value is that three indicators moved in the desired direction together. Participation increased, employment increased and unemployment declined. The gains were visible for women, and rural employment absorption was strong. Demanding that every new worker immediately move into a high-wage formal job sets an unrealistic standard for a diverse lower-middle-income economy.

That is fair. Structural transformation is gradual, and agricultural employment can be productive. The caution is about inference, not dismissal. Quarter-to-quarter sector shares are sensitive to seasonality. Without earnings and hours, it is impossible to know how much welfare improved. Without a longer comparable series under the revised quarterly design, it is difficult to separate trend from noise.

An empirical test for the claim

A useful test would follow districts or states across quarters and compare changes in employment with rainfall, crop calendars, rural wages, MGNREGA demand, formal payrolls and non-farm output. If the improvement is mainly seasonal agricultural absorption, it should be concentrated in crop-intensive areas and partly reverse after harvest. If it reflects broader labour demand, gains should persist and appear in real wages, hours and non-farm employment.

For women, the analysis should separate paid self-employment, unpaid household enterprise work, regular wage work and casual labour. A rise in participation accompanied by real earnings and more paid hours would support the opportunity interpretation. A rise concentrated in unpaid work alongside falling household income would support the distress interpretation.

What would change the judgement

The assessment would become more positive if the October to December and January to March rounds show that rural participation and employment gains persist after the seasonal peak, urban regular employment accelerates, and real earnings rise. It would strengthen further if women’s gains appear in paid work and hours rather than only in unpaid family activity.

It would become more cautious if the worker-population ratio falls back, agricultural employment reverses without non-farm absorption, or participation rises while real wages decline. The July to September release is good news about labour absorption. India should now ask the harder question, which is whether the new work raises productivity and bargaining power.

Sources

MoSPI press note · PLFS Quarterly Bulletin, July to September 2026 · September 2026 monthly PLFS release for comparison

excerpt.rendered: Employment and participation improved together in July to September. Seasonal agriculture, urban stagnation and the content of women’s work define the next test.

title.rendered: The case for India’s fertiliser subsidy depends on what it buys farmers

content.rendered:
On 11 November 2026, the Union Cabinet approved nutrient-based subsidy rates for phosphatic and potassic fertilisers for the rabi season from 1 October 2026 to 31 March 2027. The package has a tentative cost of ₹62,370.02 crore, ₹24,417.73 crore more than the comparable rabi 2025-26 requirement. That is an increase of about 64.3%. The decision is an understandable response to an external price shock. It is also a reminder that India still protects farmers from volatile world prices through a system that weakens the price signal for choosing the right nutrient. Cabinet decision, 11 November 2026 · Official Cabinet briefing

The higher subsidy is justified as temporary insurance against a supply shock during sowing, but it should not become a substitute for reform. The right test is not whether a bag remains cheap. It is whether farmers receive the mix of nutrients their soils and crops require, whether supplies arrive before the purchase window closes, and whether the fiscal cost produces more output rather than more imbalance.

What changed, and what did not

The Cabinet fixed per-kilogram support for four nutrients in covered fertilisers. For rabi 2026-27, the rates are ₹94.21 for nitrogen, ₹66.11 for phosphorus, ₹2.38 for potash and ₹10.42 for sulphur. The scheme applies to phosphatic and potassic products such as DAP, NPKS grades, MOP and SSP. Urea remains outside this nutrient-based system and continues under a separate administered-price subsidy. That distinction is central to the economics.

A nutrient-based subsidy sounds neutral because the payment follows the nutrient content of a product. It is only partly neutral when the most widely used nitrogen product is governed by a different regime. The retail price of urea is held at a low administered level, while prices of many P and K products have more room to reflect import costs. Farmers therefore compare distorted relative prices, not the underlying agronomic value of nutrients. The rabi package cushions the P and K side of that comparison, but it does not remove the structural asymmetry.

The arithmetic inside a bag

The official nutrient rates allow a transparent calculation. A 50 kg bag of DAP contains roughly 18% nitrogen and 46% phosphate measured as P2O5. Applying the Cabinet-approved rates gives an illustrative subsidy of about ₹2,368 per bag. The calculation is 9 kg of nitrogen multiplied by ₹94.21, plus 23 kg of phosphate equivalent (P₂O₅) multiplied by ₹66.11. Product-specific support can differ because the notification may include special provisions and because nutrient conventions matter, but the exercise shows why the fiscal exposure rises quickly when global input costs move.

These are analytical illustrations, not retail-price quotations. They hold bag weight and standard nutrient grades constant and exclude any product-specific additions. Their purpose is to expose the mechanism. Government absorbs a large part of the difference between a market-linked delivered cost and the price a farmer faces. The immediate incidence falls on the Exchequer. The intended benefit reaches farmers through lower prices and more reliable availability, while manufacturers and importers receive compensation for selling below full cost.

Why timing matters as much as the headline amount

Fertiliser is a working-capital purchase made before harvest income arrives. A farmer who cannot finance the required input at sowing may reduce application, substitute towards a cheaper nutrient, borrow at a high rate, or change the crop. A subsidy paid through the supply chain can relax that constraint if stocks are present at the local retailer when demand peaks. A large sanctioned amount after the purchase window is much less valuable.

That makes distribution and logistics part of fiscal policy. The relevant operational indicators are product-wise stocks at district level, the share of retailers reporting shortages, the time from import or factory dispatch to sale, and the gap between official and realised retail prices. An aggregate national availability number can conceal shortages where the crop calendar is tight. The government should publish these indicators weekly during the rabi peak.

The distributional question

A per-bag price subsidy does not deliver equal rupee support to all farmers. A cultivator buying ten bags receives roughly ten times the embedded support of a cultivator buying one comparable bag. Larger irrigated farms and input-intensive crops can therefore capture more of the fiscal benefit in absolute terms. Tenant farmers and sharecroppers may receive less if access to formal channels or land-linked systems is weaker. Consumers can still benefit indirectly if the subsidy prevents a production shortfall and moderates food prices.

The package can also shift income between domestic producers, importers and farmers. If reimbursement is delayed, firms finance the subsidy receivable and may ration supply or carry higher interest costs. If prices are capped while import costs rise, the fiscal authority bears the marginal shock. If support is fixed while market costs continue rising, part of the shock can return to the farmer. A serious assessment must therefore track payment delays and landed-cost assumptions, not only the approved outlay.

The deeper problem is nutrient imbalance

Independent scrutiny points to a persistent relative-price distortion. PRS notes that India’s all-India N:P:K consumption ratio deteriorated to 10.9:4.4:1 in 2023-24 against a commonly cited benchmark of 4:2:1. The exact agronomic requirement varies by soil and crop, so no national ratio is a prescription for every field. The broad direction is still clear. Nitrogen is used heavily relative to potash. PRS analysis of the 2026-27 demands for grants

A recent ICRIER policy brief reaches a similar conclusion with state-level evidence. It argues that nitrogen use moved from below to above recommended levels while the potassium deficit deepened. Its central claim is economic rather than educational. Farmers respond to relative prices, procurement incentives, irrigation and cropping patterns. Information campaigns alone cannot overcome a large price wedge. ICRIER, Repurposing India’s Fertiliser Policy towards Nutrient Optimisation

Excess nitrogen can impose costs that are not priced into a bag. These include nitrate leakage, nitrous-oxide emissions, soil deterioration and lower nutrient-use efficiency. Because the farmer does not bear the full social cost, a subsidy that further reduces the private price can amplify an externality. The policy problem is not that every subsidy is wasteful. It is that the subsidy should reward the output and resilience society values without encouraging the wrong input mix.

The fiscal trade-off

The rabi package alone is about ₹62,370 crore. The Union Budget allocated ₹1,70,799 crore to urea and nutrient-based fertiliser subsidies for the whole of 2026-27, according to PRS. The rabi P and K decision is not directly comparable with that annual total because the time periods and subsidy components differ. It nevertheless shows how an external price shock can consume fiscal space quickly. Every additional ₹10,000 crore used to defend an input price is ₹10,000 crore unavailable for irrigation maintenance, agricultural research, income support, nutrition or deficit reduction unless revenue rises or another item is cut.

A crude cost-per-beneficiary calculation would mislead because the subsidy also protects output and consumer prices. A better counterfactual asks what would happen without it. How much would application fall, which crops would change, what would happen to yields, and how much of the retail-price increase would pass into food inflation? Those are estimable questions. They require variation across products, districts and timing, not a national before-and-after comparison.

The strongest case for the package

The strongest counterargument to reform during a shock is practical. Rabi sowing cannot wait for a new transfer architecture. World fertiliser markets are concentrated, India imports important inputs, and abrupt retail-price increases could reduce application when farmers face limited credit. A known bag price is easy to understand and politically credible. Reform that transfers money late or excludes tenants could be worse than the existing system.

That argument supports stabilisation now. It does not justify preserving the same design indefinitely. Temporary insurance should come with a transition plan. A farmer-linked benefit neutral across nutrients, delivered before sowing and portable for tenants, could separate income protection from the relative price of a specific product. Pilot programmes should be evaluated against the existing subsidy on crop yield, nutrient balance, farmer expenditure, retailer availability and exclusion errors.

What would change the judgement

Three findings would make the present design look stronger. First, district-level evidence that the higher subsidy prevented shortages and materially increased balanced P and K application. Second, credible data showing that output gains and avoided food-price pressure were large relative to the fiscal cost. Third, proof that reimbursement reached suppliers quickly without excessive rents or leakage.

The judgement would weaken if nitrogen imbalance worsens, if large farms capture a rising share of support, if subsidy arrears delay supply, or if the rabi package becomes the annual baseline after the external shock fades. The Cabinet has bought insurance for one planting season. The next policy decision should buy better incentives.

Sources

Cabinet approval of rabi 2026-27 NBS rates · Official Cabinet briefing with nutrient rates · PRS budget analysis · ICRIER policy brief

excerpt.rendered: The ₹62,370 crore rabi package is defensible as shock insurance. Its lasting value depends on balanced nutrients, timely supply and a reform path.

title.rendered: At Antalya, adaptation finance needs a route from pledge to local delivery

content.rendered:
Climate finance after Belém · Part 5 · COP31 opening-week agenda

The adaptation question at COP31 in Antalya is what happens between a pledge and a working project. The UNFCCC’s summit programme includes an event on the Pacific Resilience Facility, illustrating attention to finance for communities with high exposure and limited administrative capacity. UNEP’s latest assessment shows how far public flows remain below estimated needs. A useful outcome would make it easier for a small government or municipality to apply, plan and receive funding on predictable terms. UNFCCC, Antalya COP31 leaders’ summit · UNEP, Adaptation Gap Report 2026

Small projects face large fixed costs

The cost of obtaining an engineer’s study, preparing a procurement plan or applying for a grant may be modest for a billion-dollar project. It can make a small project uneconomic for a local authority. A community may know which road floods, which clinic loses cooling or which well becomes saline. It may lack staff to prepare the documentation several separate funds require. A shared preparation facility can lower that fixed cost and compare similar designs across places.

Imagine ten municipalities that each need a $500,000 project and face $50,000 of individual preparation costs. If a shared platform produces the same usable work for $200,000 in total, it releases $300,000 for other uses. Some costs cannot be pooled, including site investigations and local consultation. The example shows the possible gain from common work, with local verification still necessary.

Funding should have an operating plan

A grant for construction will achieve less if there is no budget for inspection, electricity or repairs. An institution assessing the project should consider who owns it after completion and how operating costs are funded. Projects can include support for training and maintenance where those inputs preserve service. Measuring whether a facility remains usable a few years later would be more revealing than judging it by how quickly the construction account closed.

A strong argument for applying rigorous safeguards is that projects can create displacement, harm ecosystems or deliver weak value. Faster decisions should come from standardising routine checks, improving technical support and identifying risks early. A small locality can be given help with evidence and still be held to a clear outcome. The alternative of removing the checks can create harm that undermines the programme.

The opening-week benchmark is whether proposals specify who supplies grants, when funds become available and which projects qualify. Follow approvals, the time to first disbursement and completion with service measures. If funds reach smaller recipients faster while oversight remains credible, the financing system has improved. An aggregate commitment with no timetable or operating plan would leave the local budget problem largely where it was.

Climate finance after Belém
Previous · Part 4 · All installments

excerpt.rendered: COP31 provides another chance to make adaptation commitments usable. The priorities are project preparation, faster disbursement and comparable public accounting.

title.rendered: India’s storage subsidy should buy dependable discharge in the hours that matter

content.rendered:
The Cabinet’s new ₹14,500 crore storage programme can help finance assets the grid will increasingly need. Its target of 92 GWh is a useful description of scale. The service bought with the money depends on where the storage is connected, how quickly it can respond, how long it can sustain output and whether it is charged when called. Procurement should buy a defined reliability service before it rewards the installation of an energy capacity. Cabinet, grid-scale storage funding · CERC tariff second amendment, Gazette 257 of 2026

Three technologies and several objectives

The Cabinet release envisages 60 GWh of pumped storage, 30 GWh of battery storage and 2 GWh from emerging technologies, with estimated total investment of ₹97,600 crore and fiscal support over FY 2026–27 to FY 2030–31. It also specifies a minimum 40% domestic content requirement for the battery projects. These are programme parameters, and the supported capacity has yet to be commissioned. The public objectives include grid reliability and domestic industrial capability. Bid evaluation should show the cost and result of each objective, including any price premium associated with the content rule. Cabinet, grid-scale storage funding

Pumped storage can provide longer discharge in suitable locations. Its costs and schedule depend on civil works, water and site conditions. Batteries can sometimes be installed faster near a constraint and respond quickly, while their useful energy and life depend on operation and degradation. Other technologies may be valuable for specific service profiles. Putting them in the same programme gives procurement room to match assets to the grid problem. It also creates a need for a meaningful common comparison.

The contract’s clock matters

Take two illustrative facilities each offering 400 MWh of usable energy. One can deliver 200 MW for two hours and the other 100 MW for four hours. If a constraint needs an extra 150 MW for two hours, the first can cover it fully and the second leaves a 50 MW gap. If the system needs 100 MW for four hours, the second can cover the whole interval. The first can also do so if its contract and equipment allow operation at 100 MW for four hours. The crucial facts are the discharge curve and the conditions of availability. Nameplate energy alone cannot determine the service.

The life of the asset matters as much as the day it starts. A tender can pay for usable capacity over time and make replacement or augmentation costs explicit. It should require a transparent treatment of charging losses and network constraints. A battery that is cheap to build can be expensive to operate if it regularly needs to charge in a costly hour. A project located where cheap power is often available may offer more value even with a higher capital bid.

Buy manufacturing learning deliberately

The strongest argument for domestic content is that a stable order book can justify supplier investment and reduce reliance on imported inputs over time. The constraint can initially increase bids or narrow the pool of suppliers. Publish cost and delivery performance, and track which capabilities expand, such as qualified components, maintenance or repeated supply to unsubsidised projects. Procurement should be able to distinguish capability that persists from assembly done only to meet a threshold.

The grid test is measured delivery in scarcity hours, usable energy after degradation, connection delays and cost per effective unit of reliability. Benchmark against firm supply, demand response or a transmission upgrade where those alternatives can solve the same problem. Strong delivery at competitive lifecycle cost would support expansion. Delays, persistent underperformance or scarce charging capacity would justify revising the location and service requirements before committing more funds.

A developer’s guarantee also needs a practical enforcement mechanism. A low bid is less valuable if poor delivery can be excused whenever the power system is under stress. Clear tests, measured state of charge and proportional remedies can make the quoted service comparable across bids.

The subsidy will serve consumers when it reduces the cost of having power available in a difficult hour. That is the result the programme should publish alongside GWh commissioned.

excerpt.rendered: The Cabinet’s 92 GWh programme will support several technologies. Comparing bids by energy capacity alone would miss differences in location, duration and service.

title.rendered: NASA’s $10 billion lunar delivery ceiling is an option to order services

content.rendered:
The economics of returning to the Moon · Part 5 · November commercial lunar procurement

NASA’s November announcement set out a Commercial Lunar Payload Services 2 framework with a combined maximum of $10 billion over ten years. A multiple-award framework gives the agency a route to order services as needs arise. The ceiling describes the maximum value across potential orders. It should be read alongside actual obligations, awarded tasks and delivery performance when judging how much NASA is spending or how large the market has become. NASA, Moon Base transportation and science procurement · US GAO, 2026 NASA major projects assessment

A framework can reduce the cost of ordering again

A buyer that expects recurring needs can qualify multiple providers and set common terms in advance. Individual orders can then specify the service, time and performance required. This can shorten procurement and make it easier to compare bids. Providers may invest in capacity if future demand appears credible. A large ceiling with irregular orders supplies weaker assurance to a company deciding whether to hire staff or build additional capability.

Suppose an agency establishes a framework with an illustrative $1 billion ceiling and awards $100 million of tasks in the first year. The first-year commitments and the maximum value measure different things. A provider cannot rely on the remaining $900 million arriving as revenue. The agency can expand orders if useful missions become available. Both sides benefit from a realistic forecast of likely orders alongside room to adjust.

Judge delivery at the level the customer pays for

A task award can finance preparation, while payment and success may depend on milestones. Track which services were ordered, what reached the intended destination and how much repeat service costs. An early failure can provide useful learning, though it also delays the user’s project. A successful delivery establishes that a provider met a particular requirement. It provides more evidence of a market when other customers can order comparable service at a defensible cost.

The strongest case for NASA as an anchor customer is that early demand supports learning and competition before other customers are ready. A risk is that providers continue to depend on one buyer whose budget can change. Compare costs and performance as orders repeat, and monitor whether other organisations use the available services. A rising ceiling has less bearing on commercial viability than credible repeat business.

The next update should distinguish the procurement ceiling, actual contract obligations and completed deliveries. The economic result will become clearer when researchers and other customers can buy reliable transport for their projects and when NASA can choose among suppliers on evidence from prior work.

The economics of returning to the Moon
Previous · Part 4 · All installments

excerpt.rendered: A multiple-award framework sets a maximum across potential orders. The economics will depend on task orders, delivery and demand after the first customers.

title.rendered: An early tax transfer can matter even when states receive the same amount

content.rendered:
The Union’s early-November tax devolution is a useful example of why state budgets need cash calendars as well as annual totals. The finance ministry says it released the regular ₹1,09,019 crore instalment on 5 November instead of the usual 10 November date for that month. The announcement advances a scheduled transfer. Its benefit depends on which states had payments due before the original date, how they would otherwise have financed them and whether the earlier cash allowed a service or payment to move sooner. Finance ministry’s 5 November tax-devolution release · Finance ministry’s February devolution announcement

A transfer has an amount and a date

An annual budget may balance on its planned figures and still contain weeks when expected cash receipts arrive after payments are due. Salaries, vendor bills and payments to agencies have particular dates. A state can bridge a short gap with existing balances, permissible temporary finance or by delaying payments. Each option has a cost or consequence. An early transfer can reduce the need for a bridge. It does not expand the state’s annual resources unless the total amount it receives also changes. The ministry’s statement describes a timing change to the regular instalment. Finance ministry’s 5 November tax-devolution release · RBI State Finances study of 2025–26 budgets

For scale, suppose a state would otherwise need ₹1,000 crore of short-term finance for five days at an assumed seven per cent annual rate. Using simple interest and 365 days, the avoided financing cost is about ₹96 lakh. This is an illustrative calculation, not a statement of any state’s balance, borrowing terms or savings. If the state already had adequate cash, the direct saving would be smaller. If the alternative was delaying important payments to smaller suppliers, the economic benefit might include costs borne outside the Treasury as well.

The benefit varies across states and recipients

A state with cash available for all due payments can use the earlier transfer to increase its buffer temporarily. Another state could use it to pay contractors or social commitments earlier. A contractor waiting for an overdue bill might have to borrow at a higher rate than the government or delay paying workers and suppliers. Advancing public cash can reduce that chain of delays when it actually results in an earlier payment. State-level outcomes should therefore be measured using payment records. The Union release alone establishes the transfer date, not when the final recipient received funds. Finance ministry’s 5 November tax-devolution release

The November announcement provides a state-wise table. Those amounts reflect the distribution of the transfer. They are not a ranking of who had the greatest cash need or who gained most from earlier access. To assess the distributional effect, compare each amount with payments due, available balances and alternative financing. A state receiving a smaller amount could benefit more at the margin if it was close to a constraint. One receiving more might simply hold the funds until the original payment schedule. Finance ministry’s 5 November tax-devolution release · PRS analysis of the Sixteenth Finance Commission report

A regular calendar can be more valuable than occasional surprises

The strongest case for advancing a transfer is that spending pressure or holidays can concentrate payments in a period when cash is tight. A timing adjustment can ease that temporary problem without changing the annual envelope. States and suppliers also benefit from predictable dates. Regularly shifting receipts at short notice can make budgets harder to plan even if some advances are helpful. A credible system should publish the calendar and explain adjustments, so treasuries know which inflows can support a payment decision. Finance ministry’s 5 November tax-devolution release · RBI State Finances study of 2025–26 budgets

It is also useful to separate acceleration from fiscal stimulus. Paying an invoice sooner can change when cash reaches households or firms. A state may also bring forward work that would otherwise have begun later. Those are meaningful timing effects. The size and persistence of the effect depend on whether actual spending changes and whether a later payment or activity is correspondingly smaller. A comparison between the early-November release and the remainder of the annual transfer programme can show which change occurred.

Measure the constraint the advance actually relaxed

Compare planned and realised cash receipts and payments in the days around the advance. Track temporary financing, overdue supplier bills and commitments accelerated. Reconcile those observations with the year’s total transfers and spending. If earlier funds lead to timely payments or lower use of expensive short-term finance, the adjustment has improved execution. If balances rise for several days and planned payment dates are unchanged, the benefit is chiefly a temporary buffer. The same transfer can produce different results across states. The right evidence is what each Treasury was able to do because the money arrived when it did. Finance ministry’s 5 November tax-devolution release · RBI State Finances study of 2025–26 budgets

The accounting relationship also matters on the Union side. A state’s earlier receipt is the Centre’s earlier cash outflow. Depending on its own cash position, the Centre may fund the advance from balances or other financing. The combined public-sector saving depends on the difference between the costs borne by each government and any private costs avoided. The simple example values the state’s bridge financing only. A full assessment would also look at the Centre’s funding and the amount the recipients would otherwise have had to borrow.

The transfer table can support a comparison of days of ordinary expenditure rather than rupees alone. A payment that covers several days of expenditure in one state may cover fewer in another. The useful calculation would use actual cash payments from a comparable period and check for seasonality. Even that ratio would not identify near-term need unless it is read alongside commitments and cash already held.

For projects, check whether there was work ready to pay for. A well-prepared contract can use cash promptly, while a project awaiting a tender, clearance or measurement cannot simply convert an advance into construction. Showing those differences would make the release calendar more useful to both governments and suppliers.

excerpt.rendered: The Centre advanced the regular ₹1.09 lakh crore devolution instalment by five days. The effect depends on which states faced a temporary cash constraint and what payments they could bring forward.

title.rendered: Testing two Artemis landers can make competition last beyond the contract award

content.rendered:
The economics of returning to the Moon · Part 4 · November Artemis III update

NASA’s November update described Artemis III as a planned 2027 demonstration involving test vehicles from SpaceX and Blue Origin in Earth orbit. It was an update on a planned mission, while the agency continued to target a landing for Artemis IV. Supporting two approaches can preserve the option to change providers or learn from different designs. The case depends on having comparable evidence and retaining credible alternatives after the early contracts are awarded. NASA, November Artemis programme update · NASA, Artemis IV mission plan

An alternative has value before it is chosen

If only one provider can deliver a service, delay or cost growth can leave the agency with limited choices. A second credible provider can make it possible to switch or revise the division of work. It can also give both companies an incentive to meet milestones. Funding two approaches has a cost, and an alternative that is too far behind the first may offer limited bargaining or scheduling value. The practical test is whether both can satisfy the same minimum requirements in time.

Suppose supporting a second development path costs $150 million, and the alternative would avert a $500 million programme delay if the primary option were unavailable. The delay avoidance alone would break even at a 30% chance of that outcome, before any competition or learning gains. Those figures are illustrative. Real value also depends on when a switch could occur and whether the second path faces the same risks.

Make comparisons useful without forcing identical designs

A procurement can define what a mission must accomplish and let providers propose different ways to do it. Comparable test criteria help the agency see how each meets the requirement and which assumptions differ. A uniform design would make some comparisons easier but can remove the value of trying two approaches. Standard interfaces can preserve choice while keeping later integration costs manageable. Contractors need a credible path to future work if early investment is to be sustainable.

The strongest case for concentrating on one provider is that scarce staff and funding can be directed at completing one system. That is more convincing when the supplier is demonstrably ahead and the agency has ways to enforce delivery and contain future prices. A second effort is easier to justify where schedule risk is high and both teams can produce decision-relevant evidence at an affordable cost.

The next comparison should cover milestone performance, integration cost and how much work would be required to switch. A mission with two participants can produce valuable learning even if only one provider serves the first landing. The enduring return is credible competition for the next service, rather than the number of companies listed in an announcement.

The economics of returning to the Moon

title.rendered: Satellite broadband is most valuable where India’s other networks struggle to reach

content.rendered:
The most valuable Indian satellite broadband connection may serve a clinic, school or relay site that has few reliable alternatives. Selling a terminal to a well-connected household is a different proposition. TRAI’s 5 November recommendations on authorisation and spectrum assignment for satellite communication network providers offer a chance to distinguish those markets. The case for easier entry is strongest where new network capacity has a clear cost or reliability advantage over extending the terrestrial network. TRAI, November satellite network recommendations · TRAI, April 2026 consultation paper

Capacity, access and the retail bill

A satellite network provider operates infrastructure. The business that sells a connection to a school or household may use that infrastructure under a wholesale arrangement. The distinction matters because licensing the upstream provider can increase physical capacity while leaving a single downstream supplier in a location. A policy that makes multiple networks technically possible can still produce limited effective competition if switching requires a costly terminal replacement or a new installation contract. Publishing comparable coverage and contract terms helps customers assess which option is real.

Capacity also has a geography and a clock. A shared radio beam serving several customers has a finite throughput at peak times. The marginal cost of adding a customer can be low when traffic is light and appreciable when the beam is congested. This creates different incentives for operators serving dispersed sites and operators selling high-volume urban subscriptions. Average speed in a brochure will be a poor test of the service an institution receives during the busiest hour.

Compare the whole service

Take a hypothetical settlement of 80 households. A reliable terrestrial link and local distribution would cost ₹24 lakh upfront and ₹3 lakh a year to operate. A shared satellite installation costs ₹4 lakh upfront and ₹6 lakh a year. Ignoring discounting and equipment replacement, the five-year totals are ₹39 lakh and ₹34 lakh. By year seven the totals are ₹45 lakh and ₹46 lakh. The ranking changes over a plausible project horizon even with no change in unit prices. These are illustrative inputs. A serious comparison must adjust for uptime, capacity, latency, replacement costs and the chance of additional customers.

The example also shows why household affordability differs from network cost. Dividing ₹34 lakh by 80 households and five years gives an average of ₹8,500 a household per year under full take-up. If only 40 households subscribe and the shared cost is unchanged, it doubles. Early demand can be too thin to justify separate retail connections. An anchor customer, such as a health centre buying a service with a clear uptime target, can support a local access point. A contract with portable equipment or defined transition terms can protect the community if fibre subsequently becomes cheaper.

An additional test is the cost of keeping a backup connection available. A low-volume backup can prevent substantial service interruptions while generating little monthly traffic. A procurement based on cost per gigabyte would undervalue that option. Availability during an outage and the time needed to restore service are better measures for this use.

Put the subsidy where access is scarce

The strongest case for a wider rollout is that uniform offerings simplify contracts and help firms learn quickly. Terrestrial networks also fail in places that appear well covered on a map, and a satellite backup can have value there. That argues for evaluating the service an area actually receives. Where public funds are involved, an open comparison across technology and shared procurement for remote public institutions could direct spending towards unmet demand without predetermining the network.

The authorisation debate should therefore be judged by wholesale terms, repeat orders from remote sites, installation delays, busy-hour performance and total cost per functioning connection. Evidence that many customers in underserved areas can switch providers without replacing expensive hardware would make a stronger case for relying on ordinary retail competition. Persistent concentration and low take-up at full price would support competitive procurement for specific services. The aim is dependable connectivity in places where geography makes it expensive to provide, with the provider paid for the service it delivers.

excerpt.rendered: Satellite network authorisation will shape who builds, who sells capacity and who can afford a connection in the places with few alternatives.

title.rendered: India’s mineral processing subsidy should buy supply that works in a disruption

content.rendered:
India’s ₹2,814 crore critical mineral processing scheme should be judged by the supply it can deliver when imports are disrupted. The Cabinet’s 4 November approval provides capital support for four plants to process lithium and nickel inputs into higher-purity materials. Building the plants in India could create useful technical capability and diversify access to refined products. Their location alone cannot guarantee resilience. A refinery can remain dependent on a single foreign source of feedstock, a proprietary process or a buyer that cannot use the product. The public return comes from reliable output that Indian customers can qualify and obtain under the conditions the scheme is meant to address. Cabinet decision on critical mineral processing · Mines ministry’s November scheme note · Business Standard on the lithium and nickel processing plan

The approved support has a defined scale and purpose

The Cabinet describes two lithium plants with a minimum capacity of 30 kilotonnes each and two nickel plants with a minimum of 50 kilotonnes each. The scheme runs from 2026–27 to 2030–31 and offers capital support of 30 per cent of eligible investment, subject to caps of ₹500 crore per lithium beneficiary and ₹900 crore per nickel beneficiary. Applicants first have to meet technical requirements, after which the selection for each mineral is based on the lowest capital support sought. Payments are to be made in three milestone-linked tranches. These are approved design parameters. Installed capacity, commercial throughput and qualified sales will need to be measured separately. Cabinet decision on critical mineral processing · Mines ministry’s November scheme note

The grant calculation also means the percentage received can differ by project. On an illustrative ₹2,000 crore of eligible investment in a lithium plant, 30 per cent would be ₹600 crore, but the ₹500 crore ceiling limits the award to at most 25 per cent of the eligible investment. A winning bid could ask for less. This example uses an assumed capital cost and abstracts from ineligible spending or timing. It shows why a project comparison should use the actual support requested and expected output. Applying 30 per cent to every project’s total investment would overstate the support in cases where the cap binds or costs are ineligible. Cabinet decision on critical mineral processing

Processing adds value only with feedstock and qualified output

A domestic processor can reduce dependence on imported refined material while still relying on imported ore or intermediates. That trade can improve resilience when feedstock can be sourced from several suppliers and the plant can handle their material. It adds less protection when the plant can use only one grade from one supplier that is exposed to the same disruption as the finished product. A technical assessment should therefore check substitute feedstocks, the time and cost of switching, and whether agreements actually give the processor access to material in adverse conditions. Announced contracts and available delivered tonnes are different measures. Cabinet decision on critical mineral processing · IEA Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026

The output side poses a second qualification problem. A customer buying a material for batteries or another demanding application needs consistent purity and performance from batch to batch. Even a plant running near design capacity can produce material for a different use if it cannot meet the buyer’s specification. Capacity estimates should specify the product and quality basis. Commercial evidence includes independently tested samples, repeat purchases and delivery under a binding contract. The first sale is useful, while repeat sales are a better indication that the processor can sustain its standards without exceptional handling. Mines ministry’s November scheme note

A commercial buyer also needs to know whether switching inputs or processing methods will require it to qualify the output again. A plant that can use several feedstocks in principle may still take weeks to adjust equipment, run tests and deliver an accepted batch. A bid should therefore specify a demonstrated switching time and an alternative supply plan, with a distinction between capacity that is operational and capacity that would be usable after qualification. An independent trial before the final subsidy tranche would make the distinction observable while the sponsor still has an incentive to address failures. Cabinet decision on critical mineral processing · Mines ministry’s November scheme note

Compare bids on service as well as the capital cheque

Least-cost bidding can protect the budget if technically qualified projects offer comparable capacity, reliability and delivery. The selection is more difficult if one bidder expects a high utilisation rate and diversified feedstock while another offers a lower grant request based on a narrow supply arrangement. To see the scale of the difference, assume a plant with 30,000 tonnes of annual product capacity gets ₹500 crore and operates for ten years. At 80 per cent utilisation it produces 240,000 tonnes, giving an undiscounted capital grant of roughly ₹20,800 per tonne. At 40 per cent utilisation the figure doubles. Those assumptions are illustrative. They exclude operating support, capital replacement and any public costs outside the grant. Cabinet decision on critical mineral processing

The policy justification is partly an insurance benefit, so ordinary utilisation is not the only consideration. A plant might be worth supporting if it can reliably deliver during rare disruptions even when its commercial utilisation is lower in normal years. That argument needs an operating model. Spare capacity without available inputs or qualified staff cannot respond to a shortage. A domestic buyer that normally sources the full requirement overseas may also need to approve the local product in advance. A procurement or supply agreement should state what is available in a disruption and what it costs to keep that option usable.

The distribution of costs also depends on location. Processing plants need utilities, logistics and a way to manage waste. The capital subsidy does not eliminate the cost of power, water or environmental controls. If those costs are covered by separate state support or by households and firms competing for the same resources, the quoted project grant understates the public cost. A comparison of bids should identify these contributions and any contingent costs. A low upfront subsidy is less attractive where the plant needs recurring concessions to sell at a competitive delivered price.

Demand uncertainty matters too. Battery makers and other buyers can change product designs, alter the material they require or delay expansion. A plant that depends on one demand projection is vulnerable to a shift in its buyers’ investment plans. A credible project has contracted demand, customers with a reason to renew and an estimate of the costs of producing for other applications. Public support should reflect those uncertainties rather than treating all output at the planned specification as guaranteed to find an Indian buyer.

The strongest argument for acting before a shortage

The international concentration of processing gives India a reason to develop alternatives before a disruption makes them urgent. The IEA’s global analysis highlights concentration and the vulnerability of supply chains, while the Cabinet identifies limited domestic processing capacity and constraints on technology and raw materials. Capital assistance can help an investor meet a high initial cost in a market where buyers are reluctant to commit before capacity exists. The stronger the coordination problem, the more valuable an early commitment can be. It remains important to ask whether a long-term supply contract, inventories of the relevant product or diversified imports could deliver some of the same protection more cheaply. Cabinet decision on critical mineral processing · IEA Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026

What would establish resilience

Track commissioned capacity, utilisation, product qualification, feedstock concentration, delivered prices and repeat orders. Test what each plant can produce if its main feedstock source becomes unavailable or if shipping lead times increase. A useful comparison is public cost per qualified tonne delivered under normal conditions and in the specific stress scenarios that justified support. If the plants diversify inputs and supply qualified materials at competitive terms, the scheme will have created an alternative Indian buyers can use. If facilities open but qualified deliveries depend on the same supply risks the programme was meant to reduce, the next rupee should address the upstream or commercial constraint. Cabinet decision on critical mineral processing · Mines ministry’s November scheme note · IEA Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026

title.rendered: A record debt stock does not tell a country what it can spend next year

content.rendered:
The sovereign debt workout · Part 5 · November International Debt Report

The World Bank’s November release put the external debt of developing countries at a record $9.4 trillion in 2025, up 5.5% from the previous year. Low- and middle-income countries paid $1.4 trillion in principal and interest that year. The headline measures a stock across economies with very different income, financing access and creditor mixes. A ministry deciding what it can spend next year needs to know the flow of principal and interest it owes, what financing will actually arrive and which liabilities can be refinanced. An increase in the aggregate can coexist with a serious cash squeeze in particular countries. World Bank, November 2026 external debt release · World Bank, International Debt Report

Write the cash equation first

External debt can rise when a country borrows for worthwhile investments or when earlier liabilities change value in the reporting currency. Debt can also fall because a country loses market access and must make repayments without receiving enough new funds. To understand the financial effect, separate gross disbursements, principal repayments and interest. Net debt flows usually focus on disbursements less principal. Net transfers can also account for interest. A country can receive new loans and still send more cash out than it receives.

Suppose a country receives $900 million in new external loans, repays $800 million in principal and pays $250 million in interest. In this simplified example it has $100 million in net debt inflows before interest and a $150 million net outflow after interest. Looking only at gross lending or the change in the stock would understate the strain on its budget and foreign exchange.

Identify the risks inside the stock

Long-term concessional debt can be easier to carry than a smaller amount of short debt issued at high yields. Currency mismatch matters where the government collects revenue in local currency and owes dollars. A private borrower with export receipts can face a different risk from the public borrower with the same principal. The relevant comparison includes who owes the debt, when it is due and how reliable their income is.

A high stock is still a legitimate warning. It can make a borrower more vulnerable to interest-rate and exchange-rate shocks and narrow the set of lenders prepared to refinance it. Better debt management can spread maturities and reduce risk, while fiscal reforms can improve repayment capacity. These policies have more value where they address the actual source of stress. Extending maturity can relieve liquidity pressure without fixing an unsustainable underlying burden.

The next update should compare debt service with revenue and exports, and net transfers with spending on essential services and investment. After a restructuring, examine the maturity calendar under adverse conditions. Those measures are what connect the global debt headline to the decisions explored in Ghana, Zambia and Ethiopia.

The sovereign debt workout
