title.rendered: Affordable housing has to pass a test of rent and commuting together

content.rendered:
A cheaper home can leave a worker with a higher cost of living if reaching work takes longer and requires a second fare. India’s urban housing programme should therefore count the homes households can occupy within reach of jobs. The September approval announcement brings cumulative PMAY-U 2.0 sanctions to 18.77 lakh houses. The approvals are a milestone for supply. Rent, occupancy, location and access will determine the programme’s value to the people it is intended to serve. MoHUA, September PMAY-U 2.0 approvals · MoHUA, PMAY-U 2.0 operational guidelines

Four routes to different needs

The September committee approved more than 29,000 additional homes across six states under Beneficiary Led Construction and Affordable Housing in Partnership. The broader scheme also has rental housing and interest subsidy routes. Those distinctions matter. A household with land and a stable place of work can benefit from assistance to build. A worker newly arrived in a city may need a rental close enough to an uncertain job, without a long commitment. Counting both in a single programme total can hide which problem the next sanction is solving. MoHUA, September PMAY-U 2.0 approvals · MoHUA, PMAY-U 2.0 operational guidelines

An owner can gain equity and protection against a rise in rents. Ownership also brings transaction costs and a risk if the buyer has to move. Rental supply gives households flexibility but must offer enforceable terms and acceptable conditions. The mix should reflect the tenure and location different households need. A housing project can be affordable on the day of allocation and unsuitable once the cost of regular travel is included.

Compare the cost a household faces

Suppose a worker can rent a room for ₹7,500 near a job or for ₹5,500 further away. The farther room requires ₹60 extra travel expense per working day and 45 additional minutes. With 24 workdays a month, the cash expense rises ₹1,440 and travel consumes 18 more hours. The cheaper rent leaves just ₹560 in monthly cash savings. Valuing the additional time at even ₹40 per hour adds ₹720 to the effective cost. These are illustrative values. The ranking will differ for people with different travel patterns, family obligations and transport options.

Reliability can dominate a similar comparison. A worker who is late once a month might lose pay or face a penalty. An unreliable return service can create childcare expenses or limit which shifts a person can accept. A simple average commute time will miss both. The location test should count trips at shift changes and show which jobs are accessible in a reasonable period without assuming every worker can afford a private vehicle.

Land is expensive near opportunity

The strongest argument for cheaper peripheral sites is that scarce well-located land can sharply increase project costs. Building at the edge may allow many more households to receive a unit and can work when employment is nearby or a funded transport connection is credible. Public authorities should compare those options on lifetime costs and occupancy, including infrastructure needed to make the land usable. Reserving some rental supply near existing employment can provide a different benefit from subsidising ownership further away.

Publish completed and occupied units by tenure, income group, location and observed commute. Compare housing plus transport expenditure, and examine how many households leave or sublet. Account for selection because families choosing a location may already work close to it. If homes remain occupied and travel costs fall, the location choice has worked. If take-up is weak or household budgets remain strained because travel is expensive, a different location or tenure mix may produce a better return from the same subsidy.

Consider the landlord’s side of a rental project too. A low advertised rent needs a maintenance budget and a way to cover vacancies. An operating contract can tie public support to habitable units and verified occupancy at agreed terms, giving the provider a reason to keep the building useful after construction.

A sanction pays for a housing opportunity. The programme earns its value when a household can live there and still reach the work that pays for everyday life.

title.rendered: The digital euro pilot should test ordinary payment failures

content.rendered:
Europe’s financial integration test · Part 4 · July provider selection

The ECB announced in July that 36 payment service providers had been selected for its digital euro pilot, following more than 50 applications. The group includes banks and non-bank providers with varied coverage and business models. A diverse pilot is useful if it exposes ordinary failure cases. A demonstration purchase in ideal conditions gives less information than a refund, a replacement device or a transaction between providers that handle disputes differently. ECB, July selection of payment service providers · ECB, digital euro pilot

Test the entire transaction

A successful payment includes initiation, authorisation, settlement and an understandable record for buyer and seller. A user whose connection drops may need to know whether an attempted transaction went through. A merchant may need to issue a partial refund. A second provider should be able to recognise the relevant message and answer a customer’s question. The quality of this experience matters to ordinary adoption as much as the speed of payment under normal conditions.

A pilot might record a 99% success rate for 10,000 attempts, leaving 100 failures. If most failures are concentrated among people on one type of device or shops using one integration, the average obscures the relevant design problem. Report success and time to resolution by payment type and participant group. These numbers are an illustration. A useful pilot has enough variety to distinguish a rare general error from a frequent problem for a small group.

Providers also have incentives

A service provider deciding how much to invest will consider the amount it can charge, ongoing support costs and the benefit of keeping customers. An established bank may already have much of the infrastructure. A smaller provider may be more responsive to niche demand and face a larger fixed cost. Pilot participation alone does not reveal whether offering the service will be viable. Record how long it takes to integrate, what support staff need and the conditions needed to maintain the product after the trial.

The strongest argument for a small tightly controlled pilot is that it makes errors easier to diagnose and limits disruption. The limitation is selection: people and merchants willing to test early may be unusually comfortable with digital products. Staged tests can begin small and then include more demanding circumstances, accessibility needs and cross-border use. The metrics should distinguish availability from observed usage.

This pilot is preparation for a potential issuance. Its value is the information it produces about what must change before broader use. The next decision should be judged by the reliability and cost of connecting providers, including the steps needed when one participant or communication service becomes unavailable.

title.rendered: India’s Russia trade target should be judged by repeat export orders

content.rendered:
India should judge the Russia trade target by whether Indian firms develop profitable export business they can repeat. At the 10 September India–Russia Business Dialogue, Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal called for annual bilateral trade to rise from around $60 billion to $100 billion by 2030. That increase would be a large achievement if it came with new customers and sustainable shipments for Indian exporters. The same total would mean less if it was reached mostly through more expensive oil imports. The objective of rebalancing trade therefore requires measuring its composition and the obstacles Indian firms face between a prospective order and payment. Commerce ministry’s 10 September statement · Business Standard on the bilateral trade baseline

The starting point makes the choice of metric consequential

Business Standard reported roughly $60 billion of bilateral trade in 2025–26, with imports around $55 billion and crude accounting for more than 80 per cent of those imports. On the rounded figures, Indian exports account for about $5 billion of the total. Going from $60 billion to $100 billion in four years implies compound annual growth of roughly 13.6 per cent. That is an arithmetic interpretation of the minister’s illustrative horizon and target, with the figures expressed in current dollars. It is a demanding target even before asking which side supplies the incremental trade. Commerce ministry’s 10 September statement · Business Standard on the bilateral trade baseline

If the entire $40 billion increase were on the import side, the target would be reached at roughly $95 billion of imports and $5 billion of exports. Indian firms would still account for about five per cent of bilateral turnover. If exports instead grew to $15 billion and imports to $85 billion, the total would be the same and the export share would rise to 15 per cent. These are scenarios for understanding the target, not forecasts. Even the second scenario would require exports to triple in the illustrative four years, equivalent to about 31.6 per cent compound annual growth from the rounded baseline. Commerce ministry’s 10 September statement · Business Standard on the bilateral trade baseline

An increase in the nominal oil price can move the headline in the opposite direction to the welfare of an Indian fuel buyer. Conversely, more competitive procurement can reduce the dollar value of imports while improving the input costs of Indian producers. A bilateral turnover target gives the same weight to a dollar of either change. Publishing export volumes, recurring product lines and the margins firms can earn after freight and financing would better capture whether greater trade is creating new opportunities in India. Reporting net exports separately can describe the balance, while the composition shows what each side is buying.

What keeps an exporter from converting interest into sales

The commerce ministry highlighted pharmaceuticals, engineering goods, chemicals, auto components, textiles, food and other sectors. The opportunities differ by product. A medicine or industrial component can require documentation, customer qualification and assurance that future batches meet the same standards. A perishable shipment depends on logistics, spoilage and how quickly it clears inspection. A buyer can express interest at a business forum and still choose a supplier with a more predictable delivery or payment process. Policy should start with sectors where several firms face a shared, identifiable obstacle to turning interest into contracts. Commerce ministry’s 10 September statement

There is a cost to the exporter between dispatch and collection. An Indian engineering firm may need to buy inputs and pay workers well before the buyer settles an invoice. Longer delivery and payment periods tie up working capital and increase exposure to a default, exchange-rate movement or documentation problem. A firm with a potentially profitable order can decline it if those costs are uncertain. The relevant metric is the expected contribution after transport, financing, compliance and losses, along with the time cash remains committed. This is particularly important for smaller exporters that have fewer banks, buyers and routes to choose from.

For example, assume a firm finances ₹1 crore in shipment costs at a simple annual rate of 12 per cent. Financing for 60 days costs roughly ₹1.97 lakh, while 120 days costs about ₹3.95 lakh, using a 365-day year. A two-month delay therefore adds close to ₹2 lakh before currency and credit risk. These are hypothetical terms. They show how reducing payment delays can increase export margins and release capacity to fill the next order. A policy that cuts one approval step is valuable to the extent it shortens the actual cash cycle or reduces its uncertainty.

Competition in the destination market sets a limit on what facilitation can deliver. A shipment that is competitive at the Indian factory gate can become expensive after freight, inventory held by the distributor and the cost of servicing a warranty are included. For machinery and components, a dependable replacement-parts network may be part of the product the customer is buying. Evidence from lost bids and repeat orders can show whether the constraint is market access, delivered price or the level of service Indian firms can provide. Those causes call for different investments.

Trade facilitation should solve the common costs first

Public agencies can help firms understand applicable product rules, arrange credible testing and identify logistics and payment constraints. Where settlement or finance is an obstacle, businesses need compliant, dependable arrangements with clear terms and reporting. A government can lower a shared entry cost by making information or testing accessible to many exporters. Covering recurring costs for every individual shipment would risk supporting sales that cannot stand on commercial terms. The useful test is whether firms expand into repeat orders after receiving help with the first fixed cost. Commerce ministry’s 10 September statement

This also limits the distributional case for a blanket export subsidy. A large incumbent with an established distributor and ample working capital may capture support for shipments it would have made anyway. A smaller manufacturer can face a more material constraint in qualifying a product or arranging finance. Published programme terms should make it possible to see whether new firms are reaching buyers and whether that support changes sales rather than merely relabelling existing business. The same logic applies to public trade missions. Introductions are valuable where they produce verification, orders and settled invoices.

A useful scorecard would also show concentration. A $1 billion rise spread across several products and buyers is more robust than a rise of the same size from one contract whose renewal is uncertain. The number of repeat buyers and exporters provides a check on that difference.

The case for counting energy trade

The strongest case for a broad bilateral target is that energy procurement can create meaningful savings and provide scale for a relationship in which other sectors develop more slowly. A country does not need balanced trade with each partner. India can gain by buying competitively priced inputs from Russia and exporting services or goods to other markets. The benefit from an energy purchase depends on the delivered price, reliability and risks, while the benefit from an export initiative depends on sales and margins. Assessing each separately avoids expecting Indian exporters to offset a goods deficit simply because the two flows involve the same partner. Commerce ministry’s 10 September statement · Business Standard on the bilateral trade baseline

What would establish that the relationship is broadening

Track non-energy exports in value and volume, repeat orders across products and buyers, payment times, and participation by firms that had not previously sold into the market. Distinguish newly cleared products from those already traded and measure how many customers return after an initial shipment. A material increase in settled, profitable sales would justify more work on the shared constraints that held them back. If headline turnover rises while the export mix stays narrow and firms report unchanged delivery and financing problems, the trade target will have advanced faster than the effort to diversify Indian exports. Commerce ministry’s 10 September statement · Business Standard on the bilateral trade baseline

    Three customs questions decide whether a trade deal’s tariff cut is real

title.rendered: India’s small current-account deficit masks a larger shift in financing

content.rendered:
India’s April–June external accounts show why a small current-account deficit can coexist with pressure on foreign-exchange financing. The RBI put the deficit at $4.2 billion, or 0.5 per cent of GDP, compared with a revised $3.4 billion and 0.4 per cent a year earlier. That small change hides a $17.2 billion deterioration in goods trade, most of which was offset by services and income flows. Meanwhile, portfolio investment shifted from net inflow to net outflow. The quarter’s lesson is that resilience in the current account and resilience in its financing depend on different sources of dollars. RBI’s April–June 2026 balance of payments release · Reuters on the April–June external accounts

Services and transfers absorbed most of the goods deterioration

The goods deficit increased from $68.9 billion to $86.1 billion. The deficit in petroleum, oil and lubricants widened from $32.2 billion to $37.6 billion. That accounts for $5.4 billion, about 31 per cent, of the overall goods deterioration using the rounded table. The remaining $11.8 billion was outside that petroleum line. Oil is material, but the quarter cannot be explained by the petroleum balance alone. It also matters that a rise in the dollar value of imports can reflect prices, quantities or a changed mix. The balance-of-payments table does not identify those contributions on its own. RBI’s April–June 2026 balance of payments release

Other current-account lines moved in India’s favour. Net services receipts rose from $47.9 billion to $51.6 billion, a gain of $3.7 billion. The primary income deficit, mainly reflecting investment income payments, narrowed by $2.8 billion to $10.5 billion. The net secondary income surplus rose by $9.9 billion to $40.8 billion. Together these changes offset roughly $16.4 billion of the $17.2 billion deterioration in goods trade. The residual, about $0.8 billion, matches the change in the headline deficit using the rounded figures. Personal transfer receipts rose to $42.9 billion, but that is a gross receipt and should not be added separately to the net secondary income line. RBI’s April–June 2026 balance of payments release

The offset reflects distinct economic activity. Services exports earn revenue from foreign customers, with the RBI reporting growth in computer, business and transportation services. Personal transfers mainly reflect remittances from Indians working abroad. A family using a remittance to finance household spending is affected by overseas labour demand and exchange rates. A services exporter financing domestic payroll faces the business conditions of its clients. Treating both as permanently available offsets would miss their separate risks. That matters especially if a global slowdown weakens demand for exported services and changes labour income or employment in countries where Indian workers are based. RBI’s April–June 2026 balance of payments release

The portfolio swing changes the immediate financing picture

Net direct investment rose from $5.2 billion to $6.1 billion. Portfolio investment moved from a $1.6 billion inflow to a $9.6 billion outflow, an $11.2 billion swing. The RBI recorded a decline in reserves of $8.1 billion on a balance-of-payments basis, against an increase of $4.5 billion a year earlier. These reserve transactions differ from the headline change in the dollar value of the reserve stock, which can also move because of valuation. They describe how the quarter’s accounts balanced on a transactions basis. The portfolio swing is one important part of the change, alongside other flows and the statistical discrepancy. RBI’s April–June 2026 balance of payments release · Reuters on the April–June external accounts

For scale, a hypothetical quarter with the same $4.2 billion current-account deficit and the same other flows, but with portfolio flows at the previous year’s $1.6 billion inflow, would have $11.2 billion more external financing available. That is accounting arithmetic. In an actual adjustment, the exchange rate, private borrowing, import spending or reserve transactions could move. The comparison shows why the financing question is consequential even when a forecast of the current-account deficit is nearly unchanged. RBI’s April–June 2026 balance of payments release

The difference also matters for Indian borrowers. A manufacturer with near-term dollar payments and little foreign-currency revenue can face higher hedging or financing costs when portfolio investors reduce exposure and the rupee becomes more volatile. A services exporter with foreign earnings can meet some dollar obligations directly. A bank or other borrower with a sizeable external maturity cannot rely on a small national current-account gap to refinance that maturity on good terms. The national accounting result aggregates positions with different currencies, durations and counterparties. Risk management belongs at that level as well as in the headline.

When a modest deficit is a sound outcome

The strongest argument for taking comfort from this quarter is that a 0.5 per cent current-account deficit is modest and the offsetting receipts are large and economically diverse. A larger goods deficit can also be consistent with productive investment, if imports include equipment that expands future output or exports. An increase in imports of capital equipment that is followed by domestic capacity and higher export earnings has a different implication from a recurring increase in an import bill with no corresponding improvement in productive capacity. Identifying the difference requires trade volumes and categories and evidence on what domestic firms are producing. RBI’s April–June 2026 balance of payments release

MoSPI’s first estimate puts April–June real GDP growth at 7.8 per cent and nominal GDP growth at 10.3 per cent. Strong domestic activity can coexist with weaker external financing because foreign portfolios respond to global rates, valuations and relative returns as well as Indian output. It can also increase import demand, depending on the mix of spending. To judge external sustainability, the useful question is what the imports enable and what dollar earnings can be expected over time. Real GDP growth measures changes in domestic activity. It gives little guidance to an external creditor on the value or timing of a borrower’s dollar cash flow. MoSPI’s initial April–June GDP estimate · RBI’s April–June 2026 balance of payments release

A response that seeks to compress imports across the board would also hit firms that need intermediate inputs and equipment to compete. A response that relies exclusively on attracting short-term portfolio flows would expose financing to movements in global rates and risk appetite. The better judgement depends on whether a pressure is temporary, whether borrowers can adjust and what other financing is available. Where the goods deterioration is due to a short price spike, smoothing the adjustment can be reasonable. A persistent financing imbalance would make it more important to assess what is supporting import demand and whether export earnings are likely to keep pace.

The type of inflow can matter even when the amounts match. A long-term investor financing a new plant can share operating risk with the firm. A short-dated foreign-currency loan creates a fixed payment obligation that can become expensive to refinance. Reporting gross as well as net flows helps reveal those exposures when inflows and repayments are both large. RBI’s April–June 2026 balance of payments release

The ratio to GDP also deserves care. A modest percentage expresses the deficit relative to the size of the economy, while the dollar amount is closer to the immediate scale of financing. A low ratio alongside shorter debt maturities or larger gross payments can still conceal exposure to rollover conditions. Both measures belong in a quarterly assessment. RBI’s April–June 2026 balance of payments release

What would make the headline deficit more reassuring

Compare non-petroleum goods balances in value and volume, to see whether the deterioration reflects prices or an underlying change in trade. Monitor the persistence and composition of services receipts and transfers, including whether growth extends across major sources. Examine financing by instrument and maturity, along with reserve transactions and the costs Indian borrowers face in hedging or rolling over debt. A quarter of net portfolio selling can reflect global repricing. Repeated outflows together with rising refinancing costs and weaker services receipts would tell a more concerning story. RBI’s April–June 2026 balance of payments release

The current-account deficit gives a measure of the gap between external current receipts and payments. It gives less guidance on how easily that gap will be financed through the next disruption. India’s April–June accounts are more reassuring where services receipts and transfers are durable. They warrant more attention where import demand remains firm, portfolio flows reverse and firms face near-term foreign-currency obligations. The next data should show which of those movements persists. RBI’s April–June 2026 balance of payments release · Reuters on the April–June external accounts

excerpt.rendered: Services and transfers absorbed most of the deterioration in goods trade. A swing in portfolio flows and reserve transactions tells a different story about financing.

title.rendered: Drip irrigation can save water on a plot while a district pumps more

content.rendered:
A drip line can reduce the water needed for a hectare of a particular crop. At district level, the outcome depends on whether farmers irrigate the same hectares, expand acreage or switch to crops with higher water demand. India’s Per Drop More Crop programme has financed extensive uptake. Its productivity case should be assessed separately from any claim that it slows groundwater depletion. A good programme can deliver more income per unit of water and still require complementary rules to reduce total extraction. PIB, Per Drop More Crop · Central Ground Water Board, 2025 national assessment

What the public subsidy buys

The August government note reports more than 115 lakh hectares brought under micro-irrigation by July 2026. Under the described scheme, small and marginal farmers receive assistance of 55%, others 45%, with support up to five hectares per beneficiary. These are programme rules and cumulative coverage measures. Whether a system works as intended depends on pressure, maintenance, water access and the farmer’s ability to replace clogged or damaged components. Subsidising installation can encourage entry. The farmer and dealer still make decisions that determine operating performance. PIB, Per Drop More Crop

A farmer using water more efficiently can raise income by planting a higher-value crop, cutting labour costs or stabilising output when water is scarce. These are legitimate benefits. If electricity or water is cheap at the margin, the same farmer has a reason to reinvest the saved water in more production. An adoption subsidy leaves that incentive largely intact.

The rebound arithmetic

Imagine a group irrigating 100 hectares at 5,000 cubic metres per hectare a season, drawing 500,000 cubic metres. After adopting drip irrigation, the same crop needs 3,500 cubic metres per hectare in this illustrative example. Keeping acreage constant cuts withdrawals to 350,000 cubic metres. Expanding irrigated area to 150 hectares increases withdrawals to 525,000 cubic metres, 5% more than before. The per-hectare improvement is 30% throughout. A programme report focused on the device’s efficiency and hectares served could show progress in both cases while district withdrawals move in opposite directions.

The aquifer adds another complication. Part of the water applied through conventional methods can return to groundwater under some local conditions. Measuring withdrawals alone can therefore differ from measuring net depletion. Local hydrogeology and whether excess application flows back into the same resource matter. Estimates should distinguish crop water consumption, withdrawals and return flows wherever the data permit.

The case for pairing incentives

The strongest argument for a broad equipment subsidy is that farmers face capital constraints and an uncertain first season. Collective rules on extraction can be hard to implement, while a device can deliver immediate yield and income gains. That is a reason to assess micro-irrigation on those grounds. Where water tables are falling, a credible extraction policy still has to deal with the value of expanded acreage. Community budgets or measured supply can make the conservation objective explicit, with safeguards for farmers who depend on a small initial allotment.

Evaluate adopters over several seasons against similar farms and groundwater units. Track hectares actually irrigated, crop choice, pump hours where measured, and changes in water levels relative to rainfall and recharge. Record systems taken out of use and the cost of keeping them running. Higher net farm income after maintenance would support the productivity case. Measured extraction falling relative to comparable areas would support the resource case. If only the first result appears, the subsidy may remain justified while the conservation claim calls for a different instrument.

The distribution of gains also matters. A farmer with secure water access can expand acreage, while one with a shallow or shared well may receive only the productivity gain on existing land. A public evaluation should report those outcomes separately, since identical equipment can change the two households’ incomes and water use in different ways.

The best use of micro-irrigation is to make agriculture more productive with each unit of water. A district saves water when the units used across all farms also fall.

excerpt.rendered: India’s micro-irrigation subsidy can lift farm productivity. Its value for groundwater depends on what farmers do with the water they save.

title.rendered: What drove India’s 7.8% growth, and what would show private investment following it?

content.rendered:
India’s economy grew 7.8% year on year in April–June, according to the national accounts released on 31 August. Household consumption and fixed investment each added about four percentage points to the expenditure-side calculation. That is a stronger domestic demand picture than the headline alone conveys. The evidence on who invested is less complete. The quarterly fixed investment line combines public and private spending, including household investment. A broad private investment recovery remains a question for company and project data. MoSPI release and statements · Contemporary Reuters coverage.

Where the 7.8% came from

MoSPI estimates real GDP at ₹81.36 lakh crore, up from ₹75.46 lakh crore in the same quarter a year earlier, on the 2022–23 base. Real private final consumption grew 7.1%, and real gross fixed capital formation grew 11.9%. The faster-growing item was the smaller of the two. That is why their contributions to GDP growth are almost identical. In constant-price crore, consumption rose from ₹41,76,184 crore to ₹44,74,278 crore. Fixed investment rose from ₹24,97,280 crore to ₹27,95,605 crore. Divide each change by the prior-year quarter’s GDP of ₹75,46,230 crore and multiply by 100. Each adds about 3.95 percentage points. MoSPI expenditure table at constant prices.

That calculation is an accounting decomposition. It describes where expenditure changed. It does not estimate the effect of a tax cut, a change in interest rates or a public project. Government consumption added about 0.47 percentage points. Exports added 2.73 points, and lower real imports added 0.29 because imports are subtracted in the expenditure identity. Changes in stocks and valuables together subtracted about 0.36 points. The change in the statistical discrepancy subtracted about 3.21 points. The pieces add to about 7.82% using the displayed figures, with a small rounding difference. A large movement in the discrepancy makes it especially important to show the full calculation. The discrepancy reconciles estimates compiled from different sources. It should not be assigned to a sector or treated as a measure of spending.

The export and import terms also need care. They are the real national-accounts estimates for goods and services. A positive net export contribution in this calculation can coexist with a large nominal goods deficit, especially when energy prices or the exchange rate move. A country can pay a larger rupee bill for the same volume of imported inputs. The balance of payments adds still more categories, including primary income and transfers. This quarterly growth contribution answers how trade volumes enter the GDP identity at constant prices. It answers a different question from how India financed its dollar payments.

The case for a broader investment recovery

There is evidence consistent with strengthening private demand. The GDP release’s indicator annex shows capital goods production up 15.2% year on year and commercial vehicle sales up 18.3%. The RBI’s separate study of 3,247 listed non-government, non-financial companies reports year-on-year sales growth of 19.4%, up from 13.9% the previous quarter. Listed manufacturing operating profit grew 21.3%, compared with 9.4% in the preceding quarter. Stronger earnings can improve the ability to finance investment internally, and machinery or vehicle purchases are closer to investment decisions than a change in sentiment. These figures support taking the private recovery hypothesis seriously. MoSPI indicator annex · RBI listed-company results.

The strongest version of the argument is that stronger household demand improved expected sales, which encouraged firms to order equipment before capacity became tight. This would let capital goods production and credit growth move together. The difficulty is identifying the buyer of the equipment and the use of the credit. Public infrastructure projects buy machinery and vehicles too. A rise in bank credit can finance working capital, refinancing or lending through other financial institutions. Better operating profits can go into debt repayment or cash reserves. The listed-company sample also has much better coverage of large companies than of the small suppliers whose expansion would make the recovery broad.

What the government accounts can tell us

The Controller General of Accounts reports ₹3,40,258 crore of Union capital expenditure through June, equal to 27.8% of the full-year Budget Estimate. The corresponding fraction a year earlier was 24.5%. Loans disbursed accounted for ₹1,00,579 crore of this year’s first-quarter figure. Those are provisional nominal cash-account figures. They provide evidence on the timing of Union expenditure, and they should not be subtracted from national-accounts investment. Loans can finance spending elsewhere and at a different time. State accounts, public enterprises and households each need to be measured on their own terms. CGA June accounts.

The distribution matters even if the aggregate investment number is eventually revised very little. A road project can raise demand for cement and construction labour before its effect on productivity appears. A highly automated plant can raise equipment spending and output with a much smaller change in headcount. Growth in listed manufacturing profits can support investment, but it says little about the cash position of an unlisted supplier waiting for an invoice to be paid. Household consumption can rise in the aggregate while spending remains weak in places facing high food prices or seasonal work losses. Employment, hours, and real pay belong alongside the output and expenditure data.

The year-on-year comparison also uses a newly revised baseline. MoSPI says the historical quarter and full-year estimates in the release incorporate new producer price indices, the revised industrial production series and updated administrative inputs. Manufacturing value added now uses separate price indices for output and intermediate inputs. When input prices rise faster than output prices, the implied price measure for value added can decline even as both sets of prices rise. The release notes this possibility explicitly. It matters during an energy shock because a reported change in real manufacturing value added can reflect production, input use and a shift in the relative prices used to deflate them. Any comparison with a previous release should identify the earlier vintage before attributing the difference to firms’ behaviour. MoSPI methodology and revisions.

For a policy reader, the strongest early signal would be a three-way agreement between realised capital spending in company accounts, physical investment indicators and a broadening of new projects across industries. Each by itself is incomplete. Together they can narrow the gap between a national-accounts total and the decisions managers are making about future capacity. Collecting the same evidence by company size and industry would also show whether the expansion is concentrated or reaches suppliers outside the largest balance sheets.

What would make the evidence convincing

The next test should track private project commitments against actual installation or commissioning. Compare investment reported by listed companies with borrowing for new projects, and check whether orders spread beyond the largest companies and government-linked sectors. Use Union and state expenditure for the same period and keep loans, transfers and direct purchases visible. If machinery orders, implemented projects and private capital spending rise together over several quarters, the private investment interpretation becomes stronger. If spending stays concentrated in public works and a small number of listed firms, the 11.9% aggregate will still be real growth in fixed investment, with a narrower implication for private demand.

This release supports two conclusions. Household consumption made a large contribution to growth, and the amount of real fixed investment rose substantially. The evidence needed to judge how widely private firms participated sits in balance sheets, project implementation and sector-level orders. That is the distinction that should guide the next report on whether the economy can sustain this pace.

excerpt.rendered: Household consumption and fixed investment each contributed about four percentage points to real growth. Company accounts and project data will help show how widely the investment recovery spread.

title.rendered: Street vendors need working capital that raises earnings after repayment

content.rendered:
India’s street-vendor credit programme will have its largest payoff where it helps viable vendors turn over stock more profitably or replace expensive borrowing. The housing ministry’s 27 August update reports 21.86 lakh loans worth ₹6,294 crore during the first year after PM SVANidhi was restructured, and reports 10.56 lakh new beneficiaries. Those figures establish substantial lending activity. They cannot establish that the businesses are earning more, that informal borrowing has fallen or that loans are reaching vendors who previously lacked access. Those outcomes should determine where the programme expands and what complementary support it finances. Housing ministry’s first-year PM SVANidhi update · Cabinet decision restructuring PM SVANidhi

The loan buys inventory, time or a cheaper source of funds

The Cabinet extended lending under the restructured scheme to 31 March 2030 and approved a ₹7,332 crore total outlay. It raised the maximum first and second loan tranches from ₹10,000 and ₹20,000 to ₹15,000 and ₹25,000. The third tranche remains ₹50,000. A tranche structure can allow a lender to extend a smaller sum while building a repayment record. It can also help the vendor move gradually towards the amount needed. The public outlay is the cost envelope for the scheme, while loan disbursements are principal extended by lenders. Comparing them as if they were the same financial measure would give a misleading account of programme costs. Cabinet decision restructuring PM SVANidhi

For a fruit seller with predictable demand, an extra stock purchase can support sales that would otherwise be lost after the stall runs out. Access to cash can also let the seller buy from a wholesaler who offers a better price for larger lots. A vendor can benefit without buying more inventory if formal credit replaces costly borrowing used for the same sales. Those are different mechanisms. The first should show up in stock availability, sales or margins. The second should show up in financing costs and the composition of borrowing, even if the business sells the same quantity.

A profitable sale is different from enough cash to repay

Suppose a vendor uses ₹15,000 to finance an incremental batch of stock. At full sell-through, assume sales of ₹18,000, with ₹1,000 of additional transport and other operating costs. That would leave ₹2,000 before financing and the vendor’s own labour. If sales are 15 per cent below the assumption and the remaining stock has no resale value, receipts fall to ₹15,300, leaving a ₹700 loss before financing. The illustrative loan principal has to be repaid in both cases. Whether more credit improves the vendor’s position depends on demand, the risk of unsold goods and the timing of payments. The rupee figures are assumptions, not typical vendor margins.

The gap between profit and cash flow can be especially important for perishable goods. Borrowing costs may be lower on a formal loan, but repayment dates may still arrive after a poor week of sales. A flexible supplier may allow delayed payment at a high implicit price, while a cheaper formal lender may offer less flexibility when receipts are volatile. Looking at the annual interest charge alone misses that trade-off. Evidence on arrears, repeat borrowing and use of supplier credit would show whether formal credit is replacing costly obligations or being added on top of them.

Eligibility and the right to trade affect the same business

A parliamentary committee’s review of PM SVANidhi, summarised by PRS, identified how local surveys and documentation affect access. A certificate or a letter of recommendation can establish eligibility, including for a vendor who was missed in an earlier survey. The application record starts too late if a person has been unable to obtain the required document. A district with few rejected applications can still have low access if unrecognised vendors never submit one. Outreach should track who applied for documentation, how long it took and who obtained a loan after receiving it. PRS summary of the parliamentary committee’s review

A secure place to trade can matter as much as more inventory. A vendor who expects to lose a selling location has less reason to borrow to expand stock and may face higher loss rates. Conversely, credit can be valuable when a vendor has regular customers and needs cash to cope with higher wholesale prices. The ministry’s 2026 update describes additional work on vending infrastructure and street food hubs. To determine whether that spending complements loans, compare outcomes for otherwise similar vendors with and without secure, usable locations, allowing for differences in footfall and product mix. Housing ministry’s first-year PM SVANidhi update · PRS summary of the parliamentary committee’s review

The first-year totals imply roughly ₹28,800 of principal per reported loan when ₹6,294 crore is divided by 21.86 lakh loans. That is a ratio of administrative aggregates. It is above the first-tranche ceiling and should not be read as the amount received by a new vendor or the typical amount available for an initial purchase. Reporting a distribution by tranche, loan size and prior borrowing would show how much of the headline volume reflects first access and how much reflects repeat lending. The distinction also matters for evaluating inclusion. A programme can reach its volume target by making larger subsequent loans while leaving the number of new borrowers well short of its goal. Housing ministry’s first-year PM SVANidhi update · Cabinet decision restructuring PM SVANidhi

Access to a digital payment record can help establish what a business sells and when, though payment data capture receipts processed digitally rather than profit. If cash purchases shift to digital payments, the number of recorded transactions can increase without an increase in sales. A vendor’s actual gain depends on the balance of revenue, inventory costs, losses, fees and borrowing costs. Payment data can help with that assessment when combined with brief, credible expenditure and stock surveys. Treating transaction volume alone as evidence of stronger livelihoods would overstate what the administrative data show. Housing ministry’s first-year PM SVANidhi update

The case for scaling before every outcome is known

The strongest argument for maintaining and extending the programme is that working-capital loans can fill a gap for viable enterprises with little collateral or formal credit history. It is reasonable to learn from actual borrowing and repayment as the programme operates. Yet repeat loans can reflect either productive growth or a need to refinance an unstable business, and repayment can be supported by money earned elsewhere in the household. A loan programme can look strong to the lender while providing only modest improvement to the borrower. The right comparison asks how vendors would have financed operations and how they would have performed without the offer. Cabinet decision restructuring PM SVANidhi · Housing ministry’s first-year PM SVANidhi update

There are credible ways to make that comparison without delaying service everywhere. A phased outreach effort can compare groups of eligible vendors receiving help with documentation or applications at different times. A panel can record revenue, stock losses, net earnings, borrowing costs and vending days before and after first access. The sample should retain applicants who were rejected, those who leave vending and those who choose to borrow elsewhere. Comparing only vendors who take and repay a second loan would omit people for whom the first loan was a poor fit.

The public return should be measured after costs

Report the number of unique new borrowers separately from the number of loans, the share progressing through tranches and how their net earnings and total debt change. Compare those outcomes with programme administration, interest support and credit losses. If vendors earn more, rely less on costly loans and repay without increasing distress, the case for expanding formal credit strengthens. If the largest gains appear only where vending is already secure, improving access to legal trading space may buy more than raising loan limits in less stable markets. The 27 August numbers show that the programme can lend at scale. The next evidence should show what that scale is doing for vendors’ incomes. Housing ministry’s first-year PM SVANidhi update · PRS summary of the parliamentary committee’s review

excerpt.rendered: PM SVANidhi has widened access to formal credit. The test is whether vendors earn more after financing costs and have enough stability to use the loans productively.

title.rendered: Chennai’s water loan should be judged by reliable hours of service

content.rendered:
The $230 million loan India has signed with the Asian Development Bank for Chennai should be judged by the reliability of service it buys. The 21 August announcement describes an investment in water supply and sanitation, including a ring-main arrangement intended to improve distribution and pressure. Those features are economically valuable if households can depend on safe water at predictable times and if the utility can continue operating the system after construction. The amount borrowed and the length of new pipe establish the scale of investment. They give limited information about who gets a better service. Finance ministry announcement of the Chennai loan · ADB’s Chennai loan announcement

What a more connected network can change

A network that can supply an area through more than one route can give the operator flexibility when a component fails or local demand changes. Managing pressure matters because intermittent or low-pressure supply can force households to store water, buy from other sources or spend time arranging delivery. These costs can differ across adjacent streets even when the citywide supply is unchanged. The project should therefore publish the distribution of service hours and interruptions, along with pressure and quality measures, for households and areas previously receiving weaker service. Finance ministry announcement of the Chennai loan · ADB’s Chennai loan announcement

Consider a hypothetical household that buys four tanker deliveries a year at ₹1,000 each and spends another ₹1,500 on coping costs such as pumping and storage. If reliable service eliminates three purchases and half of the other cost, the household saves ₹3,750 annually before tariff changes. An extra ₹200 on the monthly utility bill would leave an illustrative net financial saving of ₹1,350. Those assumptions are neither typical Chennai costs nor a recommended tariff. They show why the household impact depends on what it previously paid to cope, the quality of the new service and the price it is asked to pay.

The same arithmetic can look different for a family that could not afford private water in the first place. Its expenditure saving may be small while its welfare gain is substantial, because it can use more safe water or spend less time obtaining it. A survey should measure time, interruptions and service quality alongside expenditures. Average monetary savings can understate benefits for the worst-served households. Conversely, an apparent improvement in willingness to pay can come from better service among high-income customers while poorer areas still experience interruptions.

The utility needs an operating plan as well as capital

Network investment can change the costs of energy, maintenance, testing and responding to failures. It can also improve cash flow if reliable service increases connections, reduces losses or makes payment more acceptable. A financial model should keep those channels separate. Savings from lower leakage depend on actual pressure management, repairs and metering. More billed volume does not provide the same benefit as cash collected. A project can improve welfare and still require an explicit operating subsidy. That choice should be visible in the utility’s budget and made with reference to the service being funded. Finance ministry announcement of the Chennai loan · ADB’s Chennai loan announcement

Sewerage also creates benefits beyond an individual customer. A connection and a working treatment chain can reduce risks for other households and the wider environment. This gives a case for using general revenue or grants to fund part of the cost where full recovery through charges would leave many households unconnected. The case should be matched to actual connection take-up and treatment performance. Financing pipes for people who cannot afford to connect gives a lower public return than a programme that identifies and addresses the connection cost in advance. Finance ministry announcement of the Chennai loan

The case for prioritising capacity first

The strongest counterargument is that expanding and modernising basic infrastructure is a prerequisite for more reliable service. It can be hard to promise an outcome before a network exists, and cost overruns or construction delays deserve attention in their own right. The correct response is to measure both. Track physical progress and then measure how each completed segment changes access, interruptions and service quality in the areas it was meant to serve. Early household measurements give the utility a baseline and can reveal whether to adjust operations or prioritise a connection before the entire project is complete. ADB’s Chennai loan announcement

Water reliability is best measured at a time scale relevant to the household. A monthly average can hide several consecutive days without supply, which is when storage is depleted and emergency purchases become necessary. The same average hours of supply can be delivered regularly or in unpredictable bursts. An outcome report should show the longest outages, how often customers receive advance notice and which areas lose service during a network failure. That information can guide operating changes even after the capital budget has been committed.

The utility should also track the time between observing a leak and repairing it. Better monitoring can initially increase the number of reported faults because more of them are discovered. A faster repair rate and improved pressure can show that the underlying service is getting better even when raw incident counts rise. The distinction matters when deciding which operating practices another city can adopt before funding a similar network.

The results that would justify replication

Publish baseline and follow-up service hours, quality failures, interruption durations, connection rates and household coping costs for comparable areas. Compare operating expenditure and cash collections with the assumptions made at appraisal. Where construction is phased, use the timing to compare neighbourhoods receiving work earlier with similar areas waiting for it, while accounting for weather and other changes. The loan will have financed lasting progress if the new system delivers safer and more predictable service to households that previously had to improvise. A large construction programme whose benefits disappear whenever pressure or maintenance falls would have a different lesson for other cities. Finance ministry announcement of the Chennai loan · ADB’s Chennai loan announcement

excerpt.rendered: A $230 million loan will help finance Chennai’s water and sanitation network. Reliable supply and lower household coping costs are the outcomes to test.

title.rendered: India’s July jobs rebound needs a second measure of work

content.rendered:
India’s July labour-market figures provide evidence that a larger share of adults worked. The next question is whether they worked enough hours and earned enough to strengthen household incomes. The Periodic Labour Force Survey shows the national worker-population ratio rising from 51.4 per cent in June to 52.5 per cent in July, while unemployment fell from 5.5 to 5.1 per cent of the labour force. That combination is stronger evidence of improved access to some work than a falling unemployment rate alone. It leaves open whether the additional work was regular, paid and likely to continue after the agricultural season. MoSPI’s July PLFS monthly bulletin · Reuters on India’s July labour-market figures

The rural gain was larger than the national average suggests

The July bulletin, for people aged 15 and older under current weekly status, puts the rural worker-population ratio at 55.4 per cent, up from 53.8 in June and 54.4 a year earlier. The urban rate was 47.0 per cent, unchanged from July 2025. Rural women’s ratio rose from 34.7 per cent in June to 37.2 in July. Urban women’s ratio rose more modestly, from 22.7 to 23.1 per cent. These comparisons point to a larger increase outside cities. The one-year comparison helps with seasonality, though variation in rainfall and the timing of crop work can still change how much labour is needed in the same calendar month. MoSPI’s July PLFS monthly bulletin

The worker-population ratio is the share of the specified population counted as working. It differs from the unemployment rate, which divides the unemployed by the labour force. A one-percentage-point change in one series therefore has a different meaning from a one-point change in the other. For every 10,000 rural women aged 15 and older in an illustrative population, moving from a 34.7 to a 37.2 per cent worker-population ratio corresponds to 250 more people classified as workers. It does not identify those people or show that they entered long-term jobs. These are survey estimates for successive periods, not a count of individual transitions. MoSPI’s July PLFS monthly bulletin

Hours and paid work can give the same headline different meanings

Suppose, for illustration, those 250 additional workers each worked eight hours in a week. They would add 2,000 hours. If they each worked 35 hours, they would add 8,750. A measure of how many people worked would register the same change in the two cases. Earnings and output could be very different, as could the value of the jobs to workers who want more hours. The example holds hours for existing workers fixed. In practice those hours can rise or fall too, which is why the change in the headcount alone cannot establish the change in total labour input.

Work in a family enterprise can generate valuable output and income even when the individual worker is not paid a wage. But the distribution of that income within the household matters. Paid employment can increase a worker’s direct control over earnings, while helping in a family business can be a better fit for local opportunities or care responsibilities. Survey evidence on employment status, hours and payment would help distinguish those circumstances. The July headline cannot establish which type of work accounted for the increase, or whether households chose the extra work because returns improved or because other income was weak.

A seasonal rise in crop work is a credible possibility, especially when rural employment rises more quickly than urban employment. It is a hypothesis about the mechanism. A test would compare crop calendars, rainfall and changes in farm and non-farm employment over comparable periods, then check whether the increase survives after seasonal tasks pass. Districts with different crop schedules offer a better comparison than treating India’s rural economy as one labour market. The distinction matters for interpreting employment as an indicator of consumption, since a brief spell of work and a recurring earnings stream support spending differently. MoSPI’s July PLFS monthly bulletin · Reuters on India’s July labour-market figures

The urban figures pose a different question

The bulletin reports urban women’s unemployment at 8.8 per cent, up from 8.4 in June, even as their participation and employment ratios rose. That combination can arise when more women enter the labour force and the increase in work is insufficient to absorb all of them. It could also reflect changes in who is searching and where, which the national aggregates cannot resolve. Evaluating urban demand requires data on job vacancies, hours and wages, including which jobs are accessible within reasonable commuting time. A growing number of applicants can be an encouraging sign of willingness to work and an indication that job creation is lagging their entry. MoSPI’s July PLFS monthly bulletin

The policy response depends on that distinction. Where firms have vacancies but applicants cannot reach jobs or fit working hours around care, transport and childcare can improve access. Where vacancies are scarce or poorly paid, training alone can expand the number of people looking for the same work. In areas where small firms want to hire but cannot count on orders or working capital, interventions aimed at firm demand might do more for sustained employment. The July release can direct investigation towards the relevant labour markets, but it is not a diagnosis of the binding constraint in any of them.

It would also be useful to separate workers who wanted additional hours from those who chose shorter schedules. A rise in short-hours work with little unmet demand for more time is different from a rise in short-hours work among people actively seeking additional paid work. The first can signal improved flexibility, the second insufficient demand for labour. Survey questions on availability for more work, combined with earnings and employment status, would help distinguish the two. This matters for deciding whether expanding access to short jobs is a useful goal in itself or whether the priority should be to increase hours and pay in existing jobs.

Why a headcount gain still matters

The strongest argument for treating July as a meaningful improvement is that a larger share of adults worked while a smaller share of the labour force was unemployed. Work with short hours can be valuable to a person who prefers it or has limited time. Seasonal work can arrive at a useful moment for a household. The increase should be taken seriously even if the bulletin cannot measure its quality in the headline. The question is whether the same improvement appears in paid work, desired hours and real income. Those measures can refine the interpretation without dismissing the evidence of a wider employment base. MoSPI’s July PLFS monthly bulletin

The timing of measurement also deserves attention. Weekly status responds to work people did in the recent reference period. That makes it sensitive to changes in current activity, including interruptions and short spells. Measures of usual employment or earnings over longer periods answer different questions about stability. Comparing them when available can show whether a better month is part of a lasting change. Where estimates are close, sampling uncertainty and rounding also matter. A small apparent difference between groups should be treated more cautiously than a change that persists across successive readings and appears in related measures. MoSPI’s July PLFS monthly bulletin

The evidence that would turn a rebound into a recovery

Track paid and unpaid work, hours actually worked and desired, and inflation-adjusted earnings where comparable estimates are available. Use seasonal comparisons and examine whether urban hiring absorbs additional participants. If rural gains persist after peak crop work and are accompanied by greater hours or better real earnings, the case for a sustained improvement strengthens. If headcounts rise while hours and pay stagnate, the immediate policy question is how to create more remunerative work for people who already have some. July’s figures justify looking for those answers in the next set of labour-market evidence. MoSPI’s July PLFS monthly bulletin

Part of a series

Reading India’s jobs data

What the monthly labour surveys and payroll data can and cannot tell us about work in India.
