Testing India’s subsidies

Semiconductors, AI compute, minerals, green hydrogen, small hydro and factory power: what each subsidy should be made to deliver.

title.rendered: India’s inland waterways should compete on the cost of a repeat shipment

content.rendered:
An inland vessel can move bulk cargo cheaply on its main leg and still lose the shipment to a truck. The shipper buys a door-to-door journey, with transfers, inventory time and a date by which the cargo must arrive. The July parliamentary reply on Maritime India Vision 2030 reports inland waterways traffic of 218.24 million tonnes in FY 2025–26, above the vision document’s stated 200 million tonne target for 2030. The next question is which routes can win repeat business on commercial terms after the full cost of the journey is counted. Parliamentary reply, Maritime India Vision 2030 · NCAER, Assessment of Logistics Cost in India

Why tonnes do not reveal the price of the alternative

Large cargo volumes can reflect several successful bulk corridors, a change in the composition of traffic or a public commitment to shift freight. A port, steel plant or power station near a navigable channel faces a different transport choice from a small manufacturer a long way from a terminal. A national tonnage total is valuable for observing scale. A route decision needs the price and service on the relevant road, rail and water options.

Low cost on the water leg depends on regular loading and commercially useful quantities. A vessel departing with a half load still incurs crew, capital and fuel costs. A return leg without cargo has to be funded by the outward customer or by some other revenue. A seasonal loss of navigability can force the company to maintain a road contract even when most traffic moves by water. The effective cost includes the capacity required for those backup weeks.

A transfer can decide the bid

Suppose road transport costs ₹1,200 per tonne door to door. A water leg costs ₹650, with ₹180 of terminal handling at each end and ₹220 of combined road connections. That totals ₹1,230 before the cost of inventory and possible delays. A plant with its own waterfront terminal can eliminate part of the ₹580 outside the main water leg. A landlocked producer may have little room to reduce it. The route can be attractive to one firm and uncompetitive for its neighbour without any difference in waterborne freight rates.

Now suppose the cargo is low value and the buyer can accept a regular, slower schedule. Inventory financing might be a small share of delivered cost. For a high-value input with a tight production window, a longer trip and less frequent service can make an ostensibly cheaper water bid costly. Publishing transit-time distributions would help shippers choose. It would also discourage investment proposals that compare a reliable road quote with the best-case sailing time.

The infrastructure case

The strongest argument for continuing public support is that terminals and channel maintenance create a common network that individual shippers cannot build. Early public investment can coordinate firms that would use a route only if several others do too. Some routes may also have environmental and road-congestion benefits. The public case should count those gains, the cost of dredging and maintenance, effects on river users and the private alternatives. A tonnage target gives little guidance on how much to spend per additional tonne moved on a specific route.

Track repeat commercial users, backhaul utilisation, year-round service days, transfer costs and the share of traffic that would move by water without recurring incentives. Compare users at a similar distance from terminals, and record cargo that returns to road after a trial. If costs fall as networks thicken and repeat users continue to renew, there is a case for scaling. If traffic depends on a few mandated flows and backup freight remains expensive, the more defensible investment may be targeted terminals and better links for the cargo that fits the route.

The government also reports initiatives to connect inland waterways to other modes. Each connection should be evaluated at the freight flows it changes. A dedicated terminal can improve a single bulk route. An open-access connection with predictable slots could serve a wider catchment if shippers can use it at commercial rates. Parliamentary reply, inland waterways and multimodal connectivity

The test is whether a shipper rebooks after paying for the whole trip.

excerpt.rendered: Traffic has expanded. Long-run viability depends on seasonal service, transfers and whether ships carry cargo in both directions.

title.rendered: China’s second-quarter slowdown made the composition of growth more important

content.rendered:
China’s growth rebalancing · Part 4 · July national accounts

China reported 4.3% year-on-year real GDP growth in the second quarter of 2026 and 4.7% for the first half. The first-quarter pace was 5.0% in the preliminary series. The slowdown strengthened the case for watching how growth is financed and sold. A factory can maintain output by cutting prices or building inventory. That can preserve production today while weakening the incentive to invest and hire tomorrow. China NBS, preliminary second-quarter GDP · China State Council, 2026 Government Work Report

Follow the gap between volume and cash

Companies pay wages, interest and suppliers in nominal currency. Real industrial activity can expand while nominal sales and profit grow more slowly if output prices fall. A highly indebted firm may then delay investment even when it produces more physical goods. A firm competing on stronger product quality or lower unit costs can cut prices and remain profitable. The same volume and price observations can have different implications depending on margins and productivity.

Consider a producer selling one million units at 100 yuan. If volumes rise 5% and prices fall 6%, revenue falls from 100 million to 98.7 million yuan. If unit costs stay at 80 yuan, gross contribution before overhead falls from 20 million to 14.7 million yuan. A strong reduction in cost would change the result. The example shows why output statistics alone cannot answer whether demand supports another round of expansion.

Test a claim of excessive capacity at the industry level

Falling prices can reward consumers and international buyers. They can also indicate excess capacity when utilisation and returns fall and producers continue investing because financing is cheap or demand forecasts are optimistic. A simple price decline is insufficient evidence. Compare capacity utilisation, inventory days, realised profits and the entry and exit of firms. Some sectors will show productivity gains while others are selling at low margins to maintain cash flow.

An argument for prioritising the real GDP number is that falling prices can be part of a successful adjustment and make higher living standards affordable. That possibility matters. It is stronger when households’ real earnings rise, firms improve productivity and credit goes to businesses with repeat demand. It is weaker when margins deteriorate and producers need to roll working capital to maintain the same activity.

The October release offers a test: did GDP recover alongside household purchases and broader investment, or did a few industries carry the improvement? The answer has implications for competitors abroad. Growing output sold profitably can sustain equipment orders and wages. Output moved mainly through price cuts can make the immediate pressure on overseas producers greater while offering them less evidence of durable Chinese demand.

China’s growth rebalancing
Previous · Part 3 · All installments · Next · Part 5

excerpt.rendered: Growth eased from 5.0% in the first quarter to 4.3% in the second. Production, profits and domestic demand can respond at different speeds.

title.rendered: The UK–India trade deal’s real test is whether firms can use it

content.rendered:
The UK–India Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement entered into force on 15 July. India’s Commerce Ministry reported that more than 50 consignments, worth over US$140 million, were flagged off under the preferential regime on the first day. It also issued the first certificates of origin through its electronic platform. Those are useful signs that the system can handle real shipments. The economic question is how many firms will keep using it after the launch, and whether lower duties generate orders that would otherwise have gone elsewhere. India’s Ministry of Commerce and Industry, 15 July release · UK Department for Business and Trade, 15 July release

The deal deserves support. It makes the UK more accessible to Indian manufacturers in sectors such as clothing, textiles and footwear, where export demand can support employment. The priority for New Delhi should now be to make the tariff preference cheap and predictable to claim, then measure whether orders, volumes and employment actually follow. The headline coverage figure tells firms where an opportunity exists. The cost of using the agreement will determine how widely that opportunity is taken up. UK Department for Business and Trade, impact assessment · CETA Chapter 3 and its rules of origin

The starting point is a services-heavy trading relationship

The UK’s June trade factsheet puts bilateral trade in goods and services at £47.9 billion in the four quarters through December 2025. That was 10% higher than the previous four quarters in current prices, before CETA entered into force. From the UK’s perspective, services accounted for £17.5 billion of its £28.7 billion of imports from India, or about 61%. Goods imported from India amounted to £11.2 billion. These are observed trade flows. The two economies already had an expanding commercial relationship against which future changes have to be judged. UK Department for Business and Trade, June 2026 bilateral factsheet

The British government’s impact assessment models bilateral trade about £25.5 billion a year higher in the long run, approximately 39% above its projected no-agreement baseline. It estimates India’s long-run GDP level about 0.06% higher and the UK’s about 0.13% higher. The pound values use projections for 2040. These estimates depend on how households and firms adjust to the agreement, including whether lower barriers are used in practice. The large percentage effect on bilateral trade can coexist with a modest GDP effect because two-way trade is only one part of either economy. UK Department for Business and Trade, impact assessment

A tariff preference is worth its margin after compliance

India’s Commerce Ministry describes zero-duty access for nearly 99% of its exports to the UK. For an individual supplier, the economically relevant figure is the margin over the duty that would otherwise apply. A product already entering duty-free offers little immediate tariff saving. A product facing a meaningful duty can be much more attractive to a UK buyer once its eligibility is established. Comparing tariffs at the product level matters because exporters competing with suppliers that already enjoy preferential access can gain a great deal from closing even a modest tariff gap. India’s Ministry of Commerce and Industry, 15 July release · CETA Chapter 2 and tariff schedules

Origin rules determine whether a product qualifies. The treaty defines when a good counts as originating and provides product-specific rules. A garment assembled in India from imported fabric may face a different qualification test from a garment whose inputs and production are traceable to domestic suppliers. Checking that test, collecting documentation and allocating staff time all carry a cost. The UK Parliament’s Business and Trade Committee identified compliance costs and complicated origin rules as reasons smaller companies may use the agreement less. India’s digital origin process is a promising first step. Exporters will still need predictable answers when a product’s eligibility is unclear. CETA Chapter 3 and its rules of origin · India’s Ministry of Commerce and Industry, 15 July release · House of Commons Business and Trade Committee, CETA scrutiny report

Consider an illustrative shipment valued at £10,000 that can save eight percentage points of duty. Its gross duty saving would be £800. If the exporter and importer incur £300 in additional verification, documentation and delay costs, the combined saving falls to £500. A shipment of £2,500 facing the same tariff margin would save £200 and could be uneconomic to claim at the same fixed cost. The rates and expenses in this example are hypothetical. The example identifies a practical target for policy: reducing the cost of the first successful claim makes it easier for a smaller firm to compete for a trial order.

Lower import duties have several claimants

India’s tariff schedule lists a 150% base rate for Scotch whisky under tariff line 22083092, a 75% preferential rate at entry, and a staged reduction to 40%. On a stylised customs value of ₹10,000, duty at the base rate is ₹15,000 and at the initial preferential rate it is ₹7,500. The customs value plus that tariff alone falls from ₹25,000 to ₹17,500, a 30% reduction in this simplified calculation. The example excludes other applicable taxes, freight changes and distribution costs. It also assumes that the shipment qualifies for the preference. India’s tariff schedule, row 1587, tariff line 22083092 · India’s Notification No. 29/2026-Customs, 14 July

The ₹7,500 saving can be divided among the UK supplier, the Indian importer, distributors and consumers. Its allocation depends on bargaining power and competition. Where consumers can easily switch brands and several importers compete, more of the cost reduction may reach retail prices. With limited distribution or strong brand power, suppliers and distributors can retain more of it. The Indian Treasury’s receipts depend on the lower rate and how quantities respond. Domestic producers can face greater competition even when retail prices adjust gradually. Comparing customs duties with actual wholesale and retail prices would show which channel mattered most.

Passenger cars show a different constraint. India’s concession for eligible UK vehicles is structured around tariff-rate quotas and staging, with details that vary by vehicle category. The size and use of the quota affect how far the concession changes competition in practice. If demand exceeds the quota, access to the lower rate can itself have commercial value. Published quota allocations, fill rates and effective duties would make it easier to see whether the main benefit reaches car buyers, overseas producers or the firms with access to the quota. CETA Chapter 2 and tariff schedules · UK Department for Business and Trade, impact assessment · House of Commons Business and Trade Committee, CETA scrutiny report

Services need their own scorecard

The Double Contributions Convention came into force alongside CETA. It addresses duplicate social-security contributions for eligible employees temporarily posted from one country to the other. That can lower the cost of a time-limited assignment and make it easier for a firm to send staff to implement a project. Eligibility for the contribution arrangement and permission to enter and work are separate questions. Professional licensing and the customer’s ability to buy the service also shape whether a consultancy, engineering firm or technology provider can turn treaty access into revenue. India’s Ministry of Commerce and Industry, 15 July release · UK government, Double Contributions Convention explainer · CETA Chapter 10, temporary movement

That matters because services already account for a majority of what the UK records as imports from India. A goods-only dashboard could capture the most visible changes and miss an important channel. Services evaluation should track the use of eligible temporary assignments, regulatory barriers reported by firms, and receipts for relevant services. Changes in how a project is delivered can matter even when the value of recorded trade takes time to respond. UK Department for Business and Trade, June 2026 bilateral factsheet · CETA Chapter 10, temporary movement

How India can tell whether the agreement delivered

The first indicator should be preference utilisation by product, shipment size and firm size. Take the value of eligible trade that claims the preference and divide it by the value of trade eligible for the preference, with the eligibility rule and tariff basis stated. Show how many firms are making a first claim and how many return with a second shipment. Pair these figures with median clearance times and the most common reasons claims are rejected. That would tell policymakers whether a poorly used concession reflects little commercial demand or an avoidable administrative cost. House of Commons Business and Trade Committee, CETA scrutiny report · CETA Chapter 27, Administrative and Institutional Provisions

The second test is additional trade. A credible evaluation would compare products receiving large tariff cuts with similar products receiving small or zero cuts. It should account for pre-existing trends, changes in sterling against the rupee, UK demand and product-specific price changes. A second comparison can use Indian exports of the same products to markets without the same tariff change. Examine both quantities and the number of exporters so that higher prices or larger shipments by established firms do not obscure whether new suppliers entered. Neither comparison by itself guarantees a causal estimate: the products receiving the deepest cuts may differ systematically from the rest.

The strongest argument for optimism is that the deal makes future access more predictable, allowing suppliers to invest in meeting buyer requirements before the first visible increase in exports. That could be more valuable than the immediate duty saving. It should show up over time in repeat orders, wider participation and investment by firms that previously struggled to enter the UK market. If utilisation remains concentrated among large incumbent exporters, India should simplify origin guidance, address recurring clearance problems through the treaty’s committees and direct practical support toward smaller suppliers. The agreement has created an opening. The next job is to find out how many Indian firms can walk through it. CETA Chapter 3 and its rules of origin · CETA Chapter 27, Administrative and Institutional Provisions

India’s trade deals

title.rendered: Ethiopia’s exchange-rate reforms have to improve access to foreign currency

content.rendered:
The sovereign debt workout · Part 3 · June and July Ethiopia reviews

In June, IMF staff and Ethiopia reached agreement on a fifth review of the country’s Extended Credit Facility, with about $468 million in potential access subject to approval at that stage. The subsequent July report covered the review and the operating framework for foreign exchange. For firms, the economic test is whether a more transparent currency market gives them a reliable way to fund imports and settle invoices. The quoted rate is only one part of that cost. IMF, Ethiopia’s fifth review staff agreement · IMF, Ethiopia fifth review staff report

A cheap official rate can be costly to use

A company buying imported inputs cares about the currency price, how long it takes to obtain dollars and whether an order can be delivered on time. If a rate is tightly controlled and currency is scarce, an importer may wait, reduce its order or pay an additional cost to find a lawful alternative. A higher market rate can raise the local-currency bill while making supply more reliable. A firm needs to compare the effective cost including delays and the risk of stockouts.

Consider a plant buying $100,000 of parts. Suppose an illustrative rate change raises the local-currency cost by 10%, while better access prevents a two-week stoppage. The value of the change depends on the production margin saved, financing and how much of the currency cost customers will bear. Another firm with spare inventory and no risk of stoppage may mostly face the higher invoice. This is why the reform can have different effects across firms at the same published rate.

Distribution and credibility determine the adjustment

Higher import prices can affect households purchasing food, fuel or medicine. Exporters may gain an incentive to bring receipts through the formal market if they can convert at reliable terms. Import competition, wage pressure and the credibility of fiscal policy can change how far prices rise. Temporary, budgeted support can ease the impact on households that are exposed, while an enduring intervention that rations the same currency may undermine availability.

The strongest counterargument is that a fast transition can produce a large price shock if markets are thin and expectations unsettled. A transparent operating framework and better liquidity can reduce instability. Fixing the price administratively without solving the shortage can allow queues to persist. A careful assessment should look at actual settlement times, volumes through formal channels and differences between quotes customers can obtain.

The next test is whether businesses can plan imports and exports with less uncertainty, and whether inflation eases after the initial adjustment. A more reliable currency market can support investment even when the exchange rate is less favourable for individual importers. That gain should appear in use, availability and production, as well as in the reported exchange rate.

The sovereign debt workout

excerpt.rendered: The IMF review points to progress and continued work on the currency market. A more flexible rate changes incentives, while payment access determines whether firms can plan.

title.rendered: India’s carbon market has a domestic job and a separate border test

content.rendered:
India should judge its carbon market first by whether it changes production and investment at home. A possible reduction in the European carbon border charge is a distinct question. The EU’s July publication put its second-quarter certificate price at €75.28, close to €75.36 for the first quarter. India’s own compliance system assigns emissions-intensity targets to designated industrial facilities. A meaningful domestic price can improve incentives and strengthen the records available to exporters. Obtaining a reduction in an EU certificate obligation depends on the European rules and evidence for a specific claim. European Commission’s dated quarterly price table · Environment ministry’s January emissions-intensity notification summary · EU Regulation 2023/956 establishing CBAM

An intensity target links the obligation to output

India’s environment ministry announced in January that an additional 208 entities in petroleum refining, petrochemicals, textiles and secondary aluminium would face greenhouse-gas emissions-intensity targets. It said the expansion brought the total to 490 obligated entities at that point. Under the compliance mechanism, an entity performing better than its assigned target can receive carbon credit certificates, subject to the rules. A plant’s compliance position depends on emissions relative to output and the applicable target. A system-wide emissions total can move differently because overall production also changes. Environment ministry’s January emissions-intensity notification summary · Bureau of Energy Efficiency’s detailed compliance procedure

Suppose a plant’s target is 1.8 tonnes of emissions per tonne of output and its actual intensity is 1.7. At 100,000 tonnes of output, the illustrative difference against the target is 10,000 tonnes of emissions. Compare a prior year in which it made 100,000 tonnes at an intensity of 1.9 with a later year in which it makes 150,000 tonnes at 1.7. Total emissions rise from 190,000 to 255,000 tonnes even as intensity falls. The numbers are assumed and do not calculate any facility’s credit award. They show why the market should report both metrics and why a policy can improve production efficiency without immediately lowering aggregate emissions.

The border charge requires a separate account

Article 9 of the original EU CBAM regulation sets out a potential reduction corresponding to a carbon price effectively paid for declared embedded emissions, subject to the relevant requirements. An announced Indian target, a quoted domestic certificate price and a payment attributable to particular emissions are different facts. A plant that receives certificates for beating a target is in a different position from one that incurs an eligible payment. The importer must be able to document the claim on the basis applicable to its goods. It should also account for rebates or other compensation where the rules require it. EU Regulation 2023/956 establishing CBAM · EU Regulation 2025/2083 on CBAM simplification · EU implementing regulation on embedded-emissions calculations

An exporter negotiating a sale can therefore keep two records. The first measures compliance and emissions reductions under the Indian framework. The second supports the importer’s assessment of embedded emissions and any carbon cost effectively paid under the applicable EU rules. Consistent underlying data may help with both, but the boundaries and evidentiary requirements can differ. A reliable commercial forecast can show the expected cost before a deduction and a separate scenario if a qualifying amount is established. That gives the parties a way to value the possibility without pricing in a reduction that has yet to be verified. Environment ministry’s January emissions-intensity notification summary · EU Regulation 2023/956 establishing CBAM · EU implementing regulation on embedded-emissions calculations

Why the domestic market still matters to exporters

The strongest case for aligning parts of the two systems is that repeated measurement and reporting impose fixed costs. Clear records and reliable verification can support business decisions in India and make it easier for buyers to establish emissions abroad. The serious risk is designing domestic targets mainly around external trade treatment. Indian sectors differ in abatement opportunities, costs and exposure to demand. A domestic rule should be evaluated by what emissions it changes, what costs it imposes and how it affects investment in facilities serving both local and foreign customers. Bureau of Energy Efficiency’s detailed compliance procedure · EU implementing regulation on embedded-emissions calculations

The distributional effect can be substantial when facilities have different starting points. A plant with access to cheaper process improvements may meet its target at a lower cost than a smaller plant dependent on older equipment or less reliable input data. A common certificate price can give both an incentive to improve. Whether they can act depends on finance, technology and the credibility of future targets. Public support is easier to justify when it addresses a specific constraint, such as access to shared measurement capacity, and when the benefit can be verified independently of the number of certificates issued.

Prices also need an interpretable denominator. A price per credit tells a plant the value of a marginal unit only if it can establish how many units its action changes and the conditions under which those units can be issued or used. Investment decisions depend on expected prices over several years, while a single published European quarterly price reflects a specific import period. A comparison can show both prices without treating them as interchangeable. The cost of reducing an additional tonne and the revenue from selling a credit may diverge because of rules, risk and trading costs. Bureau of Energy Efficiency’s detailed compliance procedure · European Commission’s dated quarterly price table

A useful public report would separate credits issued for performance, credits surrendered for compliance and verified changes in production. This helps identify whether the market provides a price signal and whether companies are acting on it. A busy trading period may improve price discovery, while the underlying changes in fuel, materials and process efficiency take longer to observe. Bureau of Energy Efficiency’s detailed compliance procedure

What the next round of evidence should show

Look at actual plant-level intensity, output, emissions, compliance costs and verified investment. For exports, examine which data European buyers use and which carbon-price deductions are substantiated in practice. A falling intensity alongside strong output can show progress even if total emissions remain high, but that trajectory should be tested against the policy’s broader goals. The scheme is building an economic incentive where companies can identify savings from changing production and a credible cost from missing targets. Border treatment can add to that case when the evidence supports it. Bureau of Energy Efficiency’s detailed compliance procedure · EU Regulation 2023/956 establishing CBAM · European Commission’s dated quarterly price table

excerpt.rendered: India’s intensity-based rules can reward cleaner production. An exporter still needs evidence of a qualifying carbon price effectively paid to reduce a European border obligation.

title.rendered: Cheaper oil gives India a chance to rebuild its emergency cushion

content.rendered:
India should use the improvement in the oil outlook to check and, where needed, rebuild the supply buffer available in an emergency. On 7 July, the US Energy Information Administration cut its forecast for average Brent in the third quarter of 2026 by $27 a barrel, to $74. That change is large enough to improve the economics of replenishing stocks. It is also a reminder of how quickly the outlook can reverse when shipping access changes. The case for buying oil for reserve depends on how much can reach a refinery during a disruption, what it costs to hold and which grades are available. A lower Brent forecast makes that calculation more favourable without settling it. EIA’s 7 July outlook · Petroleum ministry’s parliamentary reply on strategic crude reserves

The change in the forecast came from assumptions about physical supply

In June the EIA expected a more prolonged period of shipping disruption and weaker global demand at high prices. The July forecast follows the 18 June memorandum between the United States and Iran and an increase in traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. The EIA now expects trade and output to return near earlier levels by year-end. It reports that Brent averaged $85 in June, $22 below May. The June figure is an observed monthly average. The $74 third-quarter figure is a forecast based on further recovery, and it does not lock in the price an Indian buyer will pay for a future cargo. EIA’s June outlook · EIA’s 7 July outlook

A forecast that falls because cargoes can move is different from a forecast that falls because consumers are buying less. In the first case there is a direct improvement in the availability of crude and potentially in the cost of shipping and insuring it. In the second, cheaper oil can coincide with weaker demand for Indian exports and tighter financing conditions. The July outlook points to improved supply and slower inventory withdrawals. A procurement decision still needs separate scenarios for renewed shipping disruption and for weaker global demand. A single assumed Brent path would hide the difference between the two. EIA’s 7 July outlook

Price relief and physical availability solve different problems

The petroleum ministry has reported 5.33 million tonnes of strategic crude storage capacity across facilities at Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru and Padur. Capacity gives an upper bound on how much the sites can hold. It cannot tell a refinery how much suitable crude it can draw during a specific disruption. A barrel already owned by a commercial partner may have different access terms from a barrel owned outright by the government. Oil stored at a site connected to one refinery may take time and equipment to move elsewhere. The relevant operational measure is compatible crude that can be released and delivered in time to offset a disruption. Petroleum ministry’s parliamentary reply on strategic crude reserves

Suppose an importer has to buy one million barrels and that the realised price of its grade falls by the full $27 revision in the Brent forecast. The gross purchase cost would fall by $27 million. At an illustrative ₹95 per dollar, that is about ₹256.5 crore. This arithmetic holds the exchange rate, grade differential, freight and other costs fixed. It is a sensitivity example, not a forecast for the Indian import bill or a saving already available to the government. For reserve procurement, the amount that matters is the actual delivered bid and the cost of financing the barrels until they are used. EIA’s 7 July outlook

A barrel of oil in a cavern provides an option on future availability. If an otherwise viable refinery would have to reduce runs because a cargo is late, an emergency barrel could help maintain supplies of diesel or other products. If the refinery cannot process the grade in storage or the relevant link is out of service, the value of that barrel at that location is smaller. Testing withdrawals and reviewing links to refineries can reveal bottlenecks that aggregate tonnage misses. Extra capacity has low value if the binding constraint is how quickly the stored oil can be moved.

The cheapest buffer depends on the kind of shock

There is a strong case for using diversified supply contracts, commercial stocks or financial hedges before buying a large amount of additional public oil. Commercial contracts can give a refiner alternative grades and routes, and futures can reduce exposure to a price rise while limiting the use of public capital. If the shock mainly affects price and replacement cargoes remain available, those tools may provide adequate protection. If routes are impaired and compatible replacement cargoes cannot arrive in time, a financial payout cannot run a refinery. The useful mix depends on how likely those states are and on the cost of the uncovered interruption.

Strategic holdings also differ from stocks that a refinery carries for routine operations. Commercial inventories are useful in an emergency, but part of their apparent size can reflect the working stock needed to keep normal production running. The March release coordinated by the IEA illustrates the role of emergency stocks in a severe market disruption. India’s own reserve decisions should take account of how much domestic working stock is actually spare, what can be delivered from strategic sites and whether alternate suppliers can meet the gap. Simply adding every tank to a national days-of-cover figure can exaggerate what is available on short notice. IEA’s March announcement of coordinated stock releases · Petroleum ministry’s parliamentary reply on strategic crude reserves

Buying into a price decline has a fiscal opportunity cost. A million barrels bought at $74 would tie up $74 million before freight, insurance and financing. With a hypothetical financing cost of six per cent annually, carrying the purchase would cost about $4.44 million a year in financing alone, before storage, maintenance or gains and losses in inventory value. Buying gradually across grades and delivery windows can reduce the risk of committing the full budget at one price. A procurement plan should identify what extra cover the first cargo adds and why that cover is worth its recurring cost. EIA’s 7 July outlook

The benefits of extra cover also vary across products and users. A disruption to a refinery serving a region heavily dependent on road freight can raise transport costs and delay deliveries before the national average fuel price moves much. A reserve release that keeps that refinery running may be worth more than an equal release where spare product imports can arrive quickly. An operational release rule should consider local alternatives, how fast they can be activated and what the government expects refiners to report about volumes received and products delivered. This makes it possible to evaluate whether emergency oil reached the users it was intended to protect.

What would justify using the opportunity now

The practical starting point is to estimate how many days of lost deliveries each refinery or region could withstand under several disruption scenarios. Include compatible strategic and commercial stock that can be physically accessed, alternate cargo lead times and limitations on refining or distribution. Then compare the cost of adding cover through stocked barrels, alternate contracts, delivery connections and other measures. The public case for each additional purchase is strongest where it fills a gap that leaves households or industrial users exposed to a material shortage. Petroleum ministry’s parliamentary reply on strategic crude reserves

If withdrawal tests and commercial supply alternatives show that the weakest regions already have enough usable cover, the decline in Brent need not trigger additional public purchases. If a short disruption would still force large cutbacks in refinery runs, staged replenishment or improvements to delivery links would have a clearer payoff. The important evidence is a reduction in days of unserved demand under a credible disruption scenario. The July price outlook improves the terms on which India can buy that protection. EIA’s 7 July outlook · Petroleum ministry’s parliamentary reply on strategic crude reserves

Part of a series

The 2026 oil shock

How a spike in crude ran through India’s inflation target, monetary policy, fuel taxes, reserves and the rupee in 2026.
