    The IEA can release oil stocks. India still has to solve its LPG bottleneck.

  • 27 Mar 2026

    Keeping India’s 4% inflation target makes sense through an oil shock

  • 3 Apr 2026

    India’s fuel tax cut moves part of the oil shock onto the Budget

  • 5 Jun 2026

    The RBI’s June pause buys time to see how far the oil shock spreads

  • 10 Jul 2026

    Cheaper oil gives India a chance to rebuild its emergency cushion

  • 9 Oct 2026

    The RBI’s October hike is a case for restraint after the first move

  • 16 Oct 2026

    The RBI’s dollar window should be judged by how well the rupee market works

All series →

excerpt.rendered: The EIA sharply cut its Brent forecast in July. India can use the reprieve to improve emergency oil coverage while preserving flexibility if supply disruptions return.

title.rendered: July’s world growth forecast hid a split between AI investment and energy costs

content.rendered:
The global economy after the energy shock · Part 3 · July IMF outlook

In July the IMF projected global growth of 3.0% in 2026 and 3.4% in 2027. The first figure was only one tenth of a percentage point below its April forecast. The stability of the aggregate hid the point of the update. Energy costs were squeezing households and businesses while technology investment and other sources of resilience were supporting activity elsewhere. A world growth number averages those experiences before it reaches the reader. IMF, July 2026 World Economic Outlook Update · IMF, April 2026 World Economic Outlook

Investment today can coexist with weaker household demand

Construction of a data centre creates orders for equipment and work for contractors. A firm placing those orders can have access to long-term financing and a customer base spread across markets. A household paying more for transport faces an immediate budget constraint. An energy-intensive manufacturer selling into a weak market may be unable to pass on costs and cut production. GDP can show a respectable net figure when these changes occur together.

For intuition, imagine two equal-sized regions whose expected growth rates are both 3%. A two-point upgrade to one and a two-point downgrade to the other leave their simple average unchanged. The gap widens from zero to four points. This is illustrative arithmetic, not the IMF’s country weighting. It explains why the country and industry breakdown is essential when allocating resources on the basis of a global forecast.

A second test for importers

A country can enjoy external demand for software and business services while paying more for imported fuel and equipment. The net effect on investment and domestic demand depends on who receives the export income and who pays the import bill. An exporter with dollars in hand can service external debt or buy equipment. A regulated distributor carrying a larger fuel bill may need to borrow locally. A strong export number and a strained domestic credit line can appear in the same quarter.

One argument for looking through sectoral variation is that investment spending spreads to wages and suppliers, and some of the energy shock may reverse. That process takes time and depends on how much of the investment is sourced locally. Imported equipment offers a narrower immediate demand benefit than local construction and services. The gains eventually depend on whether capacity is used productively. Counting planned spending as future output leaves that question open.

The useful follow-up is to compare orders and construction with household spending, employment and financing conditions in the economies facing higher energy costs. The October IMF update can then be read against those separate indicators. A durable improvement would be broader than a strong quarter for a small group of investment-heavy industries.

The global economy after the energy shock
Previous · Part 2 · All installments · Next · Part 4

excerpt.rendered: An investment surge and a fuel shock can offset in the global aggregate while leaving exposed households and firms with sharply different outcomes.

title.rendered: India’s rural employment guarantee needs to count requests for work

content.rendered:
India’s new rural employment law will provide better income insurance if a worker can reliably turn a request for work into an offer and a payment. The Viksit Bharat Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act came into force on 1 July. It raises the statutory guarantee from 100 to 125 days per eligible rural household, while the ministry has announced a new wage schedule with a daily rate of at least ₹300. Those changes are potentially valuable. Their effect depends on a part of the system that rarely gets the same attention as the headline entitlement, the local record of who asked for work and when. Text of the VB-G RAM G Act · Gazette notification on the commencement of the Act · Ministry of Rural Development’s 1 July implementation announcement

The past baseline is closer to 50 days than 100

PRS’s analysis of the 2026–27 rural development grants puts average employment under the previous programme at about 48 days per participating household over the preceding decade and at 50 days in 2024–25. Fewer than one in ten participating households completed 100 days over the longer period covered. An average below the previous ceiling does not tell us how many households wanted more work. Some may have preferred a shorter spell of public employment, while others may have faced rationing or poor access. The data do suggest that raising the ceiling alone will directly benefit only households that would otherwise have reached it. PRS analysis of the Rural Development demand for grants

The distinction matters because a job guarantee can act as insurance when other income falls. A household that normally uses only a few weeks of public employment may depend on additional work after a crop loss or a reduction in private hiring. For such a household, the economic value of the programme is the option to obtain income when it is scarce. A day offered after the household has already borrowed at high cost or migrated may have less value than a day offered during the period of need. Tracking just total person-days treats those outcomes as equivalent.

The application starts the clock

The Act provides for an unemployment allowance when an eligible applicant is not provided work within 15 days of receipt of the application or, for advance applications, the later date from which work is sought, subject to its conditions. This is an enforceable mechanism only if requests are captured and dates can be established. If a worker is verbally told to return next month and no request is registered, the official record can show neither waiting time nor unfulfilled demand. A dated acknowledgement, available through a channel that works locally, gives workers a way to establish the date and administrators a way to audit it. Text of the VB-G RAM G Act

A simple illustration shows the size of the income difference. Suppose a household is offered 80 days at ₹300 a day when it would take 100 days at the same wage. The gap is ₹6,000 in gross earnings, before travel and other costs. Raising its statutory ceiling from 100 to 125 days changes nothing in the illustration while the offer stays at 80 days. A household already receiving 100 days that is offered all 25 additional days could earn ₹7,500 more at the illustrative wage. The difference between those cases is a reason to report where the extra days go and how many requests remain unmet. Text of the VB-G RAM G Act · Ministry of Rural Development’s 1 July implementation announcement

An apparent fall in unmet demand could mean that officials have improved job offers or that some applicants have stopped trying. A useful district report would show requested days, dated offers, days worked and payments, together with the number and value of allowances that became due and were paid. A household survey that includes people without a recent recorded application can check whether the official denominator has shrunk for administrative reasons. Offers at inaccessible sites or times should also be recorded separately from offers that workers can reasonably take up.

Seasonal calendars should reflect local labour markets

The law requires states to notify in advance a period totalling 60 days covering peak sowing and harvesting seasons during which programme works cannot be undertaken. The strongest argument for this provision is that public works can compete for labour when private demand is highest, leaving farm operations harder to schedule. But peak dates differ by crop, irrigation and location. Landless workers can lose an outside option where public work pauses while private hiring is weak. A calendar that fits irrigated districts can be poorly timed in areas where sowing waits for uncertain rainfall. Text of the VB-G RAM G Act · PRS analysis of the Rural Development demand for grants

The quality of those calendars should be evaluated against local hiring, wages and the concentration of unmet public work requests on either side of a pause. A fall in programme work in a notified period has a different interpretation if private employment and wages rise at the same time. A fall in both sources of work suggests a gap in income insurance. Advance publication also has practical value. It lets households plan and lets local officials prepare works so the programme can reopen quickly when the notified period ends.

Wages have to reach the worker while the income matters

The ministry’s rollout announcement reports an interim allocation of about ₹95,692 crore. An allocation helps fund the transition. It does not establish how many applications will be accepted in a district or when a worker will be paid. The legal text provides for compensation for certain wage delays, measured from closure of the muster roll. Separately recording the dates of work, muster closure, payment processing and receipt in the worker’s account would show where a delay originates. A report starting only after muster closure can miss time spent waiting for the roll to close. Ministry of Rural Development’s 1 July implementation announcement · Text of the VB-G RAM G Act

Late payment is also distributional. A family with savings can wait for arrears without changing its spending much. A family borrowing for groceries during the same period may lose some of the value of the wage to interest. Reporting a median payment time would miss that cost if a minority of workers face very long waits. District data should show the share of workers still unpaid at several intervals and test whether the longest delays cluster in particular villages, banks or types of work.

The administrative counterargument is that a district cannot guarantee an immediate response everywhere. Work needs technical approval, safe conditions and supervision, and spending on projects with little public value weakens the case for sustained funding. A prepared list of viable works helps reconcile those constraints. Districts with seasonal demand can identify maintenance and small projects in advance, estimate labour requirements and ensure that applications are not deterred simply because the first preferred project is not ready. An allowance and a complaint record can reveal the cost of preparation failures that would otherwise remain hidden.

What would establish that the transition worked

The first useful comparison is with the same districts and seasons under the previous system. Record the share of documented requests that receive an offer on time, days worked per household, wage delays and payments of unemployment allowance. Interpret changes alongside rainfall, crop schedules and private hiring. A rise in days worked among households previously near the ceiling would show that the extra entitlement has practical value. Improved offer and payment times for households that had never reached 100 days would show a broader improvement. Text of the VB-G RAM G Act · PRS analysis of the Rural Development demand for grants

If the reports show few unmet requests while independent surveys find large numbers of workers unable to register them, the first fix belongs at the point of application. If requests are recorded but jobs are unavailable, the evidence points to a different constraint, such as work planning or funding. A 125-day guarantee is worth more when the system reveals those failures and responds to them. The central indicator should be what happens after a household asks for work.

excerpt.rendered: The new rural jobs law offers 125 days per household. Its effectiveness as income insurance depends on whether requests are registered, work is offered and wages arrive on time.

title.rendered: India’s invoice-finance rules make buyer approval a critical bottleneck

content.rendered:
A small business cannot pay wages with an invoice that its customer has yet to accept. The RBI’s new Trade Receivables Discounting System directions set out the platform through which eligible receivables can be financed and assigned to a financier. They specify that discounted factoring units are without recourse to the seller for buyer default under the framework. This can transfer a meaningful risk away from a small supplier. The economic benefit depends on how quickly the receivable becomes financeable and how much working capital the business must carry until then. RBI’s Trade Receivables Discounting System Directions

An invoice has a date, an acceptance and a due date

A supplier can deliver goods, issue an invoice, wait for the buyer to acknowledge it, and then wait to receive payment. Discounting can shorten the period after acceptance by giving the supplier cash in exchange for the assigned receivable. It has less immediate effect on the time before a claim is accepted or on goods genuinely disputed. The platform can organise bids and settlement for the financeable unit. The buyer’s conduct and the evidence available for resolving a dispute determine whether a supplier can use the platform promptly. RBI’s Trade Receivables Discounting System Directions

For illustration, assume a ₹10 lakh invoice is due 60 days after delivery and is accepted immediately. At a simple annual discount rate of 12 per cent, a 60-day cost is about ₹19,726 on a 365-day basis, ignoring fees. If acceptance takes 20 days, the supplier can finance the remaining 40 days for about ₹13,151 at the same rate. Suppose it must fund the first 20 days separately at 18 per cent, costing about ₹9,863. The two costs sum to about ₹23,014. The rates, terms and common principal are assumptions. The point is that a lower reported discount charge can coexist with a higher total cost when the supplier must finance an earlier delay.

Competition among financiers has to reach small invoices

Several lenders may bid for the obligations of a large buyer they know well. An invoice from a smaller or less familiar buyer can receive fewer offers, regardless of the supplier’s own performance. The ability to assess buyers and diversify exposures matters to pricing. A platform that reports an attractive average rate can still give a poor picture of access if many invoices receive no bids. Report the number of bids, the time to finance and the amount financed for different buyers and invoice sizes, including unsuccessful attempts. RBI’s Trade Receivables Discounting System Directions

Small firms also differ in their ability to challenge delays. A supplier with several buyers can insist on clear acceptance and payment terms with less risk of losing its largest contract. A firm dependent on one buyer may accept slow confirmation rather than dispute it. Finance can help that firm bridge the delay once the invoice is eligible. It can also make late payment less visible if everyone focuses on whether the financier entered the transaction. Reporting the full delivery-to-cash interval gives policymakers a way to see whether the buyer’s behaviour has actually improved.

The strongest case for prioritising the finance layer

A competitive market for accepted receivables can be valuable even if acceptance is imperfect. It gives suppliers a way to obtain cash earlier and can price the risk of the buyer separately from the risk of the supplier. The requirement that discounting be without recourse to the seller for buyer default matters because it limits a particular exposure after sale of the receivable. A financier still needs to check the buyer and the validity of the claim, and the platform has to ensure that the assignment is properly recorded. Lower rates and risk transfer are worthwhile gains that should be measured on their own terms. RBI’s Trade Receivables Discounting System Directions

The next question is how much earlier the supplier can fund production. In the illustrative case, a firm that needs the money to buy inputs for its next order cannot simply wait twenty days without a cost. It may borrow elsewhere, ask its own suppliers for credit or pass up the order. A reduction in acceptance time can therefore change output and sales as well as interest expense. To evaluate the effect, compare the time firms actually receive cash with dates in the purchase contract and track whether production or order fulfilment improves.

The data should follow the entire transaction

Track delivery, invoice issue, acceptance, the first financing offer, disbursement and final payment as distinct events. Publish delays and outcomes for both financed and unfinanced invoices, with a breakdown of the reasons claims did not enter the system. A growing financed volume is stronger evidence if eligible small suppliers receive funds earlier at lower all-in cost. If rates on accepted invoices fall but the time to acceptance rises, the next fix belongs earlier in the chain. That is where a financing tool meets the economic reality of supplying a more powerful customer. RBI’s Trade Receivables Discounting System Directions

Some disputes are genuine. A blanket rule treating any delay as unreasonable would make buyers bear the risk of deficient goods or inconsistent records. A useful design sets out what evidence establishes delivery, how a buyer records a dispute and how long resolution usually takes. Publishing distributions for both disputed and undisputed invoices can reveal patterns without assuming every invoice is payable. Where documentation is clear and delays still cluster around particular buyers, suppliers and policymakers have a stronger basis for asking why. That evidence can complement financing without replacing ordinary commercial safeguards. RBI’s Trade Receivables Discounting System Directions

An additional check is whether customers extend payment terms after finance becomes easier to obtain. A supplier may still prefer a cheaper discount, while part of the gain accrues to a buyer that pays later. Comparing contractual maturities and actual payment dates alongside discount costs can reveal that shift.

excerpt.rendered: TReDS lets small suppliers turn receivables into cash. The rate they obtain matters, but so does the time between delivery and a financeable invoice.

title.rendered: India’s open-market buybacks will be judged by the price companies pay

content.rendered:
SEBI’s decision to restore share buybacks through stock exchanges can improve how Indian companies return surplus cash. It can also make it easier for a company to spend shareholders’ money supporting its share price at a poor valuation. Which result dominates depends on the price paid, the uses the company gives up and the regulator’s ability to see how orders affect the market. The board’s 19 June approval is best understood as a change in how a capital-allocation decision can be executed. It gives investors a reason to examine the completed purchases and the alternatives available to the board at the time. SEBI’s 19 June board decision · Business Standard’s account of the approved framework

The exchange route changes who can sell and at what price

A tender offer asks shareholders to offer their stock on specified terms. When the offer is oversubscribed, rules determine how many of those shares the company accepts. In an exchange buyback, the company places orders and buys shares from sellers in the market at the prices its orders can obtain. Shareholders who trade before or after its purchases may face a different price. The ability to buy over a period can be valuable when sellers arrive gradually or the value of the shares is uncertain. It also means that access to the buyback does not carry the same economics as an opportunity to tender at a common stated price. SEBI’s consultation on the exchange buyback route · The announced timetable and execution rules

The approved framework is intended to restore the route from 1 August. As reported following the decision, the purchases would have to be completed within 66 working days from opening, with at least 40 per cent of the funds used in the first half of the period. Companies would disseminate information electronically as well as through newspaper advertisements. Their orders would go through normal trading, without a separate window or an on-screen label identifying the company as purchaser. These are details of the framework announced after the board meeting. On 26 June the exchange route has yet to reopen under that decision. SEBI’s 19 June board decision · The announced timetable and execution rules

A higher earnings-per-share figure can coexist with a loss of value

Consider an illustrative company with ten crore shares and an estimated equity value of ₹1,000 crore, including surplus cash. That is ₹100 per share. Suppose the company spends ₹80 crore to repurchase one crore shares at ₹80 each. If the only change in the value of the business is the cash distributed, the remaining equity is worth ₹920 crore across nine crore shares, or about ₹102.22 per share. A continuing shareholder gains because the company buys below the assumed value. Now suppose the company instead repurchases one crore shares for ₹120 each. On the same assumptions, the remaining equity is worth ₹880 crore, or about ₹97.78 per share.

Both transactions remove one crore shares. If net earnings were unchanged, both would raise earnings per share by roughly 11.1 per cent. The purchase price determines whether value moves towards the continuing shareholders or towards the investors who sold. The example holds operating value fixed, ignores taxes and assumes the cash is surplus. In an actual company, lost interest, new debt, a different risk profile or a forgone investment can change earnings and equity value. An executive bonus linked to earnings per share can nevertheless reward the smaller share count before any of those costs are visible in the accounts.

The hardest input is the value per share. A board with a reliable estimate of spare cash and a defensible valuation range may rationally use the market route when shares trade below that range. A board forecasting a recovery in cyclical earnings may be particularly prone to mistaking optimism for a margin of safety. Investors should look for the assumptions behind the board’s willingness to pay and compare the actual purchase price with the value implied by plausible lower earnings. Where the business has a profitable investment available, the return forgone on that investment belongs in the same decision.

Execution rules shape the company’s incentives

The front-loaded spending requirement addresses the concern that an issuer might announce a large buyback and then buy very little while benefiting from the signal. On an illustrative ₹100 crore authorisation, the 40 per cent requirement would imply ₹40 crore of purchases in the first half of the window. The commitment makes an announcement more informative about intended demand. It can also put pressure on a company to buy during a rising market after an early price discount has disappeared. An issuer should therefore take account of both daily trading capacity and the risk of overpayment before it commits to a programme size. The announced timetable and execution rules

Removing the visible purchaser label can reduce opportunities to trade around known issuer orders. It also makes it harder for a seller to identify in real time how much of the demand comes from the issuer. Exchange surveillance and post-trade transparency become more valuable in that setting. The same ₹40 crore of purchases could be modest in a highly liquid stock and large relative to typical turnover in a smaller one. Market quality should be examined in relation to volume, spread and order-book depth. A price move in the days the company is active has a different interpretation if the share falls back as soon as the buying ends. SEBI’s consultation on the exchange buyback route · The announced timetable and execution rules

Why flexibility can still be worth having

The strongest argument for the route is that a company with genuinely excess cash can spread its orders over time and avoid fixing a tender price in advance. Existing shareholders who prefer to hold can continue to do so, and willing sellers trade through the existing market. When the stock is liquid and the purchases are modest relative to ordinary turnover, using that market can reduce execution costs. That flexibility is economically useful, especially when a company’s estimates of its capital requirements have changed. It does not establish that an individual buyback offers good value. SEBI’s consultation on the exchange buyback route

A repurchase also changes ownership weights. Investors who sell none of their holdings own a larger fraction of the company after shares are cancelled. The effect is arithmetically predictable and can matter when voting power is already concentrated. In the example above, a holder of one crore shares would go from 10 per cent to about 11.1 per cent without acquiring additional shares. Disclosure of the share count and any material shift in control helps separate the cash-return rationale from other effects of the transaction.

For a shareholder who needs liquidity, the exchange route can offer the ordinary market price and the chance of finding a buyer when the company is active. A tender can offer a more predictable quoted price, with uncertainty over the fraction accepted. For a shareholder who remains invested, the main exposure is to the value and risk of the company after the cash has gone. Comparing the two routes should therefore include both seller access and the financing position of the continuing company. The board’s case for a repurchase is weaker if the plan leaves little room to refinance obligations or sustain productive capital expenditure.

What evidence would make the reform look successful

SEBI should evaluate programmes by size and stock liquidity, comparing execution prices with observable trading benchmarks and checking activity for signs of concentrated buying. Issuer disclosures should make it possible to reconstruct actual spending, shares retired, average price and cash or debt remaining after the transaction. Investors should also compare those outcomes with what directors said before authorising the buyback. Announcement returns alone cannot tell whether a company bought cheaply or simply signalled stronger prospects. Trading patterns after the programme ends and subsequent financing decisions provide additional evidence. SEBI’s 19 June board decision · SEBI’s consultation on the exchange buyback route

The reform would earn confidence if companies use the route to return excess cash at defensible prices and if trading remains orderly in less liquid shares. Evidence of purchases concentrated near mandated spending deadlines, followed by price reversals or costly new financing, would support tighter execution safeguards. SEBI has widened the choice of route. The board of each company still has to show that the price and the use of cash served the shareholders who stayed. SEBI’s 19 June board decision

excerpt.rendered: SEBI’s decision to restore exchange buybacks gives companies more flexibility. The benefit to continuing shareholders depends on execution price and what the cash would otherwise earn.

title.rendered: CERC’s storage tariff makes the value of a charged battery visible

content.rendered:
A battery can be installed at a power station and still be unable to deliver electricity when the grid needs it. The Central Electricity Regulatory Commission’s second tariff amendment, published in April, supplies a framework for specified integrated storage at generation and interstate transmission facilities whose tariffs fall under the commission’s jurisdiction. The economic test is whether payment reflects the ability to discharge in valuable hours and accounts for the electricity required to charge. The investment is worthwhile where the resulting service costs less than a credible alternative. CERC tariff second amendment, Gazette 257 of 2026 · CERC, draft tariff regulations amendment

A power rating is one part of the product

The amendment addresses integrated storage that uses a common connection with eligible generating stations or transmission systems. It defines measures including declared capacity, the battery’s ability to discharge and relevant energy consumption. The scope matters. Its arrangements address regulated projects within the stated framework. A standalone merchant project with a different contract and revenue sources can have a different incentive to charge or discharge. CERC tariff second amendment, Gazette 257 of 2026

A 100 MW device can deliver 100 MW at an instant under its rated conditions. A 200 MWh usable energy budget can sustain that rate for two hours when fully charged. During a four-hour shortage, another device with the same power rating and twice the energy can provide a different service. A device already used in an earlier hour has less remaining energy unless it can recharge. For the buyer, capacity means an amount available at a specified time for a specified duration.

Charging carries a price

Suppose a battery delivers 200 MWh at a time when the avoided cost of energy is ₹8 per kWh. At an assumed round-trip efficiency of 80%, it requires 250 MWh of charging energy. If that energy costs ₹3 per kWh, it costs ₹7.5 lakh and the discharged energy has an illustrative gross value of ₹16 lakh. The energy spread is ₹8.5 lakh before fixed costs, degradation, charging constraints and any reserve value. If the charging price rises to ₹6.50 per kWh, the input cost becomes ₹16.25 lakh. The energy spread alone becomes slightly negative. A separate reliability value could still justify keeping the battery charged.

Who decides to charge and who pays are important questions. A service provider paid for availability has a reason to preserve charge for contracted hours. If someone else pays the energy cost, the provider’s charging choices need rules or incentives that discourage unnecessary expense. When the dispatch centre can call the device for grid support, accounting has to show who received the benefit and when a call displaced another promised service.

Compare the service with the next-best asset

The strongest argument for a predictable tariff is that an integrated device can provide benefits that are difficult to sell separately. It may defer an upgrade, help a generating station vary its output or provide a service to the wider network. Stable compensation can finance an investment that a volatile short-term price would undersupply. The danger is paying for capital and assuming the operating benefit. Record usable energy at the required times, actual dispatch, charging input and degradation, and compare performance with the alternative the project was intended to replace.

In a location with repeated short-duration constraints, measured availability and reliable discharge might justify additional storage. Where constrained periods last longer than the asset can serve, a grid upgrade, longer-duration resource or demand response could have more value. The relevant comparison includes the full life of each option and its effect on expected scarcity, including the value of services that can be provided at the same time without double counting.

Battery life makes the comparison dynamic. Calling an asset more often can earn additional revenue while advancing the date at which usable capacity falls below the contract requirement. Reporting both delivered energy and retained capability makes it easier to compare a heavily used project with one kept mostly in reserve.

A regulated tariff can make integrated storage financeable. Its economic value is the availability of usable electricity in the hours a purchaser would otherwise have to cover at greater cost.

excerpt.rendered: The integrated-storage framework brings a useful distinction into tariff design. A battery’s power rating, available energy and charging cost all matter.

title.rendered: Bonn’s adaptation talks put a price on measuring results

content.rendered:
Climate finance after Belém · Part 3 · June Bonn climate conference

At the June Bonn climate conference, the subsidiary bodies circulated draft text on the global goal on adaptation. That was a step in negotiating how to make progress visible. It raises a practical problem for the finance agenda that emerged from Belém. Governments need indicators comparable enough to aggregate and close enough to actual projects to guide decisions. A count of projects financed is easy to report. A measure of the disruption they prevented takes more work and is often more valuable. UNFCCC, Bonn draft on the global goal on adaptation · UNFCCC, joint note by the Bonn conference chairs · UNFCCC, Belém political package

Measure a service before declaring a success

A new embankment can be counted as complete when construction ends. The economic outcome depends on how much it reduces expected loss and whether it shifts water risk to a nearby community. A warning system can be counted by devices installed, messages delivered or people able to act on the warning. Each describes a different step. If a programme rewards devices installed, a contractor may have little incentive to test whether messages reach people when they need them.

A simple reporting framework can record the problem, the assets financed and the service result. For a health facility that needs backup cooling, the service result could be the share of extreme-heat hours it remained safe to operate. An upper-income city and a poorer district may have very different starting points. Report the initial exposure and improvement as well as the current level. Otherwise a high score may reward places that already faced fewer barriers.

The problem of the disaster that did not happen

A quiet year after investment provides little evidence about what would happen in a severe event. Compare similar events, model a transparent counterfactual and inspect routine readiness. An evacuation route can be tested in drills even if no real evacuation is needed. A water system’s performance under lower flows can be measured before a rare extreme drought. Pair event outcomes with evidence on how the system is expected to respond.

The strongest case for a uniform list is that donors and countries need a common reporting language. A long list with insufficient staffing can turn into a paperwork exercise. A smaller common core and locally selected measures would allow broad comparisons and still recognise different hazards. Grants for data collection and evaluation can be legitimate project costs when the findings change future spending.

The next test is whether a city applying for finance can describe its expected outcome in terms a funder accepts and the public can verify. If the indicators help direct money towards projects that preserve services and reduce losses, the technical work at Bonn will matter to budget choices. If reporting focuses on the number of approved activities, the information will do less to separate good investments from easy ones.

Climate finance after Belém
Previous · Part 2 · All installments · Next · Part 4

excerpt.rendered: Adaptation indicators can make funding more accountable. They work best when they measure services and allow comparison against local exposure.

title.rendered: India’s green hydrogen certificate is only as credible as its power records

content.rendered:
India’s green hydrogen certification portal will create economic value if it lets industrial buyers verify the emissions they are paying to avoid. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy launched the portal on 17 June under the Green Hydrogen Certification Scheme of India. An administrative portal can make applications and compliance easier. What makes the resulting certificate worth paying for is the ability to trace the electricity used, apply a consistent emissions boundary and prevent two users from claiming the same renewable generation. Without those conditions, a simpler process could make it easier to sell a label while leaving buyers uncertain about the underlying product. MNRE’s green hydrogen certification launch · India’s 2023 green hydrogen standard

An emissions standard makes a difficult purchase comparable

Hydrogen looks the same at the point of use regardless of how it was produced. A refinery buying it can specify purity, pressure and delivery terms and test them on arrival. It cannot inspect the delivered molecule to find out which generator supplied the electrolyser. India’s 2023 standard sets a threshold of two kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent per kilogram of hydrogen, averaged over 12 months. For electrolysis, the accounting boundary covers operations including water treatment, electrolysis, purification, drying and compression. The boundary is relevant to procurement because a buyer should be able to compare a certified supplier with another supplier on a consistent basis. India’s 2023 green hydrogen standard

The economic problem is asymmetric information. A producer knows its operating hours and power purchases in greater detail than a buyer, while the buyer cannot independently monitor each plant at reasonable cost. A credible certificate reduces that cost and allows bidders to compete on both price and emissions. It also changes what happens after contracts are signed. If power costs rise, a producer might be tempted to switch operating hours or change its source of electricity. Clear rules for periodic verification and correction of material errors make the emissions promise enforceable over the contract term.

Electricity drives both cost and emissions

Consider an illustrative electrolyser that uses 50 kilowatt-hours of electricity per kilogram of hydrogen. At ₹3 per kilowatt-hour, electricity alone costs ₹150 per kilogram. At ₹5, it costs ₹250. These are assumed power prices and an assumed electricity requirement. Neither figure includes capital recovery, water, maintenance or delivery to the buyer. A producer offered cheap electricity only during solar hours also needs to weigh the lower power price against fewer operating hours over which to recover the cost of its equipment. A bid built on a low tariff and a high annual utilisation rate needs to show that both assumptions can hold at the same site.

The same illustration shows the importance of the power record. At 50 kilowatt-hours per kilogram, power with an attributed emissions intensity of 0.04 kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent per kilowatt-hour contributes two kilograms of emissions per kilogram of hydrogen. It would use up the entire threshold before emissions from any other covered inputs are added. The 0.04 figure is a calculated break-even under the stated assumption. It is neither a national grid emissions factor nor a separate legal limit on electricity. The producer’s full compliance calculation has to use the applicable accounting rules and emissions boundary. India’s 2023 green hydrogen standard

The comparison should account for the gap between contracting for renewable power and physically drawing electricity at a particular time. An electrolyser that runs more hours can make better use of its equipment. If the extra hours rely on more emissions-intensive generation, the climate benefit can shrink. More granular verification can expose that gap, while imposing costs for metering, data reconciliation and balancing. Procurement can require bidders to show how much renewable supply they can demonstrate at the intended operating profile and what a tighter matching requirement would do to the delivered price. That information would help decide how far to go beyond the national minimum in a specific contract.

Refinery contracts are a practical demand test

The ministry says contracts have been awarded to supply 30,000 tonnes a year to four refiners, IOCL, BPCL, HPCL and NRL. At the illustrative electricity requirement above, supplying that amount would use 1.5 terawatt-hours a year if all contracted tonnes were delivered by electrolysis at that efficiency. The volume equals 0.6 per cent of the mission’s 2030 annual production capacity target of five million tonnes. These comparisons show the scale of a relatively concrete demand commitment. An award is different from a commissioned plant or an audited record of deliveries. MNRE’s green hydrogen certification launch · Cabinet approval of the National Green Hydrogen Mission

Refineries are useful early buyers because they already use hydrogen. A contract can replace part of an existing input and compare the certified product with the plant’s incumbent supply. The buyer needs terms for missed deliveries, quality, emissions verification and any continued reliance on its existing hydrogen plant. The same firm can serve as a buyer for a long-term contract and retain its conventional supply for continuity. The avoided emissions then depend on how much conventional production actually falls when the green volume arrives. A producer’s certificate and a buyer’s displacement calculation answer different parts of the same investment question. IEA Global Hydrogen Review 2025 on demand

The allocation of risk will also affect who bids. A buyer that can cancel without compensating the supplier after the plant has been built may receive few credible offers or pay a higher premium. A producer that receives a fixed payment regardless of whether the buyer needs the hydrogen can leave a public refiner paying for unused capacity. A minimum volume commitment tied to verified availability, with separately priced additional volumes, would let the two sides share that risk. Publishing utilisation and payment data would show whether a low winning bid remains inexpensive once the contract is used.

The original mission approval put the programme’s initial outlay at ₹19,744 crore. To judge public support for an individual project, compare the net subsidy with verified incremental emissions reductions over the supported period. For illustration, if a buyer pays a green premium of ₹60 per kilogram and independently verifies a reduction of eight kilograms of emissions per kilogram substituted, the premium works out to ₹7,500 per tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent. These are hypothetical inputs, not an estimate of a refinery contract or a recommendation on the right subsidy. The calculation shows how a plausible product premium can have very different public value depending on the incumbent fuel, actual utilisation and verified displacement. Cabinet approval of the National Green Hydrogen Mission

How much verification is worth paying for

There is a reasonable case for avoiding overly demanding reporting requirements at the start. Smaller suppliers may face significant fixed costs to build audit systems, and a standard that requires very granular power procurement can raise prices and slow the first round of investment. The cost is worth bearing where the evidence materially changes the emissions claim or makes contracts more financeable. Where simpler records can independently establish the same result, a more elaborate process could consume resources while adding little assurance. Common measurement rules and audit trails would make it easier for suppliers to provide credible evidence without each buyer demanding an entirely different reporting system.

The test is the evidence from actual deliveries. Publish volumes contracted, commissioned, delivered and certified as separate quantities. Report enough about the verification process for buyers to assess repeatability, including how corrected certificates and overlapping claims are handled. At refinery level, track independently verified conventional hydrogen displacement, delivered price and the utilisation of the new supply. If projects repeatedly deliver contracted tonnes with a documented emissions reduction and the premium narrows across successive procurements, certification is supporting a market. If awards rise while deliveries and verified displacement lag, the first question should be which constraint is binding, whether it is power supply, financing, operations or the buyer’s willingness to pay. MNRE’s green hydrogen certification launch · IEA Global Hydrogen Review 2025 on demand

Part of a series

Testing India’s subsidies

Semiconductors, AI compute, minerals, green hydrogen, small hydro and factory power: what each subsidy should be made to deliver.

title.rendered: Nepal’s remittance windfall gives it room to invest and a risk to manage

content.rendered:
Nepal can use unusually strong remittances to build resilience and finance investment, provided it treats them as income earned abroad whose growth may slow. Nepal Rastra Bank reports that remittances in US dollars rose 31.9 per cent to $11.55 billion in the first nine months of FY2025/26. The IMF’s June assessment projects remittances at 33.1 per cent of GDP for the full year and real output growth of three per cent. These figures are compatible because income sent by migrant workers supports spending and foreign exchange without being domestic output. The policy question is how to improve what the economy can produce while those flows are strong. Nepal Rastra Bank’s nine-month macroeconomic release · IMF’s June Nepal assessment and indicator table

Households earn the flows and decide how to use them

A family may spend a transfer on food, housing, education or repaying debt. Those uses can improve welfare and investment in human capital. A transfer can also finance imports or be deposited at a bank, which may then lend to businesses. The amount converted into investment depends on opportunities, the cost of lending and confidence that a project can earn a return. It would be a mistake to assume that an increase in bank deposits automatically finances productive domestic activity. Some of the proceeds can stay liquid or finance assets whose returns depend on continued household transfers. IMF’s June Nepal assessment and indicator table · Nepal Rastra Bank’s nine-month macroeconomic release

There is a difference between the household’s spending choice and the central bank’s reserve position. A worker sends income, the household receives purchasing power and an intermediary handles the currency conversion. The eventual effect on official reserves depends on net foreign exchange transactions and the policy response. Stronger receipts can help meet demand for imported goods and reduce the need for financing from abroad. They do not put each dollar into the Treasury’s budget. A fiscal strategy should distinguish private remittance income, tax revenue arising from activity and official foreign-currency assets. IMF’s June Nepal assessment and indicator table

How a large flow can cushion a shock and amplify another

Using the IMF’s full-year projection as scale, a hypothetical ten per cent fall in remittances would equal about 3.3 per cent of GDP if nominal GDP were held fixed. This is the size of the gross receipt shock, not a prediction of a 3.3 per cent fall in GDP or reserves. Households could draw savings, lower spending or reduce imports. Exchange rates and other flows could respond. The example shows why changes in employment, wages and living costs in migrant destinations can matter for Nepal’s external account even when domestic production initially changes little. IMF’s June Nepal assessment and indicator table

There are distributional effects even within Nepal. A household with a migrant worker can experience a direct loss when a transfer falls. Another may be exposed through local construction, retail or services that rely on remittance-funded demand. Banks can face repayment pressure if loans were assessed on the assumption of stable foreign income. A stress test should identify which regions and lenders are most exposed to particular labour markets abroad. It should also distinguish a change in how funds are recorded from an actual loss in workers’ income, since greater use of formal channels can raise measured receipts without an equivalent increase in total transfers.

Invest where a productive return is credible

The strongest case for using the moment to invest is that external liquidity can make it easier to import equipment and intermediate goods, while stronger deposits can increase the availability of finance. Nepal can gain if a project expands output, lowers a recurring cost or creates durable earnings in foreign currency. A project funded on the assumption that remittances will permanently sustain demand is riskier. Lenders should test the cash flow under weaker transfers and lower asset prices. Public investment should be judged by the service or productive capacity it creates, with finance sized to the fiscal obligations the project imposes. IMF’s June Nepal assessment and indicator table

A competing argument is that attracting more finance into domestic projects can lower the return migrants and their families earn if promising opportunities are scarce. Families may rationally prefer liquid savings, a home or schooling to a business exposed to uncertain demand and approvals. The appropriate response is to reduce genuine costs of productive activity and improve access to investments with transparent terms. Encouraging borrowers to take more risk because the country has high reserves could leave households worse off. Investment requires a credible project, not simply an available pool of savings.

For public projects, compare foreign exchange earned or saved with the foreign exchange required to build and maintain the asset. A project that imports machinery initially can still improve the external account over its life if it raises reliable exports or reduces recurring imports. A project that mostly increases demand for imported inputs may have a strong domestic social case but a weaker external-financing case. Both belong in the appraisal. When the country’s apparent room to spend depends on unusually strong transfers, showing which projects will remain viable after growth in those flows slows is particularly important.

The timing of flows also matters. A seasonal rise in transfers does not necessarily translate into a similarly timed increase in funds available for a public project or a bank’s long-term lending book.

What the next data should show

Track remittances by destination where possible, the maturity and concentration of bank lending, import composition and evidence of investment coming into operation. A rise in equipment imports and export capacity has a different implication from a rise in consumption imports or land prices. Compare domestic wage and employment opportunities with the income households can earn abroad. If stronger transfers accompany sustainable lending and more domestic productive capacity, the windfall will have broadened the economy’s options. If reserves improve while exposure to the same foreign labour markets and local asset cycle grows, that vulnerability should be priced into fiscal and financial decisions. IMF’s June Nepal assessment and indicator table · Nepal Rastra Bank’s nine-month macroeconomic release

excerpt.rendered: Remittances are supporting reserves even as the economy slows. Nepal’s opportunity is to finance more productive investment while managing exposure to jobs and wages abroad.

title.rendered: The ECB’s June increase exposes Indian exporters to two different risks

content.rendered:
An Indian exporter can gain on a euro invoice and lose on the next order. The June increase in the European Central Bank’s rates matters through both routes. Currency conversion influences the rupee value of sales already contracted. The buyer’s financing conditions influence inventories, payment terms and the volume it will order. A hedge can manage much of the first exposure. The second belongs in a credit and demand assessment. ECB, 11 June monetary policy decisions · ECB, official interest-rate history

The combination the ECB faced

The ECB decided on 11 June to raise all three policy rates by 25 basis points, with the deposit facility rate set to rise to 2.25% on 17 June. In its new baseline, headline inflation was projected at 3.0% in 2026 and 2.3% in 2027, while growth was projected at 0.8% and 1.2%. The ECB attributed the higher inflation path and weaker 2026 growth outlook in part to the consequences of the Middle East conflict for energy prices and incomes. These were staff projections under assumptions. A European buyer’s experience will depend on its country, energy use, debt and customer base. ECB, 11 June monetary policy decisions

Higher euro rates can strengthen the currency if they change relative expected returns. Weaker expected growth or heightened geopolitical risk can pull in the other direction. An exporter should avoid making its entire plan contingent on a single exchange-rate response to the announcement. The credit effect may be easier to trace. Banks and suppliers decide how much working capital to provide a buyer and the interest rate or terms at which it can finance stock.

Inventory is a financing decision

Assume an Indian company ships goods invoiced at €1 million. An illustrative move from ₹95 to ₹98 per euro lifts unhedged revenue by ₹30 lakh at conversion. Suppose its European customer then cuts an otherwise comparable subsequent order by €150,000. At ₹98 per euro that removes ₹1.47 crore of gross revenue. The effect on profit depends on variable costs, spare production capacity and whether the goods can be sold elsewhere. The two numbers make the exposures visible without assuming a forecast for the euro or the order book.

Changes to payment terms can be as important as order cuts. Extending settlement on €1 million from 45 to 75 days adds €1 million for 30 days to the supplier’s receivables exposure. At an illustrative annual financing cost of 8%, that adds roughly €6,575 before accounting for credit risk. The buyer has effectively asked the supplier to finance more of its operations. An exporter that hedged the euro amount still needs a plan for the extra month, including how the hedge is settled or rolled.

Where the effect could be small

The strongest counterargument is that a quarter-point move is modest and many European buyers finance themselves at fixed rates or from cash. Goods with few substitutes or essential use may also see little change in order volumes. The June increase is better treated as a prompt to identify sensitive buyers than as a prediction of an across-the-board export slowdown. Orders for discretionary goods, or from distributors with leveraged inventories, deserve closer attention than sales with guaranteed volumes and short settlement periods.

A test can use order frequency, cancellations and days receivable across the exporter’s European customers. Match those outcomes to buyer size, product and terms agreed before the rate decision. Examine euro-priced sales separately from sales settled in dollars or rupees. If collections stay stable and repeat orders hold up, currency movements may remain the larger near-term exposure. If receivables lengthen among leveraged buyers despite steady euro prices, working capital and buyer concentration deserve the larger share of management attention.

Longer terms also make buyer concentration visible. A firm that sells to several solvent customers can tighten terms selectively. A firm dependent on one distributor may accept a delay to protect shelf space, using its own bank line to carry a risk previously financed in Europe. That renegotiation belongs in the margin calculation.

June’s decision makes the distinction concrete. An exchange-rate gain shows up on an invoice. The profitability of a trading relationship depends on whether the next invoice is issued and paid.

excerpt.rendered: The euro value of an invoice can rise while a European customer’s ability to finance the next order deteriorates.

title.rendered: India’s current-account surplus conceals a widening non-oil trade gap

content.rendered:
The Reserve Bank of India reported a preliminary current-account surplus of $7.1 billion for January–March 2026, equivalent to 0.7% of quarterly GDP. A year earlier the surplus was $13.7 billion, or 1.4% of GDP. The encouraging part of the release is the capacity of services receipts and transfers to offset a large goods deficit. The concern is that the goods gap widened even as the measured net petroleum deficit narrowed. India’s external position will be more resilient if it can sustain services income and address the composition of the non-oil gap. RBI, 8 June balance-of-payments release, Table 1

Where the $6.6 billion deterioration came from

RBI Table 1 puts the merchandise deficit at $83.4 billion, compared with $59.3 billion a year earlier. That is a widening of about $24.1 billion. Net services receipts improved by $7.1 billion to $60.4 billion. Net secondary income rose by $9.8 billion to $41.3 billion, and the net primary-income outflow narrowed by about $0.8 billion. Together those offsets were roughly $17.7 billion. Subtracting them from the worsening goods balance gives approximately $6.4 billion of deterioration, close to the reported $6.6 billion change in the current account once the rounded line items are taken into account. RBI, 8 June balance-of-payments release, Table 1

Personal transfer receipts, mainly remittances, rose from $33.9 billion to $43.5 billion on the RBI’s figures. These are receipts. The current-account identity uses the broader net secondary-income balance. Mixing the gross receipt figure with other net components would overstate the amount available to offset the merchandise deficit. This accounting distinction matters when a large remittance figure is used to explain a quarterly surplus. RBI, 8 June balance-of-payments release, Table 1

Petroleum narrowed the gap in the quarter

The RBI’s petroleum, oil and lubricants category had a net deficit of $26.3 billion, down from $30.2 billion a year earlier. Subtract that category from the total goods balance and the remaining deficit is approximately $57.1 billion, compared with $29.1 billion a year earlier. That is an increase of about $28.0 billion. The $3.9 billion improvement in the petroleum balance partially offset the widening elsewhere. This decomposition uses the categories in the RBI release and does not identify which non-petroleum products caused the change. RBI, 8 June balance-of-payments release, Table 1

A larger non-petroleum deficit can reflect very different economic developments. Capital goods imports can support an expansion in domestic productive capacity. Higher intermediate imports can reflect growth in assembly or export production. A rise in final consumer imports or weaker non-oil exports has a different implication for future foreign-currency earnings. Without a product-level split, there is little basis for concluding that the wider gap reflects either a healthy investment cycle or a loss of competitiveness. Compare import volumes, unit values and end-use categories, then test whether the sectors buying more inputs subsequently raise output or exports.

The gross flows narrow the set of explanations. Using the RBI’s rounded petroleum and total-goods entries, non-petroleum imports increased from about $131.5 billion to $158.0 billion, while non-petroleum exports edged down from $102.3 billion to $100.8 billion. The import side drove most of the change. That still leaves price, volume and product mix to be explained. An analyst should start with the largest contributors to the increase in import value, then check whether unit values rose or buyers imported more at similar prices. A higher nominal import bill driven by a few expensive products calls for a different response from a broad shift toward foreign final goods. RBI, 8 June balance-of-payments release, Table 1

There is a policy risk in using the widening balance as a target by itself. A restriction that reduces the import of inputs used by exporters can improve the measured goods balance in the near term while making later exports less competitive. An intervention should be justified by evidence on the underlying problem, such as supply risk, persistent barriers to domestic production or a missing capability. For an investment-led import surge, a better test is whether capital goods are installed and used and whether the resulting production eventually generates income or exports.

The financing side has its own vulnerabilities

Net foreign direct investment rose to $4.2 billion in the quarter from $0.4 billion a year earlier. Net foreign portfolio outflows increased to $12.0 billion from $5.9 billion. The RBI also reported $7.2 billion of reserve accretion on a balance-of-payments basis during the quarter, while reserves declined by $23.6 billion on that basis over the full financial year. A positive current account for one quarter and outflows from traded assets can therefore coexist. The sustainability question depends on the type and maturity of financing, not just its headline total. RBI, 8 June balance-of-payments release, Table 1

Reserve movements also require a definition. A change measured on a balance-of-payments basis excludes valuation effects, while the nominal dollar value of the reserve stock can move as reserve currencies and gold are repriced. The RBI’s separate reserve-variation release makes that distinction explicit. A financing dashboard should show the two measures together and avoid inferring the scale of intervention directly from a change in gross reserves. It should also distinguish direct investment, portfolio flows and shorter-term funding, which can react differently to a change in global risk appetite. RBI, 8 June balance-of-payments release, Table 1 · RBI, 8 June sources of variation in foreign-exchange reserves

An oil stress test belongs in the next quarter’s outlook

A narrower petroleum deficit in the March quarter says little about the size of the June-quarter oil bill. At its 5 June meeting the MPC pointed to elevated energy prices and supply-chain disruptions and held the repo rate at 5.25%. The U.S. EIA’s 9 June outlook assumed that disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz would keep Brent near an average of $105 a barrel in June and July. That is a forecast conditional on supply and demand assumptions, with a different time window from the RBI’s observed trade data. RBI, 5 June Monetary Policy Committee resolution · RBI Governor’s statement, 5 June · U.S. EIA, 9 June Short-Term Energy Outlook release

For a transparent stress test, every sustained $10 increase in the price of one million net barrels a day over 90 days adds about $900 million to the bill, with volumes and other terms held constant. The calculation is a sensitivity, not a claim about India’s net import volume. Refined-product export prices, changes in volumes, contract terms, freight, and sourcing discounts can alter the result. Putting oil sensitivity alongside the non-oil gap shows why the next quarterly deficit could move even if the underlying competitiveness of Indian exporters is unchanged.

The services and transfer offsets should also be monitored separately. Services exports depend on overseas clients and the mix of activities India sells, while transfers depend on earnings and employment abroad. Changes in global demand can affect both without showing up immediately in merchandise orders. The quarterly release shows the strength of these offsets in aggregate. Testing their resilience requires more detail on the markets and sectors generating receipts, as well as attention to whether nominal receipts are rising because of prices, exchange rates or additional activity. RBI, 8 June balance-of-payments release, Table 1

A practical scorecard would track three series before the next balance-of-payments release: the non-petroleum trade gap by product, services receipts and financing flows split by instrument. Compare them against previous March and June quarters to avoid interpreting a seasonal change as a structural one. Then publish an oil-price scenario separately. If the goods gap widens in capital inputs and exports subsequently expand, that is consistent with an investment explanation. A wider gap in consumption goods, weak export volumes and reliance on short-duration financing would warrant a more cautious reading of the same headline balance.

The strongest case for optimism is the demonstrated resilience of services and transfers. For 2025–26 as a whole, the RBI puts net receipts from services, income and transfers together at $312.0 billion, up from $264.0 billion. The full-year current-account deficit was still $25.2 billion, or 0.6% of GDP. A sustained expansion in services can finance useful imports and support domestic income. The evidence that would strengthen that judgement is rising export volumes and productive investment alongside stable financing and lower vulnerability to commodity shocks. Until that evidence is clear, the right policy focus is the composition of the goods deficit and the durability of the offsets that finance it. RBI, 8 June balance-of-payments release, Table 1

excerpt.rendered: Services and transfers kept the March-quarter current account in surplus. The goods data point to a larger non-oil deficit and a separate financing challenge.

title.rendered: June’s growth downgrade made fertiliser a second channel of the energy shock

content.rendered:
The global economy after the energy shock · Part 2 · June World Bank outlook

The World Bank’s June outlook put world growth at 2.5% in 2026, down from 2.9% in 2025, with roughly two-thirds of economies downgraded against its January projections. It also projected substantially higher fertiliser prices. For importers with a crop season approaching, the latter may be the more actionable forecast. A farmer deciding on application rates today faces consequences months after the cargo that supplied the dealer was bought. World Bank, June 2026 Global Economic Prospects · World Bank, full June outlook

The cash obligation arrives before the harvest

Higher energy costs can affect the price or availability of fertiliser and the cost of moving it inland. A wholesale buyer needs funding for a more expensive inventory. A dealer needs the cash or credit to supply farmers before payment. A farmer pays for inputs while output prices and rainfall remain uncertain. Any link in that chain can cut purchases in response to a higher bill. A reduction in use can later lower yields, though the effect depends on crop, soil and whether the original rate was already above its economically useful level.

Take a dealer purchasing 1,000 tonnes at $400 per tonne. A 25% increase in unit cost requires another $100,000 for the same stock. If the dealer has a $400,000 financing limit, the same budget now buys 800 tonnes. A public programme that holds the retail price fixed can shield farmers from the price increase. Timely compensation and adequate wholesale financing are still necessary if dealers are to stock the same quantity.

Compare what the forecasts are built to measure

The June outlook also projected Brent to average $94 in 2026 under an assumption about the easing of severe disruptions. A comparison with April’s IMF forecast needs care. The institutions differ in how they aggregate national growth rates and in the data available at publication. The World Bank’s downgrade against its own prior outlook is a cleaner starting point than subtracting the June World Bank number from April’s IMF number. World Bank, June 2026 Global Economic Prospects · IMF, April 2026 World Economic Outlook

Governments have a defensible case for temporary support where a missed planting window causes a loss that cannot be reversed. Blanket support can become expensive when world prices stay high. Its benefit may concentrate among buyers who would have applied the same amount anyway. Monitoring supply and stockouts by district can help target support to places where availability genuinely constrains production. Follow-on changes in retail price, application rates and harvest yield would help identify who gained from the policy.

The immediate test is whether dealers can finance inventories and farmers can buy inputs on time. At harvest, the same policy can be assessed against quantities and output. That timeline explains how an energy disturbance can still be visible in food prices after the price of crude has changed direction.

The global economy after the energy shock
Previous · Part 1 · All installments · Next · Part 3

title.rendered: The RBI’s June pause buys time to see how far the oil shock spreads

content.rendered:
The Reserve Bank of India’s decision to leave the repo rate at 5.25 per cent is defensible even though it now expects substantially higher inflation. India faces a rise in the price of imported energy that reduces purchasing power at the same time as it pushes up prices. Raising rates immediately would add a financing shock to an economy already absorbing that loss of income. The case for waiting depends on what happens to prices beyond fuel and the industries that use it directly. Once the shock spreads to wages, unrelated services and longer-term expectations, the cost of waiting rises quickly. RBI’s June 2026 MPC resolution

The forecast revision is a change in the trade-off

In April the Monetary Policy Committee projected real GDP growth of 6.9 per cent and CPI inflation of 4.6 per cent for 2026–27. Its June projection has growth at 6.6 per cent and inflation at 5.1 per cent. The projected inflation peak in the October–December quarter is 5.9 per cent, up from 5.2 per cent in April and close to the 6 per cent upper tolerance limit. The forecasts are conditional and do not record any realised quarter. Their direction is important. Inflation and growth moved against the committee simultaneously, which is consistent with a deterioration in supply conditions and purchasing power. RBI’s April 2026 MPC resolution · RBI’s June 2026 MPC resolution

The monthly evidence also shows how much information is still in transit between prices. The June resolution puts March and April headline inflation at 3.4 and 3.5 per cent. The governor reports that wholesale price inflation moved from 3.9 per cent in March to 8.3 per cent in April. The indices cover different items, weights and points in the supply chain. Subtracting one from the other would not estimate next month’s consumer inflation. The contrast tells the committee where to look for pressure, especially in firms buying industrial inputs whose own selling prices can be adjusted only when contracts renew. RBI’s June 2026 MPC resolution · RBI governor’s June policy statement

A change in the fuel price level can lead to two different inflation paths

The RBI says petrol and diesel prices rose cumulatively by 7.4 and 8.4 per cent, respectively, and estimates that those increases add about 36 basis points directly to headline inflation. To illustrate the scale, if a hypothetical headline reading would have been 4.00 per cent with no direct fuel effect, adding 36 basis points would make it 4.36 per cent, holding every other component fixed. This is a calculation in percentage points for an illustrative reading. It does not subtract 36 basis points from the annual forecast to recover what the RBI thinks inflation would have been without the conflict. RBI’s June 2026 MPC resolution · RBI governor’s June policy statement

A one-time rise in the fuel price still leaves households with a lower real income if wages are unchanged. Once the higher price is in the comparison period, its direct contribution to year-on-year inflation drops out unless prices rise again. The lasting problem begins when transporters reprice freight, manufacturers raise prices on new orders, workers bargain for catch-up wage increases and firms make further price changes in anticipation of higher costs. Households may then start to expect repeated increases. The same direct impact can be followed by very different inflation outcomes, depending on the breadth and durability of those responses.

The composition of core inflation matters for that judgement. The resolution reports that CPI excluding food and fuel was 3.7 per cent during January to April. Core excluding precious metals was lower, and the committee projects core inflation of 4.7 per cent for the full year. Precious metals can push the aggregate higher without signalling that an ordinary service business has gained pricing power. At the same time, a rise in a broad set of core services would matter even if gold prices happened to fall. A reliable assessment needs both the published aggregates and the distribution of price changes underneath them. RBI’s June 2026 MPC resolution

Borrowers absorb a hike at different speeds

Higher policy rates matter through bank lending rates, funding costs and the exchange rate, with different lags. The governor reports that the cumulative 125-basis-point repo reduction from February 2025 had been accompanied through April 2026 by weighted average rupee lending rate declines of 83 basis points on fresh loans and 89 basis points on outstanding loans. These are observed changes in rates on loan portfolios, affected by composition and repricing. They illustrate why the cost of reversing part of the easing would arrive unevenly across loans and lenders. RBI governor’s June policy statement

A large exporter with foreign-currency receipts can have a natural hedge against some imported input costs. A small domestic supplier buying imported chemicals and selling on a fixed-price contract may have no such offset. If the latter also faces a working-capital rate that resets quickly, its input and interest costs can increase before it can renegotiate. The distributional implication of a rate decision therefore depends on borrowing, pricing power and contractual timing. A household buying less because its fuel bill rose may contribute to slowing demand even if its mortgage rate has yet to change.

The distribution also changes when the government absorbs part of the oil cost through taxes, subsidies or public-sector balance sheets. A smaller rise at the pump can protect household spending now, while the fiscal cost shows up in foregone revenue, greater borrowing or less room for other expenditure. The RBI should track the duration of that cushion. If households and firms expect tax relief to expire, the next observed fuel increase could coincide with delayed price adjustments elsewhere. The same crude price can therefore produce different inflation paths under different domestic pass-through policies. RBI governor’s June policy statement

The strongest case for tightening early

The argument for a pre-emptive hike is strongest if currency weakness and a prolonged energy shock begin moving expected inflation above target. A rate move could help anchor expectations and reduce the chance of further pass-through through the rupee, though the exchange-rate response would also depend on the dollar, oil payments and investors’ appetite for risk. The 5.9 per cent third-quarter projection leaves little room for an additional surprise. A weak monsoon could add food inflation precisely when businesses are testing how much of their costs they can pass on. RBI’s June 2026 MPC resolution · RBI governor’s June policy statement

Measures that support orderly foreign-exchange and money-market conditions can buy time for the committee to observe that evidence. The governor’s account of liquidity operations illustrates why market rates can be managed around the existing stance. A policy rate set mainly to defend a particular exchange rate would affect borrowers across the economy, including those with little exposure to imported inputs. Foreign-exchange operations also have costs and cannot permanently offset an underlying rise in the import bill. The committee should judge the rate by the outlook for medium-term Indian inflation and output, with market functioning addressed through instruments suited to it. RBI governor’s June policy statement

What would end the case for waiting

A handful of higher fuel and freight quotations would confirm the direct mechanism the committee already expects. Evidence of generalisation would look different. A wider share of categories would record persistent price increases, particularly services with modest direct fuel exposure. Surveys would show longer-horizon expectations moving up, and pay settlements and business price intentions would indicate that households and firms expect the increases to last. Looking at sequential price changes alongside year-on-year inflation would help distinguish current momentum from favourable or adverse comparison months. RBI’s June 2026 MPC resolution

If those indicators rise together while activity remains resilient, the case for tightening strengthens even before the forecast peak. If energy-related categories explain most of the increase and broader demand and pricing indicators weaken, the pause remains justified. The judgement is about the persistence and breadth of inflation at the horizon monetary policy can affect. A close approach to the tolerance limit deserves attention, and the evidence that determines the next rate move is how price-setting behaviour changes as the shock reaches households and businesses. RBI’s June 2026 MPC resolution

Part of a series

The 2026 oil shock

How a spike in crude ran through India’s inflation target, monetary policy, fuel taxes, reserves and the rupee in 2026.

title.rendered: India should measure ration reform by the grain households receive

content.rendered:
India’s new ration-distribution scheme should be judged by whether eligible households receive their full allotment on time. An electronic record of a completed transaction can help establish that. A rise in recorded transactions can also conceal people who were turned away before a sale was logged, or households that took home less grain than the machine recorded. The distinction matters because the Cabinet’s ₹25,530 crore central commitment to SARTHAK-PDS over five years brings together physical delivery and digital monitoring. The two need a common outcome that can be verified independently of the systems they finance. Cabinet decision on SARTHAK-PDS · Business Standard’s coverage of the scheme

What the Cabinet decision pays for

SARTHAK-PDS combines central assistance for moving foodgrains within states, handling them and paying fair-price shop margins with the technology and administrative reforms previously organised under SMART-PDS.
