excerpt.rendered: The EU finalised legislation for a €90 billion loan. The budget value depends on the uses, the disbursement timetable and the liability carried by the lender.

title.rendered: India’s rural roads programme should pay for reliable journeys

content.rendered:
Finishing a bridge on a rural route can create more value than upgrading several additional kilometres of road. The Cabinet on 18 April extended Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana-III, which upgrades routes from rural habitations to markets, secondary schools and hospitals. It revised the outlay to ₹83,977 crore from ₹80,250 crore. The case for continuing the programme is strongest where an incomplete link, weak bridge or seasonal interruption still makes the journey unreliable. Delhi and the states should judge projects by the trips that become possible at an acceptable cost. Kilometres completed are useful for monitoring construction and incomplete as a measure of access. Cabinet decision extending PMGSY-III · PMGSY-III programme guidelines

Fix the part of the network that sets the cost of the journey

The extension gives roads in hills and roads and bridges in plains until March 2028, with hill bridges given until March 2029. The Cabinet decision allows tendering of certain works already sanctioned and permits the sanction and award of 161 pending long-span bridges on already sanctioned alignments, at an estimated ₹961 crore. The ₹3,727 crore increase in the overall outlay is about 4.6% of the original allocation. That is a revision to the programme envelope. It should be kept separate from the eventual incremental spending on the bridges and from the value of the work already completed. Cabinet decision extending PMGSY-III

A missing crossing can determine whether all the adjacent spending is useful. A road that ends at a river a vehicle cannot cross in the monsoon is effectively two separate links. Completing the crossing can shorten the whole trip or allow a bus operator to run a schedule through the year. This is why a project should be ranked by the journey it improves and the availability of other routes. Extending a high-quality road that already has a good alternative may be worth less than making a shorter, unreliable route usable. Appraisals should include detours, waiting times and closures, alongside normal running times. Cabinet decision extending PMGSY-III · PMGSY-III programme guidelines

For illustration, suppose a crossing saves ₹200 on each of 15,000 freight trips a year. That is ₹30 lakh in annual freight savings at existing volumes. Separately, 1,000 regular passengers each making 30 round trips a year could save 20,000 hours in total if each round trip becomes 40 minutes faster. At an assumed ₹75 per hour, that adds ₹15 lakh in time savings. These are illustrative figures, before maintenance, safety or gains from trips that would not otherwise occur. They show how a shorter route can be evaluated even when the project carries few kilometres. Use local counts and values of time for a real appraisal.

The worked example can be carried into the investment decision. If the ₹45 lakh annual benefit lasts ten years and is discounted at an illustrative 8%, its present value is about ₹3.02 crore. The appraisal would deduct construction and maintenance costs and add any independently estimated safety or access benefits. A shorter closure-free life or benefits that accrue only in the dry season would reduce the estimate. New trips can add benefits as well, but they should be valued using evidence of what travellers are willing to pay or save, rather than assuming every new journey is worth the full time saving. The assumptions should be visible before the project is selected.

A road expands options and changes where work happens

A study by Sam Asher and Paul Novosad uses eligibility thresholds in an earlier rural roads programme to estimate the effect of new connections. It finds a shift out of agricultural work, with limited evidence of large short-run gains in village income, assets or agriculture. One interpretation is that the road made it easier to take work outside the village. That is a gain for some households and a reason to keep local enterprise outcomes separate from residents’ earnings. The evidence comes from new connections under an earlier programme. Upgrading a link that is already used can have a different effect. The study is useful because it challenges the assumption that every road will raise output in the place where it is built. Asher and Novosad, American Economic Review

The benefits can be uneven within a village. A farmer with saleable surplus and access to a truck can benefit immediately from more buyers. A household that sells little output may gain more from lower bus fares, access to health care or the chance to take paid work in a nearby town. A paved road does not guarantee a scheduled vehicle. Where there is little competition among operators or traffic is too thin, travel costs can fall less than engineering estimates suggest. In those cases the missing complement may be a regular service, usable loading space at the market or a safe route to the pickup point. A monitoring survey should ask who uses the route and who still cannot. Cabinet decision extending PMGSY-III · Asher and Novosad, American Economic Review

Maintenance determines whether the benefit persists

The strongest case for extending the construction programme is that stopping halfway through a network can waste earlier investment. There is also a strong argument for moving maintenance up the list. A bridge approach that washes out or a road surface that becomes unsafe can recreate the very detour the project was built to remove. The programme’s guidelines provide for routine maintenance through the initial contracts and address subsequent responsibilities. The policy question is whether funds and inspections are available when those responsibilities fall due. A state that can afford a new link but cannot preserve access on existing roads may get a better return from repair and drainage than from another upgrade. PMGSY-III programme guidelines · ILO study on rural road maintenance

Market access can also alter bargaining. When a grower can get a perishable crop to two wholesale markets instead of one, the local buyer has to compete with a credible outside option. That can raise the farm-gate price even if the farmer rarely changes buyer. The opposite is possible for a local trader protected by the cost of entry, or for a village shop now facing competition from larger markets. Those distributional effects can be tested by recording price differences for comparable grades, transport charges and the number of active buyers before and after a link opens. This offers a clearer measure of integration than the amount spent on the road. Asher and Novosad, American Economic Review

For the same reason, the benefit calculation needs a life-cycle cost. A cheap construction bid can become an expensive route if it requires frequent resurfacing or prolonged closures. Spending more on drainage or a more durable crossing may be economical in a flood-prone area. A useful procurement score would report construction cost, scheduled maintenance, expected renewal and the number of days a route is likely to remain open under realistic weather. Publishing actual closures and maintenance payments would make it easier to detect a contractor or design that wins on price while imposing costs on travellers after completion. PMGSY-III programme guidelines · ILO study on rural road maintenance

Measure access after the work is finished

Measure journey times and prices to the specific markets, schools and hospitals the projects are meant to serve, including during the monsoon. Record days closed, bus frequency, freight charges and emergency travel times. Compare routes where the missing link is completed with similar routes that are still waiting, checking whether their pre-completion trends were comparable. Track residents who find work outside the village as well as businesses that open inside it. A rise in reliably completed trips, at lower total cost and with maintained roads, would justify prioritising similar projects. A programme that hits construction targets while journeys remain seasonal would need to change which links it funds and how it maintains them. Cabinet decision extending PMGSY-III · Asher and Novosad, American Economic Review

excerpt.rendered: The extension of PMGSY-III gives India time to complete critical links. Its returns depend on year-round travel to markets, schools and hospitals, including after construction ends.

title.rendered: India’s small-city loan guarantee should reward a credible second loan

content.rendered:
The best test of a municipal loan guarantee is the loan a city can get after proving it can repay the first one. The housing ministry has launched the operational guidelines for the Urban Challenge Fund and its credit repayment guarantee. The Cabinet’s February decision set out a ₹5,000 crore guarantee scheme to help eligible smaller cities and urban local bodies in hilly and North-Eastern states access market finance. A guarantee can fill a gap when a lender lacks a record of a city’s performance. It can also allow a weak borrower to postpone a problem. The terms for the next borrowing help distinguish those cases. Housing ministry’s launch of the operational guidelines · Cabinet decision on the Urban Challenge Fund

A smaller guarantee can test the original rationale

The Cabinet description provides cover of up to ₹7 crore or 70 per cent of the first loan, whichever is lower. After successful repayment, the corresponding second limit is ₹7 crore or 50 per cent, whichever is lower. The ₹7 crore cap matters. On an illustrative first loan of ₹10 crore the guarantee would cover up to ₹7 crore, leaving at least ₹3 crore outside the guarantee. On a ₹20 crore first loan, the same cap is equivalent to 35 per cent. On a ₹10 crore subsequent loan the percentage limit brings maximum cover down to ₹5 crore. These figures describe the maximum face amount of cover under the stated rules. Recoveries and payout conditions determine the actual losses. Cabinet decision on the Urban Challenge Fund · Housing ministry’s launch of the operational guidelines

For the lender, a guarantee can reduce expected loss without improving the borrower’s ability to generate cash. Its economic value is strongest where the city has a feasible way to pay but the bank has little evidence on payment behaviour, financial controls or performance over time. The first loan can produce that evidence if timely repayment comes from the stated source. If the lender is repaid through an unexpected state rescue, a good repayment statistic may reveal less about the city’s capacity. Record the source of payments, cash reserves drawn down and any extra transfers made to meet the schedule.

A guarantee shifts risk to a wider balance sheet

Suppose 100 eligible cities each have a ₹10 crore loan with maximum first-loan cover of ₹7 crore. The face value of that illustrative exposure is ₹700 crore. If five of the loans default and a full ₹7 crore guarantee is paid on each, the gross cash payout is ₹35 crore before recoveries. This is a stress example, with assumed defaults and no estimate of the programme’s likely losses. Defaults can be correlated when the same state delays transfers or construction costs rise across several towns. That is a reason to report concentration by state, revenue source and project type as well as total guarantees issued.

The April announcement distinguishes ₹90,000 crore earmarked for projects, ₹5,000 crore for project preparation and capacity building, and ₹5,000 crore for the guarantee sub-scheme. These instruments tackle different constraints. A first-time borrower may need help preparing audited records, understanding its own cash flow and specifying a service before any lender can evaluate it. A guarantee applied at the end of that process can overcome uncertainty the lender cannot resolve. Applied in place of preparation, it can protect the lender while leaving the city with an asset it cannot operate on the planned terms. Housing ministry’s launch of the operational guidelines · RBI’s chapter on municipal own revenue

The case for insuring genuine public-service risk

A small city can face borrowing costs that reflect unfamiliarity or a limited lender market even when its finances are sound. A guarantee can widen competition, lower rates and help a city bring a worthwhile project forward. The strongest objection is that a lender with substantial protection may do less scrutiny, or that only cities expecting difficulty choose the guarantee. Leaving some risk with the lender helps, but how much matters depends on the shape of the loss-sharing and recovery terms. A programme can compare the pricing and participation of lenders with and without protection for similar borrowers and project types. Cabinet decision on the Urban Challenge Fund · PRS review of the February Cabinet decision

City residents should also be able to see the repayment source before the project is committed. A service charge, property-tax allocation and state payment put the burden on different people. For a low-income household, a higher basic-service charge may outweigh part of the improvement the project delivers. An identified budget subsidy can protect access if the city or state can credibly fund it. Leaving the shortfall unspecified makes it easier to approve the investment and harder to keep the service available once repayments begin.

Timing matters for the lender and the city. A grace period can help when construction precedes revenue, but interest that accrues during a delay is still a cost. Before a loan is approved, estimate who pays if procurement takes longer or the asset opens partway through a billing year. A plausible project can appear to default if the debt schedule assumes cash arrives sooner than the service can produce it. Reporting construction and payment dates together would reveal whether problems come from poor revenue forecasts or a mismatch between finance and project delivery.

The transition to a second loan should be evaluated for cities that applied and were turned down as well as those that obtained a guarantee. Otherwise, the observed borrowers will be the group lenders already found most promising. Compare application terms and track whether initial rejections can be resolved with better accounts, stronger transfers or a redesigned project. That helps distinguish an information problem from a genuine inability to repay.

Follow the borrowers after the first transaction

The published record should follow applications, rates, maturities, project completion, actual repayment sources and access to subsequent loans. A second loan on improved terms and with less guarantee cover would support the case that the programme is building credit histories. If rates stay high or borrowers need an equivalent public backstop again, identify whether the constraint is lending competition, erratic municipal revenue or the project itself. Financial inclusion for cities has succeeded when it widens the set of services they can sustainably deliver. A first disbursement is only the beginning of that test. Housing ministry’s launch of the operational guidelines · Cabinet decision on the Urban Challenge Fund

excerpt.rendered: A first municipal borrowing can be hard even for a viable project. The new guarantee will prove its value if a city builds a repayment record and can later borrow with less protection.

title.rendered: India’s March jobs data show why participation deserves equal billing

content.rendered:
India’s March labour survey gives more reason to watch participation than to dwell on a two-tenths rise in unemployment. The national unemployment rate for people aged 15 and above rose from 4.9% in February to 5.1% in March. Over the same period female labour-force participation fell from 35.3% to 34.4%, and the share of rural adults working fell from 56.3% to 55.5%. These are monthly survey estimates, with room for seasonal and sampling variation. They are nevertheless a useful warning about what the headline can miss. If people who need work stop looking, the unemployment rate can improve at the same time that their opportunities worsen. MoSPI’s March 2026 labour bulletin · March PLFS bulletin and methodology · Moneycontrol on the March survey

The denominator determines the story

Under the survey’s current weekly status approach, the labour-force participation rate measures the share of the population in the labour force. The worker-population ratio measures the share employed. The unemployment rate is the share of the labour force that is unemployed. The three are linked. Multiply participation by one minus the unemployment rate to obtain the employment share, up to rounding. The weekly reference period makes the measure responsive to recent conditions. It can classify a person as working after a small amount of qualifying activity, so it should be read alongside hours and earnings when the question is whether people can make a living. March PLFS bulletin and methodology

A numerical example shows why the distinction matters. Take 1,000 adults, of whom 560 are in the labour force and 28 are unemployed. The unemployment rate is 5% and 532 are working. If ten unemployed people stop searching without finding work, the labour force falls to 550 and unemployment to 18. The measured unemployment rate falls to about 3.3% even though 532 people still work. The employment share stays at 53.2%. Conversely, a rise in unemployment can be consistent with an improving economy if new entrants begin looking for jobs before finding them. The March survey cannot establish that either example caused the monthly change. It shows why all three indicators belong together. March PLFS bulletin and methodology

In the published national figures, overall participation fell from 55.9% to 55.4%. Applying the February unemployment rate to the March participation rate gives an implied employment share of about 52.69%, compared with about 53.16% in February. Applying March’s higher unemployment rate then brings the implied share to about 52.57%, close to the published 52.6% after rounding. On that ordering, roughly 0.48 percentage points of the decline comes from participation and about 0.11 from the unemployment rate. This is an accounting calculation using rounded aggregates. It cannot show that particular workers dropped out or establish why the proportions changed. Its policy implication is narrower. A response aimed only at people counted as unemployed would miss most of the movement in the employment share, so a fuller diagnosis should ask what happened to entry, exit and hours. MoSPI’s March 2026 labour bulletin

The rural and urban readings suggest different movements. Urban unemployment edged up from 6.6% to 6.8%, while the urban employment share slipped only from 47.0% to 46.8%. Rural employment fell by 0.8 percentage points, a larger change than the urban one. A policymaker focused only on the urban increase in unemployment would miss that decline in the share of rural residents working. A full explanation would compare labour-force entry and exit, crop work and other rural activity. The survey covers people across the country, and a national rural average need not describe conditions in any particular district. MoSPI’s March 2026 labour bulletin · March PLFS bulletin and methodology

Female participation is where the policy question sharpens

The March bulletin puts women’s participation at 38.9% in rural areas and 25.2% in urban areas. A higher rural figure does not by itself show better opportunities. Some rural women can work in a household enterprise or farm near home, while urban employment may offer a different mix of earnings and hours to those who are able to take it. Participation may rise because an attractive job becomes available or because household income falls and another member has to earn. It may fall because someone takes up education or cannot find work compatible with caregiving. These mechanisms have different welfare implications, even when they move the indicator in the same direction. MoSPI’s March 2026 labour bulletin · March PLFS bulletin and methodology

The case for making job access a policy priority is strongest when there are vacancies that workers cannot reasonably reach. The money wage matters, but so do commuting costs, reliable transport, care responsibilities and the ability to predict shifts. Consider a job that adds ₹8,000 a month to household income before expenses. If travel costs ₹2,000 and paid care another ₹3,000, the monthly cash gain is ₹3,000 before the value of time spent travelling. This is an illustration, not a survey estimate. A shorter commute or a workable childcare option could make that job viable without any change in its posted wage. Policies that address those costs can enlarge the set of jobs a person can accept.

That logic also cautions against treating all increases in participation as evidence of success. A household that sends a second member to work because its main income fell may be worse off even if both adults are counted as employed. A programme that produces more short spells of unpaid household work may change the employment rate without delivering the income or security people sought. Monthly indicators help locate where to ask these questions. Detailed employment status, hours worked and real earnings show whether a change in participation represents a better choice or a response to financial pressure. March PLFS bulletin and methodology

One month is evidence to investigate, with limited power to settle the cause

The strongest counterargument is that monthly estimates are noisy and employment in agriculture changes with the calendar. The March bulletin is the twelfth release in the monthly series, after the survey methodology was modified from January 2025. There is still a short history for comparing the same month across years on this design. Without standard errors for the relevant comparisons, small movements should be interpreted cautiously. The practical response is to look for repetition across months and independently measured outcomes, rather than attributing March’s changes to a single event or programme. If rural employment rebounds and hours and earnings strengthen in comparable groups, the case for concern weakens. MoSPI’s March 2026 labour bulletin · March PLFS bulletin and methodology

The distribution matters as much as the average. Look separately at paid employment, own-account activity and work in a household enterprise, and distinguish people who did some work from those who obtained the hours they wanted. A school leaver looking for a first job and a worker supplementing an unreliable farm income face different constraints. Well-designed placement and transport programmes can be evaluated against similar groups that did not receive the intervention, tracking sustained work and net earnings after travel and care costs. That evidence is more useful for deciding where to spend than a national target for adding a certain number of people to the labour force.

What would change the diagnosis

Track female participation, the employment share and unemployment together by rural and urban location, and cross-check them against hours, earnings and the types of work people report. A durable rise in participation accompanied by more paid work and stronger real earnings would support the view that opportunities are widening. Repeated declines in the employment share with a steady unemployment rate would justify asking who stopped looking and why. Local programmes should be judged by sustained work at wages that make it worth taking, alongside the ability of workers to reach those jobs. The March numbers are a reason to make that evidence routine. MoSPI’s March 2026 labour bulletin · March PLFS bulletin and methodology

Part of a series

Reading India’s jobs data

What the monthly labour surveys and payroll data can and cannot tell us about work in India.

title.rendered: Data centre electricity demand makes grid connection the scarce input

content.rendered:
Who pays for the AI buildout? · Part 4 · April IEA update

The IEA estimated that electricity demand from data centres rose 17% in 2025, compared with 3% growth in global electricity demand. Demand from AI-focused facilities grew faster still in its analysis. Those are global figures. A utility deciding whether to approve a new site faces a local question: can the connection deliver power when the facility needs it, and who will finance the network and generation it requires? IEA, Key Questions on Energy and AI · IEA, April 2026 electricity demand update

An annual energy figure can hide the peak

A continuous user can need a large amount of firm power during the busiest hours. Buying the same quantity of renewable energy over a year does not ensure supply in every hour. A site may be able to shift some processing away from tight periods, depending on the type of workload and its service commitments. That flexibility can save money if a utility is willing and able to pay for it. The opportunity depends on a measurable response when called.

A 100 MW site operating at an average of 80% of that rating would consume about 701 GWh in a 365-day year, ignoring losses and auxiliary boundary differences. Its contribution to the local peak can still be close to 100 MW if demand coincides with the system’s tightest interval. Those hypothetical figures show why tariff design can charge separately for total electricity and reserved capacity.

Separate the site’s cost from the benefit to other users

A dedicated line may primarily benefit the new customer. A new substation can also relieve an existing constraint and help nearby industry. The public decision should allocate costs on the basis of which benefits are shared and how much of the investment remains useful if the original customer leaves. An upfront contribution or minimum-payment commitment can reduce the burden on other users when a large load turns out smaller than promised.

The strongest argument for welcoming large data loads is that steady sales can support grid investment and spread fixed costs. That is more plausible where the operator commits for long enough and the new capacity improves reliability for others. It is less convincing where a costly upgrade precedes a short commitment or a major buyer can exit easily. Compare forecasts with metered load and confirmed commissioning dates, and revise the connection plan when projects are delayed.

The next data release should be read alongside waiting times for grid connection, investment in generation and network upgrades, and how those costs are recovered. Those measures show whether the buildout is buying more usable power or bidding for scarce capacity already needed by other users.

Who pays for the AI buildout?
Previous · Part 3 · All installments · Next · Part 5

title.rendered: Delhi’s new transit zoning will be tested by who can live near a station

content.rendered:
A metro line makes nearby land more valuable because more of the city can be reached from it. Delhi’s April transit-oriented development changes can turn some of that gain into more homes and better access. How much reaches residents depends on the number and kind of units delivered, how landowners and developers divide the gains, and whether streets and stations can serve more people. The city should measure the price and availability of the homes that result. Delhi Development Authority, notified TOD policy · MoHUA, Delhi TOD policy and charges · MoHUA, National Transit Oriented Development Policy

Extra development rights can be valuable without producing cheaper homes

The April notification and the ministry’s explanation describe corridor-based development along metro lines and around specified rail stations. The ministry describes a potential area of about 207 square kilometres, and a maximum floor area ratio up to 500 for qualifying plots of at least 2,000 square metres with the specified road width. It also describes the requirement to earmark 65% of permissible floor area ratio for residential units within a specified size. These provisions increase the potential building area under defined conditions. Affordability still depends on price, tenure and delivery. Delhi Development Authority, notified TOD policy · MoHUA, Delhi TOD policy and charges

An owner offered additional buildable space can ask a developer to pay more for the parcel. A developer will compare the price of acquiring it, construction costs, charges and likely sales or rents. Buyers can benefit if many additional projects become viable and increase supply. Where few parcels qualify or assembly takes a long time, a significant share of the immediate value can accrue to the owner. The timing of price gains and actual construction can differ by years.

The residual calculation

Take an illustrative plot where permissions create an additional 1,000 square metres of marketable floor area. Suppose completed space can sell at ₹1.5 lakh per square metre, generating ₹15 crore. If incremental construction, finance and marketing cost ₹9 crore and charges are ₹2 crore, the gross residual is ₹4 crore before the developer’s required return and other risks. The owner and developer can bargain over this residual. If sale prices are lower or infrastructure obligations rise, the amount that can support a higher land bid shrinks. The example isolates the mechanics and supplies no estimate of actual prices on a Delhi corridor.

A floor-area charge can capture some of the public value created by transit and finance station access, water and sewerage. A charge above the available residual can prevent construction. A low charge in a high-demand corridor can leave much of the windfall with landowners. The appropriate schedule can differ with market and infrastructure conditions. A transparent record of costs, charges and approvals helps policymakers update it without having to guess which assumption failed.

Follow residents as well as buildings

The strongest argument for a clear density rule is that more supply near good transport can improve affordability even without a deep subsidy on every unit. That response requires enough completed units and a reasonable construction timeline. Existing tenants can face rent increases or temporary displacement before supply materialises. Smaller dwelling size also provides limited assurance of affordable monthly cost in a high-priced location. Monitoring should include both the new units and households moving out of redeveloped properties.

Track permit applications, completions and occupancy by size and tenure, plus changes in rents, tenant retention and walking access. Compare corridors where similar plots fall inside and outside eligibility, with care about prior differences. If completions rise and more households at relevant incomes can live within easy reach of stations, the policy is delivering on its objective. If land prices rise before a thin pipeline of construction, check the barriers to building and the availability of affordable rental options.

Timing is another distributional choice. Phased redevelopment and enforceable return arrangements can matter to existing tenants who depend on a nearby job or school. A project can add net housing capacity while temporarily imposing expensive moves on households with little room to absorb them.

The best use of a transit-created land gain is to make it possible for more people to live close enough to use the service. Delhi can measure that directly.

excerpt.rendered: The city can permit more homes along rail corridors. Affordability will depend on land bids, delivery costs and who can occupy the extra floor space.

title.rendered: The IMF’s April forecast depended on how long the energy shock lasted

content.rendered:
The global economy after the energy shock · Part 1 · April IMF outlook

The IMF’s April projection of 3.1% world growth in 2026 came with a consequential assumption: the Middle East conflict would remain limited in duration and scope. That condition should sit beside the number whenever it is used. An oil shock that lasts a few weeks can be financed out of stocks and cash. A disruption that reaches several purchasing and wage cycles can change what firms produce and what households can afford. IMF, April 2026 World Economic Outlook · IMF, April forecast briefing

Where a price shock becomes a cash problem

A country importing more fuel than it sells abroad loses purchasing power when import prices rise. The domestic distribution depends on tax, contracts and pricing policy. A regulated utility may absorb the cost while its retail tariff stays fixed, then recover it from customers or the public budget. An industrial buyer paying the prevailing market price may see the effect on its very next order. The same national exposure produces several cash-flow paths.

For a scale comparison, consider an importer buying 100,000 barrels a day. A $15 increase adds $135 million to a 90-day bill at unchanged volumes. A company with inventory and a borrowing line may bridge the quarter. If the extra cost persists for a year, the bill rises by about $548 million. These are illustrative figures. Volume adjustment, contracts and currency movements will alter the realised cost. The example shows why the length of the disruption is a separate risk from the daily price.

What to look for after the spring release

A central bank has limited ability to lower the international cost of fuel. It can influence whether households and firms expect a broad sequence of future price increases. The evidence should come from measures that capture durable pressure, such as the breadth of services price changes and wage settlements. A rise in pump prices can depress consumption elsewhere before it triggers either effect. The fiscal position and bank lending conditions determine how much private spending can adjust without a sharp drop in activity.

There is a legitimate case for using a single baseline for budgeting. Firms and ministries need a number around which to organise plans. For an import-dependent economy the baseline works better with a second set of operating assumptions: higher settlement costs, longer shipping times and tighter access to credit. An explicit reserve policy can tell a utility when it has enough time to replace stock and when conservation or extra purchases become necessary.

The next update in this series follows what happened when the World Bank moved its forecast in June. The comparison to keep is the change in assumptions and in each institution’s own forecast, alongside the time firms and governments have available to respond.

The global economy after the energy shock
All installments · Next · Part 2

title.rendered: Europe’s first carbon border price belongs in the export contract

content.rendered:
The European Commission’s first carbon border certificate price gives importers and exporters a usable reference for contract negotiations. The price for covered imports in the first quarter of 2026 is €75.36 per certificate. The publication on 7 April concerns the quarter in which the goods were imported. Authorised declarants will begin buying certificates in February 2027 for 2026 imports. The separation between the economic exposure and the purchase date creates a question for Indian exporters now. Which party will carry the cost, finance it and bear the risk that the required certificate quantity is different from the one used to price the order? European Commission’s first certificate-price announcement · European Commission’s dated quarterly price table

Price and quantity need separate estimates

The 2026 price is calculated quarterly using EU emissions allowance auction information. The amount owed also depends on the number of certificates required under the applicable rules, which can reflect the embedded emissions calculation and adjustments. A quoted certificate price cannot be multiplied by a product’s gross emissions to get every exporter’s actual charge. The important accounting is to estimate the eligible certificate quantity separately from the price. Contracts can then identify how the parties will reconcile the expected quantity with the amount ultimately established. European Commission’s first certificate-price announcement · EU Regulation 2023/956 establishing CBAM · EU Regulation 2025/2083 on CBAM simplification

For illustration, assume the applicable calculation results in 120 chargeable certificates for a first-quarter shipment. At €75.36 each, the assumed liability is €9,043.20. If the required number turns out to be 150, the difference is €2,260.80 at the same quarter’s price. These numbers assume the certificate quantity after applicable adjustments and are not an estimate of any sector’s liability. They show how uncertainty in production evidence or the final calculation can matter even after the quarter’s published price is known. European Commission’s dated quarterly price table

The legal obligation and the economic incidence can differ

The authorised declarant bears the regulatory obligation. A buyer can nonetheless seek to recover part of the cost through lower purchase prices or ask the exporter to finance the work needed to verify emissions. Where the product is readily available from other suppliers, the buyer has a stronger bargaining position. Where a component is hard to substitute and shipment delays carry large costs, more of the bill may remain with the buyer or be passed further down the value chain. The allocation depends on the contract, market conditions and the quality of alternatives. EU Regulation 2023/956 establishing CBAM · EU implementing regulation on embedded-emissions calculations

Currency and timing can change the cost to a supplier that quotes in rupees or dollars while facing a possible charge tied to euros. In the illustrative 120-certificate example, a move from ₹90 to ₹95 per euro changes the rupee equivalent by about ₹45,216 if the amount is fully borne by the exporter. The exchange rates are assumed. The example excludes hedging and finance costs. It shows why the agreed currency and the date used for conversion matter if the buyer later deducts a euro amount from a price negotiated months earlier.

Choose a rule the two parties can verify

A contract can allocate the charge explicitly, define which records establish the certificate quantity and state which party bears the effect of a reporting error. A supplier is better placed to control the integrity of its production records. An importer may control the timing of import and elements of its compliance process. Allocating a risk to the party that can influence it can improve the incentive to prevent errors. A vague adjustment clause can leave both parties contesting the same bill after delivery, when changing the production data or the customer is no longer easy.

The strongest case for simply quoting one fixed all-in price is that commercial partners need predictability and repeated reconciliation can be costly. That can work where emissions are well documented, the relevant import quarter is clear and both firms can bear ordinary fluctuations. For a new product or an importer with less experience, an agreed provisional estimate and a transparent reconciliation formula may avoid a large risk premium. The balance depends on the size and variability of the expected charge, the reliability of the records and the value of simplicity to the buyer. European Commission’s first certificate-price announcement · EU implementing regulation on embedded-emissions calculations

Import timing also matters when goods are manufactured, shipped and cleared in different periods. The date of production alone does not fix the quarter for the published certificate price. If shipping or clearance takes longer than expected, a buyer could face a different reference price while the supplier has already committed to its original invoice. A useful agreement should define the import event that determines the reference price and how the two parties will handle a delay. This can matter for a narrow-margin order even when each firm knows its own operating costs well. European Commission’s first certificate-price announcement · European Commission’s dated quarterly price table

The delay until certificate purchases can look like free working capital. A buyer expecting to meet a known obligation later can set aside funds, while a business that makes no provision may face several quarters of liabilities arriving in a short period. The distinction matters for cash management and for comparing competing offers. An exporter that agrees to share the cost should model when its share could be deducted and what evidence would support the deduction. A lower expected charge can still create a larger liquidity problem if its timing is uncertain. European Commission’s first certificate-price announcement

The first price creates a testable benchmark

Compare contract terms before and after publication, which suppliers are asked for verified data and who absorbs any adjustment to the assumed charge. Track costs as a share of the sale price across products with different emissions and margins. A price published before cash settlement can make the terms clearer, especially if the parties agree on the quantity and the source of the data. If later disputes cluster around unsupported emissions values or the handling of multiple quarters, the first price will have solved the easier part of the commercial problem. European Commission’s first certificate-price announcement · European Commission’s dated quarterly price table

excerpt.rendered: The first CBAM certificate price is €75.36. The commercial cost of that figure depends on which emissions are chargeable and who agrees to absorb the bill.

title.rendered: Artemis II turned part of the lunar programme’s uncertainty into evidence

content.rendered:
The economics of returning to the Moon · Part 2 · April crewed flight and return

Artemis II launched on 1 April and returned its crew to Earth after a lunar flyby. For the Artemis programme, the economic importance of a crewed test lies in what NASA can learn about the system under conditions a ground test cannot fully reproduce. Flight evidence can improve the next procurement or reduce the need for contingency. Its value depends on how directly the observations apply to subsequent missions. NASA, Artemis II mission record · NASA, Artemis II return to Earth

A successful flight resolves questions within its scope

NASA can compare equipment and crew experience with models and earlier tests. It can then change maintenance requirements, confidence in operating costs or the order of later tests. Evidence from a flyby has narrower scope than evidence about completing a landing and working on the surface. The programme should carry forward the findings that are relevant and keep separate budgets and readiness checks for unresolved tasks.

A simple example helps explain the value. Suppose engineers have two plausible explanations for why a subsystem may require more servicing than expected. One calls for a design change that would cost $20 million. The other can be addressed in normal servicing for $2 million. If a flight measurement can distinguish them before production is repeated, it can prevent unnecessary expense or identify a change early. These amounts illustrate a decision and do not estimate actual costs.

Separate learning from repeatability

A one-off mission can rely on exceptional staffing and preparation. A programme intending to fly repeatedly has to understand which tasks can be standardised and which will require specialist effort each time. A flight can reveal work that had been underestimated. That may raise the expected cost while improving the accuracy of the plan. Cost reductions are more credible when they survive several missions and include the staff and facilities needed between flights.

The strongest reason to draw confidence from the flight is that real operation reveals interactions among people, hardware and procedures. An important limit is that one success supplies limited evidence about rare problems. Repeat testing, transparent review and realistic operating assumptions give the programme a way to learn without overreading one observation. That matters most when contracts and schedules involve several providers.

The next economic update should connect findings to changes in cost or schedule and distinguish issues resolved from work that remains. Observations used to change a design, supplier requirement or future test can be recorded without assuming every detail is public. The durable return from Artemis II will include the uncertainty it removed and the costly mistakes the programme can avoid as a result.

The economics of returning to the Moon

title.rendered: India’s new insolvency route can preserve more value if lenders act early

content.rendered:
India’s insolvency reform will improve recoveries if it gets viable companies into restructuring before their businesses disintegrate. The amendment that received assent on 6 April creates a creditor-initiated process for eligible companies and allows incumbent management to continue under oversight. It also sets a shorter timetable. The law provides for commencement through separate government notifications, so the new route should be understood as the design Parliament has approved. The economic test is whether lenders begin earlier, preserve viable operations and obtain better recoveries after allowing for time. A quicker process is useful only if it protects enough value to justify the powers it gives financial creditors. The April 2026 amendment as published in the Gazette · PRS Legislative Research on creditor-initiated resolution

Why time before admission matters

The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India reports that 1,376 cases that produced resolution plans by December 2025 took an average of 619 days to conclude, after excluding time the adjudicating authority excluded. That is a historical average among cases ending in approved plans. It does not include every case that entered insolvency, and says little about the time between the first sign of distress and formal commencement. That pre-process period matters. Customers can move to other suppliers, skilled workers can leave and orders can expire. A business whose assets would have earned more together can become a collection of machines and receivables before a buyer gets a chance to bid. IBBI’s December 2025 quarterly data

The Board also reports about ₹4.11 lakh crore realised through resolution plans against about ₹12.99 lakh crore in claims in the relevant cases, roughly 32% by that comparison. The same report records realisations above estimated liquidation value. These comparisons use different baselines. Claims describe what creditors are owed. Liquidation value approximates what a break-up might yield at entry. A restructuring can beat liquidation value and still leave creditors with a large loss on their claims. Neither ratio establishes what recovery would have been if lenders had acted earlier. That requires comparing cases with similar asset quality and distress at entry, and taking account of the time until money actually arrives. IBBI’s December 2025 quarterly data

Consider two plans each paying a lender ₹50 crore in a single instalment. At an assumed discount rate of 12% a year, receipt after six months is worth about ₹47.25 crore at the start, while receipt after two years is worth about ₹39.86 crore. The difference is about ₹7.4 crore in present value before legal costs. A later payment could still be preferable if a longer sales process finds a materially better buyer or if the shorter timetable leads to an unreliable commitment. The exercise puts a price on delay. The best bid still depends on the size and reliability of the payment.

The new process changes bargaining as well as the clock

The creditor-initiated route gives specified financial creditors a way to start after default, subject to the approvals and debtor representations set out in the statute. The approval threshold for eligible initiating financial creditors is at least 51% of the relevant debt by value. The law sets 150 days from commencement, with provision for an extension of up to 45 days on the specified approvals. The board or partners ordinarily retain management during the process, with oversight by the resolution professional and powers for the committee of creditors and tribunal. Keeping managers in place can preserve knowledge, contracts and relationships that would be costly for an administrator to rebuild. The April 2026 amendment as published in the Gazette · PRS Legislative Research on creditor-initiated resolution

The price of that continuity is the risk that incumbent management has information and incentives other creditors cannot see. A business in distress may have little reason to reveal which assets are most valuable or where transactions with related parties have moved cash. An insider may benefit from delaying a sale or controlling access to records. A credible resolution professional, prompt disclosure of cash flows and independent valuation are essential. The process also needs a workable path to transfer control or move to the ordinary route when existing management obstructs a fair resolution. The new structure is strongest when continuity protects operations and oversight protects the sale process. The April 2026 amendment as published in the Gazette

Suppliers can carry losses that secured lenders can absorb

A large lender can spread losses across a loan book. An unpaid supplier may have most of its working capital tied up in one debtor. If a quick process preserves a viable buyer, suppliers can benefit from future orders and from recovering some existing bills. If it moves quickly mainly because banks settle among themselves, smaller creditors may have little opportunity to verify what they are owed or challenge an unfair assumption. The rules should give them timely notice, a credible way to submit and correct claims, and enough information to compare what a plan offers with the relevant alternatives. These protections can improve the quality of a decision without turning every step into litigation. The April 2026 amendment as published in the Gazette · PRS Legislative Research on creditor-initiated resolution

The strongest argument against additional process is that delay itself often harms those suppliers. A stalled company can stop buying from them long before the final court order. Requiring a tribunal hearing for every operating decision can destroy much of the advantage of an earlier restructuring. The balance is to identify the decisions where oversight has the highest value: contested admission, disposal of important assets, conflicts of interest and the treatment of different classes of creditor. Faster agreement on ordinary operating decisions makes sense when those safeguards are credible. A good process distinguishes the actions that keep the business trading from those that decide who bears the permanent loss. The April 2026 amendment as published in the Gazette

The amendment also enables rules for coordinated proceedings involving companies in a group. That could prevent a viable operating company and the entity that holds essential assets from being sold on incompatible timetables. Coordination is valuable when a joint sale preserves operating links or makes the business intelligible to bidders. Creditors lent to individual legal entities, however, and a joint process can obscure which assets secured which loan. Common information and coordination can often capture part of the benefit while preserving a transparent account of claims and recoveries by entity. The eventual rules should make clear when coordination changes the administration of a case and when it changes the distribution of value. The April 2026 amendment as published in the Gazette · PRS Legislative Research on creditor-initiated resolution

There is also a selection problem in comparing the new route with the old one. Lenders may send relatively healthy companies through the faster process and leave the hardest cases to ordinary insolvency. Higher recoveries among the first group would then partly reflect which companies entered, rather than an effect of the route. Evaluation should compare debtors with similar sector, size, days in arrears and going-concern prospects, and report cases that convert to the ordinary process along with successful ones. Otherwise a faster median for completed cases may conceal time spent by firms that tried the new route and failed to resolve. The April 2026 amendment as published in the Gazette · IBBI’s December 2025 quarterly data

Judge the reform by earlier entry and lasting recoveries

Publish the time from default to commencement, from commencement to plan approval and from approval to cash recovery. Report recovery in present-value terms alongside recoveries relative to claims and estimated liquidation value. Include the treatment of operational creditors, repeat defaults and the survival of the underlying business after restructuring, with at least a year of follow-up for resolved cases. If eligible cases begin sooner and preserve more value without shifting unexplained losses onto suppliers, the case for expanding the route strengthens. If recoveries look better only because healthier companies were selected or because plans defer payments beyond the reported dates, the evidence is weaker. The point of the shorter clock is to save a business while it can still be saved. IBBI’s December 2025 quarterly data · The April 2026 amendment as published in the Gazette

excerpt.rendered: The April insolvency amendment creates a quicker creditor-led route. The gains depend on early action, credible valuation and safeguards for suppliers and other creditors.

title.rendered: India’s port cargo record raises a question about where ships still wait

content.rendered:
A port can handle more cargo because it became more efficient, because traffic moved from a rival, or because demand grew until the same assets were used more intensively. India’s major ports recorded 915.17 million tonnes in FY 2025–26, 7.06% higher than the previous year. The milestone matters. A decision to build another berth or improve an inland connection requires evidence about where users now lose time and what it costs them. Ports Ministry, FY 2025–26 major port traffic · UNCTAD, Review of Maritime Transport 2025, chapter II

Throughput measures a flow

The April release compares total traffic at major ports with an annual target of 904 million tonnes. The scope matters. The figure covers the major ports in the release, and tonnes are a weight measure across cargo types. A tonne of coal, a tonne of steel and a tonne inside a container can make different demands on cranes, storage, access roads and scheduling. The traffic result establishes scale. Port performance depends on handling and waiting time by cargo type and on the supply of connections to the hinterland. Ports Ministry, FY 2025–26 major port traffic

A ship’s turnaround can fall if loading becomes faster. The container may then spend another day at a terminal waiting for collection. An exporter needs its cargo loaded before a sailing cutoff and its supplier or warehouse to manage the intervening time. A facility can improve one step while the bottleneck moves to a rail slot, a gate queue or the paperwork needed before a truck can leave. Measure the whole trip to learn where investment will matter.

Queues make average capacity misleading

Suppose a terminal can handle 1,000 identical units a day and receives an average of 900. If arrivals are exactly regular, the spare 100 is enough. If 1,200 units arrive on one day and 800 on the next, the first day leaves a backlog of 200 and the second day clears it. The two days have the same average as a steady 1,000 units per day. In a real port, bad weather, late vessels and staggered truck arrivals can produce a more persistent queue. A plan based on annual throughput divided by annual nominal capacity ignores the shape of daily demand.

The users’ costs can be large before the annual number looks strained. An extra day for a shipment worth ₹2 crore carries roughly ₹6,575 in financing cost at 12% a year, before detention fees, storage charges and production effects. A factory that runs out of a single input can lose much more. This is why the 90th percentile of transit time can be a better indicator for investment than the average.

Choose the investment after locating the wait

The strongest case for building capacity ahead of demand is that port projects take time. A facility that waits until congestion is obvious can lose business for years. Overbuilding has a real cost too, particularly if the new berth relies on rail or road capacity that is still missing. Scenario planning can identify the early works that remain useful across traffic paths, including a shared connection or better appointment system. Evidence of repeated queues at the same berth would strengthen the case for dedicated capacity there.

It is also worth comparing shipper choices across nearby ports. A terminal can lose an important service even while annual tonnage rises because bulk traffic fills the difference. Report scheduled container calls, cancellations and the destinations a shipper can serve directly. A port that improves those links can make the entire supply chain more dependable.

Report anchorage wait, berth service time, container dwell, gate queues and inland departure reliability separately. Split them by cargo type and busy periods. A cheaper scheduling change that reduces delays can buy time before a large civil works decision. If delays remain after those changes and are concentrated where physical capacity is tight, investment is easier to defend. Higher throughput is a milestone. Less time and capital tied up per shipment is the return a shipper can use.

excerpt.rendered: Major-port cargo crossed 915 million tonnes. The next investment decision depends on how traffic translates into ship and cargo delays.

title.rendered: Cheap central loans make state capital spending easier to fund and harder to assess

content.rendered:
India’s long-maturity interest-free loans to states can make productive infrastructure easier to finance. Their value is harder to judge from the deficit or capital-spending headline alone. The RBI’s study of state budgets says consolidated state fiscal deficits rose to 3.3 per cent of GDP in 2024–25 after staying below three per cent in the preceding three years. It attributes much of the excess over three per cent to 50-year interest-free central loans under the Special Assistance to States for Capital Investment scheme. That finding makes the source and terms of financing essential to interpreting the higher deficit. RBI State Finances study of 2025–26 budgets · Union Budget 2026–27 expenditure profile

Two governments see a different financial transaction

For the Union, a loan creates a financial claim and requires funds to be made available today. For a state, it provides financing for spending and creates a liability that has to be repaid on the agreed terms. Counting both the Union disbursement and the state’s spending as two separate investments would overstate the combined public investment if the state uses the same funds to pay for a single asset. To measure economic activity, trace when the implementing body pays for work and when the work becomes usable. To measure fiscal risk, follow the financing and repayment obligations separately. RBI State Finances study of 2025–26 budgets · Union Budget 2026–27 expenditure profile

The concession can be large even though the principal remains due. In a stylised example, suppose a ₹100 crore interest-free loan is repaid in full after 50 years. At an assumed six per cent discount rate, the present value of that final payment is roughly ₹5.4 crore. If repayment were instead in equal instalments beginning much earlier, the present value would be higher. The example does not state the scheme’s repayment schedule or calculate its actual subsidy. It isolates the value of long deferral and explains why face value and economic cost are different measures.

A cheaper loan should change the choice of project

A state may bring forward a road, drainage network or other project when its usual financing cost makes it hard to fund. This can improve welfare if the project generates benefits earlier or would otherwise never proceed. The same loan can also replace ordinary finance on a project already scheduled. That frees resources for another use, which could itself be valuable. The two cases should be reported differently. A fair test compares the original state investment plan, the project funded by the loan, the timing of delivery and where any freed borrowing capacity or revenue went.

The RBI notes that consolidated state capital expenditure was 2.7 per cent of GDP in 2023–24 and 2024–25 and was budgeted at 3.2 per cent for 2025–26. A budgeted rise gives a benchmark for later comparison. It does not show how much work was executed or what would have happened without the central assistance. State-level analysis should distinguish approvals, loan releases, state payments, completion and use. One state may advance a project that was ready. Another can receive financing and face unresolved land or procurement issues. The finance works differently in those cases. RBI State Finances study of 2025–26 budgets

The case for concessionary finance

The strongest argument for the scheme is that infrastructure with benefits over many years is poorly matched to high near-term debt service, especially for a state facing a tight annual budget. A long, cheap loan can protect useful investment from a temporary financing constraint. The concern is that very cheap capital can weaken scrutiny of projects with uncertain benefits or high future operating costs. A state should appraise the service, maintenance and other commitments even when the Union provides the initial finance on attractive terms. The public return depends on the project, not simply on the gap between the loan terms and market borrowing. RBI State Finances study of 2025–26 budgets · Union Budget 2026–27 expenditure profile

A practical example is a facility needing recurring staff or maintenance after it opens. Its public cost includes those expenses and any other funding required to operate it at planned capacity. The state can show that in a forward budget and identify the department responsible. A project that becomes unusable for lack of maintenance can have a very low financing cost and a poor overall return. Reporting the two measures together gives legislators a basis for comparing projects even when their capital finance is equally concessional.

A useful appraisal would also account for delays. If the same asset opens a year later than planned, its users lose a year of benefits even if the construction cost is unchanged. Concessional finance may prevent that delay where the constraint is the timing of payment or procurement. Where the obstacle is administrative, extra finance may simply increase the balance held by the implementing agency. Tracking the dates of approvals, releases, contracts and work makes it possible to estimate how much of a timing improvement came from the loan.

The consolidated fiscal ratio should be accompanied by the stock and terms of liabilities. A state financed mainly with long obligations at predictable rates can face a different cash profile from one with the same reported debt ratio and several near-term repayments. Fiscal sustainability depends on interest, maturity, revenue and the use of borrowed funds. The borrowing source identified by the RBI makes that comparison more informative than a simple ranking by deficit. RBI State Finances study of 2025–26 budgets

The next accounts should connect finance to additional service

Publish funds released and spent, estimated completion dates, operating plans and the amount of additional investment relative to earlier budgets. Compare cash outlays with physical delivery and evidence of use. Where the central assistance speeds work and the state sustains the completed service, the concession has a credible return. If releases rise while projects stall or operating funds remain unassigned, the next improvement should address those constraints. A higher measured deficit can be consistent with good investment, and the evidence is in what the public can use and how long it remains available. RBI State Finances study of 2025–26 budgets · Union Budget 2026–27 expenditure profile

title.rendered: India’s fuel tax cut moves part of the oil shock onto the Budget

content.rendered:
India’s ₹10-per-litre cut in excise on petrol and diesel buys time for the government and state-owned fuel retailers. It also shifts part of the cost of expensive oil onto the central Budget. The 27 March measures reduced special additional excise to ₹3 per litre on petrol from ₹13 and to zero on diesel from ₹10. The government said the lower tax would reduce losses absorbed by oil marketing companies while consumers were being shielded from higher pump prices. That is a defensible emergency measure if it keeps fuel available and the shock proves temporary. Its fiscal cost should be measured openly and its continuation should depend on the conditions that justified it. Petroleum Ministry’s 27 March statement · Reuters, 27 March

Follow the rupees through the pump price

The tax cut is on one component of the retail price. Other duties and state taxes still enter the bill. If the pump price is unchanged and no other component changes, the buyer pays the same amount and the Centre collects ₹10 less per litre. The amount available to cover the supplier’s costs rises by ₹10. This is support for the supply chain relative to the price the consumer would otherwise pay. It is different from a ₹10 reduction at the pump. The actual impact on a company’s margins also depends on what it pays for refined products or crude, its refinery yield and the wholesale and retail mix. Petroleum Ministry’s 27 March statement · Reuters, 27 March

An illustrative price stack makes the incidence clear. Suppose a litre sold at ₹100 includes ₹30 in taxes and leaves ₹70 before supplier costs. A ₹10 cut that holds the retail price at ₹100 leaves ₹80 before supplier costs. If instead the full cut is passed through and the retail price falls to ₹90, the supplier keeps ₹70. If product costs rise ₹14 at the same time and the pump price holds, the tax measure covers ₹10 of the extra cost and the supplier still absorbs ₹4. This is simplified arithmetic with fixed other tax components. Actual state taxes, logistics and selling terms can make the split different. The example shows why a tax announcement and the observed pump price are both needed to establish who gained. Petroleum Ministry’s 27 March statement

The scale depends on how many litres are sold and for how long the lower rate applies. For illustration, 100 crore litres sold at the lower rate imply ₹1,000 crore less central excise at unchanged volumes. Apply the cut to five times that quantity and the mechanical difference is ₹5,000 crore. Contemporary reporting cited a government estimate of roughly ₹5,500 crore of net revenue cost over a fortnight after allowing for new export duties. That was a prospective estimate based on assumptions about sales and exports. The exchequer’s actual loss will depend on the volumes, the dates for which each rate applies and the response of exporters and consumers. PTI on the projected fiscal cost

The financing strain arrives before the full effect on profits is visible. Consider a distributor paying an additional ₹14 per litre for product and selling 30 crore litres during a month at unchanged pump prices. Before the excise cut, the extra cost is ₹420 crore on those sales, under the simplified assumptions above. After the ₹10 cut, the uncovered increase is ₹120 crore. If suppliers are paid before retail proceeds arrive, the company still needs liquidity to finance the higher gross cost of inventories in the interim. This example is a cash-flow illustration. It shows why the government should monitor borrowing, inventory and settlement timing as well as margins when judging whether retailers can keep fuel moving.

Export levies can help domestic supply and reduce export returns

The Centre also imposed a ₹21.50-per-litre export levy on diesel and a ₹29.50 levy on aviation turbine fuel. These levies reduce the proceeds a refiner receives from exporting, making a domestic sale more attractive at the margin. Their effect depends on the difference between the domestic price and the export netback, which is the revenue the refiner retains after costs and levies. If exporters continue to ship the same volumes, the levy raises revenue. If enough cargoes are redirected into India, it can improve domestic availability but the levy will collect less than a static projection. The two objectives can therefore pull in different directions. Government update, 29 March · Reuters, 27 March

A duty can change where existing output is sold faster than it changes how much a refinery can produce. Refineries cannot freely change the proportions of every product they make, and a sale into the domestic market depends on local storage, transport and buyers. A levy that is too high for too long can also reduce the incentive to procure costly crude and run the plant hard when product markets are tight. The useful indicator is whether more usable fuel reaches the places that were short, alongside refinery runs, stocks and export volumes. An increase in the domestic share of a smaller total output would tell a different story from a genuine improvement in supply. Government update, 29 March

Who benefits from smoothing the shock

A sharp increase in diesel can spread through freight, farm operations and construction. Preventing a sudden rise can therefore benefit businesses and households that never buy diesel directly. The strongest case for the intervention is that a short disruption might otherwise force immediate price changes across the economy, even if the cost of oil later recedes. Maintaining supply and avoiding a temporary loss of purchasing power can be worth a temporary fiscal cost. Petrol and diesel relief across the board also reaches those with the largest fuel purchases. A household using little private transport receives less direct support than a household with several vehicles, even if both benefit from more stable freight costs. Petroleum Ministry’s 27 March statement

The longer the shock lasts, the stronger the argument for a more targeted response. A lower tax on every litre reduces the incentive to conserve fuel and can become expensive to reverse. A targeted transfer can focus on the people or activities where the loss would do most harm, although it requires identifying them and getting money to them quickly. Some indirect costs are hard to target in real time. That is a good argument for temporary smoothing and for preparing more focused measures if the disruption persists. It is a weaker argument for absorbing an open-ended difference between domestic prices and the cost of replacement supply.

Some of the burden also depends on decisions by states. A state that levies a percentage of a tax-inclusive base can see receipts change when the base changes, while a fixed component responds differently. The central excise announcement does not establish what happened to the total tax collected on each litre across states. A defensible budget tally would separate the Union and state effects and use state-level retail prices and volumes. That also matters when comparing alternatives. A policy that costs little in the central accounts can still be expensive for states or the fuel companies. The national picture requires following the cash through each entity.

Make the exit depend on observable costs

Publish the excise forgone, revenue from export levies, domestic sales and inventories, and the gap between relevant product prices and retail realisations. A reduction in under-recoveries should be distinguished from a return to normal margins and from a fall in the landed cost of crude. If supply normalises and margins recover, the case for maintaining the full tax cut weakens. If availability remains poor or the cost gap persists, compare targeted support and gradual adjustment of pump prices with the cost of prolonging the existing measures. The fiscal decision should be explicit. A stable pump price can buy time for adjustment, and the Budget should show what that time costs. Petroleum Ministry’s 27 March statement · Government update, 29 March
