title.rendered: Smart meters can fix one part of a power utility’s cash shortfall

content.rendered:
A distribution utility can lose money because electricity disappears in the network, because supplied units never reach a bill, or because bills are issued and remain unpaid. These failures need different remedies. India’s Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme finances smart metering alongside infrastructure work. The March parliamentary reply gives a large sanctions figure. The best use of that capital is to diagnose losses feeder by feeder and show which of them can be reduced with a meter, a better network or a change in collection and subsidy practices. Parliamentary reply, distribution reform · CEA, National Electricity Plan, Transmission

A sanction buys a project

The ministry reports ₹2.83 lakh crore of sanctioned distribution infrastructure work, including smart meters. It separately describes about ₹1.53 lakh crore for loss-reduction infrastructure and ₹1.31 lakh crore for smart metering, with rounding across the figures. The infrastructure includes substations, distribution transformers and feeder segregation. The scheme targets lower aggregate technical and commercial losses and a smaller gap between cost and revenue. A sanctioned amount tells us the size of the programme and the intended allocation. Commissioning, maintenance and collection determine realised effects. Parliamentary reply, distribution reform

A meter makes consumption visible and gives a utility better data for billing. A line upgrade can reduce physical energy loss and improve service voltage. Billing changes can help a utility collect more, though a household with unreliable supply or a mistaken bill may have a valid dispute. A state that promises to pay a subsidy also has to transfer funds on schedule. Faster metering alone cannot put that transfer in the bank.

Decompose the gap

Suppose a utility receives 100 units and bills 80. It collects the equivalent value of 90% of billed energy at a common tariff. On this simplified basis, it realises the equivalent of 72 units and aggregate loss is 28%. If metering and billing increase billed units to 88 while collection stays at 90%, realisation rises to 79.2 and loss falls to 20.8%. If better billing instead comes with a fall in collection to 82%, realisation is only about 72.2 units. Billing has improved while cash recovery has hardly moved.

That arithmetic is a diagnosis, not a prescription. A feeder serving irrigators with metered supply may need a dependable subsidy settlement and a clearer schedule. A congested urban transformer can lose units through physical heat and equipment strain. Replacing it may improve reliability even if the measured collection rate was already high. Investment returns should include fewer outages and reduced technical loss where these benefits can be measured, alongside revenue improvement.

Use comparable feeders and count customer effects

The strongest case for buying meters at scale is that standardisation lowers procurement costs and the data improve planning throughout the network. An isolated meter pilot may miss the benefits of having all relevant points measured. The strongest reason to phase installation is to learn which operational changes turn data into collections and service. A useful evaluation can pair similar feeders and introduce installation in stages, tracking supply, billed units, verified payments, outages and dispute resolution. A comparison using only aggregate utility revenue may confuse the effects of tariff revisions, collections and metering.

Customer outcomes deserve a separate panel. Measure billing corrections, contested disconnections, resolution time and whether customers can reconcile measured use with the bill. A reduction in arrears that comes with frequent erroneous bills would impose private costs the utility ledger omits. If metering increases collection and reduces disputes alongside better reliability, the case for acceleration strengthens. If the billing gain stalls at payment, the state should look at subsidy transfers, repayment arrangements and complaint handling before buying the next round of devices.

The audit should check whether the utility controls what it is being asked to change. A meter operator can report outages in its data feed. Collection policy and transfer of a state subsidy may be outside that contractor’s role. Assign outcomes to a party able to act before tying payments to the result.

The point of the programme is to convert delivered electricity into a reliable public service and a viable stream of revenue. A meter can reveal which part of that job remains unfinished.

excerpt.rendered: India’s distribution reform finances meters and network upgrades. A utility should show how much each intervention changes losses, collections and service quality.

title.rendered: When India rationed commercial LPG, who lost supply first?

content.rendered:
India’s Petroleum Ministry reported on 28 March that commercial LPG allocation had risen to 70% of its pre-crisis level. The higher allocation helps businesses facing a shortage of cooking and process fuel. It also forces a choice about who gets the next available cylinder. The government has prioritised household supplies and directed the additional commercial allocation towards selected industries, with preference for processes that cannot switch easily to natural gas. The right test is whether the policy keeps essential services and hard-to-replace production running, while showing where other users remain short of fuel. 28 March government briefing · Official allocation and priority rules.

Allocation is a decision about quantities

The government’s 27 March letter approved an extra 20 percentage points of commercial LPG allocation, taking the total to 70% of the pre-crisis level. On a comparable baseline of 100 cylinder-equivalents, a rise from 50 to 70 expands the allocation by 40% relative to the lower starting point. It still leaves 30 cylinder-equivalents below the earlier benchmark. That arithmetic describes the scale of the allocation decision. Actual availability at an outlet also depends on deliveries, existing stocks and whether demand in the district has changed. A national allocation share does not describe the entitlement of an individual restaurant or workshop.

The 28 March briefing said commercial entities had uplifted 33,781 tonnes of non-domestic LPG since 14 March and reported more than 54 lakh household refills delivered the previous day. One is a cumulative tonnage and the other is a one-day cylinder count. Putting them side by side helps describe the government’s priorities. It does not show the relative shortage across households and firms. To measure that, publish ordered and delivered quantities for each category against a comparable pre-crisis period. State-level figures would make it possible to distinguish a national supply constraint from a problem getting cylinders to the places that need them. 28 March volumes and reporting periods.

What the priority list buys

Giving priority to industrial processes with few immediate substitutes can avoid losses that exceed the price of the fuel. A shortage at a dyeing unit, for example, can interrupt work for garment suppliers downstream. The value of keeping that line running depends on the output that would otherwise be lost and the availability of alternative capacity. The same litre-equivalent of energy may have a different value in a process that can switch to piped gas within days. A priority rule tied to technical substitutability has a stronger economic case than one based only on the size or political visibility of a sector. Priority sectors and specialised heating criteria.

The same logic should be applied within a sector. A large manufacturer may have dual-fuel equipment or access to a supplier that a smaller unit lacks. A small firm with a single oven and little inventory can lose an entire batch when one delivery fails. Firms that can document their operations may navigate a priority system more easily than informal businesses. Reviewing allocation by plant and district, or publishing the criteria and a simple appeal route, would help keep the rule tied to substitution costs. The goal is to allocate scarce fuel to uses where a missed delivery destroys the most value or threatens a service people depend on.

The cost reaches workers and customers

Restaurants facing a lower allocation can shorten opening hours, simplify menus or switch to dishes that use less fuel. Reuters reported kitchens making such changes earlier in March. That response reduces the amount of LPG needed per meal, but it can cut sales and change the work available to cooks, delivery workers and suppliers. Electricity and piped gas can help where equipment, tariffs and connections make the switch practical. The option is much less useful to a business that needs a new connection or an expensive equipment replacement. Reuters reporting on changes in kitchens.

Imagine a kitchen normally using 20 commercial cylinders a month. If it receives 14 and cooking activity scales directly with fuel, six cylinders’ worth of work is exposed. Suppose menu changes reduce fuel used per serving by 15% without affecting the quality or price of the meals. Fourteen cylinders can then support about 82% of the original serving volume, because 0.70 divided by 0.85 is about 0.82. That is a scenario and assumes all cylinders have the same usable contents. Real kitchens have fixed fuel use at opening, changes in demand and dishes that cannot be prepared with less heat. The example shows why a 30% fuel gap need not translate directly into a 30% revenue loss.

When prices or alternatives can do more

The strongest alternative to administrative allocation is to let higher commercial prices direct fuel to users willing to pay most for it and encourage rapid switching. That approach can make sense where customers can buy from multiple distributors and change fuels without interrupting essential work. Willingness to pay also reflects access to cash. In a sudden shortage, the highest bidder may simply have the largest balance sheet, while a small supplier at a critical point in a production chain cannot raise cash quickly. A time-limited priority rule, alongside transparent prices and alternatives, can preserve output in those cases. A rule that outlasts the shortage can slow switching and reward firms that remain on the list.

There is a separate choice about protecting households. Shielding household cylinder availability limits the immediate welfare cost of losing a basic cooking fuel, particularly where reliable electricity and piped gas are unavailable. That choice shifts more of the short-run adjustment onto commercial users. The distributional question includes their workers and customers. A business that closes early may save fuel while sending workers home with fewer hours. A household may retain access to its cylinder but face higher prices for prepared food. Tracking both channels gives a more complete account of the policy than a count of household refills alone.

State allocation orders add a further step between the national decision and the cylinder that reaches a business. The Petroleum Ministry reported that 28 states and union territories had issued orders for non-domestic supply, with public oil marketers supplying remaining areas. A district with low stocks and a long replenishment route may see a slower improvement than a district with the same formal allocation near a bottling plant. Publishing deliveries against local orders would help separate the logistical problem from the choice of priority sectors. It would also show where a change in truck routes or bottling schedules could restore activity faster than a new allocation formula. State and distributor arrangements.

The timing of that comparison matters. If deliveries are counted from a different start date in each state, cumulative totals favour places that started reporting earlier. Daily or weekly data with a common cutoff and a clear definition of uplift would allow a fairer comparison.

The next release should report deliveries alongside allocations, with the figures broken down by household, hospitality and industrial use. The most useful comparisons would include failed orders, waiting times, relevant changes in output, and successful switches to alternatives. If delivery improves fastest where substitution is hardest and the disruption to work and services eases, the priority rule will have a stronger case. If aggregate uplift rises while shortages persist in the same districts and businesses, the problem may be distribution or eligibility. The 70% allocation is a useful decision to track. The economic outcome is how much activity the available fuel kept going. Background on the supply shock and why oil stocks address a different bottleneck.

excerpt.rendered: The increase to 70% of pre-crisis commercial LPG allocation raised a distribution question for India’s restaurants and factories. Deliveries and substitution will show which activity the policy preserved.

title.rendered: Keeping India’s 4% inflation target makes sense through an oil shock

content.rendered:
India is right to keep headline inflation as the Reserve Bank’s target through the next five years. The Finance Ministry’s notification retains a 4% target with a lower tolerance level of 2% and an upper one of 6%, from 1 April 2026 through 31 March 2031. The decision comes at a moment when energy costs are testing the difference between a price shock and an inflation process. The RBI should explain which part of the increase it expects to fade, which part could spread to other prices and what it would do if that spread becomes visible. A stable target is useful precisely because the correct policy rate can change with the source of the shock. Gazette notification on the inflation target · Reuters on the renewed target

The midpoint is the target, and the band allows for shocks

The monetary framework gives the committee a point target of 4% and room for temporary deviations. The RBI’s review describes the accountability test as a deviation outside the tolerance band for three consecutive quarters. The rule makes prolonged misses consequential. It does not require a change in the policy rate after one monthly print or treat 6% as the objective whenever inflation is below it. The published February CPI reading, at 3.21% year on year on the new base, is a useful starting point. It measures prices before the recent phase of the energy shock and cannot settle where inflation will be once firms and households respond. Gazette notification on the inflation target · RBI’s review of the monetary policy framework · MoSPI’s February inflation release

The reason to keep the midpoint unchanged is that an inflation target also coordinates behaviour. A firm writing annual contracts and a household negotiating wages have to form a view of next year’s prices. An announced increase in the target in response to a shock could cause them to revise that view even if the immediate price rise would otherwise have faded. That would make a temporary shock more persistent. Maintaining the target preserves a reference point while allowing the RBI to explain why it is willing to take time to bring inflation back toward it. The credibility of that explanation depends on the quality of its forecasts and whether it follows through when inflation broadens. RBI’s review of the monetary policy framework

Headline inflation answers a welfare question that core cannot

The strongest argument for a core target is that food and fuel prices can move for reasons the repo rate cannot quickly fix. Higher rates will not produce more onions, replenish imported energy or clear a shipping bottleneck. A central bank that tried to reverse every such move could depress investment and employment while the original shortage persisted. Core measures can help identify underlying pressure. The problem with a core target is that food and fuel are part of the spending households actually need to finance. If those prices rise persistently, they can affect wage demands, discretionary spending and the prices businesses set. The headline is the right object for the public commitment, while measures of persistence and breadth inform the policy response. RBI’s review of the monetary policy framework

A simplified calculation illustrates the difference. Take a hypothetical economy where an energy-sensitive group represents 10% of the household basket and its price rises 12% once, starting from base weights. With all other prices unchanged, that lifts the overall price index by 1.2%. If the group then stays at the higher level and everything else is flat, the direct contribution to year-on-year inflation drops out once the comparison month also contains the higher price. If transport, packaged goods and services reprice repeatedly in response, the contribution becomes wider and more persistent. The assumed 10% weight is illustrative. The new CPI groups household energy, transport and related items in ways that require more detail for an actual estimate. MoSPI’s February inflation release

The distinction does not make a one-off rise harmless. A household with fixed cash income still loses purchasing power when prices settle at a higher level. Lower-income households may also have less room to reduce fuel or food use without giving up other essentials. Governments can address some of that distribution through targeted transfers or measures that relieve supply constraints. Blanket price suppression has its own costs. If a retail price stays flat because a public enterprise absorbs the increase, the household index can look better while the financial burden accumulates elsewhere. Monetary policymakers should look through the right price movements and still account for the economy-wide cost of the shock.

A stable target is compatible with different policy paths

The RBI’s 2025 review says headline inflation averaged 4.9% after the adoption of flexible targeting in its sample, against 6.8% in the preceding period of the same series. That is a useful record and an imperfect estimate of what the framework caused. Food supply, global energy, fiscal decisions and the pandemic also changed across those periods. A stronger test is whether medium-term expectations remained anchored through shocks and whether inflation returned toward the target without unnecessarily large losses of activity. The review records that the MPC met under the accountability provision in November 2022 after a sustained overshoot. The framework can therefore accommodate volatility while still requiring an explanation when the breach persists. RBI’s review of the monetary policy framework

Suppose the initial oil shock weakens real household demand and firms in most sectors still struggle to raise prices. A pre-emptive tightening would then impose a second cost on borrowers and investment. Suppose instead that the rupee depreciates, wage settlements accelerate and services prices start rising across categories even as the original fuel increase slows. That would make a stronger case for resisting the spread. These are different scenarios, not forecasts. The committee can make its reaction function clearer by showing how its projected headline path changes under each and explaining the evidence that would switch its preferred response. Publishing a single conditional path without its most consequential assumptions leaves too much of the decision implicit.

Flexibility should be symmetric. A sustained fall below 2% can be a sign that the economy is weak enough to justify easing, even when cheaper food has initially helped households. For a borrower facing fixed nominal payments, lower expected inflation raises the real burden of the debt at a given interest rate. The same monetary regime should therefore require the committee to explain persistent undershoots. A temporary fall in a few fresh food prices is different from broad disinflation accompanied by slower sales and investment. The case for waiting or acting should rely on the breadth of the movement and what it implies for the forecast, just as it does when inflation is above the midpoint. Gazette notification on the inflation target · RBI’s review of the monetary policy framework

Forecasts would be easier to evaluate if the RBI separated its assumptions about world oil prices, the rupee and domestic pass-through. The same imported cost shock can reach the CPI quickly if retail prices adjust or more slowly if duties, contracts or company margins absorb it. A forecast that assumes one of these paths should state it. The committee should then compare the realised path with the forecast and explain whether the error came from energy prices, the exchange rate or the behaviour of domestic prices. This is useful accountability even when inflation stays within the band. It would help readers judge whether a change in the outlook warrants a change in the rate.

Judge the framework by what it explains when the outlook changes

Track household and business inflation expectations at several horizons, the breadth of price rises beyond food and energy, and evidence that wage and margin decisions have begun to respond. Also watch lending and demand so that the committee can distinguish persistence from a shock that is already squeezing spending. If expectations and broader prices remain stable, patience through a temporary overshoot can be consistent with a credible target. If the pressure spreads or expectations move, the case for a policy response strengthens. Keeping the same 4% anchor is sensible. The value of that decision will be measured by how clearly the RBI explains and manages the trade-offs around it. Gazette notification on the inflation target · RBI’s review of the monetary policy framework

title.rendered: Maharashtra’s fiscal room is smaller after salaries, pensions and interest

content.rendered:
Maharashtra’s 2026–27 Budget should be read through its existing commitments as well as its projected deficit. The budget puts the fiscal deficit at 2.8 per cent of gross state domestic product and estimates a revenue deficit of ₹40,552 crore. PRS calculates that salaries, pensions and interest together are budgeted at ₹3,38,385 crore against ₹6,16,099 crore of revenue receipts. Those figures do not establish that the government cannot finance a worthwhile new priority. They show why the headline deficit ratio gives limited information on how much of the annual budget can be redirected if receipts disappoint or a new need appears. Maharashtra Finance Department’s 2026–27 budget documents · Maharashtra’s 2026–27 budget statement and estimates · PRS’s analysis of Maharashtra’s budget and committed expenditure

Committed spending identifies a constraint, not a judgement of value

Salaries finance staff who deliver public services. Pensions reflect promises already made. Interest reflects the cost of earlier borrowing. Combining them is useful because adjusting them quickly can be difficult or disruptive, though their economic roles differ. Dividing the projected ₹3,38,385 crore by ₹6,16,099 crore gives roughly 55 per cent of budgeted revenue receipts. Subtracting those commitments leaves about ₹2,77,714 crore of revenue before other obligations. This residual is an accounting benchmark. It still has to finance operating supplies, transfers, programmes and many other costs, and is not a measure of cash available for new initiatives. PRS’s analysis of Maharashtra’s budget and committed expenditure · Maharashtra’s 2026–27 budget statement and estimates

The sensitivity of the residual matters. Suppose revenue receipts are two per cent below budget, a shortfall of about ₹12,322 crore, and salary, pension and interest commitments are unchanged. The residual after those items falls by about 4.4 per cent, more than twice the proportional fall in receipts. This is a hypothetical sensitivity rather than a forecast. A government can respond by changing other spending, using balances or financing a larger deficit if permitted. The calculation shows why a modest revenue surprise can put more pressure on parts of the budget that are easier to adjust.

The mix of the remaining spending matters

A state might postpone routine maintenance because it is easier than changing a statutory payment. That can raise future repair costs and reduce the value of investments already made. Cutting a public programme can have different effects depending on who relies on it and whether there is a practical substitute. A budget review should distinguish the cost of existing services, new discretionary programmes and spending needed to keep assets usable. Some revenue spending can support durable public benefits. A reduction in revenue spending is therefore not automatically an improvement in the quality of expenditure. PRS’s analysis of Maharashtra’s budget and committed expenditure

The revenue sources also have different risks. PRS puts own revenue at about 73 per cent of budgeted revenue receipts, with the remainder coming from central tax shares and grants. Own taxes depend partly on economic activity, prices and collection. Transfers depend on Union collections, the formula and the grant schedule. A prudent cash and borrowing plan should assess those sources separately. Two states with similar revenue totals can have different options if one can change its tax policies or timing of collections and another depends more heavily on decisions taken elsewhere. PRS’s analysis of Maharashtra’s budget and committed expenditure · Finance ministry’s February devolution announcement

The strongest case for the headline ratio

A deficit-to-output measure is useful because it expresses annual financing needs relative to the scale of the state economy and provides a common comparison with fiscal rules. It also captures spending categories that a narrow measure of committed outlays would miss. The ratio is still affected by the assumed size of nominal output and by whether revenue and spending estimates are realised. A budget can meet a headline target while deferring useful spending or carrying large upcoming obligations. The stronger assessment uses both the fiscal ratio and the cash and expenditure decisions the state would face if assumptions fail. PRS’s analysis of Maharashtra’s budget and committed expenditure · Maharashtra’s 2026–27 budget statement and estimates

The budget estimates capital outlay of ₹97,498 crore, approximately unchanged from the previous year’s revised estimate. Protecting that amount across the board is not itself an investment strategy. Some projects may be close to completion and yield a useful service soon. Others may face delays or need a credible operating budget. Tracking which projects are advanced or deferred provides a better measure of how fiscal pressure changes investment. Report both the immediate cash consequence of adjusting an outlay and the impact on the future service it was intended to provide. PRS’s analysis of Maharashtra’s budget and committed expenditure · Maharashtra’s 2026–27 budget statement and estimates

It also matters how commitments evolve. A salary revision can change several years of spending, while a temporary rise in interest due to the payment calendar may be concentrated in one year. Pension expenditure depends on the terms of past promises and the number of people receiving them. Publish projections by category under a consistent set of assumptions and reconcile revisions with changes in policy, timing and the number of beneficiaries or employees. This would give legislators more information on how today’s decisions alter the room available in a later budget. Maharashtra’s 2026–27 budget statement and estimates · PRS’s analysis of Maharashtra’s budget and committed expenditure

Another useful comparison is the amount left after commitments at different points in the year. Budgeted revenue can arrive late even if the annual forecast is met, while payroll and debt service cannot usually be moved as easily. A separate cash forecast can show when suppliers, projects or programme payments face pressure and whether that pressure is expected to reverse. It is possible to face a timing problem without a permanent deterioration in revenue.

What later accounts should reveal

Compare actual receipts with the Budget by source. Track the largest recurring payments, the time to pay suppliers and the progress of capital projects. If revenues fall short, publish which other costs changed and whether changes were temporary or structural. Evidence of sustained service delivery and useful completed investments would strengthen the case that the state can accommodate its commitments. Delayed bills, weaker maintenance or repeatedly deferred capital projects would point to pressure that the published deficit ratio could conceal. The budget’s flexibility is best judged by the decisions that remain possible after the commitments are met. PRS’s analysis of Maharashtra’s budget and committed expenditure · Maharashtra’s 2026–27 budget statement and estimates

excerpt.rendered: A fiscal deficit of 2.8 per cent of state output tells only part of the story. The flexibility to fund new priorities depends on what is already committed and how receipts perform.

title.rendered: India’s e-bus guarantee can lower bids if cities keep paying on time

content.rendered:
An electric bus operator can price the vehicle, electricity, staff and maintenance. It must also price the possibility that the city pays late. India’s PM e-Bus Sewa payment-security mechanism addresses that risk for covered contracts. It can make competitive bids cheaper where operators previously charged a meaningful premium for municipal payment delays. The fiscal test is whether the mechanism turns late payment into an occasional, quickly recovered exception. Parliamentary reply, bus payment security · Parliamentary reply, awards and depots

Tender, award and operation are different stages

The March parliamentary replies report tenders concluded for 6,228 buses under PM e-Bus Sewa as of 28 February and letters of award issued for 4,720. They also report ₹500 crore disbursed to the implementing agency to establish the fund in FY 2025–26, alongside progress on state mandates and supporting infrastructure. Tenders and awards measure procurement progress. Buses on the road need executed contracts, usable depots, chargers, staff and a payment stream able to cover service. Parliamentary reply, bus payment security · Parliamentary reply, awards and depots

Under a gross-cost model, a public authority can retain fare revenue and pay an operator to run specified service. This makes it easier to integrate routes and offer fares based on policy. It leaves the authority with the risk that revenue falls short of contract payments. The private operator can manage maintenance and staffing. It can do little to improve a city’s budget or enforce a political decision to pay on time. A credible guarantee can move financing risk to a party better able to carry it.

The amount due still has to be funded

Suppose a bus is paid ₹65 per service kilometre and runs 200 paid kilometres daily for 300 days. Annual payments are ₹39 lakh before other terms. If the operator waits two extra months on an even stream of payments, about ₹6.5 lakh is tied up on average under that delay. At 12% annual financing cost, carrying it costs about ₹78,000 a year. Across 100 buses, the illustrative cost is ₹78 lakh. If bidders previously included that cost and a premium for unpredictable delay, reliable payment can lower the bid. These assumptions describe one cash-flow mechanism and are not official contract rates.

A guarantee can also change conduct. A city expecting the fund to cover each shortfall may invest less effort in timely budgeting. Automatic recovery and reporting can preserve discipline while still giving the operator certainty. Where the authority has a persistent gap between fares and obligations, the answer is an explicit service subsidy or a redesigned network. Repeated calls on the guarantee are evidence that the underlying budget needs attention.

Buy reliable bus service

The strongest argument for the mechanism is that a small central fund can unlock several years of private investment and reduce differences in bidding across cities. That requires timely invocation and predictable repayment. The public should see how often it pays, how long advances remain outstanding and whether tender prices fall after controlling for vehicle specifications and route requirements. The comparison should include kilometres actually delivered, breakdowns, cancellations and charging constraints. A cheap winning bid has little value when trips disappear.

There is a further allocation problem at the depot. If the public authority provides charging infrastructure, its delay can leave the operator with financed buses and no way to earn contracted revenue. If the operator controls the depot, it can bear more responsibility for availability. The contract should specify the remedy for each kind of delay and disclose whether that risk changed the bid.

Passenger outcomes deserve their own test. Reliable frequency on a route people use can raise the value of service without adding a bus to the fleet. Publish missed trips by time and route, alongside the money owed to operators. If bids become more competitive and service is dependable with occasional, quickly recovered advances, the mechanism has solved a real financing problem. If arrears recur and cancellations persist, the city’s contract and operating budget need attention before it orders more vehicles.

excerpt.rendered: Payment security can reduce a risk premium in bus contracts. Its success depends on deployment, service standards and how quickly cities repay advances.

title.rendered: A hotter year changes the risks that public investment has to carry

content.rendered:
Climate finance after Belém · Part 2 · March WMO climate assessment

In March 2026, the World Meteorological Organization put the 2025 global mean surface temperature at about 1.43°C above the 1850–1900 average, with a stated uncertainty of ±0.13°C. Its January estimate was 1.44°C. The March assessment placed the temperature reading alongside ocean heat and other indicators. A one-year global anomaly and the long-term Paris temperature thresholds answer different questions. For a city or insurer, the economic decision turns on how a shifting climate changes local extremes and the value of protection. WMO, 2025 temperature estimate · WMO, State of the Global Climate 2025

The average can leave the decision unresolved

A city facing more dangerously hot days may need cooling at clinics and schools, reliable electricity and plans for outdoor work. A coastal town may face higher expected flood losses and costs of insuring property. A national or global average cannot specify those needs on its own. Engineers and budget staff require data on the frequency and severity of local events and an account of which people and services are exposed.

Suppose a flood would impose $50 million of losses, and its annual probability under a simplified model moves from 2% to 4%. Expected annual loss rises from $1 million to $2 million before changes in exposure. A protective investment costing $600,000 annually could be worth considering if it avoids a large share of that extra loss. The calculation is illustrative and leaves out correlated events, uncertainty and the value of public services that cannot easily be priced. It shows how a small probability change can alter an investment decision.

Plan for uncertainty that is hard to resolve quickly

A municipality can spend too much preparing for an unlikely case, particularly if it locks itself into expensive construction. It can also wait for a precise forecast and lose time needed for a project with long lead times. Designs that can be expanded in stages can be useful. A drainage upgrade that works at several plausible rainfall levels has a more defensible return than one that is valuable only under an exact model result. Maintenance should be budgeted from the start.

There is a case for spending first on low-cost measures such as warnings, shade or moving critical equipment out of harm’s way. Those can lower losses now and produce evidence for later capital spending. They have limits where a major utility repeatedly fails. Compare outcomes against the services that matter, including safe temperatures, days of operation and hours of interruption.

The link to climate finance is practical. A funder should ask how the project performs under a range of local conditions, who receives the protection and who will maintain it. That is how a global signal can inform a project decision without pretending that the temperature anomaly predicts the loss at a particular site.

Climate finance after Belém

title.rendered: Britain’s March rate hold shows how central banks can wait through an energy shock

content.rendered:
A central bank facing dearer energy has two problems. Households can buy less with the same income and some firms will try to pass through higher costs. Tighter credit can slow the second process, while doing little to improve the first. The Bank of England’s March decision to leave Bank Rate at 3.75% illustrates why the useful policy question is how the shock is transmitted. India’s answer depends on its own prices, wages, fiscal choices and credit conditions. Bank of England, March MPC minutes · Bank of England, March minutes PDF

The data that would justify patience

The Monetary Policy Committee voted unanimously to hold at its March meeting. Its discussion distinguished the effect of global energy prices from the possibility of more durable pressure on domestic wages, costs and price-setting. A rate hold allows time to observe those decisions. Monetary policy still has to respond if broader inflation becomes persistent or expected inflation starts to drift. The minutes describe a range of possible paths rather than a promise about the next meeting. Bank of England, March MPC minutes

An energy price jump can cause a one-off increase in the overall price level, with a year-on-year inflation contribution that later fades. A repeated series of increases or widespread repricing of services can keep inflation elevated after the original shock. The separation is difficult in real time. Electricity contracts reprice at intervals. Transport charges and industrial inputs can affect consumer goods with a lag. A central bank looking only at current core inflation can miss costs that have yet to appear in the index.

How the same shock can yield two decisions

Consider an illustrative household spending ₹30,000 a month, with ₹3,000 devoted to energy and travel exposed to the price shock. A 10% increase in that portion costs ₹300 a month at the same quantities, or 1% of its initial budget. If its wages remain fixed, it can absorb the increase by cutting discretionary spending. If nominal wages and the prices of labour-intensive services then rise to restore margins and purchasing power, the shock can spread even after energy prices stabilise. These are alternative mechanisms and require different evidence.

India’s fiscal treatment of fuel and power can change the timing. A tax adjustment can reduce the immediate price households see at the pump. A regulated electricity tariff can postpone the adjustment and leave a utility with higher costs to recover later. The measured inflation path reflects those decisions alongside international prices. The relevant comparison is the change in consumer costs, utility balance sheets and government revenue taken together.

The cost of a false signal

The strongest argument for tightening early is that an unanchored expectation is expensive to restore. Central banks work with lags. By the time wages and services show broad acceleration, a small rate rise may no longer suffice. The case is most compelling when surveys, firms’ pricing plans and actual wage settlements move in the same direction. A rise in one near-term household expectation series after a visible fuel increase gives weaker evidence about the medium-term anchor.

The case for patience strengthens when wage growth is slowing, credit conditions are already restrictive and firms report limited ability to pass on costs. Evidence from job postings, turnover and service margins can help resolve the trade-off. A central bank should be explicit about the observations that would end the hold. That gives markets a reaction function they can test without relying on promises about a future rate path.

Food prices can further complicate the comparison. A simultaneous improvement in vegetable supply can pull down the headline Indian index while energy-intensive services are becoming more expensive. Tracking the fraction of categories with rapid price increases, alongside a weighted aggregate, gives a better read on breadth. Comparing wholesale and retail movements can show whether the shock is still passing through distribution.

India can use the British decision as a useful comparison. The analysis should travel across borders. The rate decision still belongs to the local economy, where the balance between weaker demand and more durable price pressure can be different.

excerpt.rendered: The Bank of England held at 3.75%. The relevant lesson for India is how to tell a temporary rise in costs from persistent domestic inflation.

title.rendered: India’s small hydro subsidy should pay for dependable power

content.rendered:
India has a case for supporting small hydro where a good site can supply power at hours when a remote grid needs it. The Cabinet on 18 March approved an outlay of ₹2,584.60 crore for projects of roughly 1,500 megawatts over five financial years from 2026–27. The scheme offers greater assistance in the north-east and districts on international borders. Those places can have attractive sites and costly alternatives for grid supply. The investment decision should turn on the value of electricity delivered through the year and the cost of doing so at a particular site. Installed megawatts alone give a poor measure of that return. Cabinet decision on small hydro · Business Standard, 18 March

The grant lowers a fixed cost and leaves several risks intact

The scheme covers projects from 1 to 25 MW. In the north-eastern and eligible border areas, the grant is limited to the lower of ₹3.6 crore per MW and 30% of project cost, with a ₹30 crore ceiling per project. Elsewhere, the corresponding figures are ₹2.4 crore per MW, 20% and ₹20 crore. The Cabinet statement expects the scheme to attract about ₹15,000 crore in investment and reserves ₹30 crore for detailed reports on roughly 200 projects. The investment figure is an expectation. The project reports are a chance to find out which sites are worth developing before larger sums are committed. Cabinet decision on small hydro

Consider a 12 MW plant that costs ₹120 crore. Under the preferential formula the per-MW amount is ₹43.2 crore and the percentage amount is ₹36 crore, so the ₹30 crore project cap binds. Elsewhere the comparable figures are ₹28.8 crore and ₹24 crore, and the ₹20 crore cap binds. The developer’s capital requirement after the grant is ₹90 crore in the first case and ₹100 crore in the second, before financing and other costs. The example isolates the grant. It does not imply that a plant in the first location will earn a better return. Civil works, construction delays, grid access and seasonal water flows can easily dominate the ₹10 crore difference. Cabinet decision on small hydro

Capacity utilisation shows why. At 45% utilisation, a 12 MW plant produces about 47.3 million kilowatt-hours in a 365-day year. At 30%, it produces about 31.5 million. The same annual fixed cost is spread across one-third fewer units in the second case, making the fixed cost per unit about 50% higher. The Central Electricity Regulatory Commission uses normative factors of 45% in several states, 40% in Punjab and 30% elsewhere for its small hydro tariff regulations. Those norms are useful benchmarks, while a feasibility study still needs site-specific hydrology and a realistic allowance for outages, silt and access to the network. CERC renewable tariff regulations

To put the scale in context, contemporaneous coverage puts existing small hydro capacity at about 5,100 MW across 1,196 sites. The proposed 1,500 MW would amount to about 29% of that installed capacity if built. Neither number tells us how much electricity will be available at the hour of greatest need. The existing fleet offers an evidence base. Before approving sites of similar design and geography, compare actual output and outage records from plants already running. If those plants routinely miss their dry-season estimates, use that evidence to lower the expected generation of new projects until the developers can show why their sites are different. Business Standard, 18 March

The grant arithmetic can also be converted into a price. Suppose the 12 MW project in the preferential area must recover its remaining ₹90 crore over 30 years at an assumed real financing rate of 8%. An annuity on those assumptions is about ₹8 crore a year. That is about ₹1.69 per unit of capital recovery at 45% utilisation and ₹2.54 at 30%, before operating costs, transmission, losses and taxes. These figures are neither tariff proposals nor social costs. A public appraisal must include the grant as part of total investment and compare the resulting resource cost with what the same budget could buy elsewhere.

The hour and location of generation determine its value

A unit of electricity supplied during a local shortage can be worth more than one supplied when the grid has surplus power. Small hydro can be valuable if water availability and local demand line up, or if it reduces the cost of moving power over a constrained network. A plant that generates most of its output during the wet season may deliver much less during a dry-season peak. A run-of-river plant with limited storage has less control over that timing than a plant with substantial water storage. A fair comparison therefore uses hourly or seasonal generation and local demand. Compare the site with alternatives that can serve the same hours, including grid reinforcement, solar plus storage or firm power procured from elsewhere. Cabinet decision on small hydro · CERC renewable tariff regulations

The strongest argument for an upfront grant is that new projects bear large construction and connection costs and investors may discount benefits that accrue to the local network. A project serving a weak grid can reduce outages or defer some upgrades that the developer cannot charge for directly. The grant can make that otherwise viable project financeable. The strongest reason to be selective is that a capital grant lowers the developer’s exposure to construction cost while leaving customers and taxpayers exposed to low generation later. Milestone payments can establish whether work was completed. A portion linked to verified delivery in critical hours would better align private incentives with the network benefit the subsidy is intended to buy. Cabinet decision on small hydro

River and community costs are part of the comparison

The Cabinet argues that smaller projects can avoid the large land and resettlement costs of major dams. Scale matters, yet even a relatively small diversion can affect downstream users, aquatic habitat and the movement of sediment. Several projects on the same river can have a cumulative effect that an appraisal of one project misses. The baseline for the evaluation should include existing irrigation, fisheries and drinking-water uses and the amount of water that remains available through dry months. Monitoring these effects should continue after commissioning. A project that clears its financial threshold because downstream costs are borne by others can still have a poor public return. Cabinet decision on small hydro

The same discipline applies to the jobs claim. The Cabinet projects 51 lakh person-days of work during construction and anticipates jobs in operation and maintenance. Person-days describe a flow of work and should be kept distinct from permanent jobs. The local gains depend on who is hired, whether earnings go to households near the project, and what workers would have earned elsewhere. Construction wages can be valuable in a remote district, particularly when work is scarce. The case strengthens if projects also leave durable maintenance jobs and more reliable power for local enterprise. Both outcomes are observable without treating the construction forecast as a result already achieved. Cabinet decision on small hydro

Choose projects against their alternatives

Publish the cost of generation and of connecting each proposed project, expected output by season, the terms of the power purchase agreement and the grant per unit of dependable supply. Show how the ranking changes under a dry year, delays in commissioning and lower prices for storage or competing generation. After commissioning, report actual output, outage hours and river-flow compliance against that appraisal. If plants supply electricity at the hours promised, support local activity and respect downstream requirements, the case for extending the programme strengthens. If construction targets are met while dry-season delivery is weak and costs rise, the project pipeline should be reassessed. The public purchase is more reliable energy at a competitive cost, and the capacity target is only a means of getting it.

Part of a series

Testing India’s subsidies

Semiconductors, AI compute, minerals, green hydrogen, small hydro and factory power: what each subsidy should be made to deliver.

title.rendered: A rush to import before tariffs can flatter the trade numbers

content.rendered:
America’s tariff reset · Part 4 · March WTO outlook

The WTO’s March outlook put 2026 merchandise trade volume growth at 1.9% in its baseline. A trade forecast published during rapid policy changes needs a read on the shipment calendar. Companies can import more this quarter because they expect a duty next quarter. The customs record then looks strong before the policy takes effect and weak after it, even if sales to final customers barely change. WTO, March 2026 Global Trade Outlook and Statistics · Federal Register, temporary import surcharge proclamation

Separate an import from a sale

A container cleared through customs can go straight into production, reach a retailer or sit in a warehouse. A company expecting higher import costs has an incentive to replenish inventory early. Its choice depends on whether it can finance stock, how long it can store the goods and the probability the expected tariff will apply. A business with perishable goods or expensive credit may be unable to act on the same forecast.

Imagine a company that normally imports 10,000 units a month and sells the same number. It brings forward 5,000 units from next month. Imports rise 50% this month and fall 50% the next. Sales and total imports across the two months stay flat. If a forecaster had only the first customs release, a false demand boom would be easy to infer. The balance sheet would already show where the extra units went.

The inventory story is testable

Compare shipments with sales, stock-to-sales ratios and new orders. Look for concentrations in goods subject to the expected duty, on routes that can deliver before the relevant deadline. If imports rise among products unaffected by a measure and sales rise too, demand is a more plausible part of the story. If stocks climb as prices and sales stay steady, a timing shift is more likely. A change in trade routes can also alter bilateral figures without changing total consumption.

The strongest counterargument is that firms may pull forward and increase total purchases when supply risks rise. Additional safety stocks can be a rational response to unreliable trade, and may remain higher after the deadline. That is a change in inventory policy with ongoing financing costs. It is still different from a lasting change in customer demand. Analysts should look for repeat orders after the stock target has been reached.

By October, the WTO would have more evidence from the first half to assess the initial projection. The comparison worth making is across product classes and orders after policy dates. If strength survives the deadlines and extends beyond a handful of categories, the trade recovery has a stronger demand foundation. If the rise unwinds with inventories, the original boost was chiefly a shift between months.

America’s tariff reset

title.rendered: America’s excess-capacity investigations need a test beyond low prices

content.rendered:
America’s tariff reset · Part 3 · March Section 301 investigations

On 11 March the US Trade Representative opened Section 301 investigations into practices connected to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing. An investigation is a process for collecting evidence and determining whether a practice is actionable. The economic issue is narrower than whether imports have become cheap. The evidence should identify a policy, how it changes capacity or pricing, and which US producers and customers bear the consequences. USTR, March 11 Section 301 investigations · Federal Register, notice of initiation

Cheap output has several explanations

A producer may sell more cheaply because it found a better production method. It may be drawing down unsold inventory after demand weakened. It may also have access to state support that keeps an unprofitable line open or encourages another round of investment. Lower prices are consistent with all three. Investment continuing despite low returns, chronically low utilisation and a demonstrable financing advantage would strengthen a claim of policy-driven excess capacity.

For example, suppose two suppliers sell the same input at $80 per unit. One lowered its cost from $90 to $70 by investing in better equipment and earns $10 per unit. The other still pays $90 per unit and can continue because an external subsidy covers the $10 loss. The buyer sees the same price, and the two production decisions have different consequences for the likely durability of supply and the need for a policy response. Real cases require estimates of unit cost and the value of support, with uncertainty around both.

An input buyer can lose when a producer gains

A duty that raises the domestic price may improve revenue for US producers of the protected input. It also raises costs for downstream firms that use it. A machine maker selling abroad may have to absorb some of the cost because its foreign rivals can continue buying at world prices. A domestic supplier able to expand quickly can limit that effect. Where replacement capacity is scarce, the burden can last.

The best argument for intervention is that strategic supply or industrial knowledge can be costly to rebuild after suppliers exit, and a supported foreign producer may be able to raise prices once competition disappears. That case deserves evidence about concentration, the ease of rebuilding capacity and how a proposed response addresses the specific practice. A broad remedy can protect existing producers while weakening users that need affordable inputs.

Compare utilisation, profitability and capacity plans across firms with and without access to the alleged support. Track US production and downstream prices by product. That would allow the investigation’s eventual findings to be assessed against outcomes. The launch notice establishes a question. The answers have to come from evidence that distinguishes a change in competitive conditions from ordinary movement in costs.

America’s tariff reset

title.rendered: Customs duty deferral is most valuable to firms short of working capital

content.rendered:
A manufacturer pays import duty before it can earn money from the goods that duty helped clear. For a company carrying costly short-term debt, the timing can be as consequential as a modest change in the tariff. India’s revised deferral rules and separate route for eligible manufacturer-importers can shorten that cash gap. The policy will have its strongest effect if entry is credible for smaller compliant firms and the state can monitor payment without creating a fresh paperwork burden. Union Budget, customs measures · CBIC, Circular 08/2026-Customs · Finance Ministry, deferred duty amendment

Two changes, with different dates

The Budget described an extension of deferral for trusted operators and a route for eligible manufacturer-importers. The amendment to the payment rules took effect from 1 March. CBIC’s February circular describes the new manufacturer facility beginning on 1 April and remaining available through 31 March 2028. It lays out conditions and an approval process. A deferral is a timing change in the duty liability. The days gained depend on when the bill of entry is returned for payment and the applicable due-date schedule, including the special treatment of March. Union Budget, customs measures · CBIC, Circular 08/2026-Customs · Finance Ministry, deferred duty amendment

A factory that imports inputs, assembles products and offers customers credit can have cash tied up across several parts of production at once. Deferring duty releases a part of that financing. For a borrower near its credit limit, the relevant return may be the ability to buy a production batch it would otherwise postpone. For a cash-rich firm, the value is closer to the interest it can earn or avoid in the period. The same nominal concession can have different effects on output.

Value the timing change

Take a shipment with ₹1 crore of duty and an illustrative 20-day deferral relative to immediate payment. At a 12% simple annual working-capital cost, the gross saving is about ₹65,753. If 12 separate shipments qualify on the same assumptions, the gross annual saving is about ₹7.89 lakh. That calculation treats each extension independently and leaves out approval costs, monitoring and credit effects. A company with a 6% cost of funds would get half the interest saving. A company facing a binding lending limit may gain more in value from liquidity than the rate calculation captures.

The public sector carries the corresponding receivable and may need short-term financing. Its borrowing cost can be lower than the private borrower’s. There can be a net financing benefit if collection remains high and administration is inexpensive. The state should track late payment and actual recovery. Treating every delayed rupee as revenue forgone would overstate fiscal cost, while disregarding defaults or administrative expense would understate it.

Make trust portable

The strongest case for narrow eligibility is that lower scrutiny and delayed collection work best for firms with a verifiable compliance history. Strict standards can protect public revenue. They can also entrench a financing advantage for firms already large enough to qualify. Publishing application times and rejection reasons, and recognising credible compliance information already held across agencies, can reduce avoidable fixed costs. Predictable review matters more for a smaller importer that cannot absorb the cost of a speculative application.

The test should compare approval, usage and arrears by firm size and prior compliance record. Observe whether deferral reduces bank line usage, shortens delays in releasing cargo or changes shipment frequency. Similar firms near an eligibility boundary can offer a useful comparison if other determinants are balanced. If only large cash-rich importers participate, the case for widening through a better-designed route strengthens. If payment delays and defaults increase sharply, tighter terms or graduated limits become easier to justify.

One operational issue is cash concentration on the due date. A manufacturer that enjoys lower average borrowing may still need a larger buffer on a single day if several declarations fall due together. Measure cash needs at the peak as well as on average. Predictability matters when the bank sets the size of the credit line.

The reform’s success will show up in reliable duty collection and fewer viable production decisions postponed for lack of cash.

excerpt.rendered: India’s trusted-importer reforms move duty payments closer to production. The benefits depend on timing, eligibility and the public cost of carrying the receivable.

title.rendered: A data centre can sit outside the balance sheet while its tenant still carries risk

content.rendered:
Who pays for the AI buildout? · Part 3 · March BIS infrastructure analysis

A company can reserve computing capacity without purchasing the entire facility. The BIS’s March review describes structures where an outside vehicle owns and finances infrastructure while a large technology company commits to leases or capacity purchases and sometimes provides guarantees. That can bring in investors suited to long-lived assets. To understand the economic exposure, follow the contract that determines who pays if demand falls or the project is late. BIS, on- and off-balance-sheet borrowing · BIS, Financing the AI boom

Read the guarantees and leases together

A real-estate investor can be comfortable owning a building that many users can occupy. A highly specialised data centre may depend on one tenant and particular equipment. Lenders will care about the tenant’s credit quality, the length of its commitment and the ability to find another buyer. A lease can transform a volatile stream of capacity sales into a predictable payment to the project. It also shifts some volume risk to the company promising to pay.

Suppose a project owes $70 million in annual financing and operating costs. A tenant promises $80 million annually for capacity for ten years. The investor has a $10 million margin before other costs if the tenant pays. If the tenant can earn only $60 million from using or reselling the capacity, it may bear a $20 million shortfall under the simplified terms. Ownership has changed hands. The party with the fixed payment still has an exposure to the asset’s use.

Risk can be distributed across several contracts

Construction delays can sit with a builder under a fixed delivery date, with an investor if contracts allow extensions, or with a tenant if it pays before service. Power costs can pass through to the customer or stay with the operator. A guarantee may cover financing under certain conditions without covering operating losses. The financial statements are a useful starting point. Analysts should also read commitments, guarantees and the terms under which they can be cancelled.

A defence of these structures is that specialised owners and lenders can manage construction and property risk better than a tenant. They can also diversify sites or customers, lowering the cost of capital. Those benefits are stronger when financing costs reflect the risks actually transferred. They are weaker if multiple projects depend on the same few tenants and have limited alternative uses.

The next disclosure should make clear the undiscounted commitments, their timing, the major counterparties and the conditions under which a project can be refinanced. Compare the exposure with the cost of owning an equivalent facility. The question is which risks each contract moves and which stay concentrated after ownership has been transferred.

Who pays for the AI buildout?

title.rendered: China’s 2026 growth target leaves a choice about who receives the stimulus

content.rendered:
China’s growth rebalancing · Part 3 · March Government Work Report

China’s Government Work Report set a 2026 growth objective of 4.5% to 5%, with the authorities aiming for a stronger result where possible. The range sits alongside a target of around 2% consumer price inflation and a goal of more than 12 million new urban jobs. These are policy objectives. A local authority trying to meet them can build another project, support households or address unpaid obligations. The same immediate GDP effect can lead to a different balance sheet two years later. China State Council, 2026 Government Work Report · IMF, China Article IV consultation

The local government’s decision

An infrastructure project generates measured investment while it is built. It can make production easier if it relieves a constraint with sustained demand. It can also leave a municipality carrying operating costs for a facility that users rarely need. A transfer raises households’ purchasing power and can support service businesses with fewer imported inputs, depending on how recipients spend it. Paying suppliers’ arrears can improve private liquidity without appearing as a new procurement announcement.

For illustration, a city can commit 100 million yuan to a facility with an annual operating cost of five million. If usage revenue and explicit operating transfers come to two million, the project creates a recurring three-million-yuan gap after construction. A similarly sized payment of already due bills has no facility to operate, although it requires financing now. The comparison shows why an annual investment figure gives little information about future fiscal room.

Fiscal incentives shape the growth mix

Local officials may be better placed to see where roads, schools or utilities need capacity. Their incentives can still favour building if access to funding is tied to approved projects and maintenance comes from a different budget. A national transfer for household services may have the opposite difficulty. Local staff have to identify eligible users and maintain service quality, and the fiscal benefit of better employment may accrue elsewhere. Clear central and local funding responsibilities can make either instrument more effective.

The case for investment is strongest where usage is constrained by an existing bottleneck and future demand can be documented. The case for household support strengthens when local services have unused capacity and households are delaying ordinary expenditure because disposable income is uncertain. Sector-level price and employment data can help distinguish the two. Low inflation across many services suggests a different problem from a shortage of transport or power capacity.

Read the next GDP release alongside local accounts, the settlement of supplier bills, employment and recurring public-service spending. The policy has made rebalancing easier if the extra activity creates durable demand and leaves manageable future obligations. Hitting the annual range alone cannot settle that question.

China’s growth rebalancing

title.rendered: The IEA can release oil stocks. India still has to solve its LPG bottleneck.

content.rendered:
On 11 March, the International Energy Agency’s member countries agreed to make 400 million barrels of oil available from emergency reserves. The following day, the IEA described a near halt in crude and product flows through the Strait of Hormuz, which had carried about 20 million barrels a day before the conflict. Releasing stocks is a sensible way to buy time. For India, its usefulness depends on which products become available, how fast they arrive, and whether they relieve a shortage of cooking gas as well as crude oil. IEA, 11 March emergency stock release announcement · IEA, 12 March Oil Market Report

India should judge its response by continuity of delivery to households and essential users and by the cost imposed on other consumers. A crude stock release can improve global supply conditions while doing little immediately for a distributor that needs propane or butane. That distinction is important when planning inventories, alternate sourcing and temporary allocation. The right measure of energy security is the supply of usable fuel at the point of need.

A reserve stock has to be converted into a flow

Four hundred million barrels is a stock. To compare it with a disruption measured per day, we need to know the delivery schedule. If all of the announced volume were released evenly over 60 days, it would amount to about 6.7 million barrels a day. Over 120 days it would average about 3.3 million. These are illustrative rates, not IEA estimates of actual releases. The agency says timing will depend on national circumstances. That makes the pace and location of physical deliveries as important for near-term prices as the announced total. IEA, 11 March emergency stock release announcement

The comparison with Hormuz also requires care. The IEA’s pre-conflict figure of about 20 million barrels a day describes traffic through a route. It includes crude and oil products. It is not a direct measure of the net global supply loss on each day, because some shipments may be rerouted and countries can use commercial stocks. The March report separately estimated that Gulf countries had cut oil production by at least 10 million barrels a day. Those measures describe different effects of the same disruption. A policy response based on the wrong denominator can overstate what a release achieves. IEA, 12 March Oil Market Report

The strongest case for releasing reserves early is that additional supply can reduce the pressure to compete for the last available cargoes and give importers time to arrange replacements. The counterargument is that a rapid drawdown leaves less protection if the disruption persists or another shock follows. A sensible release plan should therefore be revised against actual ship movements, refinery demand and commercial inventories. The March EIA outlook illustrates the uncertainty: its price path depends on assumptions about the duration of shipping disruptions and the restoration of supply. IEA, 12 March Oil Market Report · EIA, 10 March Short-Term Energy Outlook release

There is also a cost to rebuilding stocks. If governments begin replenishing reserves while physical supply is still constrained, their purchases can add to the pressure the release was meant to ease. If they wait too long, protection against another disruption remains weaker. The sensible way to decide is to use evidence on cargo arrivals, private inventories and replacement capacity. A published framework for releases and replenishment would make it easier to judge whether the reserves are being used to bridge a physical interruption or to hold prices near an unstated target.

India’s exposure is larger for LPG than a crude headline suggests

At its 12 March briefing, the government said imports accounted for about 60% of India’s LPG consumption and that roughly 90% of those imports came through Hormuz. Multiplying the two shares gives an indicative exposure of about 54% of consumption to that route before substitution or inventory use. It is an estimate of exposure, not an observed shortfall. The same briefing said about 70% of crude was then being sourced through routes other than Hormuz. The crude and LPG shares describe different supply chains and timeframes. They help explain why refiners can maintain crude purchases while cooking-gas distributors face a tighter market. Government of India, 12 March inter-ministerial fuel supply briefing

A barrel of crude can be converted into several products. What a refinery can produce depends on the crude grade, its equipment and how it is operated. Increasing LPG output may be possible, but it can change what else the plant makes or sells. The government said its 9 March order directed refineries to maximise LPG yields and route relevant streams to the three public-sector oil marketing companies for household cooking gas. It also reported a 28% increase in LPG production over five days. That percentage is relative to a domestic production baseline and cannot be read as replacing 28% of national LPG demand. Government of India, 12 March inter-ministerial fuel supply briefing

A better supply dashboard would start from daily tonnes of domestic LPG production and usable inventory, then add committed cargoes with their arrival dates and confidence ranges. Compare the result with average and peak deliveries to households, essential services and commercial users. This would clarify whether the bottleneck lies in international procurement, refinery production, port handling or distribution. The policy response differs at each stage. An additional ship helps little with a short-term problem at a bottling plant, while more cylinders cannot replace a missing cargo.

Priority allocation trades one shortage against another

Prioritising cooking gas and essential institutions has a strong welfare case. Many households have limited short-run alternatives, and disruptions to hospitals or institutional kitchens can have costs beyond the price of the fuel. The government’s briefing said it was giving priority to essential non-domestic users while reviewing allocations to restaurants, hotels and others. Those businesses also employ workers and can struggle to operate when fuel deliveries are uncertain. The economic cost of prioritisation is therefore borne partly by the users receiving less supply. Government of India, 12 March inter-ministerial fuel supply briefing

Temporary allocation should be predictable enough for businesses to plan. Publish the categories receiving priority and allow periodic review as cargoes arrive and demand changes. Where supply is short, assess delivery times and refill availability by region and customer group. A stable official price can be valuable to households, yet the effective cost rises if people have to spend time searching for fuel or switch to a more expensive alternative. Measuring the number of cylinders delivered alongside waiting times gives a clearer picture of who is protected.

Across-the-board price relief would also change the way the shortage is allocated. When the marginal cargo is expensive, subsidising every unit raises the cost to the public budget and can leave less fuel for users with few alternatives. Targeted support for households with limited options, combined with clear supply priorities, can protect essential consumption at a lower fiscal cost. The trade-off is that targeting needs reliable distribution and timely records. In a short emergency, simple priorities may be easier to administer, but their coverage should narrow once supply improves.

What would count as success

The release should be judged first by the usable flow it adds during the disruption. In India, the more relevant tests are whether household refill times stay manageable, essential users receive fuel, commercial allocations become more predictable and refineries can normalise their product mix as alternatives arrive. The RBI’s latest published current-account figures also give a reason to watch the cost of substitution. Before this shock, the December-quarter deficit stood at $13.2 billion, or 1.3% of GDP, in the preliminary release. More expensive cargoes and freight can raise the dollar bill even if quantities are maintained. RBI, preliminary December-quarter balance of payments

The policy case for emergency releases and priority allocation is strongest while the supply disruption is severe and substitutes are limited. If alternate cargoes arrive reliably and refill delays ease, the case for broad allocation controls weakens. If crude supply improves while LPG deliveries remain strained, the priority should shift toward securing LPG-specific cargoes and fixing distribution constraints. India’s response will work when the fuels households and businesses actually use reach them in time, at a cost that can be sustained.

Part of a series

The 2026 oil shock
