title.rendered: India should pay for new UPI acceptance before it pays for more volume

content.rendered:
India’s early case for subsidising low-value merchant payments was the case for building a network. A customer values a payments app when shops accept it. A shop values the system when customers use it. A subsidy can get both sides over that threshold. As the network becomes routine, the same subsidy increasingly pays for transactions that would have occurred anyway. A new round of support should start by identifying merchants who would lose reliable acceptance without it. DFS, incentive scheme evaluation release · Cabinet, FY 2024–25 UPI incentive rules

The denominator changes the answer

The FY 2024–25 Cabinet scheme had an estimated outlay of ₹1,500 crore. For qualifying payments up to ₹2,000 to small merchants, it offered an incentive of 0.15% of value under zero merchant discount rate. The February evaluation release describes growth in digital transactions and UPI’s rising share. That history is relevant to the scale the policy has helped build. Volume grew alongside wider smartphone use, other changes to the payments ecosystem and shifts in customer habits. Counting transactions gives the size of the rail. It supplies limited evidence on the extra volume attributable to a subsidy. Cabinet, FY 2024–25 UPI incentive rules · DFS, incentive scheme evaluation release

A ₹500 qualifying payment generates 75 paise at the stated rate. Imagine two groups each generating one million such payments. In the first, 20% of payments would have been made in cash without the incentive. In the second, that share is 2%. Total incentive cost in each is ₹7.5 lakh. The cost per additional digital payment is ₹3.75 in the first group and ₹37.50 in the second. These shares are assumptions to illustrate the arithmetic. The gap would be larger if the second group’s additional transactions merely switched from another digital instrument.

Who gets the margin?

A no-fee QR sign can be genuinely valuable to a vendor. It can reduce cash handling, widen the pool of customers and leave a transaction record. The infrastructure still has operating costs. Banks, app providers and merchant acquirers bear costs for systems, dispute handling, settlement and support. A payment linked to transaction value favours the flow a provider can measure easily. It may have little connection to the fixed cost of training a merchant, replacing a broken device or providing reliable support in a district with thin coverage.

A targeted scheme could pay for a merchant becoming active and remaining active through several months, with extra weight for locations where sustained acceptance is low. That would create a direct incentive to support adoption. It would also create a risk of duplicate or nominal registrations, so retention should be measured using activity from different customers and over time. Paying for service availability or timely dispute resolution could make providers compete on features that matter once acceptance is widespread.

A credible case for paying the providers

The strongest counterargument is that a transaction incentive helps cover recurring costs on a rail expected to operate continuously. If provider revenues fall below reasonable operating costs, the first service cuts may be in low-value segments. That risk warrants a serious cost comparison. It is a case for identifying which functions need support and how much they cost. Processing a transaction, maintaining redundancy and resolving a disputed payment each have different cost drivers. A transparent procurement or service payment could fund the last two more directly than a flat share of purchase value.

An evaluation should count substitution across payment modes too. A customer who switches from a card to UPI may reduce some acceptance costs for a shop without expanding participation. The shop that accepts its first digital payment can change which customers it serves. Those are distinct benefits and can justify different funding.

Policymakers should compare matched cohorts of merchants with similar pre-policy activity and local conditions. Measures should include new active outlets, retention, failed payments and complaints, with results split by geography and merchant size. A phased redesign could make that evidence stronger. If acceptance or reliability fell sharply after a carefully measured reduction in a mature cohort, the case for recurring volume support would improve. If both held while uptake rose in previously underserved markets, the fiscal case would favour shifting the marginal rupee towards entry and service quality.

excerpt.rendered: A scheme that subsidises transactions can expand a payments network. At UPI’s scale, the relevant question is which merchants would otherwise be left out.

title.rendered: The Urban Challenge Fund needs a repayment plan for every project

content.rendered:
The Urban Challenge Fund can impose useful discipline on city investment if a financing decision reveals how the asset will be paid for and operated. The Union Cabinet has approved ₹1 lakh crore of central assistance, with support of up to 25 per cent of project cost and at least 50 per cent to be raised from market sources. A bank, bond investor or private partner may ask questions a grant application can skate past. The most important is what cash will cover repayment after construction, and what happens if users or revenues turn out to be fewer than expected. Cabinet decision on the Urban Challenge Fund · Government’s February Urban Challenge Fund FAQ

The project share is a financing rule

Market finance can come from municipal bonds, bank loans or public-private partnerships. The remaining funding can come from the state, the urban local body or other sources. The headline projection of ₹4 lakh crore of investment follows from applying the central share to a larger project pool. It expresses the government’s ambition for the scheme. It says little on its own about bids, projects reaching financial close or completed works. The actual financing mix will vary by project, and private investment can still rely on future payments from the city or guarantees from government. Cabinet decision on the Urban Challenge Fund · Government’s February Urban Challenge Fund FAQ

Take a hypothetical ₹100 crore project with a ₹25 crore Union grant, ₹25 crore of state or local capital and a ₹50 crore ten-year loan at eight per cent. If the loan is repaid in equal annual instalments, the annual debt service is about ₹7.45 crore. Assume the service costs ₹3 crore a year to run and maintain. The project would need approximately ₹10.45 crore of annual cash before allowing for reserves, major repairs or a margin for uncertainty. The assumed rate and maturity are illustrative. The calculation identifies an ongoing obligation that the upfront funding shares alone do not show.

Suppose the city expects ₹12 crore in billed charges, collects 80 per cent and has no other committed support. It would receive ₹9.6 crore, leaving a shortfall of about ₹85 lakh under those assumptions. A higher charge might increase collections, reduce use or increase unpaid bills. These are different outcomes for a service used by lower-income households. The financial assessment needs a credible payment and use forecast rather than a multiplication of projected connections by the tariff. It should also show what other spending the city would cut if the forecast proves optimistic.

The strongest case for a market test

A lender has a reason to examine cost escalation, construction schedules and revenue estimates. That scrutiny can improve the projects chosen and discourage officials from approving assets they cannot afford to operate. It can also favour cities with established revenue systems and projects with cash flows lenders can observe. A flood channel can protect public assets and households without generating a stream of monthly bills. A water network can improve public health for people who are not the direct paying customer. Those benefits belong in a social appraisal even when they do not provide debt service. Cabinet decision on the Urban Challenge Fund · World Bank urban resilience study

One response is to state explicitly which cash flow supports a loan. A charge can fund a part of a service with direct beneficiaries. Property tax or a predictable state payment can finance part of a wider public benefit if the legal and budget arrangements are credible. Public grants can pay for justified benefits that cannot be collected through the project. If a guarantee is used, report who bears losses and how much debt is covered. A structure that relies on an open-ended public promise can satisfy a lender while leaving the original fiscal risk in place. Cabinet decision on the Urban Challenge Fund · RBI’s chapter on municipal own revenue

Distribution matters at the project selection stage

A wealthy city can prepare projects, hire advisers and show collections to lenders. A smaller city may struggle with those steps even when its residents have a more urgent service gap. The Cabinet’s separate guarantee provision recognises a financing obstacle for eligible smaller cities. The fund’s competition should test whether such cities reach financial close at manageable costs and whether the resulting works remain viable after the first grant. If only the best-resourced corporations can satisfy the administrative requirements, the public return from preparation support could be greater than the return from offering more finance to projects already able to borrow. Cabinet decision on the Urban Challenge Fund · Government’s February Urban Challenge Fund FAQ

The maturity of the finance also has to match the life and risk of the asset. A short loan against a long-lived network can require large annual payments before new connections produce revenue. Extending the term can make the annual payment smaller while increasing the duration of exposure to a revenue miss. A variable rate can leave a city paying more just when its other costs are rising. An appraisal should show the results under several maturities, rate paths and take-up assumptions. The lowest quoted rate is useful information only with the associated term, security and refinancing obligations.

A credible report would also distinguish genuinely incremental projects from works a city would have funded anyway. Bringing an existing project under a new funding window can free up local funds for other work, and that can be valuable. It is a different claim from the fund having created an entirely new investment. The fiscal record should show the previous plan, the changed source of finance and what the freed-up money paid for.

What should appear in the first set of awards

Publish project cost, grant share, source of market finance, debt-service schedule, projected operating costs and the public support relied on in a weak revenue scenario. Later compare those assumptions with contracts, receipts and service outcomes. The reform would earn confidence if projects move faster, borrow on defensible terms and operate without repeated rescue transfers. A pipeline of approvals with few completed financing agreements would point to an appraisal or credit constraint. A pipeline that closes and then depends on unexpected transfers would show that the real cost was deferred. Both outcomes are observable if the fund reports the financing and the service together. Cabinet decision on the Urban Challenge Fund · Government’s February Urban Challenge Fund FAQ

excerpt.rendered: India’s new urban fund requires market financing. Its public value depends on which risks lenders test and which costs cities can repay without sacrificing essential services.

title.rendered: India’s new inflation basket changes what a food shock means

content.rendered:
India’s new consumer price index is a better starting point for monetary policy because it reflects more recent spending patterns and measures prices that the previous basket missed. The first release on the 2024 base puts January inflation at 2.75%. The last December estimate on the 2012 base was 1.33%. Treating the difference as an acceleration of 1.42 percentage points within a single unchanged basket would overstate what the two headlines establish. Both the month and the measurement system changed. The useful question is how much price pressure has changed for comparable items, and how the new basket will translate future shocks into the headline the RBI targets. MoSPI’s first CPI release on the 2024 base · MoSPI’s December CPI release · Reuters, 12 February

The decline in the food weight has two distinct components

The Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation updates expenditure weights using the 2023–24 Household Consumption Expenditure Survey. It also adopts the international COICOP 2018 classification, dividing consumption into 12 categories. The published weight of food and beverages is 36.75%, compared with 45.86% under the old classification. Part of the 9.11 percentage point difference comes from classifying expenditure differently. For example, restaurant and accommodation services now have a separate division. To isolate the effect of the updated spending pattern, hold the classification fixed. MoSPI’s first CPI release on the 2024 base

The ministry provides both bridges. Under the old classification, applying the updated weights takes food and beverages from 45.86% to 40.10%, a 5.76 percentage point decline. Under the new classification, applying the older expenditure weights would put the category at around 42.62%, compared with 36.75% using the updated survey. Both comparisons point to a meaningful reduction in the food share under consistent definitions. The total difference between the published headline weights combines that underlying change with the classification change. The distinction matters when judging whether families have shifted consumption away from food or whether a type of expenditure was simply moved to another division. MoSPI’s first CPI release on the 2024 base

To see why it matters for policy, suppose prices for the items in the old food and beverages group rise 10% together while all other prices stay flat, starting from base-period relative prices. Applying weights of 45.86% and 40.10% to that same shock gives contributions of about 4.59 and 4.01 percentage points, respectively. The example holds the category and price shock fixed and changes only the weight. The approximate difference is 0.58 percentage points. It is an illustration rather than a decomposition of January inflation. Actual contributions depend on the detailed indices, relative prices and which parts of the basket are moving. MoSPI’s first CPI release on the 2024 base

Rural housing changes the coverage of the index

The old CPI had no separately measured rural housing group. The new system includes rural house rent, with a weight of about 2.46% in the rural basket. That figure is smaller than the 11.76% for the entire rural division covering housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels. The larger number should not be described as rent. The distinction is material if a region’s utility tariffs move while actual rents remain unchanged. The new release puts January housing inflation at 2.05% nationally, with rural and urban readings of 2.39% and 1.92%. These are observations under the new measurement system, which provides a way to follow the two segments separately. MoSPI’s first CPI release on the 2024 base

A national average is useful for a single monetary policy rate, but spending shares vary substantially by household. A low-income family that buys much of its food and has little scope to substitute when prices rise may experience a much larger squeeze than the revised headline suggests. A renting household in a fast-growing town can face an increase where the national rent index moves slowly. A change in CPI weights therefore changes the aggregate measurement of purchasing power. It does not redistribute income across these households or replace the need for separate evidence on food affordability, wages and rent burdens. That matters if the index is used to assess welfare payments as well as interest rates. MoSPI’s first CPI release on the 2024 base

Coverage also expands beyond housing. The number of weighted items rises from 299 to 358, and the ministry now uses online prices for some purchases alongside its market surveys. For categories such as air travel or streaming subscriptions, this can give a better view of how the service is actually bought. It also changes the measurement questions. A promotional fare can be unavailable for most dates, and a subscription can change its features along with its price. A meaningful comparison needs stable specifications, collection rules that reflect how consumers buy and an explanation of how temporary discounts and unavailable prices are handled. MoSPI’s first CPI release on the 2024 base

The overlap can help, if it is used for the right purpose

Both CPI vintages are available for 2025 at the general level. The ministry uses the ratio of the average new to the average old index in that overlap to rescale earlier all-India series. Multiplying an old index by a constant preserves growth rates within the portion transformed that way. It does not recreate what the historical inflation rate would have been if today’s basket and classification had been in use. The ministry limits direct linkage to the general index because the classifications differ. An analyst estimating food pass-through or the persistence of services inflation should avoid mechanically joining category histories across the break. MoSPI’s first CPI release on the 2024 base

There is a reasonable objection to putting too much emphasis on the break. The RBI still has to take decisions in real time, and a new index can be operationally valuable from its first release. A reading of 2.75% under the new definition is a useful estimate for January. The mistake would be to infer all of the change in underlying pressure from the jump relative to the last old-series headline. The overlap and the detailed items provide an alternative. Compare movements within the new basket through the recent months, check their breadth and use genuinely comparable price series for areas where the aggregate groups were recast. MoSPI’s first CPI release on the 2024 base · Reuters, 12 February

The policy consequences run in both directions. A smaller food weight can reduce the headline response to a temporary vegetable shortage. It can also make slow-moving categories more influential when their prices rise persistently. The RBI’s usual interest-rate channel works on spending and financial conditions with a lag. It has limited ability to increase the current supply of vegetables or rented homes. A more representative headline makes the target more useful, while the policy response still depends on the source and persistence of the pressure. Measures of inflation excluding volatile categories should be reconstructed from clearly documented definitions before their old thresholds are reused. MoSPI’s first CPI release on the 2024 base

January’s rural and urban headline rates, 2.73% and 2.77%, are close. Their food inflation rates, 1.96% and 2.44%, are further apart. This is a reminder that two similar headline numbers can conceal different sources of pressure. A useful release would let readers trace the difference to the categories and items that contributed most, rather than asking them to infer household conditions from the national average. A district with rising staples prices and a city with rising rents can call for different responses from local policymakers even when the national policy rate remains appropriate. MoSPI’s first CPI release on the 2024 base

What to look for in the next readings

The case for treating January as evidence of wider inflation would strengthen if price increases persist across several large categories, with independent support from wage, rent and selling-price data. If the rise is concentrated in a few food items or reflects the month used as a comparison, a broader tightening response would be less well supported. MoSPI can help by keeping both 2025 vintages accessible and publishing detailed bridges with clear category definitions. Researchers should document which version of the data they use when they assess RBI decisions or estimate inflation persistence. The new basket will earn confidence by making those comparisons more informative and reproducible. MoSPI’s first CPI release on the 2024 base

excerpt.rendered: The first CPI on the 2024 base puts January inflation at 2.75%. Updating the basket is overdue, and the published bridge shows which comparisons survive the change.

title.rendered: The case for Mumbai–Pune high-speed rail depends on time saved beyond the train

content.rendered:
The published estimate of around 48 minutes between Mumbai and Pune describes the train journey expected after a proposed high-speed corridor is built. The benefit to passengers is the time and expense they save door to door. The benefit to the wider economy depends on whether people can make trips they previously avoided, what they pay and which other investments the project displaces. India’s appraisal should test those margins before treating a fast timetable as a measure of economic integration. Ministry of Railways, Budget corridor proposals · Union Budget 2026–27 speech

What the Budget is proposing

The Budget identifies seven high-speed corridors as links between major cities, including Mumbai–Pune. The Railways ministry subsequently gave indicative travel times for several routes. An indicative journey time can inform an appraisal. The operating timetable, fare, station locations and network connections will determine what passengers experience. A business traveller near both stations faces a different choice from a student needing two local trips and a tight connection at the end. Ministry of Railways, Budget corridor proposals · Union Budget 2026–27 speech

Rail can add value even for travellers who already have a reasonable road or conventional train option. Greater predictability may let them attend a meeting and return the same day. A dependable service can expand access to specialist hospitals, markets or job interviews. How frequently that happens depends on when services depart and when the desired activity takes place. A peak-hour commuter needs a different schedule from someone travelling twice a month.

Add the minutes back

Take an illustrative trip where the best existing option takes 210 minutes door to door. A high-speed service takes 48 minutes on board, with 35 minutes reaching the station, 20 minutes for access and waiting, and 40 minutes at the far end. Total time is 143 minutes and the saving is 67 minutes. At an assumed ₹300 per hour, the time saving is worth about ₹335 before differences in reliability and comfort. If a second passenger lives close to both stations and has much shorter transfers, their willingness to pay can be considerably higher. These are scenario inputs and a method for comparing trips.

The difference also matters for a project’s public return. Rail revenue depends on the fare users will pay and the number of journeys. Wider gains can include less road congestion or reduced local emissions, which need separate evidence on which trips are displaced. Revenue and time savings should be measured consistently in appraisal. A rail ticket is an expense for a traveller and revenue for the operator. Adding it as an extra social benefit would double count a transfer.

Compare the right alternative

The strongest case for a dedicated line is that it offers speed and capacity a congested mixed-use railway may struggle to deliver. It can also make a reliable schedule possible with less interference from slower trains. The alternative comparison should still include improvements to existing routes, including timetable reliability and station access. Faster intercity service may be valuable under a wide range of assumptions. An appraisal should show how much extra benefit the dedicated investment offers over the best conventional option.

Publish results for fares, ridership and time savings by origin and destination, including alternative station locations and transfer assumptions. Test utilisation across times of day and the sensitivity of the economic return to construction cost. If the main benefits survive reasonable changes in access time and fare, a stronger case for the corridor emerges. If they depend on a station catchment that passengers cannot reach reliably, local links may offer better returns before the next commitment.

Land and construction costs belong in the same scenarios. A central station can improve access and require expensive acquisition or tunnelling. A peripheral site can lower construction costs and lengthen trips for most riders. Comparing designs on total discounted costs and benefits makes that trade-off explicit.

For Mumbai and Pune, a train under an hour would be an operating achievement. A stronger labour and business connection requires trips people can afford and complete when they need them.

excerpt.rendered: The Budget proposes a fast intercity link. The return depends on station access, service frequency and what the corridor can deliver that cheaper upgrades cannot.

title.rendered: India’s caregiver training target needs a labour market on the other side

content.rendered:
India’s plan to train 1.5 lakh caregivers can address a skills gap. It will create a durable care workforce only if employers and households can finance jobs workers are willing to keep. The Union Budget proposes multiskilled training combining core care and allied skills, including support with assistive devices. The target measures training, not hires or people receiving care. The investment case depends on the tasks graduates can perform competently, the terms on which services are bought and whether workers remain in the occupation after their first assignment. Union Budget 2026–27 speech, care ecosystem section · ILO brief on unpaid care and labour-force participation

A training seat is only one side of the market

Demand for care can be substantial even where few households can pay enough to support a stable job. Needs may be intermittent, geographically dispersed or difficult to schedule. A worker has to spend time travelling, coordinating with families and waiting between assignments. An hourly price that looks attractive to a household can translate into modest monthly earnings after those unpaid hours. A training programme can improve competence and confidence. It does not automatically create a way for multiple buyers to support reliable hours and reasonable working conditions.

Consider a hypothetical caregiver paid ₹200 for each billed hour, working 22 days a month with four billed hours per day. Gross billed revenue is ₹17,600. If another two hours per day go to travel and coordination, the gross revenue per hour of work-related time falls to about ₹133 before travel, intermediary fees or other expenses. At six billed hours per day with one additional hour of travel, monthly revenue is ₹26,400 and about ₹171 per hour of work-related time. These are assumed prices and schedules. The comparison shows why organisation and utilisation can matter as much as the quoted wage rate.

The buyer needs assurance about the service

Families can have difficulty comparing qualifications and working out which tasks a worker is trained to perform. A credible certificate can reduce that information gap if it reflects demonstrated competence. The assessment should distinguish routine assistance, tasks that require supervision and tasks outside the worker’s role. Clear terms protect both sides. If the programme rewards enrolments and certificates without checking skills in practice, it can expand the number of credentials while families still rely on informal referrals or ask workers to perform services they are not equipped to deliver. Union Budget 2026–27 speech, care ecosystem section · ILO brief on unpaid care and labour-force participation

For workers, mobility matters. A certificate recognised by several providers can make it easier to change employers or locations. The value falls if an employer recognises it only for a narrow set of jobs or if a worker must pay a new fee each time they take an assignment. Evaluating progression requires following pay, job continuity, actual duties and the reasons workers leave. A higher first placement rate is useful evidence, while retention and improved conditions show whether the occupation offers a viable career.

Different services need different ways to pay

A household may be able to purchase a few hours a week and be unable to finance intensive or long-duration care. Public programmes, insurance where applicable, institutions and households can support different parts of the market. Each arrangement should identify what service is covered, how workers are paid and what quality standards are enforced. Subsidising training can lower a fixed entry cost. Subsidising demand can help people obtain care they otherwise could not afford. If demand is the main constraint, producing more graduates alone may lower earnings or increase turnover without improving coverage. Union Budget 2026–27 speech, care ecosystem section · ILO brief on unpaid care and labour-force participation

The strongest case for acting first on training is that providers cannot build dependable services without workers whose skills they can trust. An initial cohort can help reveal demand and lower the cost of entering the market. A phased approach would compare outcomes for different locations and training providers before scaling every course. Some locations may need employer coordination or a reliable mechanism for referring clients. Others may already have enough demand and simply need training that matches it. Evidence of vacancies, repeat contracts and retention can distinguish those cases. Union Budget 2026–27 speech, care ecosystem section

There is a practical risk in paying training providers largely for completions. A provider can choose a course that is easy to fill and assess even where employers are looking for different abilities. Linking some payment to independently verified retention can strengthen the incentive to match training with vacancies. It can also encourage providers to select only candidates likely to find work anyway. Report results for all entrants, including people who leave before assessment, and compare with similar people not offered the course at the same time.

The training budget should also be evaluated against the additional capacity it produces. An illustrative programme spending ₹1 crore on 500 participants costs ₹20,000 per participant. If 250 are in sustained care jobs that they would not otherwise have obtained, the cost per additional sustained job is ₹40,000. Both numbers use assumed inputs and omit benefits to care recipients. The difference illustrates why counting seats tells the government little about the value it received. Evidence on additional employment and service quality is needed to evaluate the next round of spending.

Test whether the capacity stays in care

Follow trainees from enrolment through assessment, first assignment and work after six and twelve months. Measure earnings after work-related costs, paid hours, retention and any progression. Also record where services become available, who can pay for them and whether families see continuity. If graduates can obtain predictable work and people who previously lacked care can access it, training has helped expand the market. If many complete courses but leave the occupation after brief assignments, investigate pay, scheduling and demand before expanding the training target. The goal is dependable care and sustainable work, with the training count serving as an intermediate measure. Union Budget 2026–27 speech, care ecosystem section · ILO brief on unpaid care and labour-force participation

excerpt.rendered: The Budget proposes training 1.5 lakh caregivers. The return depends on who can hire them, what families can afford and whether the jobs offer enough pay and continuity.

title.rendered: Bangladesh needs to recognise bank losses before deciding who pays

content.rendered:
Bangladesh’s banking repair will be credible when it establishes the size of losses and allocates them in a way that protects payments and sound lending. In its January Article IV assessment, the IMF reports that real growth slowed to 3.7 per cent in FY2025 from 4.2 per cent in FY2024, that inflation remained elevated and that tax revenue weakened. The IMF calls for an assessment of undercapitalisation, clarity on fiscal support and credible restructuring and resolution plans. These are connected questions. When the budget is already constrained, the timing and form of support can determine whether a bank repair restores confidence or merely transfers hidden losses to the state. IMF Board’s Bangladesh Article IV assessment · World Bank’s October 2025 Bangladesh Development Update

A liquidity shortage and an equity shortfall require different remedies

A bank can hold sound long-term loans while facing withdrawals it cannot meet immediately. Short-term liquidity can bridge the timing gap if assets can ultimately cover liabilities. A bank whose assets are worth less than its liabilities has a deeper problem. Borrowing extra cash lets it pay some depositors now while creating another liability. It can buy time for an orderly response, yet it cannot restore equity on its own. Establishing which problem dominates requires a realistic estimate of recoverable asset values, related exposures and how quickly losses could be realised.

Take a hypothetical bank with assets recorded at 100, deposits and other debt of 92 and reported equity of eight. A review finds that expected recoveries on loans are 12 lower than the recorded values. At adjusted asset value 88 the bank is four short of covering its liabilities. A cash loan of five increases both assets and liabilities by five and leaves the shortfall unchanged. An injection of four restores equity to zero under these assumptions, which still leaves no capital buffer. The example ignores taxes, other adjustments and different creditor priorities. It shows why the size of a liquidity facility does not identify the cost of recapitalisation.

The budget can bear costs in forms that look different at first

The public cost can arrive through cash, government bonds used for recapitalisation, guarantees, or losses associated with continued support. These instruments have different payment dates and risks. A guarantee can have little immediate budget cost and become expensive later if recoveries disappoint. A recapitalisation bond can avoid a large cash payment at inception while creating interest and redemption obligations. Reporting the face value, expected loss and stress case for each commitment gives taxpayers a better picture of exposure. Protecting financial stability can justify public action, provided the cost and terms can be examined. IMF Board’s Bangladesh Article IV assessment

Weak revenue makes that transparency more important. The IMF says the FY2025 fiscal deficit was contained partly through under-execution of capital and social spending while the tax ratio fell. A low deficit attained by delaying expenditure can leave little room to meet a new recurring obligation. The distributional question is what services, investments or taxes change if public support is needed. Stabilising payments protects depositors and businesses that use banks every day. The case for support is weaker where earlier owners retain value despite losses or where assistance finances further lending on the same unsound terms. IMF Board’s Bangladesh Article IV assessment · World Bank’s October 2025 Bangladesh Development Update

How to protect the useful parts of the system

The strongest case for moving cautiously is that rapid recognition of losses, without a clear plan to protect payment services and eligible depositors, can deepen a loss of confidence. An asset review should be paired with liquidity arrangements for viable banks and a credible resolution route for institutions unable to recover. The timing should keep ordinary transfers and payroll functioning. It should also explain how exposures are valued, who is responsible for decisions and which institutions require ownership or management changes. Gradual execution can be justified by operational constraints. Repeated postponement without credible information leaves the fiscal and banking risks harder to price. IMF Board’s Bangladesh Article IV assessment

The cost of delay shows up in credit allocation. A bank that cannot recognise a loss may keep financing an existing borrower to avoid marking the loan down. A healthier business with fewer connections can be rationed even when it has a productive use for credit. That pattern can persist while aggregate credit volumes appear stable. A useful test is whether new lending becomes available to viable firms on transparent terms after a repair, and whether the volume of repeatedly restructured weak loans declines. The goal is a system that can take and price risk again. IMF Board’s Bangladesh Article IV assessment · World Bank’s October 2025 Bangladesh Development Update

A credible programme also needs a way to monitor what happens to the original loans after resolution. Recoveries may come from collateral, operating cash flows or a sale of claims. Estimating them at an optimistic value can make a public vehicle appear solvent on paper while taxpayers retain the downside. Publish recoveries against the initial valuation and disclose material changes. If the assets are sold, the comparison should include the cost and time of collecting them directly. The amount recovered, and when, matters to the final fiscal bill.

An asset review also needs rules for comparable loans. A borrower that can recover after a temporary shock should be assessed against a realistic cash-flow path. A firm whose loan has been renewed repeatedly without a viable business should not receive the same valuation. Publishing the assumptions and getting independent review can help ensure that asset quality is measured consistently across institutions. IMF Board’s Bangladesh Article IV assessment

Evidence that the repair is working

Track independently assessed capital, new non-performing exposures, recoveries, depositor confidence and access to sound credit. Report the cost and timing of public support separately from central-bank liquidity. Stronger reported capital would be more persuasive alongside credible asset valuations and better credit allocation. If weak banks remain dependent on support while losses are repeatedly deferred, a narrower fiscal deficit will provide limited reassurance. The January assessment makes clear why banking, revenue and growth have to be assessed together. IMF Board’s Bangladesh Article IV assessment · World Bank’s October 2025 Bangladesh Development Update

excerpt.rendered: The IMF’s January assessment links banking weakness to weak tax revenues and inflation. A credible repair starts with identifying losses, protecting deposits and setting clear terms for public support.

title.rendered: India’s wild-animal crop cover needs a price for prevention as well as loss

content.rendered:
An elephant or a herd of wild boar can destroy a field while leaving the village average yield almost unchanged. That kind of loss is a poor fit for a broad area index. A February parliamentary reply explains that states can notify crop damage from wild animals as an add-on under India’s crop insurance, with individual assessment and the additional cost borne by the state. The approach is promising where harm is concentrated and farmers would otherwise shoulder the local cost of a public conservation objective. It should be paired with targeted prevention and a claims process that is inexpensive to use. Parliamentary reply, wild-animal add-on · PMFBY, revised operational guidelines

The risk sits at the field boundary

An area-wide yield contract pools common shocks. A field next to a wildlife corridor may have much greater exposure than another field in the same village. Individual assessment can address that variation. It creates a need for proof, inspections and timely notice. Farmers then weigh the expected payment against the time spent applying, uncertainty over eligibility and the need to preserve evidence. When that fixed effort is high relative to a small claim, measured take-up can be low even if the benefit would matter to the household.

States have a practical reason to define eligibility carefully. A blanket statewide add-on can spend money and inspection capacity where the risk is slight. A narrow zone can make support more accurate but will miss some damage outside it. A transparent boundary with a procedure for reviewing repeated verified losses gives the state a way to adapt. Publishing exposure by crop and area can also reveal where planting choices and seasonal movement make prevention more valuable than a larger sum insured. Parliamentary reply, wild-animal add-on

Compare claims with damage avoided

Take an illustrative cluster of 100 farms. Suppose each has a 10% annual chance of ₹20,000 of verified damage. Expected losses are ₹2 lakh a year, before administration and correlated events. If collective prevention costs ₹80,000 a year and halves expected losses, it saves ₹1 lakh of crop damage at a cost of ₹80,000. A residual insurance layer still has value because households care about volatility and the loss might be concentrated among a few. This arithmetic assumes average annual costs and a reliable prevention effect. It is a way to compare interventions, not a district estimate.

Who pays for prevention matters. One farm’s protective action may shift animals to a neighbour. A shared intervention may generate benefits across the cluster while imposing concentrated costs on some landholders. This is a case for local coordination and evaluation at a geographic scale large enough to observe displacement. The state can pay for verification and shared prevention where benefits extend beyond a single farm, while paying individual claims for losses that still occur.

Avoid paying twice and avoid paying too late

The strongest argument for keeping the add-on small is that some states already compensate wildlife damage through other mechanisms. A second channel can duplicate benefits or send farmers between offices. An integrated claim record and a clear rule for which programme pays first can help. Evidence requirements should be proportionate to the sum at stake. Random verification after simpler processing of small, credible claims is a possibility where the governing rules allow it and error can be measured.

An actuarial estimate should also allow for clusters of claims in a bad year. Spreading modest expected costs across many farms provides a useful benchmark. It can understate the contingency a state needs if damage is highly correlated in time. The fiscal plan should identify who covers an exceptional season.

Compare take-up, inspection time, claimant expenses, payments and repeated damage across areas with comparable exposure. Track damage just outside the notified boundary. If individual claims turn out to be costly to verify and preventive measures reduce losses across the wider area, more spending should go towards those measures. If damage remains concentrated despite prevention and claims can be verified promptly, the insurance layer has a stronger case. Farmers should be able to see which risk they have insured and what the state is doing to reduce it.

excerpt.rendered: State-financed add-on protection can cover losses missed by a yield index. Its design should reward prevention and make verified claims practical.

title.rendered: What the India–US trade framework actually offered exporters

content.rendered:
The US–India joint statement released in India on 7 February describes a path to an 18% US reciprocal tariff for covered Indian goods. A separate US executive order does something immediately measurable. It removes the additional 25% Russian-oil duty for eligible entries from 12:01 a.m. Eastern Standard Time on 7 February, or 10:31 a.m. IST. That is the change an importer can put into a customs calculation today. The 18% framework rate, possible product exemptions and other preferences need to be read with the implementing documents and their dates. That distinction matters for deciding whether to ship an existing order or commit to future capacity. Joint statement · US order ending the Russian-oil duty.

Three prices for a covered shipment

Consider a product with a customs value of $100 to which the prior 25% reciprocal rate and 25% Russian-oil surcharge both applied. Ignore ordinary duties and all other costs and hold the price fixed. Its starting cost after those additional duties was $150. Removing the oil surcharge while the reciprocal rate remains 25% takes the example to $125. If the 18% reciprocal rate is implemented for the same line, the cost becomes $118. The oil order accounts for $25 of the $32 difference between the two endpoints. Implementation of the framework rate would account for the remaining $7. Actual entries can differ because of exemptions, valuation, classification and ordinary duties. Previous reciprocal schedule · February framework.

The two steps have different commercial effects. An importer that can identify an entry after the oil-order cutoff has a specific cost change to discuss with its supplier. A buyer considering contracts for the next season wants to know the reciprocal rate, how origin will be verified and whether the terms can change. The framework says either country may modify its commitments if the other changes the agreed tariffs. That clause preserves negotiating flexibility and also affects how confidently a buyer can price a long contract. The more expensive it is to switch suppliers, the more a buyer values a preference it can rely on after the first shipment.

Which exporters stand to gain

The statement lists textiles and apparel, leather and footwear, plastic and rubber, organic chemicals, home décor, artisanal products and some machinery among the originating goods for which it describes an 18% rate. It also describes removal of the reciprocal duty for identified goods including generics, gems and diamonds and aircraft parts, subject to successful conclusion of the interim agreement. Those lines can face distinct treatment. An exemption can be worth much more to a producer than a seven-point rate reduction, but only if the product qualifies and the importer can claim it. Auto parts preferences depend on the terms of a proposed tariff-rate quota. The statement also links negotiated outcomes for generic pharmaceuticals and ingredients to the findings of a US Section 232 investigation. Product coverage and conditions in the joint statement.

The benefit can be shared. A US buyer that accepted a higher price during the surcharge can now ask for part of the relief. An Indian producer that had cut its own price to retain business can try to restore its margin. Who succeeds depends on the contract, alternative suppliers and capacity. A factory close to full use may keep more of the gain because the buyer has fewer options. A supplier with idle capacity and one large customer may take a smaller margin increase in exchange for firm orders. Repeated orders, customs unit values and factory utilisation would help separate these outcomes. The export guarantee announced in November is most valuable where a viable order is held up by a cash-flow or credit constraint. India’s export-credit response.

India’s concessions also have buyers and sellers

India says it will eliminate or reduce tariffs on US industrial goods and a range of food and agricultural products. The list includes some animal-feed inputs, tree nuts, fruit, soybean oil, wine and spirits. A lower landed price can help Indian businesses that use the imports. It can also compress margins for domestic sellers of competing products. For a feed input, the distributional analysis should start with who uses it, which local crop or input it displaces, and how much of a lower feed cost reaches meat, dairy or egg prices. The details of phase-in, quotas, technical standards and origin will determine the size of the change. India’s proposed concessions.

The statement also records India’s intention to buy $500 billion of specified US products over five years. Dividing by five gives $100 billion per year as a simple scale comparison. That arithmetic is neither an annual schedule nor a signed set of contracts. Purchases of aircraft, fuels and technology take place on different timelines. Some could replace imports from other suppliers rather than increase total Indian imports. An evaluation should compare new purchases with existing plans, relative prices and shifts in sourcing. The import bill and trade diversion are distinct questions. Joint statement purchase intentions.

Standards may ultimately do as much as tariffs to determine trade. If Indian and US authorities accept compatible test results, a supplier may be able to use one set of checks for more customers. The savings can be large for a firm that sells low volumes because the cost of certification has to be spread across fewer units. Poorly designed mutual recognition can leave essential safety questions unresolved or create overlapping obligations. The framework describes further work on conformity assessment and sector-specific standards. The relevant evidence will be the procedures firms must follow, the time each approval takes and the number of eligible suppliers that actually use them. Framework provisions on standards and licensing.

Origin rules have a similar fixed-cost effect. A producer that buys locally and can document its inputs may claim relief more easily than a smaller supplier relying on several imported intermediates. The benefit of the preference should be compared with the cost of proving eligibility on a real order.

What would make the framework durable

The strongest argument for responding quickly is that the oil duty removal is operative and a credible expectation of lower rates can unlock orders even before a final agreement. For buyers with established suppliers, the cost of waiting can exceed the risk of preparing the next contract. The strongest caution is that investments in capacity are harder to reverse than a shipment. A factory considering machinery should ask whether it would still earn a return if rules of origin raise costs or a quota limits access. The February order also provides for US monitoring and possible recommendations for further action if Russian oil imports resume. The order states the US administration’s account of India’s oil commitments. Actual import flows would be separate evidence. Executive order and monitoring provision.

The next useful comparison is between the framework and the customs instructions that importers can actually use. Record the effective rate by product, the date and time that determines eligibility, and the paperwork required to claim it. Then compare order volumes and repeat buyers with similar products receiving different relief. A credible, durable improvement in market access would show up in those orders and, with a lag, in investment. The immediate case is narrower. The separate order removes a defined surcharge for covered entries. The rest of the commercial gain depends on what is implemented and how easily firms can use it.

excerpt.rendered: The US removed a defined oil-related surcharge on Indian goods. The commercial value of the framework’s 18% rate, quotas and exemptions depended on the implementing instruments and who could use them.

title.rendered: India’s Budget makes a credible capex bet. Execution will decide the return.

content.rendered:
The Union Budget presented on 1 February plans ₹12.22 lakh crore of central capital expenditure in 2026–27, while targeting a fiscal deficit of 4.3% of GDP, down from the revised estimate of 4.4% for 2025–26. This is a defensible direction for India. More of the spending plan is directed toward capital formation as the Centre continues gradual consolidation. The case depends on whether the extra allocation leads to completed assets that improve productivity and encourage private investment. Finance Minister’s Budget 2026–27 speech · Ministry of Finance, fiscal and expenditure estimates · Ministry of Finance, debt and deficit targets

The baseline changes the size of the increase

The 2025–26 Budget initially allocated about ₹11.2 lakh crore to central capex, while the revised estimate is about ₹11 lakh crore. A ₹12.22 lakh crore allocation is about 11.1% higher than the revised estimate and about 9.1% higher than the original allocation, using these rounded figures. The first comparison describes the intended increase from the latest spending estimate. The second shows how much larger the new plan is than the last plan. Both matter because a headline percentage can look more ambitious when a prior allocation was revised downward. Finance Minister’s Budget 2026–27 speech · Ministry of Finance, fiscal and expenditure estimates · Ministry of Finance, debt and deficit targets

The capex increase from the revised estimate is modestly above the Budget’s nominal GDP growth assumption of 10%. The rounded numbers imply that central capex rises from about 22.2% of total expenditure to 22.9%. That is useful evidence about the spending mix. The volume of roads, equipment or power infrastructure the government can procure depends on what happens to their own prices. A price index for those inputs and a measure of physical progress would make the real increase easier to judge. Ministry of Finance, fiscal and expenditure estimates · Finance Minister’s Budget 2026–27 speech

State spending is part of the investment channel

The government’s effective capital expenditure measure is ₹17.15 lakh crore. It adds ₹4.93 lakh crore in grants for creation of capital assets to the Centre’s ₹12.22 lakh crore of capital expenditure. The latter already includes ₹2 lakh crore in special assistance as loans to states for capital expenditure. Adding the loans again would double-count them. The distinction is useful because the Union can provide finance while a state or another recipient is responsible for delivering the asset. Ministry of Finance, fiscal and expenditure estimates · Union Budget 2026–27 documents

State assistance has a larger effect when it allows a viable project to proceed that would otherwise be delayed. If a state substitutes the Union’s funds for expenditure it had already budgeted, the combined increase can be smaller. Delays can also reflect unresolved land acquisition, incomplete designs, procurement disputes or limited capacity at the implementing agency. In those cases, approving a larger transfer does little by itself. Track the sanction, release, expenditure and date the asset becomes operational. Each measures a different stage, and large gaps can show where a policy is constrained.

What would persuade private firms to invest?

Public investment can raise the return to private projects by lowering costs that firms cannot address individually. Better freight links can reduce inventories and missed deliveries. Reliable power can improve utilisation of existing machinery. Urban transport can widen the pool of workers reachable within a reasonable commute. The gains depend on the fit between the public asset and the constraints facing firms. The Economic Survey’s account of the shift toward capital expenditure makes that question more important as the programme expands. An average fiscal multiplier cannot settle the merits of an individual project. Economic Survey 2025–26

The strongest counterargument is that a larger programme can tie up labour, equipment and financing before assets are usable. It can also divert attention from spending that makes existing infrastructure productive. A public hospital needs staff and supplies. A railway line needs maintenance and reliable connections to the places it is meant to serve. Where operating or complementary investments are underfunded, a high capital allocation can generate a low service return. The appropriate project comparison includes operating costs and a credible alternative, such as upgrading an existing asset where demand does not justify a new one.

A practical test is to compare investment in areas that gain access to a completed asset at different times. If improved freight connectivity is the mechanism, examine delivery times and logistics expenses first. Then track business registrations, industrial power demand and investment where relevant. A comparison should check trends before completion because routes are often chosen for places already expected to grow. Report how much the result changes when fast-growing areas and overlapping interventions are taken into account. That is more informative than attributing every new factory in a corridor to the project.

The financing assumptions deserve their own test

The Budget puts non-debt receipts at about ₹36.5 lakh crore and expenditure at about ₹53.5 lakh crore. The difference is roughly ₹17 lakh crore using the rounded figures. If nominal GDP were 1% below the budgeted level and the rupee deficit stayed unchanged, the 4.3% ratio would rise to about 4.34% through the denominator alone. A weaker economy can also reduce tax receipts and affect expenditure. An assessment should run both effects separately and show how sensitive the financing requirement is to plausible changes in revenue. Finance Minister’s Budget 2026–27 speech · Ministry of Finance, debt and deficit targets

The Finance Ministry’s projected decline in central government debt from 56.1% to 55.6% of GDP is meaningful within its stated scope. The trajectory over several years depends on the primary balance, borrowing costs and nominal growth. Central debt and the combined liabilities of the Centre and states are different measures. Looking at both is useful when the central strategy depends in part on state investment. It also matters when deciding what fiscal space actually exists in an economic downturn. Ministry of Finance, fiscal and expenditure estimates · Ministry of Finance, debt and deficit targets

The Budget speech estimates gross market borrowing at ₹17.2 lakh crore and net market borrowing from dated securities at ₹11.7 lakh crore. The gross figure includes issuance required to refinance maturing debt. The net figure is more directly relevant to the amount of additional financing raised from that channel. The borrowing calendar, maturity profile and market demand determine how the plan affects yields. A single ratio cannot show whether there will be pressure in a particular part of the government bond market. Finance Minister’s Budget 2026–27 speech

Revenue strength and spending quality belong in the same assessment

The Finance Ministry projects gross tax revenue to grow 8% over the 2025–26 revised estimate and revenue receipts to grow 5.7%, against its 10% nominal GDP growth assumption. These are distinct aggregates: gross tax revenue includes amounts before tax devolution, while the Centre’s revenue receipts also include non-tax receipts. A slower rise in receipts can constrain spending even when nominal GDP meets the forecast. For the debt path, follow whether receipts fall short because of weaker economic activity, policy changes, or shifts between tax and non-tax sources. The appropriate response can differ materially across those explanations. Ministry of Finance, fiscal and expenditure estimates

Execution also needs to be assessed when revenue disappoints. Capital projects with multi-year contracts cannot always absorb an abrupt cut without delay costs, while some commitments elsewhere in the Budget are relatively rigid. Setting a contingency plan at the start of the year can protect projects closest to delivering services and postpone projects that have yet to clear design or land approvals. That ordering helps preserve returns to money already spent. It also gives Parliament a clearer basis for evaluating midyear revisions: the issue is which projects change, what is saved, and what service is delayed.

Measure the return from sanction to service

The Budget’s direction deserves support. Its performance should be judged against a public scorecard that follows revised estimates and actual expenditure through project award, delivery and use. Report physical outputs alongside outcomes such as travel time, reliability or private investment in areas served. If delivery is timely and service indicators improve, the case for sustaining capex strengthens. If allocations repeatedly exceed execution or assets remain underused, the next Budget should prioritise resolving delivery constraints and financing the operation of existing assets. The purpose of the extra spending is better economic infrastructure and public services.

excerpt.rendered: The Union Budget raises planned capital spending while narrowing the deficit target. The return depends on execution, how states use the funds and whether completed assets unlock private investment.

title.rendered: Alphabet’s capex guidance is a forecast of spending. Utilisation will determine the return.

content.rendered:
Who pays for the AI buildout? · Part 2 · February earnings guidance

Alphabet told investors in February that it expected 2026 capital expenditure in the range of $175 billion to $185 billion. The range was management guidance. It described expected company-wide capital spending, with technical infrastructure an important part. The size of the number makes it easy to read the announcement as a forecast of new AI output. A better question is how much capacity enters service, how quickly customers use it and at what margin. Alphabet, February 2026 earnings call · Alphabet, fourth-quarter and full-year results

Paying for equipment and earning from it follow separate calendars

Capital expenditure records spending on assets. A facility can be paid for before it is connected to the grid. Servers can be installed before they reach expected utilisation. Once assets are put in use, accounting depreciation spreads their reported cost across estimated useful lives. Cash went out at acquisition, and the lifetime value comes from the stream of capacity sold or used internally. These three clocks explain why a large capital-spending year can produce less immediate revenue than some investors expect.

Take a project with capacity to supply 100 units of computing time per day, fixed operating costs of 600 and a contribution of 10 per unit used. At 80 units of demand its daily operating contribution after fixed costs is 200. At 50 units it loses 100 on the same basis. This is an illustrative operating model, before depreciation and financing. Small differences in utilisation can matter once the system is built and fixed costs are committed.

The alternative to waiting can be expensive too

A cloud provider can underbuild and turn down customers. Lost contracts may send buyers to a rival and weaken demand for other services. Building early gives the firm spare capacity to meet demand and develop products. The cost is idle equipment or a need to lower prices if the market does not grow as expected. Management’s judgement depends on evidence from order books, customer retention and the pace at which earlier capacity filled.

For outside observers, capital spending is more informative alongside cloud revenue, operating margins, backlog definitions and the timing of facility openings. A rising backlog can be valuable if commitments are durable and customers can pay. It needs to be compared with promised delivery dates and cancellation terms. Internal uses should be measured through cost savings or additional revenue, rather than treated as costless demand.

The next capex announcement should therefore be read alongside what happened to earlier assets. More spending is compatible with both strong returns and a more expensive race for scale. Revenue per unit of capacity and a credible schedule for commissioning can help tell those possibilities apart.

Who pays for the AI buildout?
