title.rendered: Japan’s rate rise puts a price on financing Indian assets in yen

content.rendered:
The Bank of Japan’s December increase matters to India even where the investor buying an Indian asset never sends money directly from Tokyo. A position can be funded in yen, hedged in another market and settled in dollars. When Japanese rates rise, the cheapest-looking leg of the trade may become more expensive at the same time that the exchange rate moves. For India, the useful question is how much leverage is sensitive to that combination and where a quick unwind could meet thin liquidity. Bank of Japan, December policy decision · Federal Reserve, 10 December policy decision

What changed in Japan

On 19 December the Bank of Japan directed the overnight call rate towards around 0.75%, effective 22 December, and raised the complementary deposit facility rate to 0.75%. Its statement cited a rising likelihood of sustained wage and price increases consistent with the 2% target. The Federal Reserve, by contrast, lowered its policy target range in December. These moves show how two central banks facing different domestic conditions can shift a funding relationship even when each changes its rate by a modest amount. Bank of Japan, December policy decision · Federal Reserve, 10 December policy decision

The simplest carry position borrows a low-yielding currency and holds a higher-yielding asset elsewhere. The interest differential is one source of return. The price of the funding currency at repayment can dominate it. Japanese policy affects both expectations and the cost of short-dated funding. The direction of the yen also depends on what investors had already priced, so a higher policy rate does not give a mechanical forecast of the exchange rate.

A return that can disappear quickly

Assume an investor borrows the yen equivalent of ₹100 crore for one year at 1% and buys a rupee asset yielding 7%, with no fees, defaults or price movement. At the original exchange rate, the position earns ₹6 crore before costs. If the yen strengthens 6% against the rupee, the amount owed becomes ₹107.06 crore and the asset is worth ₹107 crore. The interest margin is exhausted by the exchange-rate move. If the position is hedged, the result depends on the forward rate, funding terms and basis rather than the change in the spot rate.

Institutional exposures vary. An Indian company with stable yen receipts can match part of its liabilities to them. A fund borrowing short to finance long assets may face repeated collateral calls even when it expects its investment eventually to pay. A foreign insurer can reallocate because domestic Japanese yields have become more attractive without having borrowed any yen at all. These channels have different implications for the speed and durability of outflows.

What to watch from India

The strongest argument for treating the decision as a small event is that markets anticipated much of Japan’s policy normalisation and investors have several funding currencies. The yen also represents just one part of the financing system for Indian assets. That is good reason to test market outcomes before attributing a move in the Nifty or the rupee to Japan. It is also good reason to track short-dated foreign exchange hedging costs and the depth of rupee markets during unsettled sessions.

A broad decline in Indian assets accompanied by yen strength could reflect a common shift in risk appetite. Evidence for a funding channel would be more specific. Look for stress in yen-funded hedges, unusually large changes in futures positioning, reduced turnover where leveraged investors normally trade, and pressure concentrated in positions with little capacity to absorb a quick exit. Comparing those episodes with domestic bond flows and company earnings revisions would help separate forced selling from a change in Indian fundamentals.

One useful comparison is the loss an investor can absorb without selling. A fully funded holder can wait for a hedge to mature. A position supported by a small collateral buffer can run out of cash while its expected terminal return is still positive. India’s aggregate inflow figures will struggle to distinguish the two.

The policy implication is modest and useful. Track funding currency and maturity alongside the nationality of the buyer. An investor’s passport describes where it is domiciled. Its liabilities tell India more about when it might have to sell.

excerpt.rendered: India’s exposure to a stronger yen runs through funding and hedging choices as much as direct borrowing.

title.rendered: Europe’s cash and digital euro proposals serve different kinds of access

content.rendered:
Europe’s financial integration test · Part 3 · December Council negotiating position

In December the Council agreed negotiating positions on the digital euro and on strengthening the role of cash. The pairing is economically important. A public digital instrument can extend the reach of electronic payments. Physical cash gives households a means of paying that needs neither an account at the point of sale nor an active electronic transaction. A credible common payments system should be judged by who can use it in normal conditions and in interruptions. Council of the EU, negotiating position on cash and the digital euro · ECB, October 2025 decision on the digital euro project

Acceptance and access are distinct

A shop may be willing to accept cash even when its customers have trouble withdrawing it. A cash machine may be nearby while essential stores decline the instrument. A digital wallet can be easy to install and hard to use for a person with an older phone or unreliable connectivity. Retail policy needs to measure the route from access to successful payment. Otherwise it can count accounts or physical outlets that fail to serve the intended customer.

Imagine a town of 5,000 residents whose nearest cash withdrawal point moves from a 10-minute walk to a 30-minute round trip by bus. Some people can adapt easily. Others face higher travel costs or rely on someone else to obtain cash. An online payment product could reduce the burden on people able to use it. Reliable physical access remains valuable for the rest and for situations where electronic service is interrupted.

An additional option can preserve competition

The case for cash includes resilience, user choice and the ability to pay without requiring an intermediary for each transaction. Its distribution and handling have real costs. The case for a digital public option includes interoperability and the ability to use a common instrument where payment is already electronic. It also creates costs for connectivity, support and compliance. Policy should compare these costs with who receives the benefits, especially when each instrument serves different users and conditions.

A counterargument is that maintaining multiple methods increases merchant costs. That matters for low-volume businesses. Standardised access and support can make an additional option cheaper, but the public benefit should justify any obligation. Evaluate businesses in rural areas and small urban neighbourhoods separately from large chains. Uptake figures for the overall market can conceal where acceptance is expensive or where losing one method would impose large costs on consumers.

The Council’s December step was a negotiating position. The next test is how final legislation and the pilot translate policy objectives into obligations, costs and accessible services. Measure withdrawal access, payment success and complaints by user group and location. That evidence can show whether the combined approach gives more people a workable choice.

Europe’s financial integration test
Previous · Part 2 · All installments · Next · Part 4

excerpt.rendered: Europe’s Council paired a digital euro negotiating position with measures to strengthen cash. The two instruments provide different services in a payment interruption.

title.rendered: India’s 125-day jobs guarantee will be tested when states run short of funds

content.rendered:
The extra 25 days in India’s proposed rural jobs guarantee are worth having. The more consequential change is who pays for the next day of work after a state exhausts its central allocation. Parliament has now passed the Viksit Bharat Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Bill, which would replace MGNREGA and raise the annual entitlement from 100 to 125 days per rural household. The Bill retains an entitlement to work and an unemployment allowance in specified circumstances. It also changes how the Centre and states finance the programme. Unless the funding rules can respond to a local shock, some of the districts that most need the extra work could face the greatest difficulty providing it. Bill text and financial memorandum · NDTV, 19 December · MGNREGA, section 22

The household’s right and the state’s budget have different limits

Under MGNREGA, the Centre bears the wages for unskilled manual work and up to three-fourths of the material component, which includes the wages of skilled and semi-skilled workers. States bear their share of materials and pay any unemployment allowance due. Under the Bill, the Centre and most states would share programme expenditure within the normative allocation in a 60:40 ratio. The ratio would be 90:10 for the specified north-eastern and Himalayan jurisdictions. The Centre would determine a normative allocation for each state each financial year under rules yet to be prescribed. The state would bear spending above its allocation. The allocation governs who pays. The separate employment entitlement governs what households can claim. MGNREGA, section 22 · Bill text and financial memorandum

Consider a state in the 60:40 group with ₹100 crore of eligible spending within its allocation. It would put up ₹40 crore. If another ₹20 crore of demand comes in and all of it falls above the allocation, the state would pay the full ₹20 crore, raising its total contribution to ₹60 crore. Had that same additional spending qualified for matching funds, the extra state contribution would have been ₹8 crore. The allocation boundary therefore raises the marginal state cost of a rupee of eligible work from 40 paise to one rupee. This simplified example leaves out unemployment allowances and administrative adjustments. The actual amounts depend on the rules and the composition of spending. Bill text and financial memorandum

The Bill’s financial memorandum estimates a nationwide annual requirement of ₹1,51,282 crore for wages, materials and administration, with a central share of about ₹95,692 crore. For comparison, the existing scheme’s Union budget estimate for 2025–26 is ₹86,000 crore. The difference is about ₹9,692 crore in central terms. The two figures have different statuses. One is a nationwide estimate in a legislative memorandum and the other is a budget allocation for the existing scheme. Neither tells us how much money will be available to a particular district in a drought. For that, the allocation formula and the timing of releases matter. Bill text and financial memorandum · Rural Development Ministry’s budget figures

An employment guarantee earns its keep in a bad year

The programme provides insurance because families can ask for work when private incomes fall. A drought can cut days of farm work and increase the number of households seeking public work in the same district. Under the new financing design, the cost of providing additional days can rise sharply just as the state faces other drought-related expenses. A state may still fund the work. It may also postpone project approvals or run out of sanctioned works in the blocks under most pressure. An entitlement that depends on the timing of a supplementary state budget is less valuable to a family that needs income this month. Bill text and financial memorandum

Administrative records cannot show all the work people wanted. The Rural Development Ministry reports 290.60 crore person-days under MGNREGA in FY2024–25 and puts women’s participation at 58.15%. The scale makes implementation at the panchayat level consequential. An offer recorded against a household’s application reveals little about how many days it received, whether the site was reachable or whether it could afford to wait for payment. And if people stop applying after being turned away informally, registered demand can fall while hardship rises. The Bill provides for an allowance where work is unavailable within 15 days under the applicable conditions. A dated receipt for a work request is what lets a worker establish when that clock started. Rural Development Ministry’s FY2024–25 figures · Bill text and financial memorandum

Women and households without land may have fewer options when local work is unavailable. A worker who can travel for seasonal employment can look farther afield. A worker who must stay near home to care for children or older relatives has a narrower choice. In a randomised evaluation of improvements to the public employment programme in Andhra Pradesh, Karthik Muralidharan, Paul Niehaus and Sandip Sukhtankar found gains in private-sector wages and employment that accounted for most of the income gains. That result applies to the reform and labour markets studied. It illustrates why a credible public-work option can affect the terms of private work as well as the incomes of people on a government muster roll. Muralidharan, Niehaus and Sukhtankar, Econometrica

The case for cost sharing is strongest when it improves project selection

A credible argument for state co-financing is that states and panchayats choose much of the work and should face some of its cost. If a project produces little of lasting value, a funding rule that puts nearly all of the wage cost elsewhere can weaken the incentive to choose a better one. The Bill prioritises categories such as water security and resilience to extreme weather. A village that builds and maintains a useful water-harvesting structure gets income support today and a potentially more productive farm economy later. Predictable annual allocations can help panchayats plan those works and buy materials in advance. That case is strongest when transfers reward useful completed assets and well-documented demand. Shifting the full cost to a state at the allocation boundary does little by itself to distinguish good projects from bad ones. Bill text and financial memorandum · Rural Development Ministry’s introduction of the Bill · The Indian Express analysis of the Bill

There is a similar trade-off in the Bill’s requirement that states designate a total of 60 days for peak sowing and harvesting when scheme work will pause. Farmers have a legitimate interest in finding labour when delaying a harvest would destroy value. A calendar that fits one crop or district can still close the public option in another place where work is scarce. It can also weaken workers’ bargaining position during the period when farmers most need them. The Bill provides for geographic differentiation in the notifications. Fine-grained calendars and a usable route to revise them when the rains move would matter more than administrative uniformity. Bill text and financial memorandum · The Indian Express analysis of the Bill

Make the funding rule respond to the same shocks as the guarantee

The Centre could start with an allocation formula that incorporates rural population, poverty and exposure to agricultural shocks, as well as past work. A formula built mainly on historical spending risks rewarding states that already had the staff, project pipeline and payment systems to turn requests into work. It can then give less to states where low spending reflected poor access in the first place. The Bill allows the Centre to consider relaxations on a state’s recommendation in cases of natural calamity and extraordinary circumstances. Published triggers for supplementary financing, linked for example to notified drought and a documented jump in work requests, would give states a clearer basis for preparing projects before their regular allocation runs out. Bill text and financial memorandum

The test is what happens after a bad harvest. Report work requested, offered and actually worked by block and month, along with the time from request to assignment, the time from work to payment and unemployment allowances due and paid. Compare districts with similar weather shocks before and after the change, paying particular attention to states nearing their allocations. Independent household surveys can check for unregistered demand. If work expands in distressed districts and workers are paid promptly without a rise in low-value projects, the case for the new model strengthens. If demand rises while days worked stall at funding boundaries, a higher statutory entitlement will have been undermined by the financing rule.

excerpt.rendered: Parliament has approved a longer rural jobs guarantee. Its value as insurance against bad harvests and weak labour markets depends on whether work can expand when a state exhausts its central allocation.

title.rendered: India’s new cess puts the use of earmarked revenue under scrutiny

content.rendered:
The new Health Security se National Security Cess Act should be judged by two things. The first is whether its capacity-based assessment improves collection. The second is whether the spending it is meant to support can be traced through the budget. The Gazette published the Act on 16 December after assent on 15 December. It provides for commencement by a separate notification. The design initially concerns specified pan masala production and measures liability through machinery or processes. For India’s fiscal federalism, the choice of a cess matters because the Constitution treats specific-purpose cesses differently from taxes in the divisible pool. The Gazette text of the Health Security se National Security Cess Act · Finance ministry explanation of the capacity-based cess · Constitution of India, including Articles 270 and 271

The collection argument is about what the government can observe

A tax on reported output depends on being able to observe production or sales. If they are hard to measure, a tax based on installed machinery and rated capacity can give the authority a different basis for assessment. The finance ministry described a structure linked to machine speed and pack weight, with separate treatment of manual processes. Capacity can be easier to verify than every item sold. It can also be a poor proxy for actual production when firms differ in utilisation. Whether it improves collection depends on how reliably the authority can identify installed capacity, idle equipment and changes in the production process. The Gazette text of the Health Security se National Security Cess Act · Finance ministry explanation of the capacity-based cess

Consider two illustrative producers paying the same ₹10 lakh monthly levy because they have comparable taxable capacity. If one sells 500,000 units and the other 250,000, the levy is equivalent to ₹2 and ₹4 per unit respectively before considering their other costs. Those numbers are assumed and do not describe the Act’s rates. The example shows why a capacity levy can penalise low utilisation while giving a producer little additional tax cost on a further unit within the same category. It may therefore alter decisions about machine size, shifts and how production is organised. That behaviour belongs in any estimate of expected revenue.

The tax-sharing question concerns the denominator

Under Article 270, specified cesses levied for specific purposes are excluded from distribution through the divisible pool. Suppose an illustrative Union tax collection is 100 units, of which ten are outside the pool, and ignore collection costs. At a 41 per cent state share of the remaining 90, aggregate devolution is 36.9 units. If 15 units are outside the pool with the same gross revenue and state share, it is 34.85 units. The arithmetic is hypothetical and does not forecast the new cess’s receipts. It shows why the composition of taxes can affect devolution while the stated sharing percentage is constant. Constitution of India, including Articles 270 and 271

The effect on a state’s ability to finance a service depends on where the money ultimately goes and under what conditions. Union spending may benefit residents in several states, including in ways that are difficult to allocate by place. A transfer through the divisible pool gives states a different degree of discretion from expenditure tied to a specific purpose. The two can both be valuable. A credible comparison should show which services the revenue supports, how it is allocated and whether it finances spending in addition to what was already budgeted. The Gazette text of the Health Security se National Security Cess Act · Constitution of India, including Articles 270 and 271

The strongest case for a dedicated levy

A levy with stated purposes can give legislators and the public a reason to check whether the proceeds support those activities. A capacity assessment can improve enforceability in a sector where reported output is unreliable. That case is strongest when the budget shows collections and related appropriations and when administration can cope with variation across firms. Earmarking can also reduce flexibility or give the appearance of new funding when a department uses dedicated receipts to replace ordinary revenue. A review should compare what changed against a credible spending baseline. The Gazette text of the Health Security se National Security Cess Act · Finance ministry explanation of the capacity-based cess

The economic incidence is not fixed by the name of the taxpayer. Producers can try to pass on costs through prices, absorb them in margins or change the products and volumes they offer. Demand and competition determine how far each is possible. The relationship between the levy and the public-health objective should therefore be assessed with evidence on prices, output and use of the proceeds. The effective tax per unit can vary across producers even under the same machinery rule, which makes the distribution of the burden an empirical question.

The capacity schedule also creates boundaries between production methods. If liability jumps at a given rated speed or pack configuration, a manufacturer can change its investment or product mix even where underlying demand is unchanged. The enforcement agency should report how many establishments are in each band and how that distribution changes after the measure takes effect. A change in the mix may be an ordinary commercial response. It is also a reason to distinguish higher assessed capacity, higher effective tax rates and improved compliance when explaining collections. The Gazette text of the Health Security se National Security Cess Act · Finance ministry explanation of the capacity-based cess

Fiscal transparency also requires a baseline that includes ordinary budget funding for the stated purposes. Suppose a department would have spent 100 units from general resources and now spends the same amount using 20 units of dedicated revenue. Twenty units have a traceable source, while the financed activity has not grown. If expenditure rises to 120 on a comparable basis, there is more evidence of additional funding. This example holds other budget choices constant.

What a transparent first account would show

Report the taxable capacity assessed, collections, administrative costs, disputes and the variation in actual production relative to that capacity. Separately reconcile the amounts collected with budget authorisations and spending on the purposes stated in the law. Report how the composition of Union taxes affects the share of gross collections available for devolution. If collection improves and the financed activities can be identified, the design has a stronger case. If it changes the tax base while the destination and additionality of spending remain obscure, that is where parliamentary scrutiny should focus. The Gazette text of the Health Security se National Security Cess Act · Finance ministry explanation of the capacity-based cess · Constitution of India, including Articles 270 and 271

excerpt.rendered: A capacity-based levy can make revenue easier to assess. Its public-finance case also depends on how spending is authorised and what the levy means for tax sharing.

title.rendered: Ghana’s primary surplus target has an energy-sector test

content.rendered:
The sovereign debt workout · Part 1 · December Ghana review

The IMF completed Ghana’s fifth review under its Extended Credit Facility in December 2025, allowing an immediate disbursement of about $385 million. It said Ghana was on track for a primary surplus of 1.5% of GDP by year-end and highlighted risks from the energy sector and state-owned enterprises. Those points belong together. An improvement in the central budget is more durable when the costs of public services are being paid and reported rather than accumulating elsewhere. IMF, Ghana’s fifth ECF review

The fiscal boundary changes the picture

The primary balance excludes interest payments and helps show whether current policy covers non-interest spending with revenue. A government can improve that balance and still face high debt service from earlier borrowing. It can also appear to save cash while a state utility runs arrears. If the utility eventually needs a transfer or guarantee support, the cost returns to the budget. An account of the wider public sector can capture risks that a narrow measure omits.

Imagine a government makes planned transfers of 100 units to an electricity distributor, while the utility’s approved operations require 120 and its other revenues fall short. If the remaining 20 become arrears to suppliers, the cash budget records 100 today. The public sector has an additional obligation it may have to recognise later. These values are illustrative. The appropriate answer depends on tariff design, service costs, who owes the bill and whether the liability is legally guaranteed.

Follow the suppliers and households

Arrears can force suppliers to borrow, reduce deliveries or increase future contract prices. A tariff increase can improve collections and impose costs on households with little room to absorb them. Targeted support may be easier to budget than a general subsidy if administration can identify eligible users and pay the utility on time. Even with transparent transfers, a company needs an incentive to control losses and improve service. Otherwise the budget may fund a rising cost for the same result.

The argument for prioritising the central primary balance is that it is a clear instrument for showing fiscal adjustment and improving debt dynamics. A credible target can support a restructuring and help lower borrowing costs. It needs complementary reporting on actual payments, contingent liabilities and maintenance backlogs so that progress is visible beyond the narrow measure. Track arrears by age and origin, and reconcile transfers with service delivery.

The next review should show whether Ghana can meet its fiscal commitment while reducing the stock of unpaid obligations and maintaining essential services. Progress on both would make the improvement more durable than a cash result achieved by asking suppliers to wait.

The sovereign debt workout

title.rendered: FIFA’s $60 ticket made the allocation rule more important

content.rendered:
The economics of the 2026 World Cup · Part 2 · December supporter ticket tier

FIFA announced a fixed $60 Supporter Entry Tier in December for fans of qualified teams, available across all 104 World Cup matches, including the final. Availability by match did not mean every supporter could buy at that price. A low price for a scarce seat shifts the allocation question from willingness to pay towards eligibility, the number of places and the method of selecting buyers. Those details determine how much the policy widened access. FIFA, December supporter entry ticket announcement

Price and allocation are joint decisions

An organiser can sell seats at prices that clear the market or reserve a share for a particular group at a lower price. The second choice can allow supporters with smaller budgets to attend. It can also lead to far more requests than seats. A lottery, priority system or association allocation then determines the outcome. Each approach can serve a legitimate objective. Publishing the number of available places and the eligibility rules makes the distribution easier to assess.

Suppose a match has 50,000 seats and 2,000 are sold in a $60 tier, with 20,000 eligible requests for them. If one ticket is requested per person and allocation is random, the illustrative chance is 10%. The price is accessible to each successful applicant and the supply limits the number who benefit. A measure of affordability should record how many people actually obtain seats on those terms, alongside the number of eligible applicants.

A seat is one part of the trip

For a travelling supporter, lodging, transport, meals and the uncertainty of obtaining a ticket can dominate the difference between ticket tiers. A $60 seat gives greater access when fans learn the allocation early enough to book transport and lodging. Awarding it after prices have risen can leave the total trip unaffordable. Local supporters can benefit even when travel is expensive for visitors, so it matters who the scheme was meant to reach.

There is a case for using higher prices elsewhere to finance the discounted tier and the cost of staging matches. Price discrimination can let more people attend without cutting the organiser’s total revenue by the full value of the discount. It can also create opaque pricing or a high effective charge once fees and packages are considered. Disclose the share of seats sold in each category, fees and allocation outcomes by match. That makes it possible to judge whether the scheme broadened access.

The next financial report can explain how ticketing fits into the organiser’s revenue. An access review needs a different measure: who received the affordable seats and whether they could use them. The face value of a ticket is only the most visible part of that answer.

The economics of the 2026 World Cup

excerpt.rendered: A cheaper ticket expands access only when supporters can obtain it and afford the rest of the trip.

title.rendered: Pakistan’s stronger reserves still need a test against payments coming due

content.rendered:
Pakistan’s December IMF reviews have reduced immediate financing pressure. The next test is whether the country can keep reserves growing when external payments are due and temporary support has to be renewed. The IMF Board completed reviews under the Extended Fund Facility and the Resilience and Sustainability Facility on 8 December, allowing access to around $1 billion and $200 million respectively. These funds can buy time for adjustment. The improvement will be more durable if recurring export and transfer receipts can cover a larger share of external payments, and if less of the remaining gap depends on short-term borrowing. IMF Board decision and indicators for Pakistan · IMF December staff report on Pakistan

The stock of reserves improved from a low base

The IMF’s December figures put gross reserves at $14.5 billion at the end of FY2025, up from $9.4 billion the previous year. That is an increase of about $5.1 billion, or 54 per cent on the rounded numbers. The same table puts the current account at a surplus of 0.5 per cent of GDP in FY2025 after a deficit of 0.6 per cent in FY2024. Those improvements predate the December release of funds. They help explain why near-term pressure has eased, while neither statistic establishes that all dollars in the reserve stock are freely available to cover an unexpected outflow. IMF Board decision and indicators for Pakistan

A reserve stock can rise for several reasons. Export and remittance receipts can exceed the amounts the private economy needs. A sovereign can borrow abroad and add the proceeds to reserves. A creditor can extend a deposit that might otherwise have to be repaid. Each can improve the near-term position. The debt created, the rights associated with particular assets and the timing of payments determine how much insurance the increase provides. To assess that insurance, look at usable assets and scheduled gross financing needs, alongside the headline stock and the maturity structure of financing. IMF December staff report on Pakistan

Suppose a country reports $15 billion in gross reserves and expects $6 billion of payments to fall due within a year. If $4 billion is credibly refinanced, the net amount it must find for those maturities is $2 billion. If only $1 billion is renewed, the amount is $5 billion. This stylised example excludes new current-account flows, other payments and valuation effects. The gross reserve number is identical in both cases. The change in rollover conditions alters the buffer that can be used for imports, intervention or other commitments. A reserve target without a refinancing calendar leaves that exposure invisible.

A current-account improvement can arise from different adjustments

A current-account surplus supported by stronger export volumes and resilient remittances gives a different outlook from a surplus driven by suppressed imports. In the second case, demand for intermediate goods and equipment may return when activity recovers, increasing the need for dollars. The IMF reports a primary fiscal surplus of 1.3 per cent of GDP in FY2025 and expects growth to increase from an estimated 3.0 per cent to a projected 3.2 per cent in FY2026. A stronger recovery would be welcome. Assessing its financing requires looking at what that growth imports and whether domestic producers can earn additional foreign exchange. IMF Board decision and indicators for Pakistan · IMF December staff report on Pakistan

The distribution of the adjustment matters. When access to foreign exchange is uncertain, small importers can struggle to finance inputs even where large firms find alternatives. Workers can bear the cost through fewer hours or delayed investment. Depreciation can improve exporters’ competitiveness while raising prices for food, fuel and inputs with little immediate domestic substitute. An external strategy that leans heavily on import compression can stabilise the aggregate in the short run at a cost to the capacity that would help earn dollars later. Sector-level import volumes and export performance are better tests of that trade-off than the headline balance alone.

Why bridge financing can be worth taking

The strongest case for official financing is that a country facing a tight maturity schedule may need time to avoid disorderly cuts and make fiscal and structural adjustments. Paying a maturing creditor on time can protect market access and reduce disruption to ordinary trade. An improvement in the quality of the adjustment is a legitimate return on that time. The risk is that each new disbursement mainly finances earlier obligations while the underlying constraints stay in place. A durable strategy should gradually reduce reliance on repeated temporary sources, even if a period of official funding is necessary to reach it. IMF Board decision and indicators for Pakistan · IMF December staff report on Pakistan

The flood-related food-price pressure identified by the IMF also complicates the immediate policy choice. A rise concentrated in affected crops calls for a different response from a broad deterioration in inflation expectations. Tight demand management can preserve confidence in the currency but may add costs for borrowers facing a real supply loss. The choice should be assessed alongside the response of imports, reserves and domestic credit. That is another reason to follow quantities and payment schedules, rather than reading every change in a reserve stock as a change in underlying capacity. IMF Board decision and indicators for Pakistan

The distinction also matters for evaluating partners. A multilateral loan, a commercial bond and a short bilateral deposit can each support the same gross reserve number. Their costs, conditions and maturity dates can differ materially. Publishing the composition of new liabilities, along with a conservative assessment of which rollovers are already agreed, would help distinguish a broadening source of finance from a concentrated dependency. IMF December staff report on Pakistan

What would make the reserve improvement durable

Track the next twelve months of maturities, actual rollovers, the sources of changes in reserves, export volumes and the cost of access to external funding. Compare import changes across fuel, consumer goods and productive inputs. Stronger exports and continued access to funding at longer maturities would improve the judgement. Repeatedly extending short-term obligations while domestic firms struggle to finance essential inputs would make it less favourable. December’s financing matters because it gives Pakistan room to demonstrate which path it is taking. IMF December staff report on Pakistan

excerpt.rendered: The December IMF reviews unlocked roughly $1.2 billion. The durability of Pakistan’s recovery depends on how much foreign exchange it can generate and retain after meeting its obligations.

title.rendered: A Fed cut cannot do the work of financing India’s external deficit

content.rendered:
India should resist the temptation to treat ₹90 to the dollar as a line the Reserve Bank must defend. On 10 December the Federal Reserve cut its policy rate by 25 basis points, and on 11 December the rupee still hit a record low of 90.4675 before closing at 90.3675. The apparent puzzle becomes easier to understand once India’s current account and its financing are considered together. India has been earning more from services and remittances. At the same time, a sharp swing in portfolio flows has made dollars harder to attract. A Fed cut can help at the margin. Durable relief depends on the returns investors expect to earn in India and on the country’s capacity to finance its import bill through a change in global risk appetite. Federal Reserve policy decision · Reuters, 11 December · RBI’s July–September balance of payments

The rate cut and the return on a rupee investment are different prices

The Fed lowered its target range to 3.50–3.75%. The median participant still put the appropriate rate at 3.4% at the end of 2026, the same as in September. The median is an assessment by policymakers under their individual economic assumptions. Investors can price a different path. US Treasury data show the two-year par yield declining from 3.61% on 9 December to 3.54% on the 10th and 3.52% on the 11th. A smaller decline than the quarter-point cut is unsurprising for an instrument that reflects expected short rates over two years as well as a term premium. The figures are daily observations. Establishing what the announcement itself changed would require intraday prices around the decision and the next Indian trading session. Federal Reserve policy decision · December FOMC projections · US Treasury daily yield data

A simple dollar-return calculation shows the size of the currency exposure. Take a hypothetical one-year rupee investment yielding 6.5% and a dollar alternative yielding 3.6%. At an initial exchange rate of ₹90, an investor converts $1 into ₹90 and ends the year with ₹95.85. If the rupee is then at ₹94, the investment converts back to about $1.020, a dollar return of roughly 2.0% before costs. The break-even exchange rate against the dollar alternative is about ₹92.52. A depreciation of about 2.8% over the year would wipe out the initial yield advantage. A fully hedged investor faces the forward rate and trading costs instead. These are assumed investment yields, and the example excludes taxes, credit losses and any change in the price of the security.

The calculation also shows why different investors respond differently. A foreign equity fund can tolerate an adverse currency move if it expects Indian earnings to grow quickly enough. A fund benchmarked to dollar bonds has less room to do so. An importer with an invoice due next week can buy dollars even if it thinks the rupee will recover next year. These buyers and sellers meet in the same currency market on very different time horizons. A decline in Treasury yields improves one part of their arithmetic. It can be outweighed by weaker expected earnings, the need to hedge a payable or a higher premium for holding India risk.

The current account improved as portfolio financing reversed

The RBI’s preliminary July–September balance of payments puts the current-account deficit at $12.3 billion, or 1.3% of GDP, against $20.8 billion and 2.2% a year earlier. The goods gap narrowed only $1.1 billion. Net services receipts rose $6.4 billion, while personal transfer receipts, chiefly remittances, increased $3.8 billion on a gross basis. Net primary income payments rose $3.0 billion, absorbing part of the improvement. A smaller deficit lowers the net amount India needs from financial flows. How that amount is financed can still change dramatically. RBI’s July–September balance of payments

Net foreign portfolio investment moved from a $19.9 billion inflow to a $5.7 billion outflow, a $25.6 billion swing. That is about three times the $8.5 billion improvement in the current account. Net foreign direct investment improved from a $2.8 billion outflow to a $2.9 billion inflow. Net external commercial borrowing and non-resident deposits also contributed less than a year earlier. The RBI records a $10.9 billion draw on reserves on a balance-of-payments basis, against an $18.6 billion addition in the comparable quarter. That measure strips out valuation changes. It helps show how the financing mix changed, even though it cannot establish which transactions moved the rupee in December. RBI’s July–September balance of payments

The quarter’s figures and the daily market tell us different things. Reuters reported on Thursday that foreign investors had sold nearly $18 billion of Indian stocks so far this calendar year. That figure concerns equities over a different period from the RBI’s quarterly net portfolio number, which covers more than stocks. Nor can either number tell us how much of a given sale was converted to dollars on the day. What the two observations do establish is that the supply of foreign risk capital can vary by much more than the current-account deficit improves. For policy, the maturity and reversibility of financing deserve as much attention as the size of the deficit. Reuters, 11 December · RBI’s July–September balance of payments

Use reserves to preserve a functioning market

There is a respectable case for intervention even if India can absorb a weaker currency. A sharp move can trigger stop orders and cause importers to rush to cover together. Dealers can quote wider spreads or cut the size they are willing to trade, making the cost of a hedge jump well beyond the movement in spot. A manufacturer with dollar debt and mainly rupee receipts can face higher debt-service costs before it can adjust prices. Intervention that restores the ability to trade in size can prevent a temporary liquidity problem from spilling into credit and prices. The IMF’s November assessment also favours flexibility with intervention to address disorderly conditions. IMF’s India Article IV assessment

A standing defence of a round number has different incentives. If importers and borrowers come to expect that the RBI will supply dollars at a particular level, hedging looks less urgent until the commitment is tested. Spot sales use reserves and absorb rupee liquidity unless offset. A persistent change in the price foreign investors require for holding Indian assets will then force a choice between larger sales and allowing the exchange rate to adjust. The same movement has uneven effects. For an importer with an unhedged $10 million bill, a move from ₹90 to ₹94 adds ₹4 crore to the cost. A dollar-earning exporter with mostly domestic inputs receives the opposite translation benefit. An exporter with imported components, hedges or a contract that allows the buyer to demand lower prices retains less of that gain.

India has room to make that distinction. The RBI put reserves at $686.2 billion on 28 November, equivalent to more than 11 months of imports. A buffer of that size can buy time through a reversal in flows. Its adequacy under stress also depends on debt repayments, usable dollar liquidity and the central bank’s forward commitments. A weekly fall in the dollar value of the reserve stock can reflect valuation changes as well as transactions. For this reason the useful checks are the RBI’s spot and forward disclosures, the balance-of-payments measure of reserve changes and the maturity of external liabilities. That combination gives a better reading of pressure than either the spot exchange rate or the headline reserve stock alone. RBI Governor’s December statement · RBI’s July–September balance of payments

Evidence of disorder would be wider bid–ask spreads, less size available at quoted prices, or a persistent gap between comparable offshore and onshore prices after allowing for different contract terms. That would strengthen the case for temporary RBI action. A sustained widening of the current-account deficit or a broad decline in direct investment, debt inflows and portfolio flows would call for a reassessment of India’s external funding needs. If trading remains orderly and the weakness is concentrated in foreign equity flows, a flexible rupee can carry part of the adjustment while services and other receipts continue to earn dollars. The practical test of exchange-rate policy is whether firms can buy and hedge foreign currency at workable prices through a shock. RBI’s July–September balance of payments · IMF’s India Article IV assessment

excerpt.rendered: The Federal Reserve eased and the rupee still set a record low. India’s balance of payments shows why a smaller current-account deficit can coexist with more pressure on the currency.

title.rendered: India’s AI copyright proposal makes the royalty formula the central bargain

content.rendered:
A single licence for training AI could solve a real coordination problem. A model developer may draw on works owned by thousands of publishers, writers and other creators. Clearing each work individually favours firms that can afford lawyers, existing data contracts and years of delay. A central licence lowers that barrier. India’s proposal then faces a harder question. Which developer owes a payment, on what revenue, and which creators get it? Those decisions will determine whether the scheme opens the market or builds a new advantage for incumbents. DPIIT, working paper on generative AI and copyright · PIB, publication of the working paper

A proposal to separate training from payment

DPIIT’s December working paper examines several ways to treat copyrighted works used for generative AI training. Its committee proposes a blanket licence for training on lawfully accessed content, a royalty due when tools are commercialised and a central mechanism to collect and distribute payments. It proposes that rates be determined through an appointed committee, with judicial review available. These are consultation recommendations. Product budgets can model the proposal as a possible future liability while current rights and contracts continue to govern their choices. DPIIT, working paper on generative AI and copyright · PIB, publication of the working paper

The timing feature matters. Upfront per-work fees consume cash before a developer knows whether a model will work or find customers. Payment on commercialisation shifts some financing risk away from the entrant. Creators then bear the risk that the use earns little. In a market with a high rate of failed experiments, that is a meaningful transfer. Its legitimacy depends on whether successful products deliver a sufficiently predictable return to the pool.

Why the base matters more than the headline rate

Suppose an illustrative company earns ₹2 crore a year directly from a model API. At an assumed 1% rate on that revenue, it pays ₹2 lakh. Another company offers an equivalent model inside an office subscription earning ₹20 crore. A 1% royalty on the whole subscription is ₹20 lakh. A formula attributing just 10% of the bundle revenue to the model yields the same ₹2 lakh as the first firm. The rate is identical throughout. The accounting definition determines whether the rule treats economically similar uses alike.

A rate based on a narrow, observable sales line is easy to administer where the model is a standalone product. It creates an advantage for a company with a bundle, advertising business or related-party transfer if the model has no separate price. A rate covering all corporate revenue would charge unrelated activity. Defined allocation rules, consolidated reporting where appropriate and small-firm safe harbours could address those problems. Any exception should have a test for businesses that grow past it, since a sharp payment cliff can discourage honest reporting or expansion.

Paying creators when attribution is noisy

Allocation among rights holders has a different measurement problem. Counting files or tokens could reward duplication and favour the most easily scraped categories. Using current popularity as the sole weight could leave work in a regional language, small research press or specialist archive with a tiny share despite its scarcity. A developer can supply corpus-level information without producing a reliable estimate of any one work’s contribution to model performance. Sampling and category-level distributions may be practicable. They are still policy choices about whose claims the pool can recognise.

The best argument for voluntary agreements is that licences can be tailored. A publisher with a specialised archive can set terms for access, attribution and updates. A blanket arrangement should make routine clearance cheaper while preserving a workable market for higher-value services such as curated data and timely access. Evidence to watch includes the fee and time required to launch a small commercial model, the share of proceeds reaching smaller rightsholders and whether commercial bundles bear a comparable burden to standalone products. A transparent distribution methodology will matter as much as the number of works the mechanism says it covers.

The proposal is most promising as a way to reduce bargaining costs. Its wider distributional claim needs a royalty base that survives bundling and a payout formula that creators can understand and challenge.

excerpt.rendered: A blanket training licence could reduce entry costs. The way royalties are measured and shared would determine who actually benefits.

title.rendered: The World Cup draw gave host cities very different events to plan for

content.rendered:
The economics of the 2026 World Cup · Part 1 · December 2025 final draw

The World Cup’s December 2025 draw and the schedule released the next day gave supporters their first detailed itinerary across the three host countries. The expanded competition had 48 teams and 104 matches. For a host city, counting matches was only the start. The teams playing, the schedule and the location of connecting fixtures shaped travel demand and determined which parts of the city would have to absorb it. FIFA, December 2025 match schedule · FIFA, final draw procedures

Demand has a date, a route and a location

A match attended largely by people who live nearby may generate high stadium demand and relatively little hotel use. A fixture attracting a large group of visitors can fill rooms, flights and trains. Several games close together can keep visitors in the city longer or create sharp peaks in staffing and transit demand. A match scheduled between two distant fixtures can produce more short trips and higher travel costs for the fans who follow one team.

For illustration, take two fixtures of 50,000 spectators each. At the first, 15,000 visitors stay two nights with two people to a room, requiring roughly 15,000 room-nights. At the second, 6,000 visitors stay one night at the same occupancy, requiring 3,000. Attendance is identical and the hotel demand differs fivefold. The example leaves out spectators staying with friends, travelling onward and other visitors who could be displaced.

Infrastructure pays when it solves a recurring problem

Organisers need transit, staff and public facilities for a short surge. A permanent improvement can be valuable where it also serves normal commuters and events. The same construction can offer weak value if demand disappears after the tournament. Temporary services, changes in frequency and walking routes can be more adaptable. The right choice depends on what the city expects to use after the last fixture.

A strong argument for committing early is that cities compete for resources and need time to prepare. Delaying every decision until demand is clear can produce expensive last-minute arrangements. Allocate irreversible capital to projects justified across a range of scenarios. Keep staffing and temporary transport flexible where the fixture mix is the key uncertainty. That allows preparation to continue without treating every match as an identical economic event.

The useful data after the draw are booking patterns, ticket take-up by buyer location and expected transport loads by hour. The next questions are which supporters can afford to attend and how lower-priced seats are distributed. Both help determine whether the schedule’s potential demand turns into actual visits and a manageable bill for each host city.

The economics of the 2026 World Cup
All installments · Next · Part 2

excerpt.rendered: The fixture schedule determines where and when fans arrive. A match count is an incomplete measure of demand and hosting cost.

title.rendered: Europe’s capital-market proposals have to reduce the cost of crossing a border

content.rendered:
Europe’s financial integration test · Part 2 · December market integration package

The European Commission’s 4 December market integration and supervision package proposed changes to the rules and oversight of capital markets. Its economic ambition is to reduce fragmentation in a region with a common currency in much of the bloc and national markets that still differ in important respects. Integration would be valuable if investors can reach more issuers, and if smaller issuers can seek capital across borders without rebuilding the legal and operational process for each market. European Commission, market integration and supervision package

Fixed costs decide who can issue

A company issuing securities pays for documentation, advisers, distribution and ongoing compliance. Some costs are fixed. A large issuer can spread them over a bigger amount and may already have staff in several markets. The fixed cost per euro raised is higher for a smaller business. The same principle affects a fund manager deciding whether to serve a second country. A genuinely common process is valuable where it removes repeated work and predictable delays.

Assume an issuer wants to raise €20 million across three markets. Suppose fixed cross-border costs fall from €600,000 to €300,000, while pricing and other terms stay the same. The one-time cost falls from 3% to 1.5% of proceeds. On a €200 million issue the same absolute saving is 0.15% of proceeds. These are invented costs. The distributional effect explains why the size of firms that begin issuing is a better test than an aggregate dominated by large companies.

Common oversight can change both costs and incentives

A more consistent supervisory approach can make it easier to know which rules apply and how they will be enforced. Centralising work may also create distance from local market practices and require new capacity at EU level. The relevant comparison is the cost of the whole process, including response times, operational failures and any duplicated national requirements. Formal harmonisation can leave similar work at several levels if responsibilities remain unclear. European Commission, market integration and supervision package · ECB, preparation phase closing report

A strong case for retaining national flexibility is that markets differ in their legal traditions and the intermediaries that support them. Uniform rules can impose avoidable costs on small local issuers if designed around large cross-border firms. Proportional requirements and a clear cross-border path can preserve local access while making expansion easier. Evidence would include issuance costs, distribution across member states and whether the average new issuer is smaller than before.

The market package and the digital euro address different layers of financial integration. One concerns trading, issuance and oversight. The other concerns payment access. They share a useful test: whether a cross-border user can complete an ordinary task with less duplicated work and predictable standards. Report those outcomes once measures are adopted and implemented.

Europe’s financial integration test
Previous · Part 1 · All installments · Next · Part 3

excerpt.rendered: The EU package aims to reduce fragmentation in trading and supervision. Cross-border financing gets cheaper when firms can remove recurring duplicative costs.

title.rendered: The RBI has cut the repo rate. The real test is who gets cheaper credit.

content.rendered:
The Reserve Bank of India was right to cut its repo rate by a quarter point to 5.25% today. With the inflation outlook revised down, keeping the nominal rate fixed would have made policy tighter in real terms. But the case for the next cut should turn partly on what happens to the credit already in the system. A homebuyer with a repo-linked loan can see a change at the next reset. A factory with an expensive overdraft and too little collateral may see none. The RBI’s announced bond purchases and dollar swap can help lower banks’ funding costs. The test is whether those savings reach firms and households whose spending actually depends on the price and availability of credit. RBI December MPC resolution · RBI Governor’s December statement

A strong GDP print can coexist with a case for easing

The latest official estimate puts real GDP growth at 8.2% in July–September, up from 5.6% a year earlier. That is a year-on-year reading for a quarter already over. The RBI projects growth of 7.0% in October–December and 6.5% in January–March, while raising its full-year projection from 6.8% to 7.3%. Stronger activity gives the MPC a reason to move carefully. It also matters how long recent supports to demand last, including changes to income tax and GST and the front-loading of public capital spending. A strong quarter offers little guidance about what borrowing costs will do to the next investment decision without a view on inflation and future demand. MoSPI’s July–September GDP release · RBI October MPC resolution · RBI December MPC resolution

The October meeting put inflation in April–June 2026 at 4.5%. Today’s forecast for that same quarter is 3.9%. Subtracting each forecast from the repo rate at the time gives a simple comparison. In October the gap was 5.50 minus 4.50, or 1.00 percentage point. Keeping the rate at 5.50 with the new forecast would have raised it to 1.60 points. After the cut it is still 1.35 points. This comparison holds the forecast quarter fixed and abstracts from bank spreads and the level of the neutral real rate. It shows why a lower nominal rate can coexist with a more restrictive inflation-adjusted setting on this measure. RBI October MPC resolution · RBI December MPC resolution

The strongest case for holding in December was that low food inflation could reverse while the impact of earlier easing was still working through the economy. The RBI itself projects headline inflation returning to 4.0% in July–September 2026. A weak rupee could raise input costs, and persistent increases in a wider set of domestic prices would make a cut harder to justify. The quarter-point move, with the MPC retaining its neutral stance, leaves room to respond to those risks. A commitment to further easing would require more evidence than the current inflation trough. RBI December MPC resolution

The same cut reaches borrowers on different schedules

The policy rate sets a reference price for very short-term rupee funds. For a loan linked directly to the repo, a cut normally feeds into the benchmark at the contractual reset. The RBI’s external benchmarking rules require at least quarterly resets and allow benchmarks other than the repo. Loans tied to a bank’s marginal cost of funds can respond more slowly, depending on the funding benchmark and the loan’s reset date. A fixed-rate loan generally leaves the borrower’s payment unchanged unless the borrower refinances. Even two borrowers at the same bank with identical balances can therefore have different cash-flow responses to the same policy decision. RBI external benchmark circular · RBI directions on interest rates on advances

For scale, take a ₹50 lakh mortgage with 20 years left, a monthly instalment, and an interest rate of 8.50%. If the rate falls immediately to 8.25% and the maturity stays fixed, the standard amortisation calculation gives an instalment of roughly ₹42,603, down from ₹43,391. The saving is about ₹788 a month. A bank that holds the instalment fixed could pass the benefit through a shorter repayment period instead. For a small firm continuously drawing ₹1 crore on a floating-rate credit line, full pass-through saves ₹25,000 in annual interest at that balance. For a firm unable to draw more against its receivables, the credit limit can be worth far more than that rate reduction.

The evidence so far points to uneven pass-through. The Governor reports that the earlier 100 basis points of repo cuts were accompanied by a 69 basis point decline in average rates on fresh rupee bank loans and 63 basis points on outstanding loans from February through October. Holding the composition of fresh borrowing fixed at January weights puts the rate effect at 78 basis points. The November data release also shows the fresh lending rate rising from 8.50% to 8.64% between September and October even as the outstanding rate edged lower. A change in who borrows and what they borrow for can move the average in either direction. Loan pricing for comparable borrowers is a better test than an aggregate monthly rate alone. RBI Governor’s December statement · RBI’s November bank rate release

Liquidity can help transmission without solving credit risk

The RBI announced ₹1 lakh crore in government bond purchases and a three-year, $5 billion dollar–rupee buy/sell swap. Buying bonds credits rupee reserves to the banking system. At the swap’s spot leg the RBI buys dollars from banks and pays rupees, with the reverse exchange agreed for maturity. At ₹90 to the dollar, full allotment would supply roughly ₹45,000 crore at the spot leg. That puts the two measures at roughly ₹1.45 lakh crore of gross potential rupee liquidity, before offsetting flows. Actual lending will depend on how banks and borrowers respond. The swap reverses at maturity. The package was announced this morning, so the amounts describe the proposed operations. RBI Governor’s December statement · The Indian Express, December 5 morning coverage

The banking system averaged a liquidity surplus of ₹1.5 lakh crore since the October meeting, according to the Governor. That makes an immediate shortage a weak explanation for the move. The more plausible purpose is to keep enough liquidity available through changes in cash demand, government balances or foreign-exchange operations. A spot dollar sale by the RBI, for instance, takes rupees out of the system. Durable liquidity can limit upward pressure on money-market rates and ease competition for marginal funding. It leaves intact the need for borrowers with viable projects, adequate capital at their lenders, and credit assessment that distinguishes cash-flow problems from insolvency. RBI Governor’s December statement

There is a distributional cost to cheaper funding. From February through October, fresh term-deposit rates fell 105 basis points while rates on outstanding deposits declined 32 basis points. A household renewing a deposit can lose interest income even as a borrower with a floating mortgage gains disposable income. Banks that reprice loans quickly while still paying older deposit rates can face a squeeze on margins. They can respond by limiting discounts or holding tighter lending standards for riskier firms. These margins matter for the spending effect of the cut because the borrowers most likely to use additional cash are often the ones with least room to borrow. RBI Governor’s December statement

What should determine the next move

Over the next several months, watch the overnight call rate relative to the repo, loan rates for comparable borrowers around reset dates, and credit limits and utilisation among smaller firms. Faster resets on secured retail loans would show that the price signal is getting through there. A sustained easing of funding costs alongside stable spreads and more credit to viable small firms would be stronger evidence of a wider effect. If secured borrowers get relief but credit conditions elsewhere barely move, the binding constraint may be collateral, perceived risk or weak investment demand. A further general cut would then have a limited payoff. Conversely, a broad deterioration in activity alongside contained underlying inflation would strengthen the case for easing again. The December decision buys time to learn which of those conditions India is actually facing.

excerpt.rendered: The RBI’s cut to 5.25% is defensible even with strong GDP growth. Whether it changes spending and investment depends on loan resets, deposit costs and which borrowers can actually get credit.

title.rendered: A late crop insurance payment can miss Maharashtra’s next sowing decision

content.rendered:
A crop insurance payment does its most urgent work when it lets a farmer buy seed, rent a pump or avoid selling an asset before the next planting window closes. Maharashtra’s district-wise claims table, released on 2 December, tells us how much was paid and how much remained pending across several crop years. It gives a useful accounting baseline. To measure whether insurance protected production, Maharashtra should add the time between loss, assessment and payment, and show how often the money arrived before the next major cash expense. Parliamentary reply, Maharashtra crop insurance · PMFBY, revised operational guidelines

What the district ledger can tell us

The figures combine applications and claims under the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana and the Restructured Weather Based Crop Insurance Scheme from 2020–21 to 2024–25, as at 31 October 2025. The table records ₹1,802.91 crore paid and ₹7.11 crore pending in Beed, and ₹603.13 crore paid and ₹18.90 crore pending in Amravati. Those balances differ in both level and proportion. They cover different crops, seasons and events. Applications can also recur across seasons. Dividing pending claims by paid plus pending claims describes the open balance in that table and supplies little evidence on the frequency or duration of late payment. Parliamentary reply, Maharashtra crop insurance

The release also reports resolution of grievances recorded through a dedicated portal and helpline. Administrative closure is a distinct outcome from a transfer arriving on time. A well-handled complaint can establish that a claim was ineligible. A late transfer can settle a complaint without reversing the interest a household already paid to fund planting. Both closure and remedy matter, and the distinction should be visible in public reporting. Parliamentary reply, Maharashtra crop insurance

The liquidity value of timeliness

Suppose a farmer expects ₹30,000 after a covered loss and needs that sum to fund a new crop. A three-month bridge loan at 24% simple annual interest costs ₹1,800. If credit is available and the farmer can plant on schedule, that is the immediate financial cost of delay in the example. If the farmer cannot borrow, the relevant loss could be the margin on a crop that was never sown or the difference between a planned and a cheaper crop. The effect depends on the household’s cash buffer, land and access to formal credit. A state-wide total collapses those differences.

Agricultural insurance also changes what farmers can finance before any claim. A credible promise to pay after a drought can make a lender more comfortable financing inputs. A history of uncertain timing weakens that benefit. Farmers may purchase less coverage or use more expensive credit even in seasons with normal rainfall. Reliability is therefore a part of the product’s price as experienced by a household.

Pay sooner without sacrificing verification

The strongest objection to pushing for speed is that a district-wide loss is hard to assess. Faster payments can invite error or costly disputes if crop, location and loss records disagree. Timeliness and accuracy can be addressed separately at several stages. A published timeline can start when insurers receive verified yield data. A separate clock can cover the government’s time to deliver that data. Where rules permit interim payment on unambiguous events, a portion can be released while more complex claims are resolved. Audits should compare error and recovery costs across claims handled at different speeds.

A useful deadline will vary across seasons and places. Comparing payment dates with the local planting calendar avoids rewarding a transfer that arrives quickly in administrative terms but too late in agricultural terms. For households with several crops, the first major input purchase after a loss may be more relevant than the next official season opening.

A district dashboard could report median and upper-tail delays by crop and season, the value paid before the next sowing window and the share of open cases awaiting a named party. It should count outstanding cases in delay statistics so that long delays do not disappear when a season closes. Surveys could compare borrowing and planted acreage among otherwise similar farmers receiving earlier and later payouts. If those outcomes are insensitive to timing, the case for investing in faster settlement is weaker. If farmers plant sooner or borrow less at punitive rates, speed is a measurable gain from insurance itself.

excerpt.rendered: District payout totals measure money transferred. The policy’s value also depends on when a household can spend it on the next crop.

title.rendered: Import receipts masked the early fall in domestic GST revenue

content.rendered:
India’s November GST release, published on 1 December, records a modest increase in overall gross collections after the September rate changes. The increase came from imports. Domestic gross receipts fell by nearly ₹3,000 crore from a year earlier while gross import GST rose by about ₹4,240 crore. That split matters because the reform was meant to change domestic prices and spending. A healthy total can reassure a finance ministry about immediate cash receipts. It offers considerably less evidence about whether lower rates stimulated domestic consumption or paid for themselves. November GSTN tables, mirrored · Reuters report, 1 December.

What the receipts actually show

Total gross GST rose from ₹1,69,016 crore in November 2024 to ₹1,70,276 crore in November 2025, an increase of ₹1,260 crore, or 0.7%. Gross domestic GST fell from ₹1,27,281 crore to ₹1,24,300 crore, a decrease of ₹2,981 crore or 2.3%. Gross import GST rose from ₹41,736 crore to ₹45,976 crore, an increase of ₹4,240 crore or 10.2%. The changes in the two rounded components sum to ₹1,259 crore, one crore below the change in the published total. On the November 2024 gross total as a common denominator, domestic receipts contributed roughly minus 1.8 percentage points and imports contributed plus 2.5 points.

The net figures tell a similar story. After refunds, aggregate GST increased from ₹1,50,062 crore to ₹1,52,079 crore, or 1.3%. Net domestic receipts fell from ₹1,17,345 crore to ₹1,15,558 crore, or 1.5%. The published net import and export component increased from ₹32,717 crore to ₹36,521 crore. The distinction matters because the timing of refunds affects cash collected in any one month. An increase in net receipts can reflect more gross revenue, fewer refunds paid that month, or both. Compensation cess is shown separately in the GSTN tables and is excluded from these headline totals. GSTN tables, including the refund and cess rows.

What a lower rate must do to preserve revenue

Most of the September rate changes became effective on 22 September. The official FAQ lists exceptions and explains how the time of supply determines which rate applies when invoices or payments straddle the change. Returns, imports and refunds move on different schedules, so a monthly collections release brings together liabilities generated at different times. November gives a fuller reading after implementation, but the published domestic total does not assign a clean treatment date to each underlying sale. GST Council effective-date FAQ.

Consider an illustrative item moved from 18% GST to 12%. Assume the tax-exclusive price is ₹100 and the entire change is passed through to the buyer. The invoice falls from ₹118 to ₹112, about 5.1%. Tax per unit falls from ₹18 to ₹12. Sales volume would have to rise by 50% for that item to generate the same tax before adjustments for credits, refunds or enforcement. With the same quantity and a tax-inclusive price held at ₹118, the tax-exclusive price rises to about ₹105.36 and the tax per unit is about ₹12.64. That example explains both why buyers can receive different shares of a cut and why stronger demand need not quickly replace the revenue lost on a specific item.

The actual reform changed different rates in different directions. Some transactions may move from informal to registered sellers. Changes in input rates can affect credits and margins, especially when the rate on inputs differs from the rate on output. The aggregate revenue test therefore has to account for the product mix and for changes in compliance. An increase in invoice volume could accompany a lower average tax rate and a lower domestic cash take. A producer or retailer can also expand its margin while still reducing the price charged to consumers. Invoice prices and sales quantities carry information that the total collections figure leaves out. GST Council recommendations.

Who gets the savings, and which governments carry the risk?

Households benefit when a lower statutory rate reaches the price they pay. The rupee gains depend on their purchases. A family spending relatively more on items whose rates fall can save more as a share of its budget than another family with the same income. Sellers benefit when part of the reduction is retained or demand increases enough to improve sales and margins. Competition, the visibility of prices and the cost of changing posted prices all influence that split. A collection series cannot establish the incidence because it combines quantities, prices and rates.

An import GST increase also needs its own explanation. Receipts at the border can rise because the tax base rose in rupee terms, more goods arrived, the mix moved towards higher-tax categories or customs valuation changed. Some tax paid at import can later be claimed as input credit subject to eligibility. Gross import receipts therefore do not measure the final tax on households and do not replace a study of domestic sales. State budgets face a related problem. A state’s reported pre-settlement collections and the receipts it receives after IGST settlement are different numbers. A comparison of fiscal effects should use the settlement basis consistently and distinguish a cash timing change from a durable change in the tax base. GSTN state and settlement tables.

A simple decomposition also points to where policy teams should look for a fiscal surprise. Compute gross domestic receipts per rupee of reported taxable sales for a consistent set of products. If the ratio falls while taxable sales rise, a lower effective rate and a wider base can be observed together. If both fall, examine invoice counts, nominal prices and quantities before interpreting the change. Build a parallel import series using the exchange rate and customs values. This would make it easier to distinguish a domestic demand response from an import contribution that could reverse the following month. For state budget planning, that distinction matters more than a small change in the national headline.

Published totals also say little about which firms experienced a cash-flow improvement. A retailer carrying inventory acquired before a rate cut may reprice it immediately while waiting for credits or clearing old stock. Another seller may need to update its invoices, reconcile returns and adjust contracts at the same time. Those short-run costs can matter more for a small firm with a thin cash cushion. An assessment that combines tax filings with actual shelf prices and credit delays would make the adjustment visible alongside the government’s receipts.

What would establish whether the reform worked

The strongest favourable interpretation is that domestic receipts held up reasonably well given the lower rates, as retailers passed on savings and households brought purchases forward or increased their volumes. That is plausible. The strongest caution is that November combines different filing periods, festival timing, nominal prices and product composition. A small decline in domestic receipts is consistent with a successful tax cut that costs revenue, a weak increase in demand, or a temporary shift in purchase timing. A single monthly total cannot choose among them.

The next useful test would compare matched products whose rates changed with comparable products whose rates did not change, across several months before and after September. Record tax-inclusive prices, quantities, discounts and any changes in package sizes. Compare the same holiday windows across years, and use an event study only where pre-reform trends are sufficiently similar. On revenue, show domestic and import receipts separately, reconcile refunds and compare state results after settlement. Evidence of sustained lower prices and higher volumes in the affected products would strengthen the case that the relief reached consumers. Until then, November’s figures establish a narrower conclusion. Import receipts covered the fall in domestic gross collections. The consumer and fiscal effects of the reform require separate tests.

excerpt.rendered: November collections rose overall as import GST offset a fall in domestic receipts. Assessing the September reform requires separate evidence on consumer prices, volumes, refunds and state settlements.

title.rendered: India’s labour codes will succeed if formal jobs become easier to offer and safer to take

content.rendered:
India brought four labour codes into effect on 21 November, consolidating 29 central laws. The package covers wages, industrial relations, social security, and occupational safety and working conditions.
