A supplier that receives fewer bookings can cut overtime and subcontracting before changing headcount. A supplier that accepts a lower dollar price may still need to pay for materials and labour weeks before it receives payment. Smaller suppliers dependent on a few US customers can have a cash-flow problem even when the larger buyer has little trouble financing the customs bill. Reuters reporting on affected industries.

This distinction should shape any Indian policy response. A temporary credit guarantee can help a viable exporter bridge a delay in payment or finance the work of qualifying for a new customer. Its value falls if the product has become uncompetitive at every price that covers production costs. Broad interest relief in that case can preserve capacity that has little demand, while shifting credit losses to the public balance sheet. Support should be judged by orders retained at viable prices, buyer diversification and repayment performance. Loan disbursals measure how much support went out. They tell us little about the sales that support preserved.

How to tell a temporary disruption from a lost market

The strongest argument for a modest long-run hit is that global supply chains are expensive to change. A buyer may have paid for audits, tooling and product development in India. Alternative factories can be booked up, and rushing a switch can generate defects, late deliveries or penalties. Those costs give Indian suppliers room to share the duty with buyers in the short run. They also give both parties an incentive to delay a decision if they think the tariff will be reversed soon. The same buyer may nevertheless start qualifying a second supplier immediately. That decision matters even if the next shipment still comes from India.

An early test is to compare US import quantities and customs unit values for narrowly defined products from India and competing suppliers, with their pre-August seasonal patterns and product-specific treatment as benchmarks. Where possible, compare the same Indian products in other destinations and separate shipments that qualified for the transit window. A fall in Indian dollar unit values alongside resilient volumes would be consistent with exporters absorbing part of the surcharge, although shifts towards cheaper variants can produce the same pattern. Sustained volume losses alongside gains from rival suppliers would point more strongly to substitution. Purchase orders and supplier qualification data could distinguish those explanations sooner than annual export totals.

The first priority for India is to find out which exporters need time to ride out a disruption and which need new buyers. The same tariff can create both problems in the same town. A policy built around the headline rate will miss the difference. A policy built around product-level exposure, repeat orders and viable margins has a better chance of preserving employment where support can make a difference.

excerpt.rendered: The United States has added a 25% duty over India’s purchases of Russian oil. For exposed Indian suppliers, the harder question is how much price, margin and market share they can give up to keep an American customer.

title.rendered: What America’s first tariff schedule meant for Indian exporters

content.rendered:
The White House’s April tariff order raises the expected cost of selling covered Indian goods in the United States. It also changes India’s position against rival suppliers. The US annex available on 3 April lists a 26% additional rate for India, 37% for Bangladesh and 46% for Vietnam. India’s Commerce Department initially cited 27% in its statement. The examples here use the US annex and treat the difference as a reason to check the applicable customs instrument before pricing an order. The economic question is whether India can gain orders from more heavily taxed suppliers fast enough to offset the rise in its own cost of access. US tariff schedule · India’s initial statement · Reuters on the announcement.

An announced rate is only part of a customs bill

The executive order schedules a 10% baseline additional duty from 5 April and country-specific rates for Annex I partners from 9 April, subject to its exceptions and transition provisions. The higher India figure is the scheduled country rate under this order. It should not be added on top of the 10% baseline. Existing duties generally remain relevant. The order also specifies exclusions, including Annex II products and articles already subject to named Section 232 measures. Pharmaceuticals, semiconductors and energy products are among the categories referenced in the Annex II provision. Exporters should compare their specific product line and terms of entry. A headline country rate is too broad to price a pharmaceutical shipment and a garment order with the same assumptions. Executive Order 14257 and annexes.

For a shipment already en route, the order sets transit provisions tied to the point at which goods were loaded and in transit on their final mode before the relevant cutoff. For an order still being negotiated, the first questions are who imports the product, who has contractually agreed to bear any duty and how quickly a customer can qualify a substitute. The customs invoice and the economic burden are different objects. An importer can pay at the border and recover some of the cost from an exporter through a lower price on the next order or from customers through a higher shelf price.

A relative advantage can coexist with weaker demand

Suppose a US importer can buy the same eligible product from India, Bangladesh or Vietnam at a customs value of $100. Hold freight and all other duties equal and exclude them from the example. At the scheduled country rates, the post-duty amounts would be $126, $137 and $146. India would be about 8% cheaper than Bangladesh and about 14% cheaper than Vietnam on that narrow comparison. Yet the Indian shipment would itself cost $26 more than before this new duty, holding the other terms fixed. The importer can therefore have two incentives at once. It may shift a larger share of its sourcing towards India while buying fewer units in total. Annex I country rates.

The ranking changes with factory prices. If a Bangladesh supplier can deliver the same specification at a $92 customs value, the $137 in the example becomes $126.04. Almost all of India’s tariff advantage has disappeared before a buyer considers lead times, defect rates or the cost of carrying inventory. An existing vendor can also improve terms temporarily to keep the order. A purchasing manager will look at the entire cost of replacing a supplier, including audits and the reliability of the first deliveries. This favours Indian factories that already have buyer approval and room to increase production. A small firm without established relationships may find the same tariff differential much harder to turn into revenue.

Tariffs can also redirect output. Factories losing American orders can offer more goods in India’s other export markets or to Indian buyers. That could benefit Indian firms purchasing cheaper intermediate goods, while increasing competition for producers selling similar goods. An assessment of India’s gain should therefore track sales to the United States, third-country markets and domestic purchasers. An increase in one destination can partly replace a sale that was lost elsewhere. The change in total production and in margins is more informative than the change in destination alone.

What the US formula measures

The US Trade Representative’s calculation uses bilateral US goods deficits and imports, together with assumptions about import price responsiveness and tariff pass-through. The document describes the tariff change that would close a bilateral goods imbalance under its simplified assumptions, including small offsetting exchange-rate and general-equilibrium effects. That exercise differs from calculating actual foreign tariffs or matching the tariff that another country charges on a particular product. A country can sell more goods to the United States than it buys because of its role in a supply chain, demand patterns or specialization. The aggregate imbalance supplies very little information about which specific Indian rules prevent US firms from selling there. USTR methodology.

The strongest case for the schedule is that market access is valuable enough to bring trading partners to the table. India and the United States are already negotiating a bilateral agreement. Targeted commitments on clearance times, testing or rules of origin could reduce real trading costs if they address documented problems. The test is whether concessions lower the delivered cost of actual shipments. The headline tariff can provide bargaining pressure. An agreement that leaves a supplier unable to qualify or a buyer unable to claim a preference may change much less than its headline implies. India Commerce Department statement on negotiations.

The distribution within India deserves the same attention as the national comparison. An exporter that imports fabrics, chemicals or components pays part of its costs in foreign currency. Currency depreciation may improve the rupee value of its dollar revenue while also increasing input costs. A labour-intensive producer with local suppliers has a different exposure. Similarly, a large exporter can carry inventory or offer longer credit to an importer while negotiations continue, whereas a small firm may have to decline the order even if the long-run price is viable. Export support would be better targeted if it addressed specific barriers to winning orders, such as certification costs and working capital, with a clear test for whether the support kept a competitive supplier in the market.

How to tell whether India wins new orders

Track US import quantities and customs values for the same product codes by origin, with an explicit record of the applicable duty on each comparison date. Where possible, compare products covered by the order with similar exempt lines and track order books as well as customs arrivals. A shipment cleared ahead of a deadline can raise one month’s imports and depress the next. A lower average unit value can also reflect a change in the mix of products rather than a price concession by the same supplier. Evidence from individual product lines and repeat orders will help distinguish durable sourcing changes from those timing and composition effects.

India’s priority should be to identify the product lines where its suppliers have an advantage that survives the buyer’s actual cost comparison. If Indian volumes and repeat orders rise against more heavily taxed rivals without a large fall in unit values, the relative advantage is likely to have mattered. If buyers buy less overall or Indian suppliers concede most of the new duty to protect orders, the gains will be narrower. Until the data arrive, the April schedule is evidence of a change in incentives. Its effect on Indian jobs, margins and investment still depends on what buyers and suppliers do with those incentives.

title.rendered: Greta Thunberg’s climate activism in practice

content.rendered:
Greta Thunberg is cited as one of the loudest voices in the fight against climate change. However, the teen activist’s actions raises doubts about her ability to perceive the complexity of the problems she strives to solve. One example of her inability to understand the carbon costs of travelling is well documented in the aptly named ‘Yacht controversy’.

Greta had reportedly chosen not to fly to the US for her big UN speech, citing high carbon emissions in the aviation industry. Rather she had opted to travel from Sweden to the US on a ‘Low carbon emission’ yacht, which took 15 days. This move was widely regarded as a visual representation of leading by example and practicing what one preaches.

It was only later that the full picture came into light. On paper, the ‘Zero carbon emissions’ sailing yacht, donated by a Russian billionaire, used a fraction of the fuel consumed by an airliner. Even disregarding the time cost of such an endeavour, when fuel consumption per person per mile is considered, the airplane is the clear winner. Moreover, to bring the Yacht back from America, team of 7 people had to be flown all the way from Europe to the US. The result was that nearly eight to ten times carbon had been released to fuel this publicity stunt than would have been released, had Thunberg taken a flight.

Despite these revelations, it would be wrong to undermine Greta’s contribution towards climate change. Her popularity has been a catalyst in bringing climate change back into the spotlight. Greta can be thought of as an important tool to get the message of climate change to the people. However, anyone who looks to her for real world solutions might be disappointed as her ability to understand the complex socio-economic nuances around climate change leaves a lot to be desired.

title.rendered: Origins of the Taliban

content.rendered:
The Taliban are back in the spotlight. To understand why and how the Taliban came to power, one must take a look at the circumstances that led up to the formation of the Taliban.

Soviet invasion and Mujahideens

When the Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan on December 24, 1979, the Afghan forces were unable to stop their advance. After toppling the existing government, the Soviets were met with fierce resistance from Islamic mujahideens, funded by the Pakistani ISI. Fearing a Soviet invasion of Pakistan occupied Balochistan, then Pakistani dictator Zia-ul-Haq approached Saudi Arabia to garner support for the mujahideen cause. A while later, the American CIA along with Saudi Arabia’s GID started supplying these mujahideen fighters with funds and weapons siphoned through the ISI.

Mullah Omar and the Taliban

One of the mujahideen leaders receiving these funds was Mullah Mohammed Omar, the founder of the Taliban. The Taliban was founded by Omar as a movement of Pakistani Madrasa educated students from the Pashtun areas of Afghanistan.

After the dissolution of the Soviet Union, the Soviet backed Najibullah government in Afghanistan collapsed, which emboldened many mujahideen groups to increase their activity. One of these mujahidden groups was the Taliban, which, in the ensuing power struggle, emerged victorious.

Taliban in Power

The military goal of the Taliban during the period 1995 to 2001 was to re-establish a unified Afghan state with Pashtun dominance within the northern areas. The Taliban sought to establish an Islamic government through law and order alongside a strict interpretation of Sharia law, in accordance with the Hanafi school of Islamic jurisprudence and the religious edicts of Mullah Omar, upon the entire land of Afghanistan. By 1998, the Taliban’s Emirate controlled 90% of Afghanistan.

UN action

Taking note of violation of human rights and terror activities undertaken by the Taliban government, in 2000, the UNSC condemned the use of Taliban territory for training of ‘terrorists’ and the Taliban for providing safe haven to Osama bin Laden. The UNSC levied severe sanctions against Afghanistan under Taliban control. In October 2001, the United States, with allies including the Afghan Northern Alliance, invaded Afghanistan and routed the Taliban regime. The Taliban leadership fled to Pakistan.

title.rendered: Quantitative easing or money printing?

content.rendered:
Money printing is one of the most controversial topics in economics. Recent media discourse though, suggests that this is the new normal. After all, it has been observed for the past few years in America, Europe and Japan. Central banks have recently changed the name to Quantitative Easing (or QE for short). This has prompted some in in finance field to speculate the demise of the dollar and more disturbingly, the return of hyperinflation. This notion though, is not reflected empirically. Central banks have been doing this for some years now and no significant rise in inflation has been noticed. It is hence logical to refute the simplistic view that QE is the same as money printing. However, to do so, one must understand the difference between ‘quantitative easing’ and ‘money printing.’

To pinpoint exactly how quantitative easing and money printing are different, one needs to know what each is. Quantitative easing refers to a policy where the central bank starts buying financial assets on a large scale from the private sector. These assets are typically government bonds, and sometimes bonds from big corporations that are very unlikely to go out of business. What differentiates QE from a normal transaction is that large scale asset purchases by the central bank are financed by ‘newly created’ money. In this case, central bank reserves, where reserves are digital accounts that private banks have at the central bank and can use to pay each other.

With QE, central bank reserves are created. But, with traditional money printing notes and coins are created. This is important because notes and coins end up in the hands of the consumer. Whereas reserves end up in the hands of financial institutions. This is again important because where money ends up first, is likely where one sees the biggest impact on prices. This explains why we have seen massively increased asset prices in countries where there has been QE, but not so much inflation.

While the central bank creates reserves. It also takes something out of the economy, namely ‘bonds.’ This is important because bonds are actually used as money in large parts of the financial sector. With money printing, the government spends more money into the economy. But, with QE this doesn’t have to be the case. If the government doesn’t simultaneously increase its spending, the central bank merely inserts one money like instrument while taking out another.

The monetary system consists of a monetary core of central bank money. First, notes and coins, and on top of that bank reserves. Then, there is a layer of money created by private banks. And then, finally, there is a layer that consists of financial instruments often used as money, but only used in some parts of the economy. So, when QE happens, reserves are added to the economy while, at the same time bonds in the financial crusts are taken out of the economy. However, the effective money supply remains the same.

This begs the question, if the effective money supply is not changed, then why bother with Quantitative Easing at all?

First, it is important to realise that reserves are more liquid than bonds and can be directly exchanged for cash with the central bank. So, when there’s crisis, reserves are safe while government bonds cannot always be relied upon for payment.

Second, the interest rate on reserves is typically lower than the interest rate on government bonds. So, what is happening here is that government bonds are getting scarcer in the monetary financial system. And what happens to things that are getting scarcer? Well, their price goes up, of course. And, confusingly, with bonds, if their price goes up, this means their interest rate goes down. And since central bankers already control interest rates on short term debt by setting the interest rate on reserves, they can now also control interest rates on longer term government bonds through quantitative easing.

Also, there is a third effect that central banks rely on, that is that by increasing the quantity of available reserves, private banks can more easily expand their lending and therefore the quantity of private bank money. This however, is not guaranteed to happen since bank lending also depends on people being willing to borrow.

Finally, by performing QE, central bankers have made government borrowing cheaper by lowering interest rates. This enables governments to spend more. Although, governments don’t always use this opportunity. If the central bank and government work in tandem, then QE becomes more like money printing because money is added to the economy and nothing was extracted from it.

Hence, quantitative easing concerns itself with buying assets with newly created reserves which makes the system safer. And since it is safer, this could in theory make banks more confident to increase their lending. At the same time, because it takes bonds out of the economy, QE will lower long term interest rates. Finally, by making interest rates lower, it could encourage governments to spend more.

There are two main reasons why QE is not money printing. The first is that QE means more bank reserves in the economy. This is important because this type of money is much more likely to get stuck in the financial sector rather than ending up with consumers. Hence, it is more likely to increase the price of assets and reduce the long term interest rates on bonds than it is to cause any significant inflation. The second key difference is that, while money printing only adds monetary instruments to the economy, QE adds core money as well as extracts financial instruments. This is another reason why we have not seen massive inflation as a result of QE.

excerpt.rendered: Money printing is one of the most controversial topics in economics. To pinpoint exactly how quantitative easing and money printing are different, one needs to know what each is.

title.rendered: Why governments want cryptocurrencies of their own

content.rendered:
Governments of many countries are considering, or are in the process of developing their own ‘Central Bank Digital Currencies’ or CBDCs. These are proposed to be akin to an official ‘Government Cryptocurrency’.The enthusiasm of states is understandable.

Firstly, digital currency is far easier to track which means that they’ll be better equipped to tackle tax evasion, money laundering and terrorist financing. A digital currency will also provide states with near total knowledge of their economy. This information could be used to form more effective economic policy with more growth and smaller recessions, but perhaps the biggest reason that states are keen on CBDCs is that CBDCs protect their monetary sovereignty.

Digital Currencies like Bitcoin and DM threaten states monetary sovereignty. Let’s use DM as an example. DM (originally called libra) is Facebook’s proposed digital currency. The worry for states, especially states with unstable economies is that citizens might start using DM as their default currency instead of their state’s currency, which would limit a country’s ability to affect monetary policy. If people aren’t using the state’s official currency, then increasing supply, manipulating interest rates and all of the standard economic tools become far less effective.

Official state CBDCs have some advantages over DM and other cryptos and states are hoping that CBDCs can dissuade citizens from abandoning their national currencies and turn to the ‘digital dollar’ instead, which leads us on to the next question: Why would citizens agree to CBDCs?

In addition to creating better economic conditions for the whole country, they’re also more hygienic than banknotes and it’s plausible that states might legally require the digital currency; entirely phasing out the physical variant. But perhaps the biggest advantage to individuals is that CBDCs will be cheaper and more convenient.

At the moment, there is an entire infrastructure of third-party private companies that facilitate mobile payment. Think of PayTm or Google Pay in the UK and India or WeChat Pay in China. One of the functions of Commercial banks is to act as middlemen between the Central Bank and the individual. Transaction fees for this, for an average person is 350 dollars a year in the US. But if the state decides to facilitate a direct connection between the Central Bank and individuals instead, then this should in theory mean lower transaction costs, making things cheaper and easier for individuals and businesses.

title.rendered: Understanding government cryptocurrencies

content.rendered:
The topic of Cryptocurrencies is in the spotlight again, with discussions about NFTs and Reddit millionaires in recent months. People are becoming increasingly interested in this little understood field and are looking at crypto as a viable investment strategy. With the most famous Cryptocurrency- Bitcoin recently becoming a 1 Trillion dollar asset class, even some governments are taking a second look at Digital Currencies, as both an opportunity and a threat.

Governments of many countries are considering, or are in the process of developing their own ‘Central Bank Digital Currencies’ or CBDCs. These are proposed to be akin to an official ‘Government Cryptocurrency’.

What are CBDCs?

CBDCs are essentially Digital Currencies issued by Central Banks. They are a blend of Cryptocurrency and normal Fiat Currency. Until last year, only 2 countries were serious about Cryptocurrency, namely China and Sweden. Since then, many more have joined, with most Central Banks, including the likes of UK and the EU, either researching or piloting some form of CBDC. Though Digital Currencies are in not on the horizon just yet, owing to complications of money laundering, terror financing and user privacy among many others, the technological foundations are solid and getting better every day.

The appropriate technology that will carry that digital currency is still about two to four years away. this further is so significant that the bank of international settlements predicts that within three years twenty percent of the world’s population will be living somewhere that uses a CBDC.

Why are Governments enthusiastic about CBDCs?

The enthusiasm of states is understandable. Firstly, digital currency is far easier to track which means that they’ll be better equipped to tackle tax evasion, money laundering and terrorist financing. A digital currency will also provide states with near total knowledge of their economy. This information could be used to form more effective economic policy with more growth and smaller recessions, but perhaps the biggest reason that states are keen on CBDCs is that CBDCs protect their monetary sovereignty.

Digital Currencies like Bitcoin and DM threaten states monetary sovereignty. Let’s use dm as an example. DM (originally called libra) is Facebook’s proposed digital currency. The worry for states, especially states with unstable economies is that citizens might start using DM as their default currency instead of their state’s currency, which would limit a country’s ability to affect monetary policy. If people aren’t using the state’s official currency, then increasing supply, manipulating interest rates and all of the standard economic tools become far less effective.

Official state CBDCs have some advantages over DM and other cryptos and states are hoping that CBDCs can dissuade citizens from abandoning their national currencies and turn to the ‘digital dollar’ instead, which leads us on to the next question: Why would citizens agree to CBDCs?

In addition to creating better economic conditions for the whole country, they’re also more hygienic than banknotes and it’s plausible that states might legally require the digital currency; entirely phasing out the physical variant. But perhaps the biggest advantage to individuals is that CBDCs will be cheaper and more convenient.

At the moment, there is an entire infrastructure of third-party private companies that facilitate mobile payment. Think of PayTm or Google Pay in the UK and India or WeChat Pay in China. One of the functions of Commercial banks is to act as middlemen between the Central Bank and the individual. Transaction fees for this, for an average person is 350 dollars a year in the US. But if the state decides to facilitate a direct connection between the Central Bank and individuals instead, then this should in theory mean lower transaction costs, making things cheaper and easier for individuals and businesses.

Limitations of CBDCs

For all its benefits however, CBDCs aren’t all rosy. There are some possible downsides, chief amongst which is giving the state total information about their citizens economic activity. This could be a slippery slope into a totalitarianism. Imagine instant e-fines for bad behaviour or limits on what kind of things you can buy.

CBDCs might also have some possible disadvantages for states. Firstly, states with less stable currencies still risk their monetary sovereignty being undermined by large state CBDCs. Taking Turkey as an example, President Erdogan’s aversion to high interest rates and habitual sacking of central government bankers, the Lira is in crisis. In response, Turkish citizens have now moved towards the US Dollar and now keep an increasing proportion of their savings in Dollars. One can imagine that, if a digital dollar was easily available, Turkish citizens wouldn’t just save in dollars, they’d use digital dollars for all of their transactions and the dollar could become Turkey’s default currency. Essentially, an easily accessible foreign digital currency would be more likely to replace an unstable state currency, thereby further undermining state’s monetary sovereignty.

The final possible downside to CBDCs is the impact they’d have on traditional banks. Essentially, commercial banks accept lots of money on the assumption that everyone wouldn’t need their money at once, lending some of that money out to other people. This is a process known as fractional reserve banking, where only a fraction of a bank’s deposits are backed by actual cash available for withdrawal, with the rest being loaned out. Banks make money on the interest from those loans. This system has fuelled the entire economy for centuries, but CBDCs might remove the need for bank deposits upon which fractional reserve banking relies. Citizens might just use their state-issued digital wallets and store all of their money in there which could undermine the entire system of money lending as we know it.

It must be stated that everything related to cryptocurrency is still shrouded in mystery. No one knows what all of this will mean. No one knows what role Central Banks might play in lending CBDCs or whether venture capital could replace bank lending or whether banks will necessarily collapse. But it’s worth noting that CBDCs have at least the potential to completely upset the financial system. Before cryptocurrencies are introduced to the mainstream, decisionmakers must face these tough questions.

title.rendered: How does cryptocurrency work?

content.rendered:
Cryptocurrencies have become a hot topic for debate; heard by most people but understood by few. One can have a hard time finding a major Bank, Accounting firm, Software company or Government that hasn’t researched Cryptocurrencies or started a ‘Blockchain’ project. Looking beyond the noise in the press releases, many people often fail to understand the basic concept of Cryptocurrency.

Cryptocurrency started when Satoshi invented Bitcoin in 2008 as a ‘peer-to-peer electronic cash system’. To enable a digital cash transfer, one needs a payment network with accounts, balances and transactions. A major problem every payment network must solve is the prevention of ‘double spending’; essentially, prevent one entity from spending the same amount twice. Traditionally, this is done by a central server that keeps records of all the balances.

In a decentralized network, ie; one used in cryptocurrencies, one does not have this server, rather, every single entity of the network does this job. Every peer in the network needs to have a full list with all the transactions in order to facilitate future. If the peers on the network disagree about even a single balance, all transaction chain is halted.

To illustrate a typical transaction using Cryptocurrency, we’ll look at the transactions on the network the transaction is a file that says Person A gives say, 10 Bitcoin to Person B and the transaction is signed digitally by Person A. Once signed, the transaction is broadcasted to the network, and can be seen by everyone on the network, though its legitimacy still ‘unconfirmed’. After a specific amount of time, the transaction gets confirmed.

The duty of ‘confirming’ transactions is assigned to ‘Miners’. Miners take transactions, stamp them as ‘legitimate’ and spread them in the network. After a transaction is confirmed by a Miner, every user has to add it to its database and the transaction becomes part of the blockchain.

For confirming transactions, the Miners are rewarded with cryptocurrency. To become a Miner, one needs to use some of their computer’s power to qualify for the task. Essentially, every Miner competes to solve a cryptographic ‘puzzle’. Finding a solution entails a Miner confirming the transaction and adding it to the blockchain. Incentivising Miners by paying them in Cryptocurrency ensures a network of independent users, maintaining the legitimacy of the transaction history.

Cryptocurrencies are the key to the complex digital cash problem of maintaining integrity and consensus across independent and potentially malicious users. And though the technology isn’t free of flaws, it is still promising and is surely to be of increasing importance in the times to come.

title.rendered: A deeper look at the Israel–Palestine conflict

content.rendered:
While one could go back hundreds of years to understand the origin of the Israel- Palestine conflict, starting from the year 1918 provides the crux of reason for this conflict.

Before first world war, the region around Jerusalem, under the Ottoman empire, was made up of a Jewish minority and an Arab majority. In the aftermath of WW1, the Ottoman empire was dissolved, and the British were given responsibility of creating a national home for Jews in Palestine by the League of Nations. Britain committed itself to this task under the Balfour Declaration.

The decades following WW1 saw a large influx of Jews into British Palestine. These Jews were part of a political movement called ‘Zionism’. Zionists wanted their own state, citing rising antisemitic persecution in Europe and influenced by a growing belief in secular nationalism, as well as traditional religious teachings. This large influx of Jews caused communal tensions which often resulted in breakout of violence between the Arabs and the Jews, both of whom believed the land to be theirs.

By the 1930s, the British began limiting Jewish immigration. In response, Jewish militias formed to fight both the local Arabs and to resist British rule. Then came the Holocaust, leading many more Jews to flee Europe for British Palestine, and galvanizing much of the world in support of a Jewish state.

In 1947, as sectarian violence between Arabs and Jews there grew, the United Nations approved a plan to divide British Palestine into two separate states: one for Jews, Israel, and one for Arabs, Palestine. The city of Jerusalem, where Jews, Muslims, and Christians all have holy sites, it was to become a special international zone.

This solution was intended to give Jews a state, establish Palestinian independence, and end the sectarian violence that the war weakened British could no longer control.

While the Jews accepted the plan, the Arabs didn’t. Palestinians saw it as an illegitimate attempt by Europeans to push them off their own land. Many recently independent Arab states, declared war on Israel in an effort to establish a unified Arab Palestine.

The newly formed Israel won the war, pushing well past their borders under the UN plan, taking the western half of Jerusalem and much of Palestine. They also expelled huge numbers of Palestinians from their homes, creating a massive refugee population whose descendants today number about 7 million. Following the war, a peace agreement was never signed and both Israel and Palestine continue to blame the other for the conflict.

In 1967, Israel and the neighbouring Arab states fought another war, ending in a decisive Israeli victory. Israel had seized the West Bank from Jordan, the Golan Heights from Syria, and both Gaza and the Sinai Peninsula from Egypt. Israel was now occupying the Palestinian territories, including all of Jerusalem and its holy sites.

In 1978 Israel and Egypt signed the US-brokered Camp David Accords and shortly after that, Israel returned Sinai to Egypt as part of a peace treaty. Over the next few decades, the other Arab states gradually made formal or informal agreements of peace with Israel.

The Israeli military’s continued occupation of Palestinian territories of West Bank and Gaza, turned the conflict into an Israeli-Palestinian struggle. The Palestinian Liberation Organization, which had formed in the 1960s to seek a Palestinian state, fought against Israel, including through acts of terrorism. The PLO initially laid claim to all of what had been British Palestine, essentially demanding an end to the Israeli state.

By the late 1980s, Palestinian frustration exploded into the Intifada, starting with protests and boycotts that soon became violent, forcing Israel to respond with heavy force. Around the same time, a group of Palestinians in Gaza, who consider the PLO too secular and too compromise-minded, created Hamas, a terrorist group dedicated to Israel’s destruction.

By the early 1990s, as the need for peace between the parties became increasingly clear, leaders from both sides signed the Oslo Accords, establishing Palestinian Authority and allowing Palestinians limited freedom to govern themselves in certain areas. However, extremists from both sides hindered its progress into the 2000s.

The absence progress in peace negotiations exhausted the Palestinian’s patience. Palestinians came to believe that peace isn’t coming, and rose up in a Second Intifada, this one much more violent than the first, following which, Israeli enthusiasm for a peaceful resolution died out too.

This stalemate continues till today, where Israeli settlers are driving out Palestinians in the West Bank, who often respond with protests and sometimes with violence. In Gaza, Hamas and other terrorist groups conduct terror attacks on Israeli civilians. Though major conflicts overwhelmingly kill Palestinians, increasing knife and petrol bomb attacks on Israeli civilians by Palestinian separatists result in similar death figures . In Israel itself, most people have become cynical and apathetic to the situation, and for the most part the occupation keeps the conflict relatively removed from their daily lives, with moments of brief but horrible violence.

There’s little political will for peace. As Israeli politics shift right under Netanyahu, the country has builds walls and checkpoints to control Palestinians’ movements. It is becoming increasingly clear that Israel is not looking for a solution to this conflict, attempting to just manage it for the time being.

excerpt.rendered: While one could go back hundreds of years to understand the origin of the Israel- Palestine conflict, looking at 20th century history of the region provides clear explanations. From the end of the first world war, to today, we explore the geopolitics of this conflict country.

title.rendered: Understanding what ails the Greek economy

content.rendered:
A decade after the financial crisis of 2008, which saw the Greek economy nosedive, Greece is still a long way from normalcy. To understand why Greece has been in a recession longer than any other country in modern history, one must look closely at the structural problems in the Greek economy and its evolution for the past 30 years.

Before the Covid lockdown, Greece’s GDP was still 25% below its pre-crisis peak, with unemployment above 20% for most of the last decade. Greece’s no-grow recovery is unparalleled in modern history, even among the most severe depressions. For context, 5 years after the great depression, US GDP per capita had risen by 35%. Likewise, after Argentina’s 2002 crisis, per capita GDP was up by 45% within 5 years. But in Greece, GDP per capita rose by less than 6%. This appalling figure begs the question ‘Why?’

To answer why Greece was doomed to fail, one has to dive deeper into the history of its economy. Greece’s failure to recover stems from its failure to qualify for the Euro. During the 80s and 90s Greece was racked with high inflation along with twin deficits in government spending and trade account. Its get out of jail card was its exchange rate. In order to make the economy more competitive, the Greek government artificially weakened the country’s currency, the Drachma. The problem with this strategy was that it failed to address the structural flaws tin the Greek economy and as a result the Greek was subject to higher interest rates on its debt.  This was the invisible hands method of keeping excessive borrowing in check.

So, when the EU decided to rollout a new currency, the Euro, Greece was highly interested in adopting it, as the new currency would eliminate Greece’s high inflation, unstable exchange rate and provide Greece with a source of cheap capital.

Ideally, to play in the same economic sandpit as Germany and France, Greece needed to reform its economy to one with sound finances, competitive international trade practices and economic sustainability. However, Greece chose to do exactly the opposite. As its government admitted in 2004, Greece was printing false GDP figures, giving an illusion of a prospering economy. For instance, counterfeit items and smuggled cigarettes, which are a part of the black economy and must not show up in official GDP figures, were being presented as legitimate economic activity. The structural problems in the Greek economy were not addressed and wouldn’t’ve been an issue till the world economy kept growing.

The ball dropped in the financial crisis of 2008. By this point, Greece had built up an unstainable debt, its economy was overinflated on cheap credit, it has one of the most non-competitive labour supply for a country with similar income and had very little high value trade.

Greece was the furthest from being a fit in Solow’s model of economic growth. The Solow model of growth outlines few fundamental factors an economy needs to grow. These include labour, capital accumulation and population growth; all the factors Greece lacked.

In aspect of labour, Greece had become uncompetitive by European standards. This was something that historically Greece had dealt with by devaluing its currency in the international market. But being tied to the euro dictated that these external devaluations would now become painful internal devaluations. In practice, this meant that average wages and pensions went down by 25%. This decimated demand; in a country dependent on domestic consumption.

To put the labour market situation of Greece into perspective, from 1995 to 2010, Greece recorded the highest increase in hourly wages of any European country at 97%, with a productivity increase of 18% in the same period. In comparison, the average European productivity growth in the same period was almost 60%. This meant that the per unit labour cost in Greece was rising sharply, becoming highly uncompetitive.

After the financial crisis and subsequent bailouts given to Greece, Greece still remained the most uncompetitive economies in the Eurozone. one statistic showed that between 2010 and 2016, Greece was the only country in the OECD to display negative productivity growth. This can be attributed to another Solow factor- Fixed Capital formation, or investment.

Since 2008, FCF has nearly halved, as businesses have invested less, further hampering their competitiveness. Until 2018, Greece’s FDI had been under the EU average, being below 2% of GDP until 2019. Greece has seen negligible growth in FDI since 2008. This is in part due to high corporate taxes, which were until recently, among the highest in the EU. These high taxes combined with a lengthy bureaucracy has disincentivised the setting up of business. Also, the instability of the Greek economy, whether it be due to protests, referendums on bailouts or being the first developed country to default on its IMF debt, acts as a catalyst to deter businesses from investing and has done so for the best part of the decade.

Another factor complementing investments, is savings. Savings are vital for economic activity as they help in increasing the capital stock. Savings can also be a proxy for investment, that is, one person’s savings can be used as capital for another person’s business. However, Greece is plagued with the lowest savings rate in the EU. It was the only country in the EU to record a negative savings rate for the whole of the 2010s. however, this was not to fuel a lavish lifestyle, as some may think, but to compensate for the brutal wage cuts and high taxes Greeks were facing. all this has had a severe impact on Greece’s population. This brings us to the final factor in the Solow model- population growth.

Population growth is important for economic growth. However, Greece has been facing a decline, rather than growth in its population numbers. This is partly due to Greece having the second oldest population in Europe and partly due to the vast number of Greeks who emigrate to other countries. Greece has lost 5% of its population to emigration, many among which were highly qualified, educated, and most importantly- productive. This brain drain has been so bad, that Greece’s population has never recovered to its peak of 2010 and has had a great impact on Greece’s export industries.

When we think about Greece, tourism is the first thing that comes to mind. This is an industry Greece seems to excel at, welcoming record numbers of tourists every year since 2011. Greece has now become the 7th most visited country in the EU and 16th in the world. The GDP share of tourism industry has grown to 25%. But even the increase in tourist numbers cannot help the Greek economy that much. Tourism is a low value-add industry with stagnant wages. So, when this low productivity industry accounts for a quarter of the country’s GDP, stagnant wages become a wider economic reality. Also, as a seasonal industry, the unemployment rates are volatile as compared to job security provided by industrialisation. An economy based on tourism also loses out on the other benefits that come along with proper industrialisation, like improvements in infrastructure, institutions and governance and work culture.

So, while tourism is a growing sector in the Greek economy, its high numbers cannot compensate for the structural issues that fester as a by-product.

Though Greece exports little, it facilitates international trade in a significant way. Greece has the largest merchant navy in the world, making up over 25% of the global fleet and over 50% of the EU fleet, owing to its strategic location and seafaring history. The shipping industry is so important to Greece that tax breaks for this sector are enshrined in its constitution. However, the contribution of shipping to the economy is a topic of contention, with many experts claiming that its real contribution to the economy is negligible at 1% to GDP instead of the 6% claimed by the Greek state. This is due to different measures of accounting used by the 2 parties. Realistically, most of the shipping activity does not happen in the country, with ships rarely docking on Greek ports, and most of the repairs, maintenance and crew coming from foreign countries. Hence, the real impact of a sizable industry and a key export market may be lower than some may believe.

The structural issues in the Greek economy are not the only reason for its failure to rebound from the recession. Another significant factor at play is the way the Greek economy was bailed out by the EU.

After the 2008 crisis, Greece received the largest bailout package in history. There were 3 separate bailout packages totalling $352 Billion. In order to avail these bailouts, Greece had to agree to some policy changes. These policy changes entailed higher taxes and cuts in wages and pensions. This resulted in a further fall in demand, deepening the recession.

Another controversial condition for this bailout was the high government surplus Greece was supposed to run. Greece was directed by the EU to run a government surplus of 3.5% of GDP till 2022 and 2.2% of GDP until 2060. This makes sense on paper. It essentially meant that Greece would be bailed out if it does not pile up more debt. However, the sustainability of running this big a government surplus has been called into question. This is because, to maintain such high surpluses, governments need to drastically decrease expenditure on a wide variety of government programs and increase taxes.

To put this surplus into perspective, an IMF study of 90 countries from 1945 to 2015 found only 13 instances where a government surplus of 1.5% could be maintained for 10 years. At the EU’s proposed rate of 3.5% for Greece, the study found only 3 instances of success (and only 1 success if natural resource rich countries are excluded). This essentially means that the proposed surplus is near impossible to sustain.

Another problem of Greece’s huge debt is that it is mostly foreign. When debt is foreign held, it is less likely to be recycled as investment to fuel economic growth. In contrast, high sovereign debt countries like Japan and China can function only because their debt is largely held by domestic institutions and investors.

The grassroot recovery though, is coming to Greece. Before the Covid-19 pandemic, 2020 was predicted to be a very good year for Greece. Investor confidence was returning, a number of economic indicators were showing positive growth and Greece’s national stock exchange, the Athens stock exchange had been the best performing stock exchange in the world in 2019. Even Greece’s banking sector- long plagued by NPAs and NPLs had seen strong growth. These changes can, in part be credited to the new government; one set to make Greece economically more competitive through a series of policy measures.

The financial market’s rapid recovery has some economists worried, as they believe that a significant portion of investment coming in is ‘Hot Money’. This means that investors are looking to profit from assets undervalued for a long time due to the economic depression, and now being traded at potentially overinflated prices. Even though recovery is around the corner, the structural problems persist. Greece still has a large trade account deficit, unemployment is high and there is a large investment gap.

Ultimately, Greece is still far from recovering to the same level of prosperity it had before the financial crisis. Over the decade, its economy had played out like a quintessential Greek odyssey. The sacrifices the average Greeks have made to ensure economic revival is testament to their resilience, and as soon as the pandemic gloom lifts, Greece can expect growth stronger than ever before.

title.rendered: Geopolitics of the Indian subcontinent

content.rendered:
A deeper analysis of the geopolitical situation of the Indian subcontinent is required; than is provided for by fiery speeches and public sentiment. To understand why this begets the notorious title of ‘the most diplomatically isolated neighbourhood’, one needs to have a holistic understanding of the economic, political and cultural aspects of the different countries of this subcontinent and how their individual pursuits leaves everybody worse off.

Going back 100 years to when lord Curzon was the viceroy of then British India, India was that its zenith of territorial expansion.That India included what today is India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Burma.


After partition, the subcontinent broke up and all the forementioned countries, with the exception of India became dysfunctional states overtime. The India of Curzon, which stretched from the Iranian plateau to the gulf of Thailand had shadow zones of influence and interest groups from Southeast Asia to the Iranian plateau and deep in Central Asia.
India lost a lot of this geopolitical weight at partition and developed as a very imperfect democracy while in Pakistan and Bangladesh, nothing seem to work. Neither military not democratic regimes were able to stabilize these countries.

Burma was the country which everyone was most optimistic about, at the end of the second World War. The country was rich with oil, natural gas and vast swaths of mineral resources. Burma however, turned into one of the world’s most neo-fascist military dictatorship because of its own ethnic problems, and the ability of the army to someone contain them to a certain extent.


Then there is Nepal, a Hindu monarchy for 200 years; it was decimated in a shakespearean tragedy, where the crown Prince killed the number of his family members before taking his own life. This leads to a devolution into instability, giving rise to communist elements in the country.
While thinking about Nepal, one must keep in mind that most of the Nepalese population lives not in the mountains, but along the border with India in the Terai plains. So India has to deal with a highly unstable Maoist influence Nepalese state, with an insecure and easily penetrable border.
Hence India lives in fear of mass number of refugees pouring into its already poor provinces of Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.


In Bangladesh, neither military nor civilian government have worked. Bangladeshi politics is almost comparable to that of Pakistan, being formally East Pakistan. There are an estimated 15 million Bangladeshi refugees in West Bengal.
It would seem to be in everyone’s interest for India to expand in a very soft power manner, simply by the dynamism of its democratic capitalism. India could strive to incorporate these countries; not in any political sense, but in a very soft economic sense.
But here, some cultural problems arise. R. Kaplan notes that when one goes to a place like Calcutta and asks the people about Bangladesh, which is about a two-hour drive away, they say ‘we don’t want an open society with these people, we don’t want Muslim fundamentalism coming in; erect a wall or something.’ This is particularly true of the younger generation of West Bengalis. The older generation has pre-partition memories of Calcutta and Dhaka being in the same realm, but the younger generation has no memory of this shared ancestry- which in turn impedes the integration of these two cultures which are essentially the same.

The concept of economic and social integration makes abstract sense to both side on paper, but the cultural isolation has made it much difficult for this to take place.The Bangladeshis hence lose out on transit fees and economic integration whereas India loses the ability to import cheap natural gas from and exert influence on Burma.
In Burma India is locked in a battle for influence with China. Because Burma has vast quantities of natural resources and is also a rearbase for around 15 ethnic insurgencies fighting inside the very underdeveloped northeast; India as a democracy cannot simply stand aside and let China essentially become the high protector of Burma, even though it has a very bad military regime. India has no option in a real politik terms, but to engage with the Burmese regime.


Coming to Pakistan, in a conventional sense relations between India and Pakistan a bit better now than they have been for a long time. The reasons for this are tri-fold. Firstly, troops had been moved to secure the border with Afghanistan, leaving the Indian border relatively sparsely guarded, secondly, the loss of political footing and diplomatic isolation that has taken place under the disastrous Imran Khan government and their crippling economic policy. So, India faces less of a threat in a conventional sense from Pakistan as compared to before but its faces a lot more of an unconventional thread.
There exists an organisation in Pakistan known as the ISI or inter-services intelligence which is comparable to the CIA , if the CIA had armed forces of its own. ISI is a state within a state, and is supporting terrorist insurgencies in Kashmir. Indian officials at the highest officers of the South block have compared ISI to Hezbollah in Lebanon.

Then we have Afghanistan, which does not have a border with India. But since the days of the Mughal dynasty, the Mughals governed from Delhi but controlled all of what is today Pakistan and two thirds of what is today Afghanistan. Afghanistan is very much a rear shadow zone of India. India is very much committed to the survival of the current Afghan government. It is absolutely critical for India for the Afghan regime to survive, in order to keep the Taliban in Afghanistan engaged and weak- which India sees as an extension of Pakistan’s influence. India sees a friendly Afghanistan as a strategic rear base to deal with its problems with Pakistan.

Lastly India has a very tense and careful balance relationship with China. On the one hand, border disputes have flared up in Dolkam and Pangong Tso. On the other hand, India and China do a tremendous amount of trade, nearing almost 150 billion dollars annually and projected to rise to 500 billion dollars within this decade. However India cannot ignore the fact that three of China’s biggest customers for Arms sales are Bangladesh, Burma and Pakistan- all India’s neighbours. And when combined with the fact that the Chinese are developing deep water ports in Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Pakistan and Burma for use by the Chinese Navy, as well as high altitude airfields in Tibet, the Indian security establishment cannot help but feel threatened by these developments; given the expansionist nature of the Chinese state.

To conclude, we see India expanding in terms of its world image, we see the expansion and engagement of its armed forces and especially its Navy in the Indian Ocean, it is being seen increasingly an adversary to Chinese influence in the region and globally. But for all its glory, India can only be compared to Gulliver- a giant with little strings tying him down. It is India’s neighbours which are bedeviling India’s progress into a formidable power on the world stage. India can exert its global power through its military cultural and economic weight but it is its immediate neighbours which are keeping India from breaking out and realising it’s true potential and hurting the growth and integration of the subcontinent in the process.

title.rendered: The hypocrisy of climate activists

content.rendered:
In the field of climate activism, it is easy to be swayed by fiery speeches of government inaction and impending climate catastrophe. But how much of what is said is true and how much is being done about it remains in the shadows. There is an urgent need to know the people behind the prominent figures in this movement and to be better informed about the ones we listen to. From the hotshots and their incompetence to the unsung heroes, the public must know the big names in climate activism

The field of climate activism is buzzing with activity. The rising awareness of climate threats is inspiring ever more youth to come out in support of climate justice. Spearheading this movement is Greta Thunberg, the teenage sensation from Sweden. Greta first came into the spotlight by refusing to go to school, choosing rather to spend her time protesting in front of government buildings. This act of defiance gave her stage in the UN to talk to the world leaders. Her speech at the UN made her a celebrity overnight, earning her an army of fans as well as critics.

While her supporters think her brave for expressing herself vividly and openly ridiculing world leaders, critics are not impressed. Questions have been raised on the ability to understand the depth of the problems concerning climate change. There is a notion amongst critics that Thunberg is overhyped and under informed. Critics claim that she should not be taken seriously, citing that the teen leader has not yet presented any viable solutions and has instead devoted her time to meet celebrities and pop sensations.

To argue further, critics point to the aptly named ‘Yacht controversy’. Greta had reportedly chosen not to fly to the US for her big UN speech, citing high carbon emissions in the aviation industry. Rather she had opted to travel from Sweden to the US on a ‘Low carbon emission’ yacht. This move was widely regarded as a visual representation of leading by example and practicing what one preaches.

It was only later that the full picture came into light. On paper, the ‘Low carbon emissions’ yacht, donated by a Russian billionaire, used a fraction of the fuel consumed by an airliner. But when fuel consumption per person per mile is considered, the airplane with the clear winner. Moreover, to bring the Yacht back from America, team of 7 people had to be flown all the way from Europe to the US. The result was that nearly eight to ten times carbon had been admitted to fuel this publicity stunt than would have been admitted, had Thunberg taken a flight.

Despite these revelations and mounting disagreements with her statements by notable experts, Greta enjoys ever-increasing support from her loyal followers.

As her popularity grows, Greta’s Twitter handle sees less tweets about climate change, and more tweets on social and political issues. Her tweets have been observed to mirror those of left-wing media outlets- dividing opinion on her further.

Since her field of work is politically and ideological inclined with mainstream left-wing thought, it must come as no surprise that she has been approached by many far-left organisations. One of these organisations affiliated with Thunberg happened to be ‘Fridays for Future’. The now infamous NGO, which took part in creation of ‘Toolkit’ had been at the centre of everyone’s attention in February. The toolkit accidentally shared by Greta on Twitter revealed plans on attacking big business and supporting farmers protest in India.

Greta’s support for this movement has raised some eyebrows and has been hailed by her critics to be a concrete example of her lack of understanding of climate issues. Greta apparently supports the maintaining of status quo in Indian agricultural sector. The climate activist, through her tweet essentially support the wasteful agricultural practices which have led to the decimation of the water table in Punjab. It would seem that she is either unaware on concerned with the fact that stubble burning in Haryana and Punjab result in a smog blanket across North India for nearly two months at the year. Both instances being examples of gross violation of environmental codes; and regardless to state, highly detrimental to the environment.

As the climate activist and an influential voice for the same, Thunberg’s lack of knowledge on basic agricultural and industrial practices are the reason enough not to take a seriously. Heavy reliance on emotions and rhetoric to drive her point across indicates an inherent immaturity that she simply does not seem able to get rid of.

 The argument that her accomplishments at a young age compensate for her lack of practical knowledge also runs aground at the mention of lesser known young climate change innovators. Taking Fionn Ferreira for example, who at 17 discovered a new way of removing microplastics from the ocean using ferrofluids. Or Niel Deshmukh, another 17 year old, who created AI based Apps to help farmers detect and diagnose various crop diseases- significantly reducing the risk and impact of Crop failures or even Param Jaggi, who, at 17 form the way to reduce carbon emissions from Car emissions and turn it into oxygen.

These individuals are among many who are over shadowed by loud climate activists. None of the abovementioned heroes have been in public light, despite being the ones who bring about actual change through their work. This is in part because the field of climate activism is dominated by obstructive political interest groups. Protests, sit-ins, public demonstrations and thought-provoking speeches constitutes the majority of activities in these circles. And in this Labyrinth the people who do real work in the field are often overlooked or pushed aside to give way to the revolutionary speech to gain public support and create hype over their cause.

It would be wrong to claim that political movements towards climate change is baseless. No movement can succeed without strong political support. However, it must be acknowledged that in the long run, disruptive activism leads to erosion of political weight and legitimacy. What the movement desperately needs is on-ground action and real and practical solution. Unchecked rhetoric will eventually result in loss of interest of the populace. It is high time that the Climate Change lobby lay the foundation for an objective approach to fighting the problem, with tangible results. As Thunberg so eloquently put it, “You must unite behind science. You must take action. You must do the impossible. Because giving up can never be an option.”

title.rendered: India’s government is spending like there’s no tomorrow

content.rendered:
Government spending or expenditure includes all government consumption, investment, and transfer payments. In the Indian economy, government expenditure accounts for 10% of GDP.

Since the non-governmental sector is not showing any signs of improvement since 2017, in accordance with Keynesian theory, the government has ramped up its spending. While the rest of the components lag far behind the desired growth rate, government spending has gone up by 15.7%. This spending spree has been going on since late 2016/ early 2017. In the 2017-18 fiscal year (FY17), government spending went up by 15.1% followed by a rise of 9.25% in FY18.

This is troubling for more than a few reasons. Firstly, this means that the poor GDP growth figures seem even worse when we account for the fact that most of it is being driven by the increase in government spending. If growth rate of the non-government component alone is considered; (which makes up 90% of GDP) it stands at a painful 2.95%. This is far below the GDP growth rate of 4.5% in FY19.

The government component accounts for merely 10% of the GDP. So, any ‘reasonable’ amount spent by the government is unlikely to make a dent in the economy. Moreover, the government does not have unlimited funds, and the current fiscal policy is not suited for this level of spending.

As the economy stagnates, the tax revenue is also proving to be a problem. From April till Oct’19, the government had collected $139.9B in tax revenue and did not meet its $327B tax goal in the FY19.

“Overall, there is likely to be shortfall of Rs. 3.5 – 3.75 lakh crore ($46.5B- $49.9B) in gross tax collections of the Centre. Therefore, revision of fiscal deficit goal of 3.3 per cent by 0.5 per cent to 0.7 per cent appears quite inevitable.”

-Mr. Subhash Chandra Garg, former finance secretary

The dividend from the RBI of $23.4B and earnings from disinvestment might lessen the load on the government. This, however is not a sane or sustainable strategy in the long run. The current trend of rapid disinvestment and privatisation of PSUs as well as arguments with the RBI over loans to the government seem to strengthen the notion that the government is spending beyond its means and must stop.

The government has to ensure that the financial environment of the country is stabilised to encourage growth of the non government i.e.; private consumption and investment sectors of the economy as their performance is crucial for a healthy GDP figure.

title.rendered: Sluggish exports are not a worry for India

content.rendered:
Net Exports refer to the difference between the total value of exports and imports of the country. India’s total exported goods represent 2.9% of its overall Gross Domestic Product for 2019 ($11.33T PPP USD). That 2.9% for exports to overall GDP per PPP in 2019 compares to 3.1% in 2018.

The exports have been saved last fiscal year by an ever expensive dollar- steadily increasing from Rs.63.4 to Rs.73.4 against the dollar between Jan and Oct 2018. This corresponded to stagnant exports in the same period.

However, a drop in its price from Oct’18 to early July’19 from Rs.73.4 to Rs.68.4 against the dollar, paired with increasing oil prices slowed down the already struggling export sector. The figures conclude a growth of -1.1% in Oct’19.

“World trade will continue to face strong headwinds in 2019 and 2020 after growing more slowly than expected in 2018 due to rising trade tensions and increased economic uncertainty,”

WTO

India’s key exports in FY2018-19 were petroleum products, followed by pearls, precious, semiprecious stones, drug formulations and biologicals, gold and other precious metal jewelry, iron and steel, as well as organic chemicals. Together, these top ten commodities accounted for about 46 percent of India’s total export.

Pharmaceutical products, automobile, transport equipment, machinery, and readymade garments are also major exports for India.

Since Indian exports contribute less than 3% to the GDP, slowdown here is not something to worry about too much. India does not rely heavily on its export market. Exports today are at the same level as they were in FY11. Exports have remained consistent for the past 9 years with the exception of a period of degrowth from early 2015 till mid 2017.

title.rendered: Investment falls as Indian economy slows

content.rendered:
In an economic sense, investment is the money spent on ‘assets’ used to create wealth in the future. The contribution of this component to the Nominal GDP is around 30%.

The growth figures for investment paint a bleak picture as it grinds to a crawling 1% over the same quarter of the previous fiscal year. India is witnessing a reverse situation since FY12. Both its savings and investment have gone down, dragging the GDP growth along.

The RBI data reveal that the Gross Domestic Savings and Gross Capital Formation (GCF) or Investment reached a new low of 30.3% and 29.1% of the GDP in FY17 – from a high of 34.6% and 36.7%, respectively, in FY12. Both marked a marginal improvement to 30.5% and 29.1% of the GDP, respectively, in FY18- the fiscal year for which comparable data is available.

Source: Business Today

In theory, investment and savings are directly linked in a way such that the negative change in savings should reflect as a positive change in investment. i.e; in a healthy economy, dissavings should ideally go towards investment. Here, however we see that a -4.1% change in savings is accompanied by an even larger -7.6% change in investment.

This points out that not only have the savings in the last 8 years not gone towards investment but rather, the size investment relative to the GDP has shrunk as well. In layman’s terms, the country’s wealth share has declined on both fronts over the last 8 years.

title.rendered: A fall in private consumption is a warning sign for India

content.rendered:
Private consumption refers to the money spent by households i.e; private individuals to buy consumer goods. This component contributes to 60% of GDP.

The growth rate of private consumption was recorded to be 3.05% against the growth rate of GDP at 4.5% in the same quarter of 2019.

Source: The Economic Times

This is problematic as it points out that the current environment does not promote consumption. Let us understand why:

A stable financial and economic environment is key to consumer confidence and sustained growth in this component. As people’s trust in financial stability erodes, their tendency to save, rather than spend increases for the foreseeable future. Effects of this can be seen in the dwindling sales of the automotive, metal and utilities sector.

This particular component is of vital interest because of its immense contribution to the GDP. Retardation here cannot be accommodated by changes in fiscal policy. Though an increase in government spending helps the economy overall, its effect will be negligible in compensating for the slowdown in private consumption. A stable socio political and financial environment is needed for this component to sustain growth.
